In plain words first The idea in one line This course builds AI from the ground up: every idea first written out in small code you can run, then used the way production teams use it, from a first training loop to agents that work in teams. Why this came about Most AI courses pick one end of the subject. Some start with a working chatbot and never explain what is inside it; others start with calculus and lose people before anything works. This course does both, in order: every idea is built from scratch in small code you can run, the maths is shown with pictures and real numbers, and only then do the lessons reach for the libraries and the production practice that teams use. Who this course is for Anyone who wants to understand AI properly, from the ground up : engineers, analysts, data scientists, product people and students. You do not need to know Python, statistics or machine learning before you start. The course teaches each of them, and each lesson names what it assumes, so you can skip what you already know. By the end you will be able to: explain, with the right technical terms, how a model learns from data, how a neural network is trained, and how a transformer turns text into predictions; build the core pieces yourself in Python: a training loop, a convolutional network, a tokenizer, attention, a small language model, retrieval and an agent loop; use the libraries and protocols that production teams use, and evaluate, secure, serve and cost what you build; design agents and multi-agent systems that hold up outside a demo. The story of this course in one page Why this came about How the parts connect The first six parts follow the history of the field: each one exists because the step before it ran into a limit. The seventh and eighth are practice. Part 1 · Foundations (Phases 0 to 3). Tools, the maths you actually need, classic machine learning and the core of deep learning, written out by hand. Everything later stands on these four phases. Part 2 · Perception (Phases 4 to 6). How models see, read and listen: convolutional vision, language from tokens to sequence models, and speech. Each modality introduces an idea the rest of the course reuses. Part 3 · Models (Phases 7 to 10). Attention and transformers in depth, generative models, reinforcement learning, and finally a small language model built end to end. Part 4 · Building with LLMs (Phases 11 to 13). Using large models well: prompting, retrieval, evaluation and serving; models that mix text and images; and the tools and protocols, such as MCP, that connect them to the world. Part 5 · Agents (Phases 14 to 16). The agent loop and everything around it: planning, memory, tools, frameworks and production engineering, then autonomous systems and teams of agents. Part 6 · Serving, Safety & Capstones (Phases 17 to 19). Running models for real users (serving engines, GPUs, caching, routing, observability, releases, security, compliance and cost), the safety and alignment work that keeps systems trustworthy, and capstone projects that build complete systems step by step. Part 7 · Projects and Case Files (Phases 20 and 21). 79 smaller projects you build and test stage by stage, from starter tools to frontier systems, and 60 real incidents from serving and agent systems to diagnose the way an interview debugging round asks you to. Part 8 · Project Library (Phases 22 to 30). 427 projects, recipes and samples from other open-licence repositories: classic machine learning and build-from-scratch projects that run here with their real output, then RAG, application, agent, multi-agent and MCP projects, Claude API recipes and Snowflake samples that you run with your own keys. Part 9 · Forward Deployed Engineering (Phase 31). A 20-lesson intensive on the forward deployed engineer's job with Claude, modelled on Anthropic's Claude FDE learning path and Frontier Academy and on other FDE programmes: discovery, scoping, building inside a customer's systems, security review, evals, cost, pilots, adoption and handover, ending in a four-day simulated deployment with a graded practical. Part 10 · MLOps and LLMOps (Phase 32). Running models as systems: reproducibility, experiment tracking and a model registry with MLflow, data contracts, point-in-time features, pipelines, CI/CD, serving, canary releases, monitoring, retraining and governance, Snowflake-native MLOps, and the LLMOps practices for prompts, evaluation data, monitoring and model upgrades. Part 11 · AI on Snowflake (Phase 33). Every Snowflake AI, ML and agent feature for one retailer, with its 2026 status: access and model governance, Horizon classification and context, document parsing, Cortex AI Functions and custom AI functions, the Cortex REST API, ML Functions, embeddings, Cortex Search, RAG and Knowledge Extensions, semantic views, Cortex Agents and the Coding Agent, CoWork, CoCo, Native Apps and Cortex AI Gateway, evaluation, the ML lifecycle, serving and Cortex Training, guardrails, agent identity and session scopes, governance with public standards, cost, a preview radar and CI/CD, ending in a graded capstone. How to study so it sticks These habits come from learning research and they make a real difference: Predict before you run. Before running a code block, write down what you expect it to print. Being wrong and then seeing why is the fastest way to learn. Recall, do not reread. At the end of a lesson, close it and write the three main ideas from memory. Then check. The quizzes and check your understanding questions exist for this. Space it out. An hour a day for a week beats seven hours on Sunday. Come back to the quiz of the previous lesson before starting the next. Explain it to someone. If you can explain attention or RAG to a colleague without notes, you understand it. Change the code. After each example works, change one thing (a number, a word, a step) and predict the effect. The Make it your own exercises guide this. Do not wait to feel ready. In plain words first Setting up a workshop Before cooking you need a kitchen: a stove, knives, a place to put things. Programming is the same. You need a terminal (a window where you type commands to your computer), a code editor (a text editor that understands code), Python (the program that runs Python code) and a project folder with its own set of add-on libraries. You do this once. If anything here feels unfamiliar, that is normal; every step says exactly what to type and what you should see. Setup from zero: four tools, one project If you have never programmed, follow this section step by step. If you already have Python 3.11 or newer and a code editor, skim it and continue at Setup below. 1. Open a terminal A terminal (also called a command line or shell) is a text window where you type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers with text. Your computer How to open a terminal Windows 10 or 11 Press the Windows key, type PowerShell , press Enter macOS Press Cmd+Space, type Terminal , press Enter Linux Press Ctrl+Alt+T, or find Terminal in your applications Type pwd (macOS, Linux) or Get-Location (Windows) and press Enter. The terminal prints the folder you are "standing in", for example /Users/asha or C:\Users\asha . Every command runs relative to that folder. Three commands are enough to move around: Command What it does Example cd <folder> Change directory: move into a folder ( cd .. goes up one level) cd Documents ls (macOS, Linux) or dir (Windows) List what is in the current folder ls mkdir <name> Make a new folder mkdir ai-course 2. Install a code editor Install Visual Studio Code (free, from code.visualstudio.com). Then, inside VS Code, open the Extensions panel (the four-squares icon on the left) and install Python and Jupyter , both published by Microsoft. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Tokenizer The program that splits text into tokens and maps each to a number Lesson 5.3 Temperature A number that divides the logits before softmax: low is confident, high is varied Lesson 1.10 Softmax The function that turns any list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1 Lesson 1.10 Gradient The list of slopes of a function with respect to each of its inputs Lesson 1.7 Gradient descent Improving parameters by repeatedly stepping a little in the downhill direction of the loss Lesson 1.7 Pretraining The first, largest stage of training: predicting the next token over a huge body of text Lesson 10.6 Instruction tuning Fine-tuning a base model on instructions paired with good responses, so that it follows requests Lesson 10.10 Why this came about Most people meet generative AI as a chat box that seems to understand them. That impression is useful for using it and useless for building with it: it hides the parts, so failures look mysterious. Teachers such as fast.ai found that showing the whole working system first, then opening it up, helps people learn faster than starting from theory. This lesson is that first look. In plain words first The words you will hear, in one breath Artificial intelligence (AI) is any technique that makes a computer do something that seems to need intelligence. Machine learning is the part of AI where programs learn patterns from examples instead of following rules a person wrote. Deep learning is machine learning with large neural networks . Generative AI is deep learning that creates new content: text, images, sound, code. A large language model (LLM) is a generative model for text, trained to predict the next word. An agent is an LLM given tools it can ask to use, inside a loop that keeps going until a task is done. AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning; generative AI and large language models sit inside deep learning. An agent wraps a model with tools and a loop. Step 1 · A language model predicts the next piece of text Here is a real language model at work. GPT-2 is a small, free model released by OpenAI in 2019; it is old and weak by today's standards, but it works exactly the way today's large models work, and it runs on a laptop. The code downloads it (about 500 MB, once), gives it the beginning of a sentence, and asks: what comes next? Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output tokens : the model does not see letters or whole words. A tokenizer later · 5.3 cut the sentence into five pieces called tokens . Ġ is how GPT-2 writes "a space before this piece", so Ġcapital means " capital". ids : each token is replaced by its number in the model's fixed list of pieces. Everything inside the model is arithmetic on numbers like these. Lesson 5.3 builds a tokenizer from scratch. vocabulary size: 50257 : GPT-2 knows 50,257 different pieces. For every one of them it produced a score. the five lines : the scores turned into probabilities, highest first. The model thinks the most likely next piece is " the" (8.5%), and " Paris" gets only 3.2%. Notice what the model is not doing. It is not looking up the capital of France. It learned, from millions of web pages, which pieces of text tend to follow which. "The capital of France is the city of..." is a perfectly common continuation, so " the" scores highest. Larger models put far more probability on " Paris", but the mechanism is identical: score every possible next token, turn the scores into probabilities. the Language as data: NLP foundations and Transformers, step by step sections show how the scores are computed; Lesson 1.10 explains the probabilities. Step 2 · Generating text is choosing a token and repeating A model only ever predicts one next token. To write a sentence, you pick a token, add it to the text, and ask again. Here the code always picks the single most likely piece (this is called greedy decoding ): Copy What you should see Copy The sentence grows one token at a time, and it is fluent but empty: "the capital of France is the capital of the French Republic". Always picking the top choice tends to produce safe, repetitive text. Real systems usually sample , picking tokens at random in proportion to their probabilities, with settings such as temperature later · 1.10 that you will drag with a slider in Lesson 7.19 . The whole game. A language model turns text into tokens, scores every possible next token, picks one and repeats. Retrieval adds your documents to the prompt; tools and a loop turn the model into an agent. Step 3 · A model that predicts text is not yet an assistant Ask GPT-2 to do something, and it does not do it. It continues the text in whatever way looks most like its training data: Copy What you should see Copy It wrote what looks like a line from a story. A model trained only to predict the next word on internet text is called a base model or pretrained model . The assistants you use (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot) are base models that were then trained further on examples of instructions and good answers, and on human feedback about which answers are better. That extra training, covered in Lesson 10.10 , is what makes them follow requests. The mechanism underneath is still next-token prediction. Step 4 · Retrieval: give the model your information Even the best assistant does not know your company's refund policy or yesterday's orders: it only knows what was in its training data. The fix is simple to state: find the relevant documents yourself and paste them into the prompt. This is called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) . Here is the idea in plain Python, with no AI at all in the search step: Copy What you should see Copy That prompt is what gets sent to the model. The model now answers from your note instead of guessing. Real retrieval replaces the word-matching with smarter search (the Retrieval (RAG) section builds it step by step), but the shape never changes: search, then put what you found in front of the model. Step 5 · An agent: a model, some tools, and a loop Some questions need an action: looking up an order, booking a slot, running a query. Modern models can reply with a structured request such as "please run lookup_order with SK-1042 " instead of text. Your program runs the function and sends the result back; the model then answers or asks for another tool. Wrap that in a loop and you have an agent . The "model" below is a stand-in written as a plain function, so you can see the loop without any AI service. In the Agents from first principles section the same loop runs with real models. Copy What you should see Copy Three things in those few lines are the heart of every agent you will build: The model decides, your code acts. The model never runs anything itself; it only asks. This is why agents can be made safe: your code chooses what tools exist, checks every request, and can ask a person for approval. The loop. The agent keeps going, one decision at a time, until it answers. Real tasks take several steps. A limit. range(5) stops a confused agent. Production agents have limits on steps, time and money. Facts come out because they were common in the text it learned from, which is also why it can be confidently wrong. ✗ "The model reads words." ✓ It reads tokens, which are often parts of words, and only ever as numbers. ✗ "An agent runs code by itself." ✓ The model only requests an action; your program decides whether and how to run it. ✗ "ChatGPT and GPT-2 work in completely different ways." ✓ Same next-token mechanism; the assistant is far larger and was trained further to follow instructions. Exercises Predict before you run Change the prompt in Step 1 to "The capital of Japan is" . Before running, guess: will " Tokyo" be the top choice? Will " the" still be near the top? (Solution P1.) Make it your own In Step 4, add a fourth note about cash on delivery ("COD is available for orders up to INR 10,000") and ask "Can I pay cash on delivery for a 5,000 rupee order?". Does the word-matching retriever pick the right note? (Solution M1.) Break it on purpose In Step 5, change stand_in_model so that it always returns the tool request, never an answer. Run the loop. What stops it, and what would happen without range(5) ? (Solution B1.) Solutions Solution P1 · The capital of Japan The run prints ' the' 9.4%, ' Tokyo' 6.7%, ' home' 6.4%, ' a' 4.2%, ' now' 3.8%. Tokyo is second, behind " the", because "is the..." is such a common pattern in web text. The lesson is not the exact numbers but the shape: a ranked list of likely continuations, not a looked-up fact. Solution M1 · A fourth note Add "cod": "COD is available for orders up to INR 10,000 in most pin codes." to NOTES . The retriever returns the delivery note ("Metro cities get delivery in 2 to 3 days..."), not the COD note. The question says "cash on delivery", the note says "COD", so they share almost no words, while the delivery note shares "delivery". This is exactly the weakness of matching words that the Retrieval (RAG) section fixes with synonyms, embeddings and hybrid search . Solution B1 · A loop with no exit The loop calls the tool five times and then stops because range(5) ends, without ever printing an answer. Without the limit it would call the tool forever (or until something crashed or the bill arrived). Every real agent needs a step limit, and a plan for what to tell the user when it is reached. Recap An LLM scores every possible next token and turns the scores into probabilities; generating text is picking one token and repeating. A base model continues text; an assistant is a base model trained further to follow instructions. RAG means: search your own documents, then put what you found in the prompt. An agent is a model that can request tools, inside a loop with limits; your code runs the tools. Q2 In the agent loop of Step 5, who actually runs lookup_order ? A The language model B The program around the model C The tokenizer D The user The model only returns a request; the program runs the function and sends back the result. Q3 What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) add to a model? A More training data, permanently B Relevant documents pasted into the prompt for each question C A bigger vocabulary D The ability to run tools RAG fetches information at question time and puts it in front of the model. a0002: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Git and Team Collaboration for AI Projects Lesson 0.4 30 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Configure git identity and use the daily workflow of add, commit, and push Create and merge branches for isolated experiments without breaking main Write a .gitignore that excludes model checkpoints and large binary files Navigate the commit history with git log to understand project evolution Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Learn. Time : about 30 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Version control is not optional. Every experiment, every model, every lesson you build here gets tracked. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Commit "Saving" A snapshot of your entire project at a point in time Branch "A copy" A pointer to a commit that moves forward as you work Merge "Combining code" Taking changes from one branch and applying them to another Remote "The cloud" A copy of your repo hosted somewhere else (GitHub, GitLab) The problem In plain words first Git keeps a history of your project as a chain of snapshots called commits . You choose what goes into the next snapshot ( git add ), take it ( git commit ), and copy your history to GitHub ( git push ). A branch is just a name pointing at one commit, so trying an idea on a branch costs nothing and leaves main untouched. You're about to write hundreds of code files across 20 phases. Without version control you will lose work, break things you can't undo, and have no way to collaborate with others. Git is the tool. GitHub is where the code lives. This lesson covers what you need for this course and nothing more. The idea Three things to remember: 1. Save often ( git commit ) 2. Push to remote ( git push ) 3. Branch for experiments ( git checkout -b experiment ) The same idea as a formula Git stores every file, folder listing and commit as an object named by a hash of its contents: where joins bytes. A folder (a tree ) is hashed from the names and ids of what it contains, and a commit from its tree id, its parent commit's id, the author and the message. So a commit id fixes the entire history behind it: change one byte in an old file and that file's id changes, then its tree's, then every later commit's. Why collisions do not worry anyone. SHA-1 gives 160-bit ids. For objects with random ids, the chance that any two share an id is about / 2 161 (the birthday bound). Git can also use SHA-256 for new repositories ( git init --object-format=sha256 ), which hardens it against deliberately constructed collisions. Worked example Hashing a file by hand The file contains hello and a newline: 6 bytes. Header: blob 6 followed by a zero byte. Hash the header plus the 6 bytes with SHA-1: ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a . Git stores the object in .git/objects/ce/013625… : the first two hex digits name the folder. Every repository in the world that contains a file with exactly these bytes stores it under this same id; that is how Git spots unchanged files instantly and why it never stores the same content twice. See it drawn Git's hash, recomputed Python's hashlib against git hash-object , then the same file with one character changed. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The two ids are identical: Git really is just SHA-1 over a short header and the bytes. Adding one ! produces an unrelated id, which is how git status knows instantly which files changed, without comparing contents line by line. The collision chance for a billion objects, about , is why nobody worries about accidental clashes. Creating one is instant, whatever the size of the repository. ✗ "Adding *.pt to .gitignore removes the checkpoint I already committed." ✓ .gitignore only affects files Git is not tracking yet. A file already committed stays tracked until you run git rm --cached on it. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Training on CPU is fine for learning. Training for real needs a GPU. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means CUDA "GPU programming" NVIDIA's parallel computing platform that lets you run code on the GPU VRAM "GPU memory" Video RAM on the GPU, separate from system RAM. Limits model size. fp16 "Half precision" 16-bit floating point, uses half the memory of fp32 with minimal accuracy loss Tensor Core "Fast matrix hardware" Specialized GPU cores for matrix multiplication, 4-8x faster than regular cores The problem In plain words first A neural network spends almost all its time multiplying large grids of numbers. A CPU has a handful of powerful cores that do this a few numbers at a time; a GPU has thousands of simple cores that do it all at once. The second limit is memory: the whole model, and while training much more, has to fit in the GPU's own memory, called VRAM . Most lessons in phases 1-3 run fine on CPU. But once you start training CNNs, transformers, or LLMs (phases 4+), you need GPU acceleration. A training run that takes 8 hours on CPU takes 10 minutes on GPU. You have three options: local GPU, cloud GPU, or Google Colab (free). The idea Copy The same idea as a formula Work. Multiplying an matrix by a one takes floating-point operations (FLOPs): one multiply and one add per term. Speed is capped twice. A chip can do at most FLOP per second and move at most bytes per second between its memory and its cores. A computation that does FLOPs per byte it moves (its arithmetic intensity ) runs at most at Large matrix products reuse each number many times ( grows with matrix size), so they hit the ceiling: compute-bound . Generating text one token at a time multiplies each weight once per token ( FLOP per byte in bf16), so it hits the ceiling: memory-bound . Decoding speed limit. For a batch of one, every new token reads all the weights once: B ​ Worked example GPU arithmetic by hand An NVIDIA H100 (SXM) is rated at TFLOP/s for dense bf16 matrix work and TB/s of memory bandwidth. Ridge point: FLOP per byte. Below it, memory limits you; above it, arithmetic does. A big matrix product, times in bf16: = 1.4 × 1 0 11 FLOPs over × 2 = 100 MB, so : compute-bound, about 0.14 ms at full speed. Chatting with an 8B model in bf16 (16 GB): at most tokens per second for one user, however many FLOPs the chip has. Quantising to 4 bits (4 GB) raises the ceiling about four times; batching many users shares each weight read among them. With Adam in full precision that is about 16 bytes per parameter, eight times the 2 bytes of fp16 inference. ✗ "Colab's free GPU is always available." ✓ It is shared and time-limited; sessions disconnect and GPU types vary. On a GPU the same product takes a few milliseconds. The torch.cuda.synchronize() calls matter: GPU work is queued and returns at once, so without them you would time the queueing, not the work. Recap What to keep from this lesson Phases 1–3 run on a CPU; from Phase 4 on, use a local GPU, Colab or a rented cloud GPU. Write device-independent code with torch.device(...) and .to(device) . Solutions Solution P1 · Seven billion parameters 7 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 14 GB, so the weights alone fit on a 16 GB card with about 2 GB left for activations and the CUDA context, which is tight but works for short inputs. Training with Adam needs 7 × 10⁹ × 16 bytes = 112 GB, far beyond one 16 GB card. That gap is why later lessons cover LoRA, quantisation and sharding. Solution B1 · Timing the queue The GPU time drops to well under a millisecond and the speedup jumps to thousands. The matrix product was only queued when time.time() read the clock; the GPU finishes it later. You measured how long it takes to launch the work, not to do it. torch.cuda.synchronize() waits until the queue is empty, so the clock includes the work. a0004: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Model APIs and Managing API Keys Lesson 0.6 30 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Store API keys securely using environment variables and .env files Make an LLM API call using both the Anthropic Python SDK and raw HTTP Compare SDK-based and raw HTTP request/response formats for debugging Identify and handle common API errors including authentication and rate limits Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Build. Time : about 30 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every AI API works the same way: send a request, get a response. The details change, the pattern doesn't. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means API key "Password for the API" A unique string that identifies your account and authorizes requests Rate limit "They're throttling me" Maximum requests per minute/hour to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage Token "A word" (in API context) A billing unit: input and output tokens are counted and charged separately Streaming "Real-time responses" Getting the response word by word instead of waiting for the full response The problem In plain words first A model API is a web address you send a request to. The request carries your API key , a secret string that says who is paying, and a JSON body that says which model to use and what to ask. The reply is JSON too. An SDK is a library that builds those requests for you; underneath, it is the same HTTP call. Starting from Phase 11, you'll call LLM APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google). In Phase 13-16 you'll build agents that use these APIs in loops. You need to know how API keys work, how to store them safely, and how to make your first API call. The idea Every API call has: 1. An endpoint (URL) 2. An API key (authentication) 3. A request body (what you want) 4. A response body (what you get back) The same idea as a formula Cost. Providers price per million tokens, separately for input (your prompt, including the conversation so far) and output (the reply): T in ​ p in ​ + T out ​ p out ​ ​ Output tokens usually cost 4 to 5 times more than input tokens, and in a chat every turn resends the history, so ​ grows with the conversation. Rate limits. Many APIs enforce limits like a token bucket : a bucket holds at most units and refills at per second; each request takes units out. You can burst up to at once, but over a long period you get at most per second. Retries. On a 429 Too Many Requests or a 5xx error, wait before retrying, doubling the wait each time up to a cap, and pick the actual wait at random ("full jitter"): ​ ∼ Uniform ( 0 , min ( cap , base ⋅ 2 n ) ) The randomness keeps many clients that failed together from retrying together. How many requests are in flight. By Little's law, with requests per second each taking seconds, on average are open at once. Worked example Budgeting a chatbot by hand A support bot handles 20,000 conversations a month, each about 3,000 input tokens and 400 output tokens, on a model priced at 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output tokens (a common mid-tier price; check your provider's pricing page): Input: million tokens, at 3 dollars per million: 180 dollars. Output: million tokens, at 15 dollars per million: 120 dollars. Total: 300 dollars a month . The output is 12% of the tokens but 40% of the bill. With a limit of 50 requests per minute and replies that take 3 seconds, requests are open at once on average, so a client that allows 4 concurrent calls is enough. Check your mental model ✗ "It's fine to paste my key into the notebook for now." ✓ Notebooks and scripts get committed, shared and screenshotted. Keys leaked to GitHub are found by scanners within minutes. Keep them in environment variables or a git-ignored .env file. ✗ "A token is a word." ✓ A token is a piece of text the model reads, often part of a word. You pay separately for input and output tokens. ✗ "The SDK and the raw HTTP call can give different answers." ✓ The SDK sends the same HTTP request. The difference is convenience: retries, types, streaming helpers. Step 1 · Store API keys safely Never put API keys in code. Use environment variables. Recap What to keep from this lesson Every model API is an HTTPS POST with a key in a header and a JSON body; the reply is JSON. Keys live in environment variables or a git-ignored .env , never in code. SDKs wrap the same HTTP call and add retries, types and streaming. Read the status code first: 401 key, 400 request, 429 rate limit, 5xx provider. See it drawn Backoff with jitter, simulated The retry formula for one client, then 100 clients that all hit a rate limit at the same moment and retry with and without jitter, then the cost formula on the worked example's numbers. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The ceiling doubles from 0.5 s until it reaches the 30 s cap, and each actual wait is a random fraction of it. Without jitter all 100 clients wait exactly 4 s and come back in the same instant, hitting the limit again; with full jitter the busiest tenth of a second holds only a handful of them. The official Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs retry this way for you (their max_retries setting); write it yourself only when you call the HTTP API directly. Solutions Solution P1 · A missing variable os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] raises KeyError: 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY' , which stops the program at that line. os.environ.get(...) returns None and carries on, so the failure shows up later as a confusing 401 from the server. For required secrets, failing early with the KeyError is the better behaviour. Solution B1 · A wrong key The SDK raises anthropic.AuthenticationError with status 401 and an authentication_error type in the body. It is raised by the client.messages.create(...) line, not by anthropic.Anthropic() : creating the client does not contact the server, so a bad key is only found on the first request. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) OpenAI's Responses API is the recommended interface for new projects; the older Assistants API was shut down on 26 August 2026. Chat Completions remains supported. OpenAI-compatible endpoints everywhere. vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, and providers such as Google (Gemini) and many inference clouds accept the OpenAI request format, so one client library can switch providers by changing the base URL and key. Keys as secrets, scoped and rotated. Providers offer project-scoped keys with spending limits; production code reads keys from a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault) rather than .env files, and secret scanning on repositories catches leaked keys. Tools through MCP. The Model Context Protocol is the common way to give models access to tools and data across Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and IDEs. a0005: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Jupyter Notebooks for Exploration Lesson 0.7 30 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Install and launch JupyterLab, Jupyter Notebook, or VS Code with the Jupyter extension Use magic commands ( %timeit , %%time , %matplotlib inline ) to benchmark and visualize inline Distinguish when to use notebooks vs scripts and apply the "explore in notebooks, ship in scripts" workflow Identify and avoid common notebook traps: out-of-order execution, hidden state, and memory leaks Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Build. Time : about 30 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Notebooks are the lab bench of AI engineering. You prototype here, then move what works into production. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Kernel "The thing running my code" A separate Python process that executes cells and keeps variables in memory Cell "A code block" An independently runnable unit in a notebook, either code or markdown Magic command "Jupyter tricks" Special commands prefixed with % or %% that control the notebook environment .ipynb "Notebook file" A JSON file containing cells, outputs, and metadata. Stands for IPython Notebook The problem In plain words first A notebook is a document made of cells. When you run a code cell, it is sent to a kernel , a Python process that stays alive between cells and remembers every variable. That memory is what makes notebooks fast to explore with, and it is also their main trap: what the kernel remembers depends on the order you clicked, not the order on the page. Every AI paper, tutorial, and Kaggle competition uses Jupyter notebooks. They let you run code in pieces, see outputs inline, mix code with explanations, and iterate fast. If you try to learn AI without notebooks, you're doing math homework without scratch paper. But notebooks have real traps. People use them for everything, including things they're terrible at. Knowing when to use a notebook and when to use a script will save you from debugging nightmares later. The idea A notebook is a list of cells. Each cell is either code or text. The kernel is a Python process running in the background. When you run a cell, it sends the code to the kernel, which executes it and sends back the result. All cells share the same kernel, so variables persist between cells. That "whatever order you click" part is both the superpower and the foot-gun. The same idea as a formula The kernel holds a state : every variable, import and object currently in memory. Running cell is a function from one state to the next, ​ ( S ) . If you run cells ​ , c 2 ​ , … , c k ​ in that order, starting from an empty kernel, ​ = f c k ​ ​ ( ⋯ f c 2 ​ ​ ( f c 1 ​ ​ ( ∅ )) ⋯ ) The result depends on the order and the number of times you ran each cell, not on the order the cells appear in the file. The notebook file stores the code and the last outputs, not the history of runs, so the only state another reader can reproduce is the one from running every cell once, top to bottom, from a fresh kernel. Worked example Three cells by hand Cells: (1) x = 10 , (2) x = x * 2 , (3) y = x + 1 . Top to bottom, 1, 2, 3: , . Run cell 2 twice by accident, 1, 2, 2, 3: , . The file looks identical. Then re-run cell 1 to "reset": , but is still 21, left over from before. Any output that uses both now mixes two histories. Check your mental model ✗ "The notebook on screen is the program." ✓ The program is whatever the kernel ran, in the order you ran it. A cell you deleted can still have left a variable behind. ✗ "If it runs on my machine, it runs for my colleague." ✓ Only if it runs top to bottom on a fresh kernel. Use Restart & Run All before you share it. ✗ " %timeit is Python." ✓ Lines starting with % or ! are instructions to Jupyter (IPython). Paste them into a .py script and you get a SyntaxError . Pick whatever you like. JupyterLab is the most common in AI work. Copy Step 2 · Keyboard shortcuts that matter You operate in two modes. a0006: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Python Virtual Environments and Dependencies Lesson 0.8 30 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Create isolated virtual environments using uv , venv , or conda Write a pyproject.toml with optional dependency groups and generate lockfiles for reproducibility Diagnose and fix common pitfalls: global installs, pip/conda mixing, CUDA version mismatches Implement a per-phase environment strategy for projects with conflicting dependencies Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Build. Time : about 30 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Dependency hell is real. Virtual environments are the cure. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Virtual environment "A venv" An isolated directory containing a Python interpreter and packages, separate from the system Python Lockfile "Pinned dependencies" A file listing every package and its exact version, guaranteeing identical installs across machines pyproject.toml "The new setup.py" The standard Python project configuration file, replacing setup.py/setup.cfg/requirements.txt Transitive dependency "A dependency of a dependency" Package B depends on C; if you install A which depends on B, C is a transitive dependency of A CUDA mismatch "My GPU isn't working" PyTorch was compiled for a different CUDA version than what your GPU driver supports The problem In plain words first A Python package is installed into one folder of one Python. If every project shares that folder, upgrading a library for one project silently changes it for all of them. A virtual environment gives each project its own folder. A lockfile writes down the exact version of every package, including the ones your packages pulled in, so the same environment can be rebuilt on another machine. You install PyTorch 2.4 for a fine-tuning project. Next week, a different project needs PyTorch 2.1 because its CUDA build is pinned. You upgrade globally, and the first project breaks. You downgrade, and the second one breaks. This is dependency hell. It happens constantly in AI/ML work because: PyTorch, JAX, and TensorFlow each ship their own CUDA bindings Model libraries pin specific framework versions A global pip install overwrites whatever was there before CUDA 11.8 builds don't work with CUDA 12.x drivers (and vice versa) The fix: every project gets its own isolated environment with its own packages. The idea The same idea as a formula A version specifier describes a set of versions , and several specifiers joined by commas mean the intersection of their sets: >=1.26 is ; <2.3 is ; together >=1.26,<2.3 is . ~=X.Y (compatible release) means >=X.Y, ==X.* ; ~=X.Y.Z means >=X.Y.Z, ==X.Y.* . ==2.* is every 2.x release. A resolver has to choose one version of each package that lies in the intersection of every constraint on it, from your project and from every dependency of every dependency; it usually takes the newest. If the intersection is empty, there is no solution: that is a dependency conflict. Pre-releases ( 3.0.0rc1 ) are skipped unless you ask for them ( pip install --pre , uv --prerelease allow ). A lockfile ( uv.lock ) records the chosen point for every package, so the next install repeats it instead of solving again. Worked example Intersecting constraints by hand NumPy releases available: 1.24.4, 1.26.4, 2.0.2, 2.1.3, 2.2.6, 2.3.1. Your project says numpy>=1.26,<2.3 : allowed {1.26.4, 2.0.2, 2.1.3, 2.2.6}. A library you use says numpy~=2.1 , which is >=2.1, ==2.* : allowed {2.1.3, 2.2.6, 2.3.1}. Intersection: {2.1.3, 2.2.6}. The resolver installs 2.2.6 . If the library said ~=2.3 instead, the intersection with <2.3 would be empty and the install would fail with a conflict, naming both requirements. Check your mental model ✗ " numpy>=1.26 in pyproject.toml means everyone gets the same NumPy." ✓ It means any version from 1.26 up. Today that might be 2.5, next year 3.0. Only the lockfile pins one exact version. ✗ "I only depend on the four packages I listed." ✓ Each of them depends on others. Matplotlib alone needs nine more, and those are what usually conflict. ✗ "Copy the .venv folder to share the environment." ✓ It contains paths and compiled files for your machine. Share pyproject.toml and the lockfile; the other person rebuilds. Build · Option 1: uv venv (Recommended) uv is the fastest Python package manager (10-100x faster than pip). It handles virtual environments, Python versions, and dependency resolution in one tool. Copy Install packages: Copy Create a project with pyproject.toml in one step: Copy Predict before you run In a new project, uv add numpy changes two files. In pyproject.toml it writes a line like "numpy>=2.5.5" . What does it write about NumPy in uv.lock , and why are there two different kinds of line? (Solution P1.) Build · Option 2: venv (Built-in) If you can't install uv , Python ships with venv : Copy Slower than uv , but works everywhere Python is installed. Build · Option 3: conda (When You Need It) Conda manages non-Python dependencies like CUDA toolkits, cuDNN, and C libraries. Use it when: You need a specific CUDA toolkit version without installing it system-wide You're on a shared cluster where you can't install system packages A library's install instructions say "use conda" Copy One rule: if you use conda for an environment, use conda for all packages in that environment. Mixing pip install into a conda env causes dependency conflicts that are painful to debug. Build · For This Course: Per-Phase Strategy You could create one environment for the whole course. Don't. Different phases need different (sometimes conflicting) dependencies. It replaces setup.py , setup.cfg , and requirements.txt in one file. Reading this output >=1.26 accepts everything from 1.26.0 up, including 2.5.4, a new major version that may break your code. ~=1.26 stops at the 1.x line, and ==1.26.* accepts only 1.26 patch releases. Libraries usually state wide ranges (so they combine with other packages) and applications pin exact versions in a lockfile. Lockfiles A lockfile pins every dependency (including transitive ones) to exact versions. This guarantees reproducibility: anyone who installs from the lockfile gets exactly the same packages. Copy Commit your lockfile to git. When someone clones the repo, they install from the lockfile and get identical versions. Reading this output Each line is a constraint Matplotlib places on another package, with its own range. None of these names is in your pyproject.toml , but the resolver has to satisfy all of them, intersected with whatever your other packages ask of the same names (NumPy appears in almost every scientific package's list). The lockfile is the record of the single version it picked for each. Common mistakes 1. Installing globally Copy Check where your packages go: Copy 2. Mixing pip and conda Copy If you must use pip inside conda (some packages are pip-only), install all conda packages first, then pip packages last. 3. Forgetting to activate Copy Your shell prompt should show the environment name: Copy 4. Committing .venv to git Copy Virtual environments are 200MB-2GB. They're local, not portable between machines. Commit pyproject.toml and the lockfile instead. 5. CUDA version mismatch Copy Break it on purpose Create a virtual environment and activate it. Open a new terminal tab without activating anything and run python -c "import numpy" , then which python in both tabs. What do you see, and why? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson One virtual environment per project (or per phase of this course); never install into the system Python. pyproject.toml states what you need, as ranges; the lockfile records exactly what you got, including transitive dependencies. Commit both, never .venv . uv does environments, Python versions, installs and locking in one tool; conda is for non-Python dependencies such as CUDA toolkits. Check which python when imports fail, and check that PyTorch's CUDA version is not newer than your driver's. Solutions Solution P1 · Two kinds of line uv.lock gets an entry with name = "numpy" and one exact version = "2.5.5" , plus the download source and file hashes. pyproject.toml records your intent , a range of acceptable versions; the lockfile records the result , the one version chosen today. Installing from the lockfile gives everyone the same bytes; resolving from pyproject.toml alone may give a newer version next month. Solution B1 · The tab without the environment In the new tab which python points at the system Python (for example /usr/bin/python3 or a Homebrew path), and the import fails with ModuleNotFoundError if NumPy was only installed in the environment. Activation only changes the PATH of the terminal it ran in. Activate in every new terminal, or let your editor pick the interpreter in .venv for you. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Run the setup script to create your course environment: Copy This creates a .venv at the repo root with core dependencies installed and verified. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) uv projects and lock files. uv init , uv add and uv lock give every project a pyproject.toml and a cross-platform uv.lock ; PEP 751 standardised a pylock.toml lock-file format (2025) that tools are adopting. Picking the right PyTorch build. uv pip install torch --torch-backend=auto selects the CUDA, ROCm or CPU wheel index for the machine automatically; otherwise use PyTorch's own index URL for your CUDA version. Conda where native libraries matter. conda-forge and pixi remain the choice when a stack needs non-Python dependencies (CUDA toolkits, GDAL, compilers) pinned together. Sources: uv projects , PEP 751 , uv and PyTorch , pixi . In plain words first A program is a recipe A program is a list of instructions, like a recipe. Python reads it from the top, one line at a time, and does exactly what each line says, nothing more. Most instructions work with values : a number such as 499 , a piece of text such as "tea" , or True . Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit ( 2nd_price is not allowed). They are case-sensitive: Price and price are different variables. In plain words first Shopping lists and phone books A list is like a shopping list: items in order, and you can add, remove or look at the third one. A dictionary is like a phone book: you look things up by a name (the key ), not by position. A loop is "do this for every item on the list". A decision is "if the cart is over 499 rupees, delivery is free; otherwise, charge 40". Step 1 · Lists: values in order A list holds several values in order, inside square brackets. You can ask how long it is, read any position (positions start at 0, and -1 means the last), and add or remove items. A shopping cart is a natural list: Copy What you should see Copy A list keeps items in order. Positions (indexes) start at 0; negative indexes count from the end. A slice [1:3] takes positions 1 and 2, stopping before 3. A list can hold any values, even a mix, and you can change it after creating it: lists are mutable . Slices work like they do for strings: cart[:2] means "from the start up to position 2", cart[2:] "from position 2 to the end". Numbers in lists come with useful built-in functions: Copy What you should see Copy sorted(prices) gives back a new sorted list and leaves the original alone; prices.sort() changes the list itself and gives back nothing. Step 2 · Tuples and sets Two more collections you will meet often: Copy What you should see Copy Collection Written as Ordered Changeable Duplicates Typical use list [1, 2, 3] yes yes yes Items you will add to or loop over tuple (1, 2, 3) yes no yes A fixed group: a coordinate, a row, a pair returned from a function set {1, 2, 3} no yes no Unique values, fast "is it in here?" checks dict {"a": 1} keeps insertion order yes keys unique Looking things up by name The duplicated "urgent" was stored once: sets keep only unique values. That is why len(tags) is 3. Step 3 · Dictionaries: looking things up by key A list finds things by position. A dictionary (dict) finds things by name: it stores pairs of a key and a value , inside curly brackets. Almost everything an AI model sends you arrives as dictionaries inside lists inside dictionaries, so this is worth practising. One order, as a dictionary: Copy What you should see Copy A dictionary maps keys to values. You look values up by key, not by position. Values can themselves be lists or dictionaries, which is exactly the shape of JSON. Reading this output order["status"] looks a value up by its key. Step 4 · Decisions with if, elif and else Programs decide what to do by testing a condition. if runs its indented lines only when the condition is true; elif ("else if") is tried only when the ones above it were false; else catches everything left. The indentation is not decoration: it is how Python knows which lines belong to which branch. Here is a delivery fee that depends on the cart total: Copy What you should see Copy Three rules make Python's decisions work: Each condition ends with a colon : . The lines that belong to it are indented (by convention, four spaces). Indentation is not decoration in Python: it is how Python knows which lines are inside the if . A line that is not indented, like the last print , runs whatever happened above. Python checks the conditions from the top and runs only the first one that is true. elif ("else if") is checked only when everything above it was false; else catches everything left. A one-line version exists for simple choices: label = "free" if cart_total >= 499 else "paid" . Idea What it means, in one line Taught in NumPy The Python library for fast math on arrays of numbers Lesson 0.14 PyTorch The most widely used Python library for building and training neural networks Lesson 3.16 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.52 Why this came about As programs grow, repeating the same lines in many places becomes a source of bugs: fix one copy and forget the others. Functions let you write a piece of logic once, give it a name, and reuse it; modules let you organize functions into files and share them as libraries. Every AI library you will use ( NumPy later · 0.14 , PyTorch later · 3.16 , LangChain later · 14.52 ) is a collection of modules full of functions and classes. And because things do go wrong, Python reports problems with detailed messages; learning to read them turns errors from roadblocks into directions. In plain words first A function is a recipe card A function is a recipe card with a name. It lists what it needs (its parameters : flour, sugar), the steps, and what it hands back at the end (its return value : a cake). You write the card once; anyone can then "call" it with their own ingredients. A module is a recipe book: a file of functions you can bring into any program with import . An error message is the kitchen telling you exactly which step failed and why. Step 1 · Defining and calling a function A function is a named piece of code that you can run whenever you need it. def defines one: it has a name, parameters (the inputs, in brackets) and usually a return line that hands back the result. Defining a function runs nothing; calling it by name, with values for the parameters, does. Watch three ways of calling the same function: Copy What you should see Copy A function is a named machine: inputs go in as arguments, the body runs, and return sends one result back to the caller. The parts of a function definition: Part In the example What it does def and a name def order_total Starts a function definition and names it Parameters (price, qty, discount=0) The inputs. discount=0 has a default , so callers may leave it out Docstring """Return the amount...""" A description in triple quotes; editors and help(order_total) show it Body the indented lines Runs each time the function is called return return subtotal - discount Ends the function and hands one value back to the caller Defining a function does not run it; calling order_total(...) does. Arguments can be passed by position (in the order of the parameters) or by name ( qty=3 ), and named arguments make calls easy to read. AI libraries use named arguments everywhere, for example model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=30, do_sample=False) in Lesson 0.2 . A function without return gives back None . A function can return several values as a tuple: Copy What you should see Copy Step 2 · Variables inside functions are private A variable created inside a function exists only while that function runs. Code outside cannot see it. This is called scope , and it is a good thing: two functions can both use a variable called total without disturbing each other. The code below proves it by trying to read an inside variable from outside, which fails: Copy What you should see Copy Variables created inside a function are local : they exist only while the function runs. This is a feature: functions cannot accidentally overwrite each other's variables. If a function needs a value, pass it in as a parameter ; if the caller needs a result, return it. Functions that only use their parameters and return values are the easiest to test and reuse. Step 3 · Functions are values too A function's name refers to a value, just like a variable. You can store functions in dictionaries and pass them to other functions. This idea is everywhere in AI code: you hand a library your function to call later, such as a tool an agent may use (the Agents from first principles section) or a scoring rule for sorting. Copy What you should see Copy lambda o: o[1] is a tiny unnamed function: "given o , return o[1] ". The key= argument tells sorted and max what to compare. The STYLES dictionary is a dispatch table : look up a function by name, then call it. The agent in Lesson 0.2 used exactly this to find and run tools. Step 4 · Modules and libraries A module is a .py file of functions and variables. import brings one into your program. Python ships with a large standard library of modules; anything else you install with uv add (or pip install ). Copy What you should see Copy You make your own module by saving functions in a file. Normally you would create shopkart_utils.py in your editor; here the code writes the file itself, so the example runs anywhere: Copy What you should see Copy You write What it means When to use it import math Bring in the module; use names as math.sqrt The default: it is clear where each name came from from math import sqrt Bring in one name; use it as sqrt When you use one or two names a lot import numpy as np Bring in the module under a short alias For libraries with conventional aliases: np , pd , plt from math import * Bring in every name Avoid: you cannot tell where names came from Tip Standard library or installed package? If import something fails with ModuleNotFoundError , the package is not installed in the environment you are running. Standard modules ( math , json , random , pathlib , datetime , csv ) never need installing. Packages such as numpy , pandas , torch and requests do: uv add numpy in your project folder. Step 5 · Reading error messages Errors are normal: professional programmers see dozens a day. When Python cannot continue, it stops and prints a traceback : the chain of calls that led to the problem, ending with what went wrong. How to read a traceback: start at the last line (what went wrong), then the line just above it (where), then walk up the call chain only if you need to know how the program got there. Read it from the bottom up : The last line names the error type and gives a message: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'str' and 'int' . This is usually all you need. The line above it shows where: the file, the line number and the code. Go there first. The lines further up show how the program got there, from the outermost call down. In big programs most of these lines are inside libraries; look for the lowest one that is in your file. Here the caller passed the text "499" instead of the number 499 , so price * qty gave the string "499499" , and subtracting a number from a string is impossible. The fix belongs at the caller, not inside order_total . These ten errors cover most of what beginners meet: Error Typical cause Example SyntaxError Python cannot read the line: a missing colon, bracket or quote if x > 3 (no colon) IndentationError Lines inside a block are not indented consistently a loop body not indented NameError A name was used before it was defined, or misspelled prnt("hi") TypeError An operation got the wrong type of value "Total: " + 998 ValueError Right type, unusable value int("forty") KeyError A dictionary key does not exist order["phone"] IndexError A list position does not exist cart[10] on a 3-item list AttributeError The value has no such method or attribute [1, 2].upper() ZeroDivisionError Division by zero total / 0 ModuleNotFoundError A package is not installed, or its name is misspelled import nump Step 6 · Handling errors with try and except Some errors are expected: a user types letters where a number belongs, a file is missing, a web service is down. You can catch an error and decide what to do instead of crashing: Copy What you should see Copy Keyword What it does try: Run these lines and watch for errors except SomeError: If that kind of error happens, run these lines instead of crashing. as e gives you the error object else: (optional) Runs only if no error happened finally: (optional) Runs whatever happened; used for clean-up such as closing a connection raise Report an error yourself, with a clear message Watch out Catch specific errors, not everything A bare except: (or except Exception: ) catches every error, including your own typos, and hides real bugs. Catch the specific errors you expect and know how to handle, and let the rest surface. the Agents from first principles section applies the same rule to agent tools: a failed tool returns a clear error to the model, but a bug in your code should still be visible. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in UTF-8 The standard way of storing text as bytes Lesson 5.3 Structured output Getting a model's reply as data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema, instead of free text Lesson 11.2 Why this came about Programs are rarely alone: they read data from files and talk to other programs over the internet. In the 2000s, web services settled on a simple convention: send an HTTP request to a URL and get JSON back, text that looks like Python dictionaries and lists. Every AI model provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and the rest) works this way: your prompt goes out as JSON, the model's answer comes back as JSON. Understanding one request and response end to end makes every AI SDK much less mysterious. In plain words first Letters and replies A file is a box on your disk with text (or other data) inside; your program can open it, read it and write to it. A web API is a program on another computer that answers requests. Calling one is like posting a letter with a precise address (the URL ), a type of request on the envelope (the method : GET "please send me", POST "please do this"), sometimes a pass in the envelope (an API key ) and a form inside (the body , usually JSON). The reply comes back with a number on the envelope saying how it went (the status code : 200 means fine, 404 means not found) and an answer inside. Always open files this way. The second argument is the mode : "r" read (the default), "w" write (replaces the file), "a" append. encoding="utf-8" tells Python how characters are stored as bytes. It is the format of nearly every web API and of most AI configuration and output. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in PyTorch The most widely used Python library for building and training neural networks Lesson 3.16 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.52 Pydantic A Python library that defines data shapes as classes and validates data against them Lesson 0.16 Structured output Getting a model's reply as data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema, instead of free text Lesson 11.2 Why this came about As programs grew in the 1970s and 1980s, keeping data and the functions that work on it in separate places became a source of bugs. Object-oriented programming bundled them together: a class describes a kind of thing (its data and its behaviour), and objects are the individual things. Python supports this style, and almost every library you will use is organised around it: a scikit-learn model is an object you .fit() and .predict() with, a PyTorch later · 3.16 layer is an object you call, a LangChain later · 14.52 chat model is an object you .invoke() . Reading library code is much easier once classes are familiar. In plain words first A blueprint and the houses built from it A class is a blueprint: "a cart has a customer and a list of items, and you can add an item or ask for the total". An object (or instance ) is one actual cart built from that blueprint: Asha's cart, Ravi's cart. Each has its own data, called attributes ( customer , items ); all of them share the same abilities, called methods ( add , total ). You already use objects all the time: a string is an object of class str , and .upper() is one of its methods. Step 1 · You have been using objects all along Every value in Python is an object : a bundle of data plus the actions that work on that data. The kind of object is its class . A string is an object of class str , a list of class list , and the methods you have been calling with a dot belong to those classes. The code asks a few values what they are: Copy What you should see Copy Everything in Python is an object: numbers, strings, lists, functions, even modules. type(x) says which class an object belongs to; isinstance(x, SomeClass) checks it. Step 2 · Writing your own class You can define your own kind of object. A class is the blueprint; each object made from it is an instance . The special method __init__ runs when an instance is created and sets up its data, called attributes . self is the instance itself, so self.items means "this cart's items". Read the class first, then the lines below it that create two separate carts: A class is a blueprint; each object (instance) made from it has its own data (attributes) and shares the class's behaviour (methods). Copy What you should see Copy Piece What it does class Cart: Defines a new class called Cart . Class names use CapitalisedWords by convention __init__(self, customer) The initialiser : runs automatically when you write Cart("Asha") , to set up the new object's attributes self The object the method is working on. Python passes it in for you: cart_a.total() becomes Cart.total(cart_a) self.items = [] Creates an attribute on this object; each cart gets its own list def add(self, ...) A method : a function that belongs to the class and works on self The key point is in the output: cart_a and cart_b are built from the same class but hold separate data. Adding to Asha's cart did not touch Ravi's. Step 3 · A readable printout, and comparing objects By default, printing an object shows something unhelpful like <__main__.Cart object at 0x7f...> . A method named __repr__ controls what is shown. Methods with double underscores, called special methods or "dunder" methods, let your objects work with Python's built-in operations: Copy What you should see Copy .add(...).add(...) works because add returns the cart itself, so the next .add is called on it. This method chaining style is common in data and AI libraries (pandas and LangChain both use it). {self.customer!r} inserts the repr of the value, which puts quotes around strings. Step 4 · Inheritance: a specialised version A class can inherit from another: it gets all the parent's attributes and methods, and can add or change some. Copy What you should see Copy PrimeCart reused __init__ , add , __repr__ and __len__ from Cart and replaced only total . Notice that __repr__ printed the discounted total: it calls self.total() , and self is a PrimeCart , so Python uses the PrimeCart version. Libraries use inheritance heavily: in PyTorch you write your own network by inheriting from torch.nn.Module ( Lesson 3.16 ), and in LangChain many components inherit from a common Runnable base class. Step 5 · Exploring an unfamiliar object When a library hands you an object, four tools tell you what it is and what it can do: Copy What you should see Copy Tool What it tells you type(obj) The object's class dir(obj) Every attribute and method name (skip the ones starting with _ ) help(obj) or help(obj.method) The documentation written in the class's docstrings Your editor Hover over a name in VS Code to see its signature and docstring; Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on a Mac) to jump to its source Notice that subtracting two dates gave an object with a .days attribute: classes can define what - means for their objects, through special methods like the __len__ you wrote above. Tip Data-only classes: dataclasses and Pydantic Many classes only hold data. Writing __init__ and __repr__ for them is repetitive, so Python offers @dataclass , which writes those methods for you, and the popular Pydantic later · 0.16 library adds validation on top. Both appear everywhere in AI code (tool arguments, structured output later · 11.2 ) and are taught in Lesson 0.16 . Check your mental model ✗ "A class and an object are the same thing." ✓ The class is the blueprint; objects are the individual things built from it, each with its own data. ✗ " self is a keyword I must pass in." ✓ Python passes it automatically: cart.total() calls Cart.total(cart) . ✗ "Changing one object's attribute changes all objects of that class." ✓ Attributes set on self belong to that one object. Exercises Predict before you run After a = Cart("Asha") , b = a , b.add("tea", 100) , what is len(a) ? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Remove self from the method definition def total(self): (so it reads def total(): ) and call cart.total() . Read the error and explain it. (Solution B1.) Make it your own Write a class Order with attributes order_id , items (a list of (name, price) tuples) and status (starting at "placed" ), and methods ship() (sets the status to "shipped" , but raises a ValueError if the order is empty) and __repr__ . (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Two names, one object len(a) is 1. b = a does not copy the cart: it makes a second name for the same object (like the variable picture in Lesson 0.9 ). Changing it through b is visible through a . To make a separate cart you would create a new one or copy it. Solution B1 · Forgetting self Python raises TypeError: Cart.total() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given . Calling cart.total() always passes the object as the first argument, so a method must accept it. The "1 was given" is self , the argument you did not type. Solution M1 · An order class Copy Guarding the change (refusing to ship an empty order) inside the class means no caller can forget the check. Agent tools in the Agents from first principles section rely on the same idea: rules live in the code, not in the model's instructions. Recap A class bundles data (attributes) and behaviour (methods); objects are instances with their own data. __init__ sets up a new object; self is the object a method works on; special methods such as __repr__ and __len__ plug into Python's built-ins. Inheritance makes a specialised class that reuses and overrides a parent's methods. Explore unfamiliar objects with type , dir , help and your editor. Check your understanding Q1 What runs when you write Cart("Asha") ? A The total method B The init method, with self as the new object and customer="Asha" C Nothing until you call a method D The repr method Creating an object calls init to set up its attributes. Q2 In class PrimeCart(Cart): , what does PrimeCart get from Cart? A Nothing; it starts empty B All of Cart's attributes and methods, which it can add to or override C Only init D A copy of every existing Cart object Inheritance reuses the parent's behaviour.
