Next : Lesson 0.15 handles tables of data with pandas. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up NumPy The Python library for fast math on arrays of numbers All ML code Array A grid of numbers of one type, with a shape All ML code Shape The size of an array along each of its axes, such as (3, 4) Debugging tensors Axis One direction of an array: rows are axis 0, columns are axis 1 Sums and means Vectorization Doing an operation on a whole array at once instead of in a Python loop Speed Broadcasting NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by stretching the smaller one Shape bugs Dot product Multiply two vectors element by element and add up the results Similarity, attention Matrix multiplication Combining two arrays so that each output is a dot product of a row with a column Neural network layers Mentioned here, taught later 2 PyTorch, Transformer This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in PyTorch The most widely used Python library for building and training neural networks Lesson 3.16 Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.8 Why this came about Python is easy to read but slow at doing arithmetic one number at a time. Scientists in the 1990s and 2000s solved this by writing the number-crunching parts in fast compiled languages (C and Fortran) and calling them from Python. NumPy (2006) unified those efforts into one library built around a single object, the array : a grid of numbers of one type, stored compactly, with fast operations on the whole grid at once. pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch later · 3.16 and nearly every AI library either build on NumPy or copy its design, so its ideas (shapes, axes, broadcasting ) appear in every later block. In plain words first A spreadsheet you can do maths on in one go A Python list is a row of boxes that can hold anything. A NumPy array is a grid of numbers, all of the same kind, packed tightly together, like a block of cells in a spreadsheet. Instead of writing a loop to double every number, you write prices * 2 and NumPy doubles all of them at once, very fast. The two ideas you must get comfortable with are shape (how many numbers along each direction) and axis (which direction an operation runs along). Step 1 · Arrays and their shape NumPy's central object is the array : a grid of numbers that all have the same type. A list of numbers becomes a one-dimensional array; a list of lists becomes a two-dimensional one, a table. Every array knows its shape (how many rows and columns), and reading shapes is the habit this lesson is building. Make one of each and ask about them: Copy What you should see Copy Arrays have a shape: the number of items along each axis. A 1-D array is a row of numbers, a 2-D array a table (rows × columns), a 3-D array a stack of tables. Reading this output dtype is the data type of every element: float64 (decimal numbers stored in 64 bits) or int64 (whole numbers). One array holds one type; that is part of why it is fast. shape is a tuple with the size along each axis . (4,) is a 1-D array of 4 numbers (the comma makes it a tuple of one). (3, 4) is 3 rows by 4 columns. ndim is the number of axes: 1 for a vector, 2 for a table. size is the total number of elements, 12. Shapes are the single most useful thing to print when AI code misbehaves. A language model's input in the Transformers, step by step section has shape like (batch, tokens, features) , such as (8, 128, 768) : 8 texts, 128 tokens each, 768 numbers per token. Step 2 · Making arrays You rarely type arrays out by hand. NumPy has functions that build them: all zeros, all ones, a run of evenly spaced numbers, or random numbers. Note the seed on the random generator: it makes the "random" numbers the same on every run, which is why your output will match this page. Copy What you should see Copy Random numbers matter in AI: models start from random values and training shuffles data. Fixing the seed makes "random" results repeat exactly, which is how this course's outputs stay the same on every run. Step 3 · Indexing, slicing and masks Picking values out of an array uses square brackets, with one position per dimension: sales[0, 2] is row 0, column 2. A colon means "all of them". The second half shows a mask : comparing an array with a number gives an array of True and False, and using that as the index keeps only the True positions. Masks are how you filter data without writing a loop. Copy What you should see Copy For a 2-D array, sales[row, column] picks one element; a : means "everything along this axis". A boolean mask is an array of True / False of the same shape; using it as an index keeps only the True positions. Filtering like this replaces most for -loop-with- if code in data work. Step 4 · Arithmetic on whole arrays Arithmetic on arrays applies to every element at once. prices * 2 doubles every price; multiplying two arrays of the same shape multiplies them position by position. This is called vectorised code. It is shorter than a loop, and much faster, because the work happens inside NumPy's compiled code. Copy What you should see Copy Operators such as * and + work element by element : the first price times the first quantity, the second times the second, and so on. Functions such as np.sqrt , np.exp and np.log apply to every element. This is called vectorization , and it is fast because the loop runs inside NumPy's compiled code instead of in Python: Copy What you should see Copy Both give the same answer ( np.isclose checks they agree up to tiny rounding differences, because adding a million decimals in a different order changes the last digits), and the vectorized version is more than ten times faster (usually 50 to 100 times on a laptop). Neural networks do billions of such operations, which is why everything in the sections from Machine learning from zero to Transformers, step by step is written with arrays, never with Python loops over numbers. Step 5 · Aggregating along an axis sum , mean , max and friends can work on the whole array or along one axis . This is where most beginners get confused, so try the figure before reading on. Which way does an axis go? Units sold: 3 days (rows) by 4 products (columns). Click a button and watch which numbers are added together. Copy What you should see Copy The rule that always works: the axis you name is the one that disappears. sales has shape (3, 4) . sum(axis=0) removes axis 0 (the 3 rows), leaving shape (4,) ; sum(axis=1) removes axis 1 (the 4 columns), leaving (3,) . argmax gives the position of the largest value, not the value itself: Monday's best seller is column 2 (soap). Language models use exactly this: argmax over the vocabulary axis picks the most likely next token. Step 6 · Reshaping and broadcasting reshape rearranges the same numbers into a different shape, as long as the total count matches: Copy What you should see Copy Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes work together. NumPy lines the shapes up from the right; an axis of size 1, or a missing axis, is stretched to match the other array. Broadcasting: when shapes differ, NumPy stretches the smaller array along the missing axis (without copying it) so the operation applies to every row. Copy What you should see Copy Broadcasting is how a neural network adds one bias value to every example in a batch ( Lesson 3.4 ) and how a transformer later · 7.8 adds position information to every token ( Lesson 7.8 ). When you see the error operands could not be broadcast together , print the shapes: one of them is not what you expected. Step 7 · The dot product and matrix multiplication Two operations deserve a preview here because the The math you need, with pictures section explains them with pictures and every model uses them constantly. Copy What you should see Copy The dot product basket @ unit_price multiplies matching elements and adds them up: here, the cost of the basket. Matrix multiplication with @ does a dot product for every row: the basket's cost at each shop, in one operation. Every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiplication followed by a simple function ( Lesson 3.4 ), and attention in a transformer is mostly dot products ( Lesson 7.3 ). Check your mental model ✗ " sales.sum(axis=0) adds along each row." ✓ It adds down the rows, collapsing axis 0 and giving one total per column. The named axis disappears. ✗ " a * b on two arrays is matrix multiplication." ✓ * multiplies element by element. Matrix multiplication is @ . ✗ "A Python loop over an array is just as good." ✓ It gives the same answer, often 50 to 100 times more slowly. ✗ "Shape (4,) and shape (4, 1) are the same." ✓ The first is a 1-D array of 4 numbers; the second is a 2-D column with 4 rows and 1 column, and they broadcast differently. Exercises Predict before you run m = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4) . Predict the shape of m.sum(axis=1) , of m[:, 1:3] , and of m.reshape(2, -1) . (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Run np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([1, 2]) . Read the message, then explain in one sentence why NumPy refuses. (Solution B1.) Make it your own Using sales and prices from this lesson, compute each day's revenue in one line (hint: one matrix multiplication), then find the best day with argmax . (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Shapes m.sum(axis=1) has shape (3,) : one sum per row. m[:, 1:3] has shape (3, 2) : all rows, columns 1 and 2. m.reshape(2, -1) has shape (2, 6) : 12 numbers in 2 rows means 6 per row. Solution B1 · Shapes that do not line up ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,) (2,) . Lined up from the right, the sizes are 3 and 2: they are neither equal nor 1, so there is no sensible way to pair the elements. Solution M1 · Revenue per day revenue = sales @ prices gives one number per day: shape (3, 4) @ (4,) → (3,) , here [1163.5 675.5 1946. ] . revenue.argmax() is 2 : Wednesday. Matrix multiplication did the "multiply each quantity by its price and add up" for all three days at once. Recap An array is a grid of numbers of one type; shape , ndim and dtype describe it. Index with a[row, col] , slice with : , filter with boolean masks. Arithmetic and math functions apply element by element and are fast (vectorization). The axis you aggregate over disappears from the shape; argmax returns positions. Broadcasting stretches shapes from the right; @ is the dot product and matrix multiplication. Check your understanding Q1 x has shape (8, 128, 768). What is the shape of x.mean(axis=1) ? A (8, 128) B (8, 768) C (128, 768) D (8,) The named axis (128) disappears. Q2 What does np.array([1, 2, 3]) * np.array([4, 5, 6]) give? A 32 B [4, 10, 18] C [[4, 5, 6], [8, 10, 12], [12, 15, 18]] D An error multiplies element by element; the dot product (32) needs @. Q3 Why is (big * big).sum() much faster than a Python loop over big ? A It skips some elements B The loop runs inside NumPy's compiled code instead of in Python, one element at a time C It uses less precise numbers D It caches the answer Vectorized operations avoid Python's per-element overhead. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Evals and evaluation sets Evals are repeatable tests that measure how well a model or system does a task; an evaluation set is the fixed list of test cases with known good answers. Introduced in Lesson 11.22, first built in Lesson 14.27, and covered in depth in Lessons 14.117 and 14.118 Lesson 11.22 Why this came about NumPy arrays hold numbers of one type, but real business data is a table: order IDs (text), cities (text), amounts (numbers), dates, true/false flags. In 2008 Wes McKinney, then working at a hedge fund, started pandas to make that kind of table as easy to handle in Python as in a spreadsheet or SQL, but scriptable and repeatable. It became the standard tool for preparing data, and data preparation is most of the work in any AI project: training examples, evaluation sets later · 11.22 , and the documents and logs an agent reads. In plain words first A spreadsheet you control with code A DataFrame is a table: each column has a name and holds one kind of value, and each row is one record (one order, one customer). You can do everything you would do in a spreadsheet (filter, sort, add a calculated column, make a pivot table, look values up in another sheet), but by writing a line of code, so you can repeat it on tomorrow's data in one click and see exactly what was done. Step 1 · A first table pandas works with tables. Its main object, the DataFrame , has named columns and numbered rows, like a spreadsheet. Real data usually arrives as a CSV file (comma-separated values); here the CSV is a string inside the program so that the example runs anywhere. Load it and take a first look: Copy What you should see Copy A pandas DataFrame is a table: named columns, each with one data type, and an index labelling the rows. Selecting one column gives a Series . Reading this output The left-most column (0 to 5) is the index : a label for each row. By default it counts from 0. NaN ("not a number") marks a missing value : order SK-6 has no amount in the file. shape is (rows, columns) : 6 orders, 5 columns. dtypes gives each column's type. amount became float64 rather than an integer type because of the missing value ( NaN is a float). paid was recognised as bool , ordered_on as a date ( datetime64 ) because we asked for it with parse_dates . Text columns show as str (pandas 3; older versions showed object ). In real work you would write pd.read_csv("orders.csv") with a file path, or pd.read_excel(...) , pd.read_json(...) , pd.read_parquet(...) or pd.read_sql(...) for other sources. Three more first looks are worth making a habit: Copy What you should see Copy describe() summarises a numeric column: how many values are present ( count is 5, not 6, because of the missing one), the mean, the standard deviation ( std , how spread out the values are; Lesson 1.10 ), and the minimum, quartiles and maximum. value_counts() counts each distinct value. Step 2 · Selecting columns and rows The first thing you do with a table is pick parts of it. One column name in square brackets gives a single column; a list of names gives a smaller table. For single cells there are two tools: loc finds by label, iloc by position counted from 0. Copy What you should see Copy You want Write Gives One column df["amount"] A Series : one column with its index Several columns df[["order_id", "amount"]] A smaller DataFrame (note the double brackets: a list of names) Rows and columns by label df.loc[1, "city"] , df.loc[0:2, ["city"]] Uses index labels and column names; 0:2 includes 2 Rows and columns by position df.iloc[0, 2] , df.iloc[:3, :2] Like NumPy: counts from 0, end excluded Step 3 · Filtering, new columns and sorting Filtering works exactly like NumPy masks ( Lesson 0.14 ): a comparison gives a True/False Series, and df[mask] keeps the True rows. Copy What you should see Copy Use & (and), | (or) and ~ (not) to combine conditions in pandas, with brackets around each one. The words and / or do not work on whole columns. pd.cut puts each number into a labelled range, a common way to turn a number into a category. The missing amount stays missing in every derived column, and sort_values puts it last. Step 4 · Missing values Real tables have holes. pandas marks a missing value as NaN ("not a number"). Before you compute anything, count the holes and decide what to do with them: ignore them, fill them with a value, or drop the rows. Each choice gives a different answer, as the three means below show. Copy What you should see Copy The two means differ: pandas skips missing values by default, but filling them with 0 drags the mean down. There is no universally right choice. Ask why the value is missing (not yet paid? a broken export?) before deciding to drop it, fill it, or keep it as missing. The same question appears when you clean data for evaluating AI systems in the Production engineering and AI system design section. Step 5 · Summarising with groupby groupby answers questions like "total sales per city" in one line. It splits the rows into groups, applies a calculation to each group, and combines the results. groupby is split, apply, combine: rows are split into groups by a key, a calculation runs on each group, and the results are combined into a new table. Copy What you should see Copy agg lets you compute several summaries at once, each written as new_name=(column, function) . df["ordered_on"].dt.day_name() extracts the weekday from each date; .dt gives access to date parts the way .str gives access to string methods ( df["city"].str.upper() ). Notice that orders for Pune is 3 but its revenue includes only two amounts: count counts rows, sum skips missing values. And Wednesday shows 0.0 : its only order (SK-6) has a missing amount, and the sum of nothing is 0. A zero that really means "unknown" is a classic reporting mistake, which is why it pays to look at counts next to sums. Step 6 · Joining two tables Data often lives in several tables linked by an ID, exactly like a database. merge joins them: Copy What you should see Copy how="left" keeps every row of the left table ( df ) and fills in matches from the right; orders without a known customer get a missing value. how="inner" would keep only orders that appear in both tables, so SK-4, SK-5 and SK-6 would disappear (and Meera's SK-7, which has no order details, would not appear either). Choosing the wrong join is a classic way to lose or duplicate rows silently: always compare row counts before and after. Step 7 · A quick chart pandas can draw charts through the matplotlib library. In a notebook the chart appears under the cell; in a script you save it to a file. Copy What you should see Copy Open revenue_by_city.png to see three horizontal bars, Goa shortest and Delhi longest. Charts are the fastest way to spot problems in data: a city with zero orders, a sudden spike, a column that should never be negative. The problem: the libraries assume more Python than the tutorials teach From the next lesson on, the code uses features that beginner Python courses often skip. None of it is hard, but reading library code is slow until these are familiar. Each section below shows one feature, what it prints, and where the course uses it. Type hints, TypedDict and Annotated A type hint is a label that says what kind of value a variable or parameter is meant to hold, such as order_id: str . Python itself does not enforce hints, but AI libraries read them: they are how a library learns what your data looks like. A TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys, Literal lists the only allowed values, and Annotated attaches extra information to a type. Run this and look at what the hints contain: Copy What you should see Copy Type hints are labels: Python does not enforce them at run time, but tools, editors and libraries read them. TypedDict declares which keys a dictionary has; Literal limits a value to a few strings; Annotated attaches extra information to a type without changing it. LangGraph reads the annotations of your state class to learn its keys and reducers ( Lesson 14.60 ), and LangChain later · 14.52 reads a function's hints to build a tool's schema (Lessons 14.4 and 14.54 ). Dataclasses and Pydantic Two ways to define a small class that mostly holds data. A dataclass writes the __init__ for you and nothing more. A Pydantic model also checks the data when the object is created, and raises an error that says exactly which field was wrong. That checking is why every agent framework later · 14.51 uses Pydantic for anything that comes from a model. Compare the two: Copy What you should see Copy A dataclass is a small class with an automatic constructor and printout, and no checking: use it for internal records and run context ( Lesson 14.61 ). A Pydantic model validates and converts data when it is created: the string "1200" became the number 1200, and a malformed ID and a zero amount were rejected with errors naming the fields. Use Pydantic wherever data comes from outside your code: model outputs ( Lesson 11.2 ), tool arguments ( Lesson 14.54 ) and API requests ( Lesson 14.71 ). JSON and JSON Schema: how your Python is described to a model A model never sees your Python; it only sees text. So whenever a library tells a model about a tool's arguments, or asks for an answer of a fixed shape, it first translates your Python into two standard text formats. Knowing them makes outputs like {'title': 'Order Id', 'type': 'string'} readable, and they appear in almost every lesson from 2.2 on. A tool definition is read straight from the function. The name, the type hints and the docstring already say everything the model needs, so generating the schema from them keeps the two descriptions from drifting apart. In plain words first A filled-in form, and the blank form JSON is data as text: {"order_id": "A-1001", "amount": 1200} . It is how data travels between your code, model providers and web APIs. JSON Schema is a description of data as text: "an object whose order_id is a string matching this pattern, and whose amount is a whole number above 0". It is the blank form with its labels and rules, not the data. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output JSON looks like a Python dictionary but is a string; False and None become false and null , and strings always use double quotes. When a model "returns JSON", it returns a string like this. From the two-line class A , Pydantic generated the whole schema: 'type': 'object' (a class is an object), 'properties' (one entry per field), 'type': 'integer' (from int ), 'required': ['x'] (no default), and two 'title' keys made from the field and class names. title is only a label; you never write it. "pattern": ... Yes: the shape of a valid value Field(description="...") "description": "..." Describe the result in the docstring if the model needs to know. Functions as values, and decorators In Python a function is a value like any other: you can pass it to another function, store it in a list, or return it. A decorator uses this. It is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, usually the original with something added. The @name line above a def applies it. Frameworks use decorators constantly ( @tool , @app.get ), so it helps to have built one: Copy What you should see Copy A function can be passed to another function and returned from one. A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, applied with @ above a definition. functools.wraps keeps the original's name and docstring, which matters because libraries read them: @tool builds a tool's name and description from exactly these ( Lesson 14.54 ). When you see @tool , @entrypoint , @before_model or @traceable , read it as "this function, wrapped with extra behavior". async and await Much of an agent's time is spent waiting: for a model, for an API, for a database. Asynchronous code lets one program wait for several things at once. An async def function can pause at an await and let other work run. asyncio.gather starts several of them together. Three lookups that each take 0.2 seconds finish in about 0.2 seconds in total, not 0.6: Copy What you should see Copy async def defines a function that can pause at await while it waits, letting other work run meanwhile. asyncio.gather started three lookups together, so three 0.2-second waits took about 0.2 seconds, not 0.6. This is how parallel tool calls and concurrent requests stay fast ( Lesson 14.5 ), and why some LangGraph features, such as node timeouts, need async nodes ( Lesson 14.68 ). Async methods in the libraries start with a : ainvoke , astream , abatch . Generators and with-blocks Two small features that appear in almost every AI library. A generator is a function that hands out its results one at a time with yield , which is how streamed model output reaches your code. A with-block runs set-up code on the way in and clean-up code on the way out, even if an error happens in between; it is how files, connections and timers are opened and closed safely. Copy What you should see Copy A generator yield s values one at a time, which is exactly what streaming is: for chunk in model.stream(...) reads a generator (Lessons 11.3 and 14.65 ). A generator can be read only once; the second list(pieces) was empty, a common streaming bug. A with block runs setup and cleanup around your code, even when an error happens: the SDK 's messages.stream(...) and database connections use it. Reading a signature A function's signature is its first line: the name, the parameters and their types. Library documentation is mostly signatures, so being able to read one is a practical skill. This example has every part you will meet: required parameters, a Literal , a bare * (everything after it must be passed by name), a default value, an optional type and **extra , which collects any additional named arguments. Copy What you should see Copy Everything after a lone * must be passed by name, which libraries use to keep calls readable ( model.invoke(messages, config=...) ). **extra collects any other named arguments, which is how many LangChain classes pass settings through to a provider. When a call fails with a TypeError , compare it with inspect.signature or the library's reference. A tool built from it would be named wrapper with no description, and LangChain refuses a tool without one ( Lesson 14.54 ). Libraries depend on the metadata decorators preserve. Keep the pieces as they pass: shown = [] , then shown.append(p) inside the loop, and save " ".join(shown) . Solution M1 · Limit concurrency Create limit = asyncio.Semaphore(3) and wrap the lookup: async def limited(oid): async with limit: return await lookup(oid, 0.2) . Then await asyncio.gather(*(limited(f"A-{1000 + i}") for i in range(10))) runs at most three at once, taking about four rounds of 0.2 seconds. This is what max_concurrency does for batch ( Lesson 14.52 ) and what protects provider quotas ( Lesson 14.115 ). Because hints are machine-readable: a library can turn a function's parameters into a JSON Schema for a tool, a TypedDict into a graph's state channels, an Annotated reducer into merge behavior, and a Pydantic model into a structured-output schema and a validator. Whether something blocks the event loop: a synchronous call (a sync HTTP client, time.sleep , CPU-heavy parsing) inside an async function stops every other request while it runs. Use async clients ( ainvoke ), run blocking work in a thread pool, and check that the server runs enough workers. A plausible wrong answer. "Async is slower than threads." Async is fast for waiting; it is slow only when the waiting is done with blocking calls. Follow-ups. How would you find a blocking call? The libraries read them, so hints are part of the behavior, not just documentation: tool schemas, state reducers and output validation come from them. "Hints are optional style." In these libraries they change what the code does. Follow-ups. Which type checker would you run, and where? a0007: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Docker Containers for AI Workloads Lesson 0.17 60 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Build a GPU-enabled Docker image with CUDA, PyTorch, and AI libraries from a Dockerfile Mount host directories as volumes to persist models, datasets, and code across container rebuilds Configure the NVIDIA Container Toolkit to expose GPUs inside containers Orchestrate multi-service AI applications (inference server + vector database) using Docker Compose Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 and 03 Type : Build. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Containers make "works on my machine" a thing of the past. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Container "Lightweight VM" An isolated process using the host kernel, with its own filesystem and network Image layer "Cached step" Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Unchanged layers are cached, so rebuilds are fast. NVIDIA Container Toolkit "GPU in Docker" A runtime hook that exposes host GPUs to containers via --gpus flag Volume mount "Shared folder" A directory on the host mapped into the container. Changes persist after the container stops. Base image "Starting point" The FROM image your Dockerfile builds on top of. Determines what is pre-installed. The problem In plain words first A Docker image is a frozen copy of everything your code needs: an operating system's files, Python, CUDA libraries, your packages. A container is that image running as an isolated process on your machine. Anyone who runs the same image gets the same environment, down to the system libraries, which a virtual environment alone cannot promise. You trained a model on your laptop with PyTorch 2.3, CUDA 12.4, and Python 3.12. Your colleague has PyTorch 2.1, CUDA 11.8, and Python 3.10. Your model crashes on their machine. Your Dockerfile works on both. AI projects are dependency nightmares. A typical stack includes Python, PyTorch, CUDA drivers, cuDNN, system-level C libraries, and specialized packages like flash-attn that need exact compiler versions. Docker packages all of this into a single image that runs identically everywhere. The idea Docker wraps your code, runtime, libraries, and system tools into an isolated unit called a container. Think of it as a lightweight virtual machine, except it shares the host OS kernel instead of running its own, so it starts in seconds instead of minutes. The same idea as a formula An image is a stack of layers, one per FROM , RUN , COPY or ADD line. Docker caches each layer under a key computed from the key of the layer below it, the instruction itself and, for COPY , the contents of the copied files: ​ = H ( k i − 1 ​ , instruction i ​ , inputs i ​ ) Because ​ contains ​ , a change at layer changes every key from upward. If layer takes ​ seconds to build, an edit that touches layer costs ∑ ​ t i ​ So put slow layers that rarely change (system packages, pip install ) near the bottom and fast layers that change often (your code) at the top. Image size. The image is the sum of its layers. Deleting a file in a later layer hides it but does not shrink the image; remove temporary files in the same RUN line that created them. Worked example Ordering a Dockerfile by hand Installing the requirements takes 4 minutes; copying the code takes 1 second. Code first ( COPY . /app , then RUN pip install ): editing one line of code changes the inputs of the COPY layer, so the pip install above it in the stack reruns. Every code edit costs about 4 minutes. Requirements first ( COPY requirements.txt , RUN pip install , then COPY . /app ): a code edit changes only the last COPY . Rebuild: about 1 second. Only editing requirements.txt costs the 4 minutes. See it drawn Docker's cache, simulated The key rule of the formula box in ten lines of Python, applied to the two orderings of the worked example. The script builds each Dockerfile once, edits the app code, and lists the layers whose key changed. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output With the code copied first, the edit invalidates the COPY layer and therefore pip install above it: the slow layer reruns on every change. With the requirements copied first, the pip install key depends only on requirements.txt , which did not change, so it comes from the cache, and only the cheap layers rebuild. Docker's real keys work this way, which is why every production Dockerfile in this lesson copies the requirements before the code. Check your mental model ✗ "A container is a virtual machine." ✓ A VM runs its own operating system kernel. A container is an ordinary process on the host's kernel with its own view of files and network, which is why it starts in a second. ✗ "The image contains the GPU driver." ✓ The driver stays on the host. The image carries the CUDA toolkit (the libraries); the NVIDIA Container Toolkit lets the container use the host's driver. The toolkit in the image must not be newer than the driver supports. ✗ "Files I write inside a container are kept." ✓ They live in the container's own layer, which disappears with docker run --rm or when the container is removed. Anything worth keeping goes in a mounted volume. Idea 1 · Why AI projects need Docker more than most GPU drivers are fragile. CUDA 12.4 code does not run on CUDA 11.8. Docker isolates the CUDA toolkit inside the container while sharing the host GPU driver through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. Model weights are large. A 7B parameter model is 14 GB in fp16. You do not want to re-download it every time you rebuild. Docker volumes let you mount a models directory from the host. Multi-service architectures are common. A real AI application is not just a Python script. It is an inference server, a vector database for RAG, maybe a web frontend. Docker Compose orchestrates all of these with one command. Idea 2 · Key vocabulary Term What it means Image A read-only template. Your recipe. Built from a Dockerfile. Container A running instance of an image. Your kitchen. Dockerfile Instructions to build an image. Layer by layer. Volume Persistent storage that survives container restarts. docker-compose A tool for defining multi-container applications in YAML. Step 7 · Useful Docker commands for AI work Copy Recap What to keep from this lesson An image is a frozen environment; a container is a running copy of it on the host kernel. Order Dockerfile lines from slow and stable to fast and changing, so the cache does the work. Models, datasets and code belong in mounted volumes; the container's own files are disposable. Solutions Solution P1 · A cache thrown away Everything from the COPY line down: the PyTorch install, the library install, and every later layer. Editing a file changes the COPY layer, which invalidates every layer after it, so a one-line change costs a multi-gigabyte reinstall. Move COPY to the end (or mount the code as a volume) and the same edit rebuilds in seconds. Solution B1 · A disappearing model Without the mount the model is gone: it was written into the container's writable layer, and a new container starts again from the image. With -v ~/models:/models the files are written to ~/models on your host, so every new container sees them and nothing is downloaded twice. Use it: the same idea with real libraries You now have a reproducible AI development environment. Smaller, safer images. Multi-stage builds, uv inside the image for fast installs, non-root users and image scanning (Docker Scout, Trivy) are standard practice; Kubernetes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator runs these images at scale. a0008: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Setting Up Your Code Editor and IDE Lesson 0.18 20 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Install VS Code with essential extensions for Python, Jupyter, linting, and remote SSH Configure format-on-save, type checking, and notebook output scrolling for AI workflows Set up Remote SSH to edit and debug code on remote GPU machines as if they were local Evaluate editor alternatives (Cursor, Windsurf, Neovim) and their tradeoffs for AI work Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Build. Time : about 20 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Your editor is your co-pilot. Configure it once so it stays out of your way and starts pulling its weight. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means LSP "Autocomplete engine" Language Server Protocol: a standard for editors to get type info, completions, and diagnostics from a language-specific server Pylance "The Python plugin" Microsoft's Python language server using Pyright for type checking and IntelliSense Remote SSH "Working on the server" VS Code extension that runs a lightweight server on a remote machine and streams the UI to your local editor Format on save "Auto-prettier" The editor runs a formatter (Black, Ruff) every time you save, so code style is always consistent The problem In plain words first An editor does more than show text. Through a language server it reads your code as you type and reports mistakes before you run anything: a misspelt variable, a missing import, a string passed where a number was expected. A formatter rewrites layout on save so you never argue about spaces, and a linter flags code that is legal but almost certainly wrong. You'll spend thousands of hours inside your editor writing Python, running notebooks, debugging training loops, and SSH-ing into GPU boxes. A misconfigured editor turns every session into friction: no autocomplete, no type hints, no inline errors, manual formatting, and a clunky terminal workflow. The right setup takes 20 minutes. Skipping it costs you 20 minutes every day. The idea An AI engineering editor setup needs five things: The same idea as a formula A type checker such as Pylance (Pyright) treats a type as a set of values : int is all integers, str all strings, float | None all floats plus None . A value fits a parameter if it lies in the parameter's set, and a type may be passed where is expected if every is a (written , " is a subtype of "). By convention int is accepted where float is expected. Containers that can be changed are stricter. A list[int] is not accepted where a list[float] is expected, even though every int is accepted as a float: a function given a list[float] may append 0.5 to it, which would break the caller's list of ints. Types like list are invariant ; read-only ones such as Sequence[float] are covariant and accept a list[int] . The checker works on the code without running it, so it can only see what the annotations say: un-annotated code is mostly invisible to it. Worked example Checking two calls by hand Copy mean(ints) : is list[int] a subtype of list[float] ? No, lists are invariant. Pyright reports "list[int]" is not assignable to "list[float]" and suggests Sequence ; mypy gives the same error. mean2(ints) : is list[int] a Sequence[float] ? A list is a sequence, and int is accepted as float in a read-only container: yes, no error. scale(3) with x: float : accepted, by the int-for-float convention. Check your mental model ✗ "Type hints make Python check types when the code runs." ✓ Python ignores them at run time. They are read by tools: your editor's type checker, Pydantic, LangChain. The demo below runs a badly typed call without complaint. ✗ "The linter and the formatter do the same job." ✓ The formatter (Black, or ruff format ) changes layout only. The linter (Ruff) finds problems such as unused imports and undefined names, and changes nothing unless you ask it to fix. ✗ "Remote SSH copies my project to the GPU box." ✓ The files stay on the remote machine; VS Code runs a small server there and shows you the remote folder. Your code runs where the GPU is. Step 1 · Install VS Code VS Code is the recommended editor. It is free, runs on every OS, has first-class Jupyter notebook support, and the extension ecosystem covers everything you need for AI work. Download it from code.visualstudio.com . Verify from the terminal: Copy If code is not found on macOS, open VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+P , type "Shell Command", and select "Install 'code' command in PATH". Step 2 · Install Essential Extensions Open the integrated terminal in VS Code ( Ctrl+` on every platform) and install the extensions that matter for AI work: Copy What each one does: Extension Why Python Language support, virtual env detection, run/debug Pylance Fast type checking, autocomplete, import resolution Jupyter Run notebooks inside VS Code, variable explorer GitLens See who changed what, inline git blame Remote SSH Open a folder on a remote GPU box as if it were local Debugpy Step-through debugging for Python Black Formatter Auto-format on save, consistent style Ruff Fast linting, catches common mistakes The file code/vscode/extensions.json in this lesson contains the full recommendations list. Copy it to .vscode/extensions.json in your project folder, and VS Code prompts you to install them when you open that folder. Step 3 · Configure Settings Copy the settings from code/vscode/settings.json in this lesson, or apply them manually through Settings > Open Settings (JSON) . The key settings for AI work: Copy Why these matter: Type checking on basic : Catches wrong argument types before you run. Saves debugging time on tensor shape mismatches and wrong API parameters. Format on save : Never think about formatting again. Black handles it. Rulers at 88 and 120 : Black wraps at 88. The 120 marker shows when docstrings and comments are getting too long. Notebook output scrolling : Training loops print thousands of lines. Without scrolling, the output panel explodes. Auto-save : You will forget to save. Your training script will run stale code. Auto-save prevents that. Predict before you run scale(x: float, factor: float) multiplies its two arguments. What does scale("3", 2) print, and would Pylance have warned you? (Solution P1.) Copy What you should see Copy Copy See it drawn What a linter catches Ruff is the linter the lesson installs. Run on a small training file with an unused import and a typo in a variable name, it finds both without running the code: Copy What you should see Copy Copy F821 Undefined name 'preds' would otherwise surface as a NameError at the end of a training run, possibly hours in. Reading this output Ruff reports two problems by rule code: F401 ( os is imported but never used) and F821 ( preds is used but never defined; the function's parameter is pred ). Neither stops Python from starting the script; the NameError would come only when execution reaches the last line, possibly after a long training run. The editor shows the same codes as squiggles while you type. Step 4 · Terminal Integration VS Code's integrated terminal is where you run training scripts, monitor GPUs, and manage environments. Set it up properly: Copy Useful shortcuts: Action macOS Linux/Windows Toggle terminal Ctrl+` Ctrl+` New terminal Ctrl+Shift+` Ctrl+Shift+` Split terminal Cmd+\ Ctrl+Shift+5 Split terminals are useful: one for running your script, one for monitoring GPU with nvidia-smi -l 1 or watch -n 1 nvidia-smi . Step 5 · Remote Development (SSH into GPU Boxes) This is the most important extension for AI work. You will run training on remote machines (cloud VMs, lab servers, Lambda, Vast.ai). Remote SSH lets you open the remote filesystem, edit files, run terminals, and debug as if everything were local. Setup: Install the Remote SSH extension (done in Step 2). Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P ), type "Remote-SSH: Connect to Host". Enter user@your-gpu-box-ip . VS Code installs its server component on the remote machine automatically. For passwordless access, set up SSH keys: Copy Add the host to ~/.ssh/config for convenience: Copy Now Remote-SSH: Connect to Host > gpu-box connects instantly. Break it on purpose Turn off files.autoSave , edit a training script so it prints something new, and run it from the integrated terminal without saving . What runs? Then save and run again. (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson VS Code plus the Python, Pylance, Jupyter, Ruff and Remote SSH extensions cover the whole course. Type checking, linting and formatting catch mistakes before you run; type hints are not checked at run time. Turn on format on save and auto-save so style and stale files never cost you a run. Remote SSH lets you edit and run on a GPU box as if it were local; set up SSH keys and ~/.ssh/config once. Alternatives Cursor cursor.com is a VS Code fork with built-in AI code generation. It uses the same extension ecosystem and settings format. If you use Cursor, everything in this lesson still applies. Import the same settings.json and extensions.json . Windsurf windsurf.com is another AI-first VS Code fork. Same story: same extensions, same settings format, same Remote SSH support. Vim/Neovim If you already use Vim or Neovim and are productive in it, stay there. The minimum setup for AI Python work: pyright or pylsp for type checking (via Mason or manual install) nvim-lspconfig for language server integration jupyter-vim or molten-nvim for notebook-like execution telescope.nvim for file/symbol search none-ls.nvim with black and ruff for formatting/linting If you do not already use Vim, do not start now. The learning curve will compete with learning AI engineering. Use VS Code. Solutions Solution P1 · A string where a float was expected scale(3, 2) prints 6 , and scale("3", 2) prints 33 : Python repeats the string twice, with no error, because type hints are not enforced. Pylance (with type checking on basic ) underlines "3" with a warning like Argument of type "Literal['3']" cannot be assigned to parameter "x" of type "float" . That warning is the whole point of the setting. Solution B1 · Running stale code The terminal runs the file on disk, which is the last saved version, so the old output appears. The editor's unsaved buffer is invisible to Python. After saving, the new line prints. This is why the lesson turns auto-save on: a training run on stale code wastes the whole run. Use it: the same idea with real libraries With this setup, your daily workflow looks like: Open the project folder in VS Code (or connect via Remote SSH to a GPU box). Write Python in the editor with autocomplete, type hints, and inline errors. Run Jupyter notebooks inline with the Jupyter extension. Use the integrated terminal for training scripts, uv pip install , and GPU monitoring. Review changes with GitLens before committing. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) AI coding assistants are part of the editor. VS Code with GitHub Copilot (chat, edits and agent mode), Cursor, and JetBrains AI are the common setups; Claude Code and similar agents work from the terminal next to any editor. Fast linting and type checking. Ruff replaces flake8, isort and Black in many projects; Pyright (Pylance in VS Code) or mypy check types; both run on save and in CI. Remote development. VS Code Remote-SSH, Dev Containers and Codespaces let the editor run locally while code runs on a GPU machine. Sources: Copilot in VS Code , Ruff , Pyright , VS Code Remote Development . Then use the Remote SSH command to connect; the status bar shows the host name when VS Code runs on the remote machine. a0009: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Data Management: Storing and Versioning Datasets Lesson 0.19 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Load, stream, and cache datasets using the Hugging Face datasets library Convert between CSV, JSON, Parquet, and Arrow formats and explain their tradeoffs Create reproducible train/validation/test splits with fixed random seeds Manage large model and dataset files using .gitignore , Git LFS, or DVC Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Data is the fuel. How you manage it determines how fast you go. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Dataset split "Training data" A named subset (train/val/test) used at different stages of the ML lifecycle Streaming "Load it lazily" Processing data row by row from a remote source without downloading the full dataset Parquet "Compressed CSV" A columnar file format optimized for analytical queries and storage efficiency Arrow "Fast dataframe" An in-memory columnar format used internally by the datasets library for zero-copy reads Git LFS "Git for big files" An extension that stores large files outside the git repo while keeping pointers in version control DVC "Git for data" A version control system for datasets and models that integrates with cloud storage Cache "Already downloaded" A local copy of previously fetched data, stored at ~/.cache/huggingface/ by default The problem In plain words first Most AI data lives on the Hugging Face Hub. The datasets library downloads a dataset once, keeps it in a cache on your disk, and gives it back as a table you can index, split and convert. For data too big for your disk it can stream rows instead. Large files such as model weights stay out of Git; you record where they came from instead. Every AI project starts with data. You need to find datasets, download them, convert between formats, split them for training and evaluation, and version them so experiments are reproducible. Doing this manually every time is slow and error-prone. You need a repeatable workflow. The idea The Hugging Face datasets library is the standard way to load data for AI work. It handles downloading, caching, format conversion, and streaming out of the box. The same idea as a formula Size. A table of rows and numeric columns stored as numbers of bytes takes bytes. Text formats (CSV, JSON) store each number as characters instead: 0.8414709848 is 12 bytes plus a separator, against 4 for a float32, and JSON repeats every column name in every row. Reading part of it. CSV and JSON store data row by row, so reading one column still means reading every byte of the file. Parquet stores each column separately (in blocks called row groups), so reading of columns of equal size reads about of the file. Within a column the values are alike, so they also compress well. Streaming. Loading a dataset needs memory for all of it; streaming one batch of rows at a time needs memory for rows, whatever is. Worked example Estimating file sizes by hand One million rows of 20 float32 features plus a label: In memory: × 21 × 4 = 84 MB. As CSV, at about 12 characters per value: × 21 × 12 ≈ 250 MB, three times larger, and every number must be parsed back from text. As Parquet, reading only the label column: about of the data, roughly 4 MB before compression. The IMDB files written in this lesson show the same effect with text columns: the review text dominates the bytes, and a Parquet read of the label column skips it. Check your mental model ✗ " load_dataset downloads the data every time I run my script." ✓ Only the first time. Later calls read from ~/.cache/huggingface/ , which is why the second run is fast and works offline. ✗ "A test split is just more training data I haven't used yet." ✓ It is the one honest measure of how the model does on unseen data. Look at it once, at the end; tune on the validation split. ✗ "Parquet is just a compressed CSV." ✓ It stores each column separately with its type, so a program can read only the columns it needs and gets numbers back as numbers, not text. Step 1 · Install the datasets library Copy Step 2 · Load a dataset Copy What you should see Copy Copy This downloads the IMDB movie review dataset. After the first download, it loads from cache at ~/.cache/huggingface/datasets/ . Reading this output DatasetDict holds the three splits IMDB ships with: 25,000 labelled reviews for training, 25,000 for testing, and 50,000 unlabelled ones ( label is -1 there). Each row has two features , the review text and its label (0 negative, 1 positive). dataset["train"][0] is one row as a plain Python dictionary. Step 3 · Stream large datasets Some datasets are too large to fit on disk. Streaming loads them row by row without downloading the full thing. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Streaming gives you an IterableDataset . You process rows as they arrive. Memory usage stays constant regardless of dataset size. Step 4 · Dataset formats The datasets library uses Apache Arrow under the hood. You can convert to other formats depending on what your pipeline needs. Copy See it drawn The same data in three formats The cell above wrote the 25,000 training reviews three times. Here are the file sizes on this page's server, and a Parquet read of one column: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Parquet is about 40 percent smaller here, and reading just the label column never touches the 20 MB of review text. Format comparison: Format Size Read Speed Best For CSV Large Slow Human readability, spreadsheets JSON Large Slow APIs, nested data Parquet Small Fast Analytics, columnar queries Arrow Small Fastest In-memory processing (what datasets uses internally) For AI work, Parquet is the best storage format. Arrow is what you work with in memory. CSV and JSON are for interchange. Step 5 · Data splits Predict before you run IMDB's training split has 25,000 rows. The code below first holds out 20 percent as a test set, then takes 12.5 percent of what is left as validation. How many rows end up in train, validation and test, and what fractions are those of the whole? (Solution P1.) Every ML project needs three splits: Train : The model learns from this (typically 80%) Validation : You check progress during training (typically 10%) Test : Final evaluation after training is done (typically 10%) Some datasets come pre-split. When they don't, split them yourself: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Always set a seed for reproducibility. The same seed produces the same split every time. Step 6 · Download and cache models Models are large files. The huggingface_hub library handles downloading and caching. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Models cache to ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/ . Once downloaded, they load instantly on subsequent runs. Step 7 · Handle large files Model weights and large datasets should not go into git. Three options: Option A: .gitignore (simplest) Copy Option B: Git LFS (track large files in git) Copy Git LFS stores pointers in your repo and the actual files on a separate server. GitHub gives you 1 GB free. Option C: DVC (data version control) Copy DVC creates small .dvc files that point to your data. The data itself lives in S3, GCS, or another remote storage backend. Approach Complexity Best For .gitignore Low Personal projects, downloaded data you can re-fetch Git LFS Medium Teams sharing model weights via git DVC High Reproducible experiments, large datasets, teams For this course, .gitignore is enough. Use DVC when you need to reproduce exact experiments across machines. Break it on purpose Run the split code twice with seed=42 , then twice with no seed argument, and print the first review of test_ds each time. What changes, and why does it matter when you compare two models? (Solution B1.) Step 8 · Storage patterns Local storage works for datasets under ~10 GB. The HF cache handles this automatically. Cloud storage is for anything larger or shared across machines: Copy DVC integrates with S3 and GCS directly: Copy For this course, local storage is sufficient. Cloud storage becomes relevant when you fine-tune on remote GPU instances. Datasets Used in This Course Dataset Lessons Size What It Teaches IMDB Tokenization, classification 84 MB Text classification basics WikiText Language modeling 181 MB Next-token prediction SQuAD QA systems 35 MB Question answering, spans Common Crawl (subset) Embeddings Varies Large-scale text processing MNIST Vision basics 21 MB Image classification fundamentals COCO (subset) Multimodal Varies Image-text pairs You do not need to download all of these now. Each lesson specifies what it needs. Recap What to keep from this lesson load_dataset downloads once and caches; streaming=True reads row by row when the data is too large. Arrow in memory, Parquet on disk, CSV and JSON only for exchange. Split into train, validation and test with a fixed seed; touch the test split once, at the end. Keep weights and data out of Git: .gitignore for re-downloadable files, Git LFS or DVC when a team needs exact versions. Solutions Solution P1 · Two splits in a row Test: 20 percent of 25,000 = 5,000. That leaves 20,000, and 12.5 percent of 20,000 = 2,500 for validation, leaving 17,500 for training. The run prints Train: 17500, Val: 2500, Test: 5000 , which is 70, 10 and 20 percent of the whole. The 0.125 was chosen because 0.125 × 0.8 = 0.1. Solution B1 · Splits without a seed With seed=42 both runs pick exactly the same rows, so the first test review is the same. Without a seed each run shuffles differently and the review changes. If you train model A on one random split and model B on another, part of the difference in their scores comes from which rows landed in the test set, not from the models. Fix the seed, or save the split, before comparing. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Run the utility script to verify everything works: Copy This downloads a small dataset, converts it, splits it, and prints a summary. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Parquet plus Arrow is the default. Columnar Parquet files and Apache Arrow memory are what pandas 3.0 (January 2026, copy-on-write and a string dtype by default), Polars, DuckDB, Spark and the Hugging Face datasets library share. Local engines for big files. DuckDB and Polars query multi-gigabyte Parquet or CSV files on a laptop, often faster than loading them into pandas. Open table formats in the warehouse. Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake add versions, schema changes and time travel on top of Parquet; Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery and AWS all read and write Iceberg. Versioning ML data. Hugging Face Hub dataset revisions, DVC and lakeFS tie a model run to the exact data it saw. Sources: pandas 3.0 , DuckDB , Polars , Apache Iceberg , DVC . a0010: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling The Terminal and Shell Essentials Lesson 0.20 35 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Use piping, redirects, and grep to filter and process training logs from the command line Create persistent tmux sessions with multiple panes for concurrent training and GPU monitoring Monitor system and GPU resources with htop , nvtop , and nvidia-smi Transfer files between local and remote machines using SSH, scp , and rsync Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Learn. Time : about 35 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line The terminal is where AI engineers live. Get comfortable here. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Shell "The terminal" The program that interprets your commands (bash, zsh, fish) tmux "Terminal multiplexer" A program that lets you run multiple terminal sessions inside one window, and detach/reattach Pipe "The bar thing" The \| operator that sends one command's output as input to another PID "Process ID" A unique number assigned to every running process, used to monitor or kill it nohup "No hangup" Runs a command immune to the hangup signal, so closing the terminal won't kill it SSH "Connecting to the server" Secure Shell, an encrypted protocol for running commands on a remote machine The problem In plain words first Every command reads from one stream ( stdin ) and writes to two: stdout for results and stderr for errors and warnings. The shell lets you connect them: | feeds one command's stdout into the next, > sends it to a file. Small tools joined this way answer most questions about a training log. And a training run should never depend on your terminal staying open, which is what nohup and tmux are for. You will spend more time in the terminal than in any editor. Training runs, GPU monitoring, log tailing, remote SSH sessions, environment management. Every AI workflow touches the shell. If you're slow here, you're slow everywhere. This lesson covers the terminal skills that matter for AI work. No history of Unix. No deep-dive into Bash scripting. Just what you need. The idea Three things running at once. One terminal. You can detach, go home, SSH back in, and reattach. The training keeps running. The same idea as a formula A pipe a | b | c sends the output of a into b and the output of b into c : it is function composition , , with each program reading lines and writing lines. The programs run at the same time; b starts working on the first lines while a is still producing the rest, so a pipeline over a 50 GB log never holds all of it in memory. Costs of common pieces for a file of lines: grep , awk , cut , wc , head : one pass, time and constant memory ( head even stops reading early). sort : time and it must see all the input before printing anything; it spills to disk for large inputs. sort | uniq -c : counts duplicates in ; uniq alone only merges adjacent duplicates, which is why the sort comes first. Streams. Every program has standard output (1) and standard error (2); > redirects 1, 2> redirects 2, and 2>&1 sends 2 wherever 1 is going. Worked example Reading a pipeline by hand grep 'loss:' train.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -n | head -1 on a 10-line log: grep keeps the 10 lines containing loss: (the warning line is dropped). awk '{print $NF}' prints the last field of each: ten numbers such as 1.0000 , 0.5000 , 0.3333 . sort -n sorts them numerically; without -n , it sorts as text, where 10.5 comes before 9.1 . head -1 prints the first: the lowest loss, 0.1000 . Check your mental model ✗ " python train.py & keeps training after I close the laptop." ✓ & only frees the prompt. Closing the terminal sends a hang-up signal that stops the job. Use nohup ... & , or better, run it inside tmux. ✗ " > train.log captures everything the script prints." ✓ Only stdout. Tracebacks and most warnings go to stderr and still land on your screen, then vanish. Add 2>&1 . ✗ "tmux is only for remote servers." ✓ It helps locally too: one window with training, GPU monitor and log tail side by side, and nothing dies if the terminal app crashes. Step 1 · Know your shell Check which shell you're running: Copy Most systems use bash or zsh . Both work fine. The commands in this course work in either. Key things to know: Copy Step 2 · Piping and redirects Piping connects commands together. This is how you process logs, filter output, and chain tools. You will use this constantly. Copy The four redirects and the pipe you need: Symbol What it does > Write stdout to file (overwrite) >> Append stdout to file 2> Write stderr to file 2>&1 Send stderr to same place as stdout \| Send stdout of one command as stdin to the next See it drawn Pipes on a real log These are the commands from this step, run on a ten-epoch log written by the first lines of the cell: Copy What you should see Copy Copy awk '{print $NF}' prints the last field of each line; sort -k4 -n sorts numerically on the fourth field, so head -1 is the lowest loss. Predict before you run The log has 11 lines. Why does grep -c 'loss' train.log print 10, not 11? And what would grep -c 'WARNING' train.log print? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Run python3 -c "import sys; print('to stdout'); print('to stderr', file=sys.stderr)" 2>&1 > both.log and then cat both.log . Is the error line in the file? Swap the two redirects and try again. (Solution B1.) Step 3 · Background processes Training runs take hours. You don't want to keep your terminal open the whole time. Copy The difference between & , nohup , and screen / tmux : Method Survives terminal close? Can reattach? command & No No nohup command & Yes No (check log file) screen / tmux Yes Yes For anything longer than a few minutes, use tmux. Step 4 · tmux tmux lets you create persistent terminal sessions with multiple panes. This is the single most useful tool for managing training runs. Copy A typical AI workflow session: Copy Reading this output Reading this screen A tmux window shows a green status bar at the bottom: the session name in brackets on the left ( [train] ), then the windows ( 0:python* , where * marks the current one). tmux ls lists sessions with (attached) next to the one you are in. If tmux attach -t train says no sessions , the server was restarted or the session was killed, and the run inside it stopped too. Step 5 · Monitoring with htop and nvtop Copy htop keybindings you'll use: - F6 or > to sort by column (sort by memory to find memory leaks) - F5 to toggle tree view (see child processes) - F9 to kill a process - / to search for a process name Step 6 · SSH for remote GPU boxes When you rent a cloud GPU (Lambda, RunPod, Vast.ai), you connect via SSH. Copy Step 7 · Useful aliases for AI work Add these to your ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc : Copy Or copy the ones you want. The key aliases: Copy See code/shell_aliases.sh for the full set. Step 8 · Common AI terminal patterns These come up repeatedly in practice: Copy Recap What to keep from this lesson stdout and stderr are separate: > file, 2>&1 both, | tee file to watch and save at once. grep, awk, sort, head, tail and wc answer most questions about logs without opening an editor. Long runs go in tmux (or nohup ... & ), never in a bare terminal. Watch the machine with htop and nvtop or watch -n1 nvidia-smi ; move files with scp and rsync over SSH. Solutions Solution P1 · Counting lines grep -c counts lines that match , and the warning line does not contain "loss", so 10 of the 11 lines match. grep -c 'WARNING' train.log prints 1 . To count matches rather than lines (when a pattern can appear twice on one line), use grep -o 'loss' train.log | wc -l . Solution B1 · Redirect order The file holds only to stdout , and to stderr appears on the screen. Redirects are applied left to right: 2>&1 first points stderr at wherever stdout points now , the terminal; then > both.log moves stdout alone to the file. Written as > both.log 2>&1 , stdout moves to the file first and stderr follows it, so both lines land in the file. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Here's when each tool comes into play during this course: Tool When you use it tmux Every training run (Phases 3+) tail -f + grep Monitoring training logs nohup / & Quick background tasks htop / nvtop Debugging slow training, OOM errors SSH + rsync Working on cloud GPUs Piping + redirects Processing experiment results Aliases Saving time on repetitive commands Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Coding agents live in the terminal. Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI and Google's Gemini CLI read the repository, run commands and edit files from a shell prompt; knowing the shell well is how you review and control what they do. Modern command-line tools. ripgrep ( rg ), fd, fzf and jq are standard additions for searching code, finding files and filtering JSON logs; tmux keeps long training runs alive after you disconnect. Sources: Claude Code , Codex CLI , Gemini CLI , ripgrep , tmux . Exercises Install tmux, create a session with three panes, and run htop in one, watch -n1 date in another, and a Python script in the third. Detach and reattach. Add the aliases from code/shell_aliases.sh to your shell config and reload with source ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc ). Create a fake training log with for i in $(seq 1 100); do echo "epoch $i loss: $(echo "scale=4; 1/$i" | bc)"; sleep 0.1; done > fake_train.log and then use grep , tail , and awk to extract just the loss values. Set up an SSH config entry for a server you have access to (or use localhost to practice the syntax). Hints Exercise 1. Start with tmux new -s practice , then split with the prefix Ctrl+B followed by " and % , and move between panes with Ctrl+B and an arrow key. Detach with Ctrl+B then d , run tmux ls , and attach again with tmux attach -t practice ; all three programs must still run. Exercise 2. Copy the lines from code/shell_aliases.sh to the end of ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc , then run source on that file. Run alias or type <name> for one of the new aliases to confirm that the shell knows it. Exercise 3. First run tail -5 fake_train.log to see the line format. Then filter with grep loss and print only the last field with awk '{print $NF}' ; the output must be 100 numbers that get smaller. Exercise 4. Copy the Host gpu block from the lesson into ~/.ssh/config and change HostName and User to your server, or to localhost and your user name. Run ssh -G gpu to print the settings that SSH will use. If you have a reachable SSH server that accepts your key, run ssh gpu to connect. Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Linux Essentials for AI Engineers Lesson 0.21 30 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Navigate the Linux file system and perform essential file operations from the command line Manage file permissions with chmod and chown to resolve "Permission denied" errors Install system packages with apt and set up a fresh GPU box for AI work Identify macOS-to-Linux differences that commonly trip up developers working on remote machines Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.3 Type : Learn. Time : about 30 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Most AI runs on Linux. You need to know enough to not be stuck. The problem In plain words first A rented GPU machine is almost always Linux with no screen, reached over SSH. Everything is a file under one root / , every file has an owner and permission bits, software is installed with apt , and long jobs run as processes you can list and stop. A dozen commands cover nearly all of it. You develop on macOS or Windows. But the moment you SSH into a cloud GPU box, rent a Lambda instance, or spin up an EC2 machine, you land in Ubuntu. The terminal is your only interface. There is no Finder, no Explorer, no GUI. If you can't navigate the file system, install packages, and manage processes from the command line, you're stuck paying for idle GPU hours while googling "how to unzip a file in Linux." This is a survival guide. It covers exactly what you need to operate on a remote Linux machine for AI work. Nothing more. File System Layout Linux organizes everything under a single root / . There is no C:\ or /Volumes . The directories you'll actually touch: Your home directory is ~ or /home/your-username . Almost everything you do happens here. Check your mental model ✗ " rm moves files to the trash." ✓ There is no trash on a server. rm -rf deletes immediately and recursively; check the path first. ✗ " Model.py and model.py are the same file." ✓ Linux file names are case-sensitive, unlike the default on macOS and Windows. An import that worked on your laptop can fail on the server. ✗ " sudo fixes errors." ✓ It runs one command as root. It fixes genuine permission problems, and makes others worse: sudo pip install writes into the system Python. Essential Commands These are the 13 commands that cover most of what you'll do on a remote GPU box. Moving Around Copy Files and Directories Copy rm -rf is permanent. There is no undo. Double-check the path before hitting enter. Reading Files Copy Searching Copy Permissions The same idea as a formula Permission bits. Each file has three groups of three bits: owner, group, others, each with read ( ), write ( ) and execute ( ). One octal digit per group is the sum of the granted bits: so 7 = rwx , 6 = rw- , 5 = r-x , 4 = r-- , 0 = --- , and chmod 754 means owner rwx , group r-x , others r-- . Defaults. New files start from 666 and new folders from 777, with the bits in the umask removed: with the usual umask 022, files get minus the group and other write bits, 644 ( rw-r--r-- ), and folders 755. Disk space. df reports free space per filesystem; du adds up the sizes of files under a folder. Model caches grow fast: a 7B model in bf16 is about 14 GB (Lesson 0.5). Worked example Permissions by hand chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 : owner (read and write), group 0, others 0. SSH refuses to use a private key that others can read, so this is the one you need. chmod +x train.sh on a 644 file adds to all three groups: , rwxr-xr-x . A folder needs to be entered: with 644 on a folder, ls can list names but cd fails. Every file in Linux has an owner and permission bits. You'll run into this when scripts won't execute or you can't write to a directory. Copy Common fixes: Copy When something says "Permission denied," it's almost always a permissions issue. chmod +x or sudo will fix most cases. See it drawn Reading permission bits ls -l shows ten characters such as -rwxr-xr-x : the file type, then read, write and execute for the owner, the group and everyone else. Each group of three is one octal digit (r = 4, w = 2, x = 1), so rwxr-xr-x is 755 and rw-r--r-- is 644 : Copy What you should see Copy Copy Predict before you run A freshly written train.sh is rw-r--r-- . What happens when you run ./train.sh , and what is the shortest fix? (Solution P1.) Package Management (apt) Ubuntu uses apt . This is how you install system-level software. Copy Common packages you'll install on a fresh GPU box: Copy Users and sudo You're usually logged in as a regular user. Some operations need root (admin) access. Copy On cloud GPU instances, you're typically the only user and already have sudo access. Don't run everything as root. Use sudo only when needed. Processes and systemd When your training hangs, or you need to check what's running: Copy systemd manages services (background daemons). You'll use it if you run inference servers: Copy Disk Space GPU boxes often have limited disk space. Models and datasets fill it fast. Copy Common space savers: Copy Reading this output Reading `df -h` Each line is one mounted drive: Size , Used , Avail , Use% and where it is mounted. On cloud GPU boxes look for a small root disk ( / , often 50 to 100 GB) and a large data disk mounted somewhere like /data or /workspace . Model caches land in ~/.cache on the small one by default, which is how a box fills up after a few downloads; point HF_HOME at the large disk. Networking You'll download models, transfer files, and hit APIs from the command line. Copy Use rsync over scp for anything large. It only transfers changed bytes and handles interrupted connections. tmux: Keep Sessions Alive When you SSH into a remote box, closing your laptop kills your training run. tmux prevents this. Copy Always run long training jobs inside tmux. Always. WSL2 for Windows Users If you're on Windows, WSL2 gives you a real Linux environment without dual-booting. Copy WSL2 runs a real Linux kernel. Everything in this lesson works inside it. Your Windows files are at /mnt/c/Users/YourName/ from inside WSL. GPU passthrough works with NVIDIA drivers installed on the Windows side. Install the Windows NVIDIA driver (not the Linux one), and CUDA will be available inside WSL2. Gotchas: macOS to Linux Things that will trip you up if you're coming from macOS: macOS Linux Notes brew install sudo apt install Different package names sometimes. brew install htop vs sudo apt install htop works the same, but brew install readline vs sudo apt install libreadline-dev does not. open file.txt xdg-open file.txt But you won't have a GUI on a remote box. Use cat or less . pbcopy / pbpaste Not available Pipe to/from clipboard doesn't exist over SSH. ~/.zshrc ~/.bashrc macOS defaults to zsh. Most Linux servers use bash. /opt/homebrew/ /usr/bin/ , /usr/local/bin/ Binaries live in different places. sed -i '' 's/a/b/' file sed -i 's/a/b/' file macOS sed needs an empty string after -i . Linux does not. Case-insensitive filesystem Case-sensitive filesystem Model.py and model.py are two different files on Linux. Line endings 
 Line endings 
 Same. But Windows uses 
 , which breaks bash scripts. Run dos2unix to fix. Break it on purpose Write a two-line script on Windows (or save it with Windows line endings), copy it to Linux, make it executable and run it. What error appears, and what is wrong with the file? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson Your work lives under ~ ; caches under ~/.cache fill disks fast, so check df -h and du -sh . Permission bits are three octal digits; chmod +x makes a script runnable. apt update then apt install for system packages; sudo only when needed, never for pip. ps , htop , kill and nvidia-smi for processes; tmux for anything long. Linux is case-sensitive and expects 
 line endings. Quick Reference Card Copy Solutions Solution P1 · Not executable bash: ./train.sh: Permission denied , exit code 126: the file has no x bit, so the system refuses to execute it. chmod +x train.sh adds execute for everyone ( rwxr-xr-x ), and it runs. bash train.sh also works without changing anything, because then bash is the program being run and it only needs to read the file. Solution B1 · Windows line endings Something like bash: ./win.sh: cannot execute: required file not found (older systems say /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter ). Each line ends in 
 , so the first line asks for an interpreter called /bin/bash , which does not exist. dos2unix win.sh , or sed -i 's/$//' win.sh , strips the  and the script runs. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Ubuntu LTS on GPU servers. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is the common cloud GPU image and 26.04 LTS (April 2026) ships NVIDIA's CUDA in its repositories; check that your driver supports the CUDA version your frameworks were built for ( nvidia-smi shows it). Schedulers, not bare machines. Training clusters run Slurm or Kubernetes (with the NVIDIA GPU Operator); a job asks for GPUs and the scheduler places it, so learn sbatch or kubectl alongside basic Linux. Monitoring tools. nvidia-smi , nvtop and DCGM exporters (for Prometheus and Grafana) are the usual ways to watch GPU use, memory and temperature. Sources: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS release , Slurm , NVIDIA GPU Operator , DCGM exporter . Exercises SSH into any Linux machine (or open WSL2) and navigate to your home directory. Create a project folder, create three empty files inside it with touch , then list them with ls -la . Install htop with apt, run it, and identify which process is using the most memory. Start a tmux session, run sleep 300 inside it, detach, list sessions, and reattach. Use df -h to check available disk space, then use du -sh ~/.cache/* to find what's taking up space in your cache. Transfer a file from your local machine to a remote one using scp , then do the same transfer with rsync and compare the experience. Hints Exercise 1. Use cd ~ , mkdir , and cd into the new folder, then run touch with three file names. In the ls -la output, check that the three files show a size of 0 and your user name as owner. Exercise 2. Install with sudo apt install -y htop , start it, and press F6 (or click the column name) to sort by MEM% . The process at the top of the list uses the most memory. Exercise 3. Use tmux new -s train from the lesson, run sleep 300 , and detach with Ctrl+B then d . Run tmux ls to see the session, then tmux attach -t train ; the sleep must still run. Exercise 4. Run df -h and read the Avail column for the file system that holds your home folder. Then run du -sh ~/.cache/* | sort -h so that the largest folder is on the last line. Exercise 5. Copy a file with scp file.txt user@host:~/ , then run rsync -avP file.txt user@host:~/ for the same file. Run the rsync command a second time: it sends almost nothing, because the file on the remote side did not change.
