a0012: Course home / Phase 0 · Dev Environment and AI Tooling Profiling and Debugging Python Code Lesson 0.22 60 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Use conditional breakpoint() and debug_print to inspect tensor shapes, dtypes, and NaN values mid-training Profile training loops with cProfile , line_profiler , and tracemalloc to find bottlenecks Detect common AI bugs: shape mismatches, NaN loss, data leakage, and wrong-device tensors Set up TensorBoard to visualize loss curves, weight histograms, and gradient distributions Before you start Needs : Lesson 1 (Setting Up an AI Dev Environment), basic PyTorch familiarity Type : Build. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line The worst AI bugs don't crash. They train silently on garbage and report a beautiful loss curve. The problem In plain words first Most broken training runs do not crash. They produce a loss that is nan , stuck, or suspiciously perfect, and Python reports nothing. Debugging AI code means checking, in order, the plain Python (wrong variable, wrong file), then the tensors (shape, dtype, device, NaN), and only then the training dynamics (loss curves, gradients). Each level has its own small tools, and most bugs are found at the first two. AI code fails differently than regular code. A web app crashes with a stack trace. A misconfigured training loop runs for 8 hours, burns $200 in GPU time, and produces a model that predicts the mean of every input. The code never errored. The bug was a tensor on the wrong device, a forgotten .detach() , or labels leaking into features. You need debugging tools that catch these silent failures before they waste your time and compute. The idea AI debugging operates at three levels: Most people jump straight to level 3 (staring at TensorBoard). But 80% of AI bugs live at levels 1 and 2. The same idea as a formula Amdahl's law. If a fraction of a program's time is spent in a part you speed up times, the whole program speeds up by 1 ​ < 1 − p 1 ​ However large gets, the untouched part sets the limit. So profile before optimising : find the part with the largest . Reading a profile. cProfile reports, for each function, tottime (time spent in its own code) and cumtime (its own time plus everything it calls). Large cumtime with small tottime means the cost is further down; large tottime is the hot spot itself. NaN spreads. and for every , so one NaN in a tensor makes its sum, mean and any loss computed from it NaN. In bf16 and fp16 the largest number is limited ( for fp16), so large activations overflow to inf , and gives NaN. Worked example Where to optimise, by hand A training step takes 100 ms: data loading 60 ms, the model on the GPU 40 ms. Make the model 10× faster: , , . The step now takes 64 ms. Instead, load batches in background worker processes ( DataLoader(num_workers=4) ) while the GPU works on the previous batch: once loading is hidden behind the 40 ms of GPU work, the step takes about 40 ms, a 2.5× gain for one argument. The profile answers which case you are in; without it, the natural instinct is to optimise the model. Check your mental model ✗ "If there's a bug, PyTorch will raise an error." ✓ Only for some: mismatched shapes in a matrix product, tensors on two devices. A log of a negative number, a loss computed on the wrong labels or data leaking into the test set all run silently. ✗ "A NaN loss means the model is wrong." ✓ Usually it means a number grew too large: a learning rate too high for the scale of the inputs, a division by zero, a log(0) . The demo in Part 3 diverges with an ordinary model. ✗ "Training is slow, so I need a faster GPU." ✓ Time the steps first. Data loading often takes most of each step, and num_workers in the DataLoader fixes it for free. Build · Part 1: Print Debugging (Yes, It Works) Print debugging gets dismissed. It shouldn't. For tensor code, a targeted print statement beats stepping through a debugger because you need to see shapes, dtypes, and value ranges all at once. Copy Call this after every suspicious operation. When the bug is found, remove the prints. Simple. See it drawn `debug_print` on a real bug torch.log of a negative number gives nan , silently. Here the helper above catches it, and notice what happens to min , max and mean once one NaN is present: Copy What you should see Copy Copy A single NaN poisons every reduction over the tensor, which is why one bad value at step 900 turns the whole loss into nan from then on. Build · Part 2: Python Debugger (pdb and breakpoint) The built-in debugger is underrated for AI work. Drop breakpoint() into your training loop and inspect tensors interactively. Copy When the debugger drops you in, useful commands: p outputs.shape to check shapes p loss.item() to see the loss value p torch.isnan(outputs).sum() to count NaNs p model.fc1.weight.grad to check gradients c to continue, q to quit This is conditional debugging. You only stop when something looks wrong. For a 10,000-step training run, that matters. Build · Part 3: Python Logging Replace print statements with logging when your debugging goes beyond a quick check. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Logging gives you timestamps, severity levels, and file output. When a training run fails at 3 AM, you want a log file, not terminal output that scrolled off screen. Reading this output The cell above printed the log file it wrote. Each line has a timestamp, a level and the message; the same lines also went to the screen through the second handler. force=True is there because basicConfig does nothing if logging was already set up earlier in the same process, a common reason for an empty log file in notebooks. Predict before you run Below, the same small linear regression is trained three times on inputs about ten times larger than usual, with learning rates 0.001, 0.01 and 1.0. Which ones bring the loss down, and which one ends in nan ? (Solution P1.) Copy What you should see Copy Copy Build · Part 4: Timing Code Sections Knowing where time goes is the first step to optimization. Copy Common finding: data loading takes 60% of training time. The fix is num_workers > 0 in your DataLoader, not a faster GPU. Build · Part 5: cProfile and line_profiler When you need more than manual timers: Copy This shows every function call sorted by cumulative time. For line-by-line profiling: Copy Copy Build · Part 6: Memory Profiling CPU Memory with tracemalloc Copy CPU Memory with memory_profiler Copy Copy Run with python -m memory_profiler your_script.py to see line-by-line memory usage. GPU Memory with PyTorch Copy When you hit OOM (Out of Memory): Reduce batch size (first thing to try, always) Use torch.cuda.empty_cache() to free cached memory Use del tensor followed by torch.cuda.empty_cache() for large intermediates Use mixed precision ( torch.cuda.amp ) to halve memory usage Use gradient checkpointing for very deep models Build · Part 7: Common AI Bugs and How to Catch Them Shape Mismatch The most frequent bug. A tensor has shape [batch, features] when the model expects [batch, channels, height, width] . Copy Run this once with a sample batch. It maps every shape transformation in your model. NaN Loss NaN loss means something exploded. Common causes: Learning rate too high Division by zero in custom loss Log of zero or negative number Exploding gradients in RNNs Copy Data Leakage Your model gets 99% accuracy on the test set. Sounds great. It's a bug. Copy Also check for temporal leakage: using future data to predict the past. Sort by timestamp before splitting. Wrong Device Tensors on different devices (CPU vs GPU) cause runtime errors. But sometimes a tensor silently stays on CPU while everything else is on GPU, and training just runs slowly. Copy See it drawn `check_shapes` on a small model The hook-based helper above prints every layer's input and output shape. Then the same model is given 5 features instead of 3: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Read the error as "a 4 × 5 batch cannot be multiplied by the 3 × 8 weights of the first layer": the second number of the input must equal in_features . Break it on purpose In the learning-rate demo, keep lr=0.01 but remove the * 10 so the inputs have their normal scale. Does it still diverge? What does that tell you about the order in which to try fixes? (Solution B1.) Build · Part 8: TensorBoard Basics TensorBoard shows you what's happening inside training over time. Copy Copy Launch it: Copy What to look for: Loss not decreasing : Learning rate too low, or model architecture issue Loss oscillating wildly : Learning rate too high Loss goes to NaN : Numerical instability (see NaN section above) Train loss decreasing, val loss increasing : Overfitting Weight histograms collapsing to zero : Vanishing gradients Gradient histograms exploding : Need gradient clipping Build · Part 9: VS Code Debugger For interactive debugging, configure VS Code with a launch.json : Copy Set breakpoints by clicking the gutter. Use the Variables pane to inspect tensor properties. The Debug Console lets you run arbitrary Python expressions mid-execution. Useful for stepping through data preprocessing pipelines where you want to see each transformation. Recap What to keep from this lesson Debug bottom-up: Python first, then tensor shape, dtype, device and NaN, then training dynamics. A targeted print of shape, dtype, device, range and NaN beats a debugger for tensor bugs. Log to a file with levels and timestamps; conditional breakpoint() stops only when something looks wrong. Time before you optimise; profile memory when you hit out-of-memory errors. NaN usually means a value grew too large; check the learning rate and the scale of the inputs. Solutions Solution P1 · Three learning rates Only lr=0.001 brings the loss down, from about 545 to about 8 after 30 steps. lr=0.01 looks fine for three steps and then climbs into the hundreds of billions. lr=1.0 overflows to inf and then nan at step 18. The inputs are about ten times larger than usual, so the gradients are too, and each step overshoots more than the one before. Solution B1 · Fix the inputs, not just the rate With inputs of normal size, lr=0.01 converges. The divergence came from the scale of the data, not from the learning rate alone. Normalising inputs (Phase 2's feature scaling) is usually the first fix, because it makes a standard learning rate work; lowering the rate until it stops exploding just trains slowly. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Here's the debugging workflow that catches most AI bugs: Before training : Run check_shapes with a sample batch. Verify input and output dimensions match expectations. First 10 steps : Use debug_print on loss, outputs, and gradients. Confirm nothing is NaN and values are in reasonable ranges. During training : Log loss, learning rate, and gradient norms. Use TensorBoard for visualization. When something breaks : Drop breakpoint() at the failure point. Inspect tensors interactively. For performance : Time your data loading vs forward vs backward pass. Profile memory if you're near OOM. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Profilers in the standard library. Python 3.15 (October 2026) adds a built-in statistical sampling profiler (PEP 799) next to cProfile ; py-spy and Scalene remain the common external profilers, and memray finds memory leaks. GPU profiling. The PyTorch Profiler (with TensorBoard or Perfetto traces) and NVIDIA Nsight Systems show where time goes between Python, data loading and GPU kernels; most "slow training" turns out to be the input pipeline. Debuggers attach to running processes. debugpy (VS Code) and Python 3.14's safe external debugger interface (PEP 768) let you inspect a long-running job without restarting it. Sources: Python 3.15 release , py-spy , memray , PyTorch Profiler , Nsight Systems , PEP 768 . Before you start Needs : Setting Up an AI Dev Environment, Python Virtual Environments and Dependencies Type : Build. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Most code in this course uses the same small set of Python idioms. Learn that set here, before the math and model lessons depend on it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it means Iterable "Something you can loop over" An object that iter() accepts, such as a list, a file, or a generator Iterator "A cursor" An object whose __next__ method returns one item per call and raises StopIteration at the end Generator "A lazy list" An iterator from a yield function or a generator expression. It makes each item on request and runs only once. Comprehension "A one-line loop" An expression that builds a list, dict, or set from an iterable, with an optional filter Closure "A function inside a function" A function that keeps variables from the function that created it Dataclass "A struct" A class whose __init__ , __repr__ , and __eq__ methods Python writes from the annotated fields Context manager "A with block" An object that runs setup code at the start of a with block and cleanup code at the end, even after an exception Seed "The random number" The start value of a pseudo-random generator. The same seed gives the same sequence. Vectorized code "Fast code" Code that applies one operation to a whole array, so that compiled code runs the loop Broadcasting "Automatic shape matching" The NumPy rules that combine arrays of different shapes by using size-1 dimensions again, with no copy The problem In plain words first You only need a small part of Python to read every lesson that follows: collections, comprehensions, functions, dataclasses, generators, with blocks and a few standard modules. Three behaviours cause most of the silent bugs: two names can share one list, a generator can be used only once, and a default argument is created once and shared by every call. And loops over numbers in plain Python are slow, which is the reason NumPy and PyTorch exist. The lessons after this phase use plain Python for the math and the models. Of the 541 Python files in the lessons, 276 import dataclasses . Also, 187 files call random.seed or create a random.Random generator. If those idioms are new to you, you read syntax when you want to read the math. Python also has behaviors that give wrong results with no error message. Two names can refer to one list, so a change through one name also changes the other. A default argument keeps its value from one call to the next. A generator is empty after one pass, so a second training epoch gets no data and the loss does not change. The last problem is speed. On our test laptop, a pure-Python loop over a million floats took about 30 milliseconds. NumPy computed the same dot product in less than one millisecond. You need to know the reason, so that you can choose between a clear loop and an array operation. Idea 2 · Names refer to objects In Python, a variable is a name that refers to an object. Assignment binds a name to an object. It does not copy the object. When two names refer to one list, a change through either name is visible through both. Numbers, strings, and tuples cannot change, so this rule causes no problems for them. Lists, dicts, and sets can change, so make a copy when you need an independent version. Predict before you run The first block in The Idioms You Need runs grid = [[0] * 3] * 2 and then grid[0][0] = 1 . What does print(grid) show: [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]] or something else? (Solution P1.) Idea 3 · A list holds pointers, an array holds numbers A Python list does not store numbers directly. It stores pointers, and each pointer refers to a full Python object. On a 64-bit build of CPython, each pointer takes 8 bytes and each float object takes 24 bytes. A NumPy float64 array stores the raw 8-byte values side by side in one block of memory. A loop over a list does a lot of work for each element. The interpreter runs one bytecode instruction at a time. For each element, it follows a pointer and checks the type of each operand. Then it calls the float multiply code and makes a Python float object to hold the result. NumPy does the same arithmetic in a loop of compiled code over the raw values. It checks the data type once for the whole array, and it makes no Python object for each element. Vectorized code describes one operation over a whole array, such as (x - mean) / std , and a library runs the loop. The vector functions in this lesson follow that rule. Each one does one array operation, so you can replace it with one NumPy call later. Idea 4 · A list holds every item, a generator holds one A list comprehension builds every item before the next line runs. A generator builds one item each time the caller asks for the next one. The memory for a list grows with the number of items. The memory for a generator stays about the same for any number of items. A generator can run only once. After the last item, it raises StopIteration on each request, so a second for loop over it gets no items. Training code reads the dataset once per epoch, so it must create a new generator for each epoch. Generator functions are rare in the lesson code. The data loaders that the deep learning lessons use are iterables of batches, so the idea is in every training loop. The figure shows both approaches on the same eight rows. The same idea as a formula Memory of a list of floats. A Python list stores one 8-byte pointer per item, and every float is a separate object of 24 bytes: (plus a small fixed header, and a list over-allocates a little so appends stay cheap). Small integers from to are shared objects, so a list of them costs only the pointers. Time. A Python loop pays the interpreter's cost per item, tens of nanoseconds; NumPy runs one C loop over the whole array, often with SIMD instructions that handle several numbers per cycle. For items, both are , but the constants differ by 10 to 100 times. Generators. A generator produces one item at a time, so its memory is in ; a list comprehension over the same items holds all . Worked example Memory by hand One million training losses as floats: List: × 32 = 32 MB ( MB of pointers, MB of float objects). numpy.array(..., dtype=np.float64) : MB; in float32, MB. sum(x * x for x in losses) : the generator never holds more than one square at a time, against 32 MB more for sum([x * x for x in losses]) . Make a new generator, or a list, for each epoch. ✗ " def add(item, bucket=[]) starts with an empty list on every call." ✓ The default list is created once, when def runs, and every call that uses it appends to the same list. Use bucket=None and create the list inside. ✗ " 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is True ." ✓ It is False : neither number is exact in binary. Compare floats with a tolerance, math.isclose or np.allclose . Learn when to use each one. A slice a[start:stop:step] includes start and excludes stop . Negative indexes count from the end. A slice of a list is a new list, so a slice of a large list copies all of its pointers. Copy What you should see Copy Copy 2. Comprehensions A comprehension builds a list, dict, or set from an iterable in one expression. It reads like the math that it describes. Copy What you should see Copy Copy A trailing if keeps only some items. The expression before for can be a conditional expression, a if condition else b . Two for clauses run in the same order as two nested loops. Round brackets make a generator expression. In sum(s * s for s in scores) , sum reads one square at a time, and Python builds no list. In zip(*matrix) , the star passes each row as a separate argument, and zip pairs the items at each position. 3. Functions, arguments, and closures A default value makes an argument optional. A keyword argument names the parameter at the call. A * by itself in the parameter list makes the next parameters keyword-only. Copy What you should see Copy Copy With keyword-only arguments, a call such as train(data, 0.1, 3) raises TypeError . The caller must write lr=0.1 , so two numbers cannot change places by accident. The inner function scale uses factor from the function that created it. Python keeps factor for as long as scale exists. A function that keeps variables from its creator is a closure. The standardizer in Build It uses a closure to keep the training statistics. A lambda is a one-expression function with no name. Course code uses it mostly as a key= function, which part 8 shows. Python evaluates a default value once, when it runs the def statement. Every call that uses the default gets the same object. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Use None as the default for a list, dict, or set. Create the new object inside the function. 4. Classes and dataclasses The @dataclass decorator writes __init__ , __repr__ , and __eq__ from the annotated fields. With frozen=True , the object cannot change after creation, and you can use it as a dict key or put it in a set. Copy What you should see Copy Copy field(default_factory=...) gives each instance a new list. It solves the shared-default problem from part 3 inside a dataclass. Special methods connect a class to Python syntax. len(ds) calls __len__ , and ds[2] calls __getitem__ . Copy What you should see Copy Copy The for loop inside list(ds) works without an __iter__ method. Python calls __getitem__ with 0, 1, 2, and so on until it gets IndexError . PyTorch map-style datasets use the same two methods, __len__ and __getitem__ . 5. Iterators and generators An iterable is any object that a for loop accepts. iter() gets an iterator from it, and next() asks the iterator for one item. When the iterator has no more items, it raises StopIteration . A for loop calls next() for you and stops at StopIteration . Copy What you should see Copy Copy A function with yield in its body is a generator function. A call to it runs none of its code and returns a generator object. Each next() runs the body to the next yield and pauses there. The second list(gen) is empty because the first one used up the generator. A generator can read a file one line at a time. Copy What you should see Copy Copy read_rows keeps one line of the file in memory at a time. It is the read_rows in the figure. It splits on commas to keep the example short. Context managers and exceptions A with statement runs setup code, then its body, and then cleanup code. The cleanup runs even when the body raises an exception. The contextlib.contextmanager decorator makes the same kind of object from a generator. The code before yield is the setup, and the finally block is the cleanup. Python does not check them when the code runs. A type checker, such as mypy, reads them before the code runs. Copy What you should see Copy Copy With from __future__ import annotations , Python stores each hint as a string, as the last line shows. Every .py file is a module. When you run a file with python3 file.py , Python sets its __name__ to "__main__" . When another file imports it, __name__ is the module name. Files, JSON, CSV, and sorting pathlib.Path joins paths with / and can read or write a whole file in one call. A key= function returns the value that Python compares for each item. sorted , min , and max all accept one. A tuple key sorts by the first value, and it uses the second value only for ties. Counting, grouping, and iterator tools These two modules hold the data structures and iterator tools that plain lists and dicts do not give you. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Counter counts hashable items, such as labels or tokens. defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time that you use a new key, so a grouping loop needs no key check. deque(maxlen=3) removes the oldest item when you add a fourth, which gives a moving window over recent losses. enumerate gives each item with its index. product gives every combination of its inputs, which is a hyperparameter grid. chain joins iterables end to end. islice takes a slice of any iterator, including a generator. The mini-batch generator in Build It uses islice . 10. Why loops over numbers are slow The dis module prints the bytecode instructions that the interpreter runs for a function. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The instructions from FOR_ITER to the jump back to it run once for each element. That is about ten instructions for each multiply and add. The exact instruction names change between Python versions. A loop gets faster when fewer of its steps run as bytecode. Built-in functions such as sum , map , and zip are written in C. Solutions Solution P1 · One row, twice [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]] . [[0] * 3] * 2 makes an outer list holding two references to the same inner list , so changing "row 0" changes the only row there is, seen twice. The comprehension [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)] evaluates [0] * 3 once per row and gives two independent rows. Solution B1 · An empty second epoch epoch 0: [4, 4, 2] and then epoch 1: [] . The first epoch reads every batch and the generator finishes; from then on each next() raises StopIteration , which a for loop treats as "done". Python gives no warning, and in a real training loop the loss would simply stop changing. Call batches(...) at the start of each epoch, as the lesson's code does. NumPy is faster for three reasons: The array stores raw float64 values, 8 bytes each, in one block of memory. A list of floats needs an 8-byte pointer and a 24-byte float object for each value. The loop runs in compiled code. NumPy checks the data type once for the whole array and makes no Python object for each element. Values that sit side by side in memory let NumPy use SIMD instructions, which process several values with one instruction. For very small arrays, the fixed cost of one NumPy call can be larger than a short Python loop. Exercise 4 finds the size where NumPy becomes faster on your machine. Copy What you should see Copy Copy NumPy compares the two shapes from the last dimension back to the first. Two dimensions are compatible when they are equal or when one of them is 1. A missing leading dimension counts as 1. A dimension of size 1 is used again along the larger dimension, and NumPy makes no copy of the data. In plain words first The idea in one line Every AI model is just matrix math wearing a fancy hat. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Vector "An arrow" A list of numbers representing a point or direction in n-dimensional space Matrix "A table of numbers" A transformation that maps vectors from one space to another Dot product "Multiply and sum" A measure of how aligned two vectors are -- the core of similarity search Embedding "Some AI magic" A vector that represents the meaning of something (word, image, user) Linear independence "They don't overlap" No vector in the set can be written as a combination of the others Rank "How many dimensions" The number of linearly independent columns (or rows) in a matrix Projection "The shadow" The component of one vector in the direction of another Basis "The coordinate axes" A minimal set of independent vectors that span the space Orthonormal "Perpendicular unit vectors" Vectors that are mutually perpendicular and each have length 1 The problem In plain words first A vector is a list of numbers, and you can picture it as an arrow from the origin to a point. A matrix is a grid of numbers that turns one vector into another: a neural network layer is exactly that. The dot product multiplies two vectors position by position and adds the results; it is large when they point the same way, zero when they are at right angles. Most of this lesson is those three ideas, seen from a few angles. Open any ML paper. Within the first page, you'll see vectors, matrices, dot products, and transformations. Without linear algebra intuition, these are just symbols. With it, you can see what a neural network is actually doing -- moving points around in space. You don't need to be a mathematician. You need to see what these operations mean geometrically, then code them yourself. Idea 1 · Vectors Are Points (and Directions) A vector is just a list of numbers. But those numbers mean something -- they're coordinates in space. 2D vector [3, 2]: x y Point 3 2 The vector points from origin (0,0) to (3, 2) on the plane The vector has magnitude + 2 2 ​ = 13 ​ and points up and to the right. In AI, vectors represent everything: - A word → a vector of 768 numbers (its "meaning" in embedding space) - An image → a vector of millions of pixel values - A user → a vector of preferences Idea 2 · Matrices Are Transformations A matrix transforms one vector into another. It can rotate, scale, stretch, or project. In AI, matrices ARE the model: - Neural network weights → matrices that transform input into output - Attention scores → matrices that decide what to focus on - Embeddings → matrices that map words to vectors Idea 3 · The Dot Product Measures Similarity The dot product of two vectors tells you how similar they are. Same direction: a ⋅ b Perpendicular: a ⋅ b Opposite direction: a ⋅ b ​ = a 1 ​ × b 1 ​ + a 2 ​ × b 2 ​ + ⋯ + a n ​ × b n ​ > 0 (similar) = 0 (unrelated) < 0 (dissimilar) ​ This is literally how search engines, recommendation systems, and RAG work -- find vectors with high dot products. Worked example Worked by hand Take a = [1, 2, 3] and b = [4, 5, 6] . Step Calculation Result Dot product 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×6 32 Length of a √(1 + 4 + 9) = √14 3.7417 Length of b √(16 + 25 + 36) = √77 8.7750 Cosine similarity 32 / (3.7417 × 8.7750) 0.9746 These are the numbers Step 1 prints. The dot product (32) grows with the lengths of the vectors; the cosine (0.97) does not, because it divides them out, which is why search and RAG usually rank by cosine. Idea 4 · Linear Independence Vectors are linearly independent if no vector in the set can be written as a combination of the others. If ​ , v 2 ​ , v 3 ​ are independent, they span a 3D space. If one is a combination of the others, they only span a plane. Why it matters for AI: your feature matrix should have linearly independent columns. If two features are perfectly correlated (linearly dependent), the model cannot distinguish their effects. This causes multicollinearity in regression -- the weight matrix becomes unstable, and small input changes produce wild output swings. Concrete example: Copy ​ and ​ are independent -- neither is a scalar multiple or combination of the other. But ​ = 2 v 1 ​ + v 2 ​ , so ​ , v 2 ​ , v 3 ​ } is a dependent set. These three vectors all lie in the xy-plane. No matter how you combine them, you cannot reach [0, 0, 1]. You have three vectors but only two dimensions of freedom. In a dataset: if feature_3 = 2*feature_1 + feature_2, adding feature_3 gives the model zero new information. Worse, it makes the normal equations singular -- there is no unique solution for the weights. Idea 5 · Basis and Rank A basis is a minimal set of linearly independent vectors that span the entire space. The number of basis vectors is the dimension of the space. The standard basis for 3D space is {[1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1]}. But any three independent vectors in 3D form a valid basis. The choice of basis is a choice of coordinate system. Rank of a matrix = number of linearly independent columns = number of linearly independent rows. If , the matrix is rank-deficient. This means: - The system has infinitely many solutions (or none) - Information is lost in the transformation - The matrix cannot be inverted Situation Rank What it means for ML Full rank Maximum possible With at least as many rows as columns (full column rank), the least-squares solution is unique. With fewer rows than columns, infinitely many solutions fit exactly. Rank deficient Below maximum Features are redundant. Infinitely many weight solutions. Regularization needed. Rank 1 1 Every column is a scaled copy of one vector. All data lies on a line. Near rank-deficient (small singular values) Numerically low Matrix is ill-conditioned. Tiny input noise causes large output changes. Use SVD truncation or ridge regression. Check your mental model ✗ "A bigger dot product always means more similar." ✓ The dot product also grows with length. A long vector pointing slightly away can beat a short one pointing the same way. Cosine similarity compares direction only. ✗ "Three vectors in 3D always form a basis." ✓ Only if they are independent. [1, 0, 0] , [0, 1, 0] and [2, 1, 0] all lie in one plane, and the matrix they make has rank 2. ✗ "The rank of a matrix is its number of rows." ✓ It is the number of independent columns (which always equals the number of independent rows). A 100 × 100 matrix can have rank 1. Idea 6 · Projection Projecting vector a onto vector b gives the component of a in the direction of b : b ​ ( a ) = b ⋅ b a ⋅ b ​ b The residual b ​ ( a )) is perpendicular to . This orthogonal decomposition is the foundation of least-squares fitting. Projection is everywhere in ML: - Linear regression minimizes the distance from observations to the column space -- the solution IS a projection - PCA projects data onto the directions of maximum variance - Attention in transformers computes projections of queries onto keys Example: , b ​ ( a ) = ( 3 ⋅ 1 + 4 ⋅ 0 ) / ( 1 ⋅ 1 + 0 ⋅ 0 ) ⋅ [ 1 , 0 ] = 3 ⋅ [ 1 , 0 ] = [ 3 , 0 ] The projection drops the y-component. This is dimensionality reduction in its simplest form -- throw away the directions you don't care about. See it drawn Projection of a = [3, 4] onto b = [5, 1] : the green arrow is the part of a that points along b , the dashed line is what is left over, and the two meet at a right angle. Idea 7 · Gram-Schmidt Process Converting any set of independent vectors into an orthonormal basis. Orthonormal means every vector has length 1 and every pair is perpendicular. The algorithm: 1. Take the first vector, normalize it 2. Take the second vector, subtract its projection onto the first, normalize 3. Take the third vector, subtract its projections onto all previous vectors, normalize 4. Repeat for remaining vectors Copy This is how QR decomposition works internally. Q is the orthonormal basis, R captures the projection coefficients. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Vector An ordered list of numbers, which can be read as a point or as an arrow Embeddings Dimension How many numbers a vector has Embeddings Norm The length of a vector Normalising embeddings Euclidean distance The straight-line distance between two points Vector search Cosine similarity How closely two vectors point the same way, from -1 to 1 Vector search Vector database A store that finds the vectors nearest to a query vector quickly Retrieval Mentioned here, taught later 4 Embedding, RAG, Embedding model, Vector search This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Embedding A learned vector that stands for a word, token, product or anything else Lesson 3.19 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.37 Embedding model A model that turns a piece of text into one vector that captures its meaning Lesson 7.13 Vector search Finding text by meaning: embed the query and return the stored passages whose vectors are closest Lesson 14.26 Why this came about Computers can only do arithmetic, so anything an AI system works with (a word, a photo, a customer, a support ticket) has to become numbers first. The most useful form turned out to be a vector , a fixed-length list of numbers, because geometry then gives meaning to arithmetic: things that are alike end up close together. From word vectors in 2013 to the " embeddings later · 3.19 " behind every RAG later · 10.37 system today, how similar are these two vectors? is one of the most-asked questions in AI. This lesson gives you the two answers everyone uses: distance and cosine similarity . In plain words first Describing things with numbers Describe snacks with two numbers: how sweet (0 to 1) and how salty (0 to 1). Masala chips are [0.1, 0.9] , chocolate is [0.9, 0.1] . That pair of numbers is a vector . Draw it as an arrow from the corner of a graph to the point (0.1, 0.9), and similar snacks become arrows pointing in similar directions. Now imagine 768 numbers instead of 2, each capturing some aspect of meaning that a model learned. You cannot draw 768 directions, but the arithmetic is exactly the same, and that is what this lesson teaches. A vector is a list of numbers that describes something. With two numbers (how sweet, how salty) every snack becomes a point, or an arrow from the origin; similar snacks point in similar directions. Step 1 · A vector is a list of numbers A vector is an ordered list of numbers that describes one thing. The example describes five snacks by three numbers each: how sweet, how salty and how spicy, from 0 to 1. Once things are lists of numbers, a computer can compare them with arithmetic, and that single idea is behind every embedding and every search in this course. Make the vectors first: Copy What you should see Copy Each number is one component (or dimension ) of the vector; this vector has 3 dimensions: sweet, salty, spicy. The order matters and is fixed: component 1 is always "salty" for every snack. Everything that follows works the same whether a vector has 2, 3 or 3,072 components. Step 2 · Adding and scaling vectors Vectors add component by component , and multiplying by a number scales every component: Copy What you should see Copy As arrows, adding means "walk along the first arrow, then the second"; scaling means making an arrow longer or shorter without turning it. The average of two vectors lands halfway between them. A famous result from word vectors ( Lesson 5.7 ) uses exactly this arithmetic: the vector for king minus man plus woman lands near queen . Step 3 · Length and distance The length (also called the norm or magnitude) of a vector comes from Pythagoras: square each component, add them up, take the square root. The distance between two vectors is the length of their difference. Copy What you should see Copy Namkeen mix is closest to masala chips, chocolate is far away: distance matches our sense of "alike". This Euclidean distance (straight-line distance) is one way to measure similarity. It has a weakness, though: it cares about how much as well as what kind . Step 5 shows when that matters. The same idea as a formula For vectors a and b with n components: length: | a | = √(a₁² + a₂² + … + aₙ²) distance: | a − b | = √((a₁ − b₁)² + … + (aₙ − bₙ)²) Step 4 · The dot product The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results. It is the single most important operation in this course: neural network layers ( Lesson 3.4 ) and attention ( Lesson 7.3 ) are built from it. Copy What you should see Copy (The code rounds to 3 decimals because, as Lesson 0.9 showed, decimal arithmetic leaves tiny errors such as 0.7800000000000001 .) The dot product is large when the two vectors have big values in the same components (both salty), and small when their big values are in different places (one salty, one sweet). Geometrically, it combines the two lengths with the angle between the arrows. Drag the arrows to feel it: Dot product, length and angle Drag the tips of the two arrows. Watch the dot product and the cosine change with the angle between them. Things to try in the figure: point both arrows the same way (large positive dot product); make them perpendicular (dot product exactly 0); point them in opposite directions (negative); keep the angle fixed but make one arrow longer (the dot product grows even though the direction did not change). The same idea as a formula a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … + aₙbₙ = | a | | b | cos θ, where θ is the angle between the arrows. Step 5 · Cosine similarity: direction, not size The last experiment shows the dot product's weakness as a similarity measure: longer arrows get bigger scores. Often you care only about direction , the kind of thing, not the amount. Divide the dot product by both lengths and you get the cosine of the angle between the vectors: cosine similarity , always between −1 and 1. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Mild chips is the same snack profile at half strength. By distance it looks further from masala chips than peanuts are, because the arrow is shorter. By cosine it is a perfect match, 1.000 : same direction. Cosine 1 means "same direction", 0 means "unrelated" (perpendicular), −1 means "opposite". When the lengths are not meaningful (a long document versus a short one about the same topic), cosine is the better measure. This is why text search with embeddings almost always uses cosine similarity (the Retrieval (RAG) section). Step 6 · Ranking by similarity: vector search in miniature Put it together: given a query vector, score every item and sort. This is, in essence, what a vector database does for millions of items ( Lesson 14.26 ). Copy What you should see Copy A common speed-up: normalize every vector to length 1 once, when you store it. Then cosine similarity is just the dot product, and one matrix multiplication ( Lesson 1.5 ) scores a query against every item at once: Copy What you should see Copy keepdims=True keeps the lengths as a column of shape (6, 1) , so broadcasting ( Lesson 0.14 ) divides each row by its own length. Step 7 · Many dimensions Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of components. You cannot picture 768 directions, but every formula above is unchanged. One surprising fact about high dimensions is worth knowing: two random vectors are almost always nearly perpendicular. Copy What you should see Copy In 2 dimensions random arrows often point roughly the same way; in 768 dimensions they almost never do. So when two embeddings have a cosine of 0.6, that is a strong signal: it did not happen by chance. It also means similarity scores from different embedding models later · 7.13 are not comparable with each other: what counts as "high" depends on the model, a point the Retrieval (RAG) section returns to. Check your mental model ✗ "A vector is an arrow." ✓ It is a list of numbers; an arrow is one way to picture it, useful in 2 or 3 dimensions. ✗ "A bigger dot product always means more similar." ✓ It also grows with length. Cosine similarity removes length and compares direction only. ✗ "Cosine similarity of 0 means the opposite." ✓ 0 means unrelated (perpendicular); −1 means opposite. ✗ "High-dimensional math needs different formulas." ✓ Length, distance, dot product and cosine are the same formulas with more terms. Exercises Predict before you run Without running code: what is the dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 0, -1] ? And the cosine similarity of [2, 0] and [0, 5] ? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Add two snacks of your own to snacks (for example pani puri and kaju katli ), choose their three numbers, and run most_similar with each as the query. Do the neighbours make sense? Which number would you add as a fourth dimension to separate snacks that still look too similar? (Solution M1.) Debugging exercise A colleague computes M @ q with M of shape (6, 3) and gets correct-looking scores, but the ranking favours snacks with large numbers in every component. What did they forget? (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · By hand Dot product: 1×4 + 2×0 + 3×(−1) = 4 + 0 − 3 = 1 . Cosine of [2, 0] and [0, 5] : the dot product is 0 (one points along the first axis, the other along the second), so the cosine is 0 : perpendicular, whatever their lengths. Solution M1 · Your own snacks Any reasonable numbers work, for example pani puri = [0.3, 0.5, 0.8] (its nearest neighbour is likely namkeen mix) and kaju katli = [0.9, 0.1, 0.0] (chocolate and gulab jamun). Three hand-picked numbers can only separate snacks along three directions; a fourth such as crunchy would split chips from gulab jamun-like sweets more finely. Learned embeddings solve this by letting a model choose hundreds of such directions from data instead of a person choosing three ( Lesson 5.7 ). Solution D1 · Not normalized They used raw vectors, so M @ q is the dot product, which grows with each row's length. Normalize the rows of M (and the query) to length 1 first, or divide each score by np.linalg.norm(M, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(q) . Then the scores are cosines and compare direction only. Recap A vector is a fixed-length list of numbers; each position always means the same thing. Vectors add component by component and scale by multiplying every component. Length uses Pythagoras; distance is the length of the difference. The dot product multiplies matching components and adds them; it combines lengths and angle. Cosine similarity divides out the lengths and compares direction only; with unit-length vectors it is just the dot product, and ranking by it is vector search later · 14.26 . Check your understanding Q1 Two document embeddings point in exactly the same direction, but one is three times longer. What is their cosine similarity? A 3 B 0.33 C 1 D 0 Cosine ignores length; same direction gives 1. Q2 What is the dot product of [1, 0] and [0, 1]? A 0 B 1 C 2 D -1 They are perpendicular: 1×0 + 0×1 = 0. Q3 Why do vector search systems often normalize vectors to length 1 when storing them? A To save memory B So that cosine similarity becomes a plain dot product, which is fast to compute for many items at once C Because embedding models require it D To make the vectors random With unit vectors, a single matrix multiplication gives every cosine. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Vector "An arrow" An ordered list of numbers. In AI: a point in high-dimensional space. Matrix "A table of numbers" A linear transformation. It maps vectors from one space to another. Matrix multiply "Just multiply the numbers" Dot products between every row of the first matrix and every column of the second. Order matters. Transpose "Flip it" Swap rows and columns. Turns an $m \times n$ matrix into $n \times m$. Critical in backpropagation. Determinant "Some number from the matrix" Measures how much the matrix scales area (2D) or volume (3D). Zero means the transformation crushes a dimension. Inverse "Undo the matrix" The matrix that reverses the transformation. Only exists when the determinant is not zero. Identity matrix "The boring matrix" The matrix equivalent of multiplying by 1. Used in residual connections (ResNets). Broadcasting "Magic shape fixing" Stretching a smaller array to match a larger one by repeating along missing dimensions. Element-wise "Regular multiplication" Multiply matching positions. Two kinds of multiplication matter and are easy to mix up: element-wise ( * ) multiplies matching positions and needs equal shapes, while matrix multiplication ( @ ) takes dot products of rows with columns and needs the inner sizes to match. Broadcasting lets NumPy and PyTorch combine arrays of different shapes by repeating the smaller one, which is convenient and occasionally a silent bug. You want to build a neural network. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A colleague builds a dense layer that takes 784 inputs and gives 128 outputs. The first forward pass stops with a shape error. Which dimensions does the weight matrix need, and how do you read an error like this one? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The matrix is 128 by 784: one row for each output and one column for each input. A matrix product needs the inner sizes to agree, so a 128 by 784 matrix times a 784 by 1 input gives a 128 by 1 output. An error means the inner sizes differ, and the fix starts with the shapes of every operand written on paper. The rule. A product of an m by n matrix and an n by p matrix gives an m by p matrix. The inner sizes, both n, must agree. For the layer in the question: Copy The rows of the weight matrix count the outputs. The columns count the inputs. Each output is the dot product of one weight row with the whole input vector. The bias. The bias holds one value for each output. Store it as a 128 by 1 column, as the lesson does, so that it adds to the 128 by 1 result element by element. A flat array of 128 values against a 128 by 1 column broadcasts to 128 by 128 with no error. When the layer runs on a batch, the bias has fewer dimensions than the output, and broadcasting repeats it across the batch. Broadcasting only stretches a dimension of size 1, so it never fixes a 784 against a 128. How to read the error. Write the shape of every operand next to the operation. Find the operation whose inner sizes do not match. That is the broken line. Decide which side is wrong. A transposed weight matrix, an input stored as a row instead of a column, and a missing batch dimension each give a different pair of numbers in the message. The lesson makes the same check for a two layer network: the first matrix is 4 by 3 and the second is 2 by 4, so a 3 by 1 input gives a 4 by 1 hidden vector and a 2 by 1 output. Plausible wrong answers. "The weight matrix is 784 by 128 because inputs come first." With a column input the matrix needs 128 rows and 784 columns. The order of the product decides which form is right, not the order in which you name the sizes. "Shapes do not matter, the framework fixes them." Broadcasting repeats only a dimension of size 1. A 784 against a 128 inner size is an error, or a silent wrong result after a reshape. "Transpose things until the code runs." A transpose that makes the code run can multiply the wrong pairs of numbers. Write the shapes down first and then change the one that is wrong. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What shape does the bias have? Expected: one value for each output, so 128 values, stored as a 128 by 1 column so that it adds to each output column. (level 2) A batch of inputs arrives as rows instead of columns. What changes? Expected: the order of the product changes, so the batch matrix times the transposed weight gives one output row for each input. (level 2) Why does a transpose appear in the backward pass? Expected: the gradient for the input needs the weight matrix with its rows and columns swapped, so that the shapes agree in the reverse direction. (level 3) How does broadcasting hide a shape bug? Expected: a dimension of size 1 is stretched to fit, so a wrong shape can run without an error and give wrong values. An assertion on the shape catches it. Where it is taught. Short answer. The star multiplies matching positions, so the first print shows 5, 12, 21 and 32. The at sign forms dot products of rows with columns, so the second print shows 19, 22, 43 and 50. A layer uses the at sign, because every output must sum over every input. Element-wise product. Both arrays have the same shape, so the star pairs each cell with the cell at the same position: Copy The order of A and B does not change the result. Matrix product. The at sign calls the matmul method. Cell (i, j) of the result is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: Copy The order matters. B times A gives other numbers. The inner sizes must agree, and the result has the rows of A and the columns of B. Which one a layer uses. A dense layer computes an activation of W times x plus b. The element-wise product appears in other places in training, for example when the learning rate scales a gradient, or when a mask zeroes some values. NumPy runs the matrix product with tuned BLAS routines written in C and Fortran, which the lesson measures as about 100 times faster than a Python loop over the same numbers. Plausible wrong answers. "Both print the same matrix, the star is another spelling of the at sign." The two operations follow different rules and give different numbers. "The at sign is the element-wise product and the star is the matrix product." The at sign calls matmul, which forms dot products of rows and columns. The star works on matching positions. "A dense layer multiplies each weight by its input, so it is element-wise." Each output also sums over all inputs. That sum is the dot product inside a matrix product. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, Julia. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A matrix is a machine that reshapes space. Learn what it does to every point, and you understand the whole transformation. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Rotation matrix "Spins things" An orthogonal matrix that moves points along circular arcs while preserving distances and angles. Determinant is always 1. Scaling matrix "Makes things bigger" A diagonal matrix that stretches or compresses independently along each axis. Determinant is the product of scale factors. Shearing matrix "Slants things" A matrix that shifts one coordinate proportionally to another, turning rectangles into parallelograms. Determinant is 1. Reflection "Mirrors things" A matrix that flips space across an axis or plane. Determinant is -1. Composition "Do two things" Multiplying transformation matrices to chain operations. Order matters: B @ A means apply A first, then B. Eigenvector "Special direction" A direction that the matrix only scales, never rotates. The transformation's fingerprint. Eigenvalue "How much it stretches" The scalar factor by which the matrix scales its eigenvector. Can be negative (flip) or complex (rotation). Eigendecomposition "Break the matrix apart" Writing a matrix as $V D V^{-1}$, separating it into its fundamental scaling directions and magnitudes. Determinant "A single number from a matrix" The factor by which the transformation scales area (2D) or volume (3D). Zero means the transformation is irreversible. Characteristic equation "Where eigenvalues come from" $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. The polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues. The problem In plain words first A 2 × 2 matrix is fully described by where it sends the two arrows [1, 0] and [0, 1] : those are its two columns. Everything else on the plane follows along, so a matrix can rotate, stretch, tilt or mirror the whole plane at once. A few special directions are only stretched, never turned: those are the eigenvectors , and the stretch factors are the eigenvalues . They tell you what the matrix does when you apply it again and again. You read about PCA and see "find the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix." You read about model stability and see "check if all eigenvalues have magnitude less than 1." You read about data augmentation and see "apply a random rotation." None of this makes sense until you understand what matrices do to space geometrically. Matrices are not just grids of numbers. They are spatial machines. A rotation matrix spins points. A scaling matrix stretches them. A shearing matrix tilts them. Every transformation a neural network applies to data is one of these operations or a composition of them. This lesson makes those operations concrete. Idea 1 · Transformations as matrices Every linear transformation in 2D can be written as a 2x2 matrix. The matrix tells you exactly where the basis vectors [1, 0] and [0, 1] end up. Everything else follows. Idea 2 · Rotation A 2D rotation by angle keeps distances and angles intact. It moves every point along a circular arc. In 3D, you rotate around an axis. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in GPU A processor built to do many simple calculations at once, which is what neural networks need Lesson 3.20 Activation function The non-linear function applied to a neuron's sum, such as ReLU Lesson 3.4 PyTorch The most widely used Python library for building and training neural networks Lesson 3.16 Why this came about Matrices were developed in the 1800s to solve many equations at once, and they became the workhorse of computing because one matrix multiplication does a huge number of multiply-and-add operations in a single, highly optimized step. Graphics cards ( GPUs later · 3.20 ) were built to multiply matrices fast for video games; in 2012 researchers realized the same hardware could train neural networks, whose every layer is a matrix multiplication . Today, "how many matrix multiplications per second" is the measure of AI hardware, and almost every line of model code you will read moves data through matrices. In plain words first A recipe card for a whole kitchen A matrix is a table of numbers. Think of a café's recipe table: one column per drink (tea, coffee), one row per ingredient (milk, sugar, water), each cell saying how much of that ingredient one drink needs. Multiply that table by today's orders (4 teas, 2 coffees) and you get, in one step, how much milk, sugar and water to buy. That is all matrix-times-vector is: many dot products done together. The same operation, seen as geometry, moves every point of space at once, which is what a neural network layer does to its inputs. Step 1 · A matrix is a table of numbers A matrix is a table of numbers with rows and columns: several vectors stacked together. The table below holds two drink recipes. Each row is an ingredient and each column is a drink, so one number answers a question such as "how much milk does one coffee need?". Build it and read a few entries: Copy What you should see Copy A matrix with m rows and n columns has shape m × n , read "m by n". Step 2 · Matrix times vector: two ways to see the same thing Today's orders are a vector: 4 teas and 2 coffees. Copy What you should see Copy All three print the same shopping list: 360 ml milk, 50 g sugar, 840 ml water. Both views are worth keeping: Rows view: each output number is a dot product of one row with the input vector. This is how a neural network computes each of its outputs ( Lesson 3.4 ). Columns view: the output is a weighted mix of the matrix's columns, with the input numbers as the weights. This is the geometric view in Step 3. The shapes follow one rule: a (3, 2) matrix times a vector of length 2 gives a vector of length 3. The matrix's column count must equal the vector's length. Step 3 · A matrix transforms space Take a 2 × 2 matrix and multiply it by every point of a flat plane. Each point moves somewhere new. The columns tell you exactly where: column 1 is where the point [1, 0] lands, column 2 is where [0, 1] lands, and every other point follows along, because it is a mix of those two. Time : about 60 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Derivatives tell you which way is downhill. That is all a neural network needs to learn. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Derivative "The slope" The rate of change of a function at a point. Tells you how much the output changes per unit change in input. Partial derivative "Derivative of one variable" The derivative with respect to one variable while all others are held constant. Gradient "Direction of steepest ascent" A vector of all partial derivatives. Points in the direction that increases the function fastest. Gradient descent "Go downhill" Subtract the gradient (times a learning rate) from the parameters to reduce the loss. The core of neural network training. Learning rate "Step size" A scalar that controls how big each gradient descent step is. Too large: diverge. Too small: converge slowly. Chain rule "Multiply the derivatives" The rule for differentiating composed functions: $\frac{df}{dx} = \frac{df}{dg} \cdot \frac{dg}{dx}$. The mathematical basis of backpropagation. Jacobian "Matrix of derivatives" When a function maps vectors to vectors, the Jacobian is the matrix of all partial derivatives of outputs with respect to inputs. Numerical derivative "Finite differences" Approximating a derivative by evaluating the function at two nearby points and computing the slope between them. Backpropagation "Reverse-mode autodiff" Computing gradients layer by layer from output to input using the chain rule. How neural networks learn. Hessian "Matrix of second derivatives" The matrix of all second-order partial derivatives. Describes the curvature of a function. Positive definite Hessian at a critical point means local minimum. Taylor series "Polynomial approximation" Approximating a function near a point using its derivatives: $f(x+h) \approx f(x) + f'(x)h + \frac{1}{2}f''(x)h^2 + \cdots$ The basis for understanding why gradient descent and Newton's method work. Integral "Area under the curve" The accumulation of a quantity over a range. In ML, integrals define probabilities, expected values, and KL divergence. The problem In plain words first A derivative answers one question: if I nudge this input a tiny bit, how much does the output move? For a loss with millions of weights you ask it once per weight, and the answers together form the gradient , an arrow pointing uphill. Training is walking the other way, a small step at a time. The chain rule is how those answers are computed through many layers, which is all backpropagation is. You have a neural network with millions of weights. Each weight is a knob. You need to figure out which direction to turn every single knob to make the model slightly less wrong. Calculus gives you that direction. Without calculus, training a neural network would mean trying random changes and hoping for the best. With derivatives, you know exactly how each weight affects the error. You turn every knob the right way, every time. Idea 1 · What is a derivative? A derivative measures the rate of change. For a function , the derivative ( x ) tells you: if you nudge by a tiny amount, how much does change? Geometrically, the derivative is the slope of the tangent line at a point. : ( x ) (slope) 0 0 0 (flat, at the bottom) 1 1 2 2 4 4 (tangent line slope at this point) 3 9 6 At , the slope is 4. If you move a tiny bit to the right, increases by about 4 times that amount. At , the slope is 0. You are at the bottom of the bowl. The formal definition: ( x ) = h → 0 lim ​ h f ( x + h ) − f ( x ) ​ In code, you skip the limit and just use a very small . That is the numerical derivative. Idea 2 · Partial derivatives: one variable at a time Real functions have many inputs. A neural network loss depends on thousands of weights. A partial derivative holds all variables constant except one, then takes the derivative with respect to that one. ∂ x ∂ f ​ ∂ y ∂ f ​ ​ = x 2 + 3 x y + y 2 = 2 x + 3 y (treat y as a constant) = 3 x + 2 y (treat x as a constant) ​ Each partial derivative answers: if I nudge just this one weight, how does the loss change? Idea 3 · The gradient: vector of all partial derivatives The gradient collects every partial derivative into one vector. For a function , the gradient is: ∂ f ​ , ∂ y ∂ f ​ , ∂ z ∂ f ​ ] The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. To minimize a function, go in the opposite direction. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Backpropagation Computing every parameter's gradient by applying the chain rule backwards through the network Lesson 3.6 Why this came about Training a model means adjusting its numbers until its predictions are good. With a handful of numbers you could try values by hand; with millions you need a rule that says, for every number at once, which way to move it and roughly how much . Calculus, developed by Newton and Leibniz in the 1600s, provides that rule through the derivative . In 1847 Augustin-Louis Cauchy described gradient descent : repeatedly take a small step downhill. Combined with the chain rule and computers, this same idea trains everything from the line fit in Lesson 2.4 to the largest language models. In plain words first Walking down a hill in fog Imagine standing on a hillside in thick fog, trying to reach the bottom of the valley. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you take a small step in the downhill direction, feel again, step again. The slope (or derivative ) tells you which way is down and how steep it is. With many directions to choose from, the slopes in each direction together form the gradient . The learning rate is your step size: too small and you take forever, too large and you overshoot the valley and may end up higher than you started. A model's "valley" is the lowest possible loss , its measure of how wrong it is. Step 1 · A slope: how much the output changes when you nudge the input Here is a loss that depends on one setting, w . It is lowest (1.0) at w = 3 . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The slope at a point is "change in loss ÷ change in w" for a tiny nudge. The code nudges w by 0.00001 in each direction and divides. A negative slope means the loss goes down as w goes up: move w up. A positive slope means move w down. At the bottom ( w = 3 ) the slope is 0: no direction improves things. The size of the slope says how steep it is: far from the minimum ( w = -1 ) the slope is −4, close to it ( w = 2 ) only −1. For this particular curve the exact slope has a simple formula, w - 3 (you can check it against the table). You will rarely need such formulas: libraries compute slopes for you automatically ( Lesson 3.6 ). What you need is the meaning: the slope tells you which way is downhill and how steep it is. Step 2 · The chain rule: slopes through several steps Models compute their output in many steps, each feeding the next. The chain rule says how a nudge at the start travels through: multiply the local slopes of each step. The chain rule: when a result is computed in steps, a small change at the start is multiplied by each step's local slope on the way through. Backpropagation ( Lesson 3.6 ) is this rule applied to every step of a network. Copy What you should see Copy Both give 18. The chain rule lets a computer find the slope of a huge calculation by working backwards through it, step by step, multiplying local slopes as it goes. That backward pass is backpropagation later · 3.6 , and Lesson 3.6 builds it in about sixty lines. Step 3 · Many inputs: the gradient Real models have many settings. The slope with respect to one setting, holding the others still, is a partial derivative . Collect them all into a vector and you have the gradient . It points in the direction of steepest increase ; so gradient descent steps the opposite way. Copy What you should see Copy At (0, 0) the gradient is [-6, 4] : the loss rises fastest if you move w[0] down and w[1] up, so to reduce it, move w[0] up and w[1] down. That is towards the lowest point (3, -1) . Nudging each coordinate one at a time costs two loss evaluations per setting. For a model with a billion settings that would be two billion evaluations for one step, which is why real training uses backpropagation, which gets every partial derivative in roughly the cost of one extra pass. Step 4 · Gradient descent The whole algorithm fits in one line, repeated: move every setting a small step against its slope. w ← w − learning_rate × gradient Gradient descent, one step at a time The curve is the loss for each value of a setting w. The red line is the slope where the ball sits. Each step moves w a little downhill. Try learning rates of 0.1, 1.0, 1.9 and 2.1. The same thing in code, for the 2-D bowl: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output 0.01 : too small. After 50 steps w has moved only part of the way; the loss is still well above its minimum of 0. 0.1 : good. w reaches (3, -1) and the loss is essentially 0. 0.45 : still converges, but by bouncing back and forth across the valley in the steep direction, each bounce a little smaller. 0.55 : too large. Each step overshoots by more than it corrects, the steps grow, and the loss explodes. This is called divergence . The steep direction (the 2 * (w[1] + 1) ** 2 term) sets the limit: there each step multiplies the distance from the bottom by 1 - 4 × learning rate , so any rate above 0.5 makes it grow. Choosing the learning rate is the most important practical decision in training. In Lesson 3.12 you will meet the standard remedies: optimizers such as Adam that adapt the step for each setting, and schedules that start small, warm up, then decay. Step 5 · What this means for real models The loss is the hill. For a language model it is the cross-entropy of Lesson 1.10 , averaged over training text. The settings are the millions or billions of parameters. Each training step computes the loss on a small batch of examples, gets the gradient by backpropagation, and moves every parameter a little against it. That is called stochastic gradient descent : stochastic (random) because each batch is a random sample of the data, so each gradient is a noisy estimate of the true one. Real landscapes are not bowls. They have flat regions, saddle points and many valleys. In practice, for large networks, gradient descent with good settings finds valleys that are good enough, though nobody can prove it finds the best one. Three ways to take the steps. Using all the data for every step (left) gives a smooth path; using small random batches (middle) or one example at a time (right) gives a noisier path that still arrives, at a fraction of the work per step. Real models use mini-batches. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . The same idea as a formula derivative: f′(w) ≈ (f(w + h) − f(w − h)) / 2h for a tiny h chain rule: if y = g(u) and u = h(w), then dy/dw = (dy/du) · (du/dw) gradient: ∇f( w ) = (∂f/∂w₁, ∂f/∂w₂, …, ∂f/∂wₙ) gradient descent: w ← w − η ∇f( w ), with learning rate η Check your mental model ✗ "The gradient points to the minimum." ✓ It points uphill, in the steepest direction at your current spot. You step the opposite way, and only a little, because the direction changes as you move. ✗ "A bigger learning rate always trains faster." ✓ Past a limit, steps overshoot and training diverges. ✗ "You need calculus formulas to train models." ✓ You need to understand slopes; libraries compute exact gradients automatically with the chain rule. Solutions Solution P1 · Special learning rates With 1.0: one step. The slope at w is w - 3 , so w - 1.0 × (w - 3) = 3 exactly: for this bowl, a learning rate of 1 jumps straight to the bottom. With 2.0: w - 2(w - 3) = 6 - w , so w flips between -1 and 7 forever, never settling. Above 2.0 it flies off (diverges). Solution M1 · A V-shaped loss The slope of abs(w - 3) is −1 on the left and +1 on the right, never smaller, so every step has the same size, 0.3. Near the bottom w keeps hopping back and forth across 3 (for example between 2.9 and 3.2) and never settles. This is why learning-rate schedules shrink the step size over training: with constant steps, you cannot land exactly at a sharp minimum. Solution D1 · Exploding loss Almost always a learning rate that is too large (or a sudden very large gradient). Try reducing the learning rate by a factor of 3 to 10 first. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Chain rule "Multiply the derivatives" The derivative of composed functions equals the product of each function's local derivative, evaluated at the right point Computational graph "The network diagram" A directed acyclic graph where nodes are operations and edges carry values (forward) or gradients (backward) Forward mode "Push derivatives forward" Autodiff that propagates derivatives from inputs to outputs. One pass per input variable. Reverse mode "Backpropagation" Autodiff that propagates gradients from outputs to inputs. One pass per output variable. Autograd "Automatic gradients" A system that records operations on values, builds a graph, and computes exact gradients via the chain rule Dual numbers "Value plus derivative" Numbers of the form $a + b\epsilon$ ($\epsilon^2 = 0$) that carry derivative information through arithmetic Topological sort "Dependency order" Ordering graph nodes so every node comes after all its dependencies. Required for correct gradient propagation. Gradient accumulation "Add, don't replace" When a value feeds into multiple operations, its gradient is the sum of all incoming gradient contributions Dynamic graph "Define by run" A computation graph rebuilt on every forward pass, allowing Python control flow inside models (PyTorch style) Gradient checking "Numerical verification" Comparing autodiff gradients against numerical finite-difference gradients to verify correctness. Essential for debugging. MLP "Multi-layer perceptron" A neural network with one or more hidden layers of neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias, then applies an activation function. Neuron "Weighted sum + activation" The basic unit: $\text{output} = \text{activation}(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \cdots + b)$. The weights and bias are learnable parameters. The problem In plain words first Every number a network computes is built from a few simple operations: add, multiply, tanh . Each one knows its own small derivative. If every result remembers which numbers it came from, you can start at the loss and walk backwards through that record, multiplying the small derivatives together (the chain rule ) and adding them up where paths meet. That walk is backpropagation , and a program that does it for you is an autograd engine . This lesson builds one in about 80 lines. You can compute derivatives of simple functions. But a neural network is not a simple function. It is hundreds of functions composed together: matrix multiply, add bias, apply activation, matrix multiply again, softmax, cross-entropy loss. The output is a function of a function of a function. To train the network, you need the gradient of the loss with respect to every single weight. Doing this by hand is impossible for millions of parameters. Doing it numerically (finite differences) is too slow. The chain rule gives you the math. Automatic differentiation gives you the algorithm. Together they let you compute exact gradients through arbitrary compositions of functions in time proportional to a single forward pass. This is how PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX work. You will build a miniature version from scratch. Idea 5 · Building an Autograd Engine An autograd engine needs three things: Value wrapping. Wrap every number in an object that stores its value and gradient. Graph recording.
