Read the code This is the multiply operation of a small autograd engine. python def __mul__(self, other): other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other) out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other), '*') def _backward(): self.grad += other.data * out.grad other.grad += self.data * out.grad out._backward = _backward return out A contributor replaces both += with = , with the comment that a gradient should be set, not added. The XOR training loop still runs and the loss still falls. What did the change break, and how do you prove it in one small test? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A value that feeds two or more operations receives a gradient from each consumer, and the chain rule says those contributions add. With assignment, the last consumer to run overwrites the others, so every shared node gets a wrong gradient, including each weight that the summed loss uses once per sample. A numerical gradient check exposes the error in one call. What the chain rule says about shared nodes. When y depends on x through two paths, the derivative of y with respect to x is the sum of the derivatives along each path. In the engine, a node that is used twice has two closures that write to its grad . The topological order runs every consumer before the node passes its gradient to its own children, so both closures run, and the second must add to the first. Why the loop still ran. In the XOR loop the loss is the sum of four squared errors, one per sample, and every weight takes part in all four forward passes. With assignment, each weight keeps only the contribution of the sample that ran last. That is still a direction that often points downhill, so the loss moves. The gradient is wrong for every parameter even so. The one-line test. Copy Here self and other are the same object. The correct gradient of x squared at 3 is 6.0. The two closures each add 3.0, which gives 6.0. With assignment the result is 3.0. The lesson's gradient_check does the same job for any expression: it compares the engine with a centered finite difference and reports the difference, which must be far below 1e-5. The other side of the same rule. Because gradients add, the training loop must set every grad back to 0.0 before each backward call. The lesson does this with a loop over the parameters. A framework does the same with a zero_grad call. Both habits come from the same fact: gradient storage is an accumulator. Plausible wrong answers. "Assignment is fine because each node has one parent." A node that feeds two operations has two consumers in the graph, and a weight in a summed loss has one consumer per sample. "The loss still goes down, so the gradients are correct." A wrong gradient can still point partly downhill. Only a numerical check proves it. "Use a running average instead of a sum." The chain rule sums the path contributions. An average divides the true gradient by the number of consumers. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why must the training loop set every gradient to zero before backward? Expected: gradients accumulate, so a second backward would stack onto the first; the loop sets each parameter's grad to 0.0. (level 3) Write the smallest expression that fails with assignment. Expected: a value multiplied by itself; the gradient at 3 must be 6.0, and assignment gives 3.0. (level 3) Why does the topological order matter for this bug? Expected: all consumers of a node must run before the node passes gradient on; with assignment the answer depends on which consumer ran last. (level 4) Where does the same accumulation rule show up in a framework you use? Expected: a tensor's grad accumulates across uses and across backward calls, which is why the optimizer's zero_grad runs before each step. Where it is taught. The chain rule and autodiff lesson builds the Value class and the gradient check that catches this bug. Explain the mechanism Automatic differentiation can push derivatives forward from the inputs or pull them backward from the output. Training frameworks pick the backward direction. Why, and in which situation would the forward direction be the better choice? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A network has millions of parameters and one scalar loss. Reverse mode seeds the output with a gradient of 1 and gets the gradient of every parameter in one backward sweep. Forward mode needs one sweep for each input variable, so it wins only when the inputs are few and the outputs are many. The two modes. Both modes apply the chain rule at every node of the computation graph. They differ in where the seed goes. Mode Seed Direction Best when Forward the derivative of one input with respect to itself, set to 1 input to output few inputs, many outputs Reverse the derivative of the output with respect to itself, set to 1 output to input many inputs, few outputs Forward mode carries one derivative through the graph. To get the gradient of a loss with respect to a million weights, you would run it a million times. Reverse mode carries the gradient of the single loss back to every node, and each node multiplies by its local derivative and passes the result to its children. What reverse mode costs. The backward sweep visits each node once, so the time is proportional to one forward pass. The engine must order the nodes first. A topological sort guarantees that a node has received the gradient from every consumer before it passes gradient on. When a value feeds several operations, the contributions add. When forward mode is the right choice. Forward mode fits a function with one or two inputs and a large output, because one sweep gives the derivative of the whole output along one input direction. Dual numbers implement it with almost no code: a pair of value and derivative, with the rule that the square of the derivative part is zero, so the product rule falls out of the arithmetic. Plausible wrong answers. "Reverse mode is more accurate than forward mode." Both are exact up to floating point rounding. The difference is the cost, not the result. "Forward mode cannot handle a composition of functions." Both modes apply the chain rule through every link. Forward mode pushes the derivative from the input side. "Backpropagation is a different algorithm from reverse-mode autodiff." Backpropagation is reverse-mode autodiff applied to the network graph, with the loss as the single output. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the backward sweep need a topological order? Expected: a node must receive the full gradient from every consumer before it passes gradient to its children. (level 3) How many forward-mode sweeps does a model with one million weights need for one gradient? Expected: one million, one per input variable, which is why nobody trains that way. (level 3) What is a dual number and how does it carry a derivative? Expected: a pair of a value and a derivative, where the derivative part squares to zero, so each arithmetic rule carries the derivative along. (level 4) Name a case in an ML system where you would pick forward mode. Expected: a function with one or two inputs and a large vector output, where one sweep gives the derivative of the whole output along one input direction. Where it is taught. The chain rule and autodiff lesson compares the two modes and builds a reverse-mode engine. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Sample space "All the possibilities" The set $S$ of every possible outcome of an experiment PMF "The probability function" A function that gives the exact probability of each discrete outcome, summing to 1 PDF "The probability curve" A density function for continuous variables. Appears everywhere due to the CLT Central Limit Theorem "Averages become normal" The centered, scaled mean of many independent samples converges to a normal distribution for any source with finite variance Joint distribution "Two variables together" $P(X, Y)$ describes the probability of every combination of $X$ and $Y$ outcomes Marginal distribution "Sum out the other variable" $P(X) = \sum_y P(X, Y)$. How models generate output The problem In plain words first A probability is a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is, and a distribution lists the probability of every possible outcome. A classifier's output is a distribution over classes; a language model's output is a distribution over the next word. Two summaries describe a distribution: its expected value (the average outcome) and its variance (how spread out the outcomes are). Computers work with the logarithms of probabilities, because multiplying many small numbers underflows to zero. A classifier outputs [0.03, 0.91, 0.06] . A language model picks the next word from 50,000 candidates. A diffusion model generates images by sampling from learned distributions. All of these are probability in action. Every prediction a model makes is a probability distribution. Every loss function measures how far the predicted distribution is from the true one. Every training step adjusts parameters to make one distribution look more like another. Without probability, you cannot read a single ML paper, debug a single model, or understand why your training loss is NaN. Explain the mechanism A language model scores a sentence as the product of the probability of each word. For long sentences the score is exactly zero, and two long sentences can no longer be compared. What went wrong, and what do you compute instead? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The product of many small probabilities underflows to zero in floating point. Add the log probabilities instead, and the sum stays a finite negative number. A more negative sum means a less likely sentence, and the order of the sentences is unchanged. Why the product dies. Each word has a probability below 1, often far below. The lesson shows the product falling to 0.0 after about 30 terms. Once the product is zero, every longer sentence gets the same score, and a comparison between them is meaningless. What the log does. The log turns a product into a sum: log(a times b) equals log(a) plus log(b). Each term is at most 0, because each probability is at most 1, so the sum is a negative number that grows in size with the sentence length but never underflows. The lesson gives the extreme case: 50 words with probability 0.01 each have a raw probability of 10 to the minus 100, and a log probability of about minus 230.26. Where you already use it. Cross-entropy loss is the negative log probability of the correct class. Training a classifier or a language model already works in log space. Log-softmax computes the log probabilities straight from the logits, so the tiny probabilities are never formed. Comparing sentences. A longer sentence has a more negative sum even when every word is likely. To compare a short sentence with a long one, divide by the token count, or report the perplexity, which is the exponential of the mean negative log probability. Plausible wrong answers. "Use a wider float type and the product will be fine." A wider format only moves the point of underflow. Fifty words with probability 0.01 give 10 to the minus 100, and a longer sentence pushes it further down. "Multiply the probabilities and take the log at the end." The product is already zero before the log, and the log of zero is minus infinity. "Clip each probability to a minimum value." That changes the score of every rare word and still underflows for a long enough sentence. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why is every log probability zero or negative? Expected: a probability is between 0 and 1, and the log of such a number is at most 0. (level 2) How do you compare two sentences of different length? Expected: compare the mean log probability per token, or the perplexity, not the raw sum. (level 2) Where does this appear in a loss function? Expected: cross-entropy is the negative log probability of the correct class, so training already runs in log space. (level 3) How do you get log probabilities from logits without forming the probabilities first? Expected: log-softmax, which subtracts the log-sum-exp of the logits from each logit. Where it is taught. The probability lesson shows the underflow, the log rules, and the log-softmax function. Lesson 1.2 helps but is not required. Depth : Core, for everyone. Time : about 70 minutes. Next : Lesson 1.7 shows how a model uses slopes to get better. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Probability distribution A list of outcomes with a probability for each, adding up to 1 Model output Softmax The function that turns any list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1 Model output Logits The raw scores a model produces before softmax Model output Temperature A number that divides the logits before softmax: low is confident, high is varied Sampling Conditional probability The probability of one thing given that another is known Language models Cross-entropy loss The surprise at the correct answer, averaged over examples: minus the log of the probability given to it Training Perplexity How many choices the model is, on average, torn between: e to the power of the cross-entropy Evaluating language models Mentioned here, taught later 3 Machine learning, Transformer, Overfitting This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Machine learning Software that learns a rule from examples instead of being given the rule Lesson 2.2 Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.8 Overfitting Doing well on the training data and badly on new data, because the model memorised Lesson 2.16 Why this came about Probability began in the 1600s with games of chance and became the mathematics of uncertainty. Machine learning later · 2.2 adopted it because real data is noisy and predictions are never certain: a good model does not just guess, it says how sure it is. A language model is, at its heart, a probability machine: for every possible next token it outputs a probability (you saw 8.5% for " the" in Lesson 0.2 ). It is trained by making the probability of the actual next token as high as possible, and judged by how surprised it is by real text. This lesson builds each of those ideas from counting. In plain words first Weather forecasts for words A probability is a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is: 0 never, 1 certainly, 0.3 "about three times in ten". A distribution lists the probability of every possible outcome, and the probabilities add up to 1, like a weather forecast that splits 100% between sun, cloud and rain. A language model gives a forecast for the next word. Softmax is the recipe that turns the model's raw scores into such a forecast. And surprise measures how badly a forecast did once you see what actually happened: a forecast of 1% rain followed by a downpour was very surprising. Step 1 · From counts to probabilities The simplest way to estimate a probability is to count. Here are the categories of 200 ShopKart support tickets: Copy What you should see Copy Dividing counts by their total is called normalizing , and it always gives numbers between 0 and 1 that add up to 1. This is a categorical distribution : one probability per category. A language model's output is exactly this shape, with one probability per vocabulary token, 50,257 of them for GPT-2. Step 2 · Sampling: letting chance choose To sample from a distribution is to pick an outcome at random, with each outcome as likely as its probability says. Picking the next word this way is how language models generate varied text. Copy What you should see Copy With 10 samples the frequencies wobble a lot; with 10,000 they settle close to [0.45, 0.3, 0.15, 0.1] . That settling is the law of large numbers , and it is why one sample says little and evaluation in the Production engineering and AI system design section runs many cases. It is also why the same prompt can give different answers: if a model samples, each run is a fresh draw. Step 3 · Conditional probability: it depends on what came before A conditional probability is the probability of something given that something else is known, written P(A | B), read "the probability of A given B". Language models compute exactly this: P(next word | the words so far). Here it is estimated by counting which word follows which in a tiny corpus: Copy What you should see Copy After "is", "delivered" has probability 0.4 because it followed "is" in 2 of the 5 times "is" appeared. This counting model is called a bigram model , and Lesson 5.25 builds and samples from one. Its weakness is plain: it only looks at one previous word. "My refund is ..." and "my order is ..." get the same forecast. Large language models condition on thousands of previous tokens, which is what makes their forecasts so much better. Step 4 · Describing numbers: mean, spread and the bell curve For numeric data, three numbers summarize a lot. The mean is the average. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation (std) is its square root, back in the original units: it says how far a typical value sits from the mean. Copy What you should see Copy Many measurements cluster symmetrically around a mean in a bell-shaped pattern called the normal (or Gaussian) distribution, described completely by its mean and standard deviation. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. It appears all over AI: the starting values of a neural network's weights are drawn from it ( Lesson 3.12 ), and normalization layers rescale values to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 ( Lesson 7.8 ). Copy What you should see Copy The last line standardizes the delivery times: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. The result is measured in "standard deviations from typical", and the 9-day delivery stands out at about 2.7. This is the same rescaling normalization layers do inside transformers later · 7.8 . Step 5 · Softmax: scores into probabilities A model's last layer produces raw scores , called logits , one per possible answer. They can be any numbers, positive or negative, and they do not add up to 1. Softmax turns them into a distribution in two moves: make every score positive with the exponential function e^x , then normalize. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The highest score gets the highest probability, but not all of it: softmax keeps every option alive. Adding 100 to every score leaves the probabilities unchanged: only the differences between scores matter. The code subtracts the maximum for exactly this reason, so e^x never overflows to infinity. Temperature divides the scores before softmax. Below 1, differences grow and the top choice dominates (0.5 gives " Paris" over 70%); above 1, differences shrink and the distribution flattens. Temperature near 0 approaches always picking the top word; this is the "temperature" setting on every model API ( Lesson 11.22 ). Play with the same five words: From scores to probabilities to a choice Five candidate next words with fixed scores (logits). Move the temperature, change one score, and sample to see how often each word is picked. Step 6 · Log-probabilities and surprise When a model generates or reads a long text, it assigns a probability to each token. The probability of the whole text is the product of them, and products of many small numbers become too small for a computer to store: Copy What you should see Copy Logarithms turn products into sums, log(a × b) = log a + log b, so models work with log-probabilities throughout. The negative log-probability of what actually happened is its surprise : near 0 when the model was confident and right, large when it gave the truth a low probability. Surprise, or negative log probability: if the model gave the right answer probability p, the loss is −log p. A confident right answer costs almost nothing; a confident wrong one (tiny p for the truth) costs a lot. Averaging the surprise over every token of a text gives the cross-entropy loss , the number a language model is trained to make as small as possible ( Lesson 5.25 ). Taking exp of it gives perplexity : roughly, "the model was as unsure as if it were choosing uniformly among this many words". Copy What you should see Copy One confident mistake (probability 0.01 for the truth, a surprise of 4.6) costs more than the other three good predictions combined, and drags the average almost down to the level of the "unsure" model. Cross-entropy punishes overconfidence hard, which is why trained models learn to hedge when they are unsure. A perplexity near 1 means "almost certain every time"; uniformly guessing among GPT-2's 50,257 tokens would give a perplexity of 50,257. The same idea as a formula softmax: pᵢ = e^(zᵢ / T) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ / T), for scores zᵢ and temperature T cross-entropy over N tokens: L = −(1/N) Σₜ log pₜ, where pₜ is the probability given to the true token t perplexity = e^L Check your mental model ✗ "Softmax picks the highest score." ✓ It gives every option a probability; picking happens afterwards (greedy or sampling). ✗ "Temperature makes a model more creative." ✓ It only reshapes the probability distribution : flatter (more varied picks) or sharper (more predictable). ✗ "A loss of 0 is achievable and good." ✓ It would mean probability 1 for every true token, which no honest model of real text can do; aiming for it on training data leads to overfitting later · 2.16 ( Lesson 2.16 ). ✗ "P(A | B) is the same as P(B | A)." ✓ P(rain | clouds) is not P(clouds | rain). The order matters. Exercises Predict before you run softmax([1, 1, 1, 1]) gives what? And softmax([5, 1]) versus softmax([50, 10]) : which is sharper? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Add three sentences of your own to corpus in Step 3 (for example about payments) and print next_word_probs for a word you added. How many sentences would you need before the forecasts look reliable? (Solution M1.) Debugging exercise A colleague writes np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum() and gets nan for scores like [1000, 999] . Why, and what is the one-line fix? (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Equal and scaled scores Equal scores give a uniform distribution: [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] . softmax([5, 1]) is about [0.982, 0.018] ; softmax([50, 10]) is about [1.0, 0.0] , much sharper, because softmax depends on differences: 4 versus 40. Scaling all scores up is the same as lowering the temperature. Solution M1 · More data Any additions work; the forecasts for words you add will be based on very few examples, so one sentence can swing them from 0 to 1. Counting models need a lot of text to estimate rare continuations; that hunger for data, and the fact that unseen pairs get probability 0, are the problems neural language models solved (Lessons 5.25 and 5.13 ). Solution D1 · Overflow np.exp(1000) is larger than the biggest number a float can hold, so it becomes inf , and inf / inf is nan . Subtract the maximum first: e = np.exp(scores - scores.max()) . Since only differences matter, the probabilities are unchanged and the largest exponent is now e^0 = 1 . Recap Probabilities are between 0 and 1; a distribution's probabilities add up to 1; normalizing counts gives one. Sampling picks outcomes at random by their probabilities; many samples settle near the true frequencies. P(next | previous) is a conditional probability; counting it gives a bigram model. Mean, variance and standard deviation summarize numbers; the normal distribution is the bell curve; standardizing rescales to mean 0, std 1. Softmax turns scores into probabilities; temperature sharpens or flattens them. −log p is surprise; its average is the cross-entropy loss; perplexity is its exponential. A Makes it sharper, concentrating probability on the top choices B Makes it flatter C Changes which word has the highest score D Makes the probabilities no longer add up to 1 Dividing by a small T enlarges differences between scores. Q3 Why do language models work with log-probabilities? A Logs are faster to compute than probabilities B Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0; adding their logs does not C Logs make every probability positive D Because softmax requires it Products become sums, which stay in a normal numeric range. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Probability is about what you expect. Bayes' theorem is about what you learn. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Prior "My initial guess" $P(\text{hypothesis})$ before observing evidence. In ML: the regularization term. Likelihood "How well the data fits" $P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{hypothesis})$. How probable the observed data is under a specific hypothesis. Posterior "My updated belief" $P(\text{hypothesis} \mid \text{evidence})$. The prior multiplied by the likelihood, then normalized. Evidence "The normalizing constant" $P(\text{data})$ across all hypotheses. Ensures the posterior sums to 1. Naive Bayes "That simple text classifier" A classifier that assumes features are independent given the class. Works well despite the false assumption. Laplace smoothing "Add-one smoothing" Adding a small count to every feature to prevent zero probabilities from unseen data. MLE "Just use the frequencies" Choose parameters that maximize $P(\text{data} \mid \text{parameters})$. No prior. Can overfit with small data. MAP "MLE with a prior" Choose parameters that maximize $P(\text{data} \mid \text{parameters}) \cdot P(\text{parameters})$. Equivalent to regularized MLE. Log-probability "Work in log space" Using $\log(P)$ instead of $P$ to avoid floating-point underflow when multiplying many small numbers. False positive "A wrong alarm" The test says positive, but the true state is negative. Drives the base rate fallacy. The problem In plain words first Bayes' theorem is the rule for updating a belief when evidence arrives. You start with a prior (how likely something was before), multiply by the likelihood (how likely the evidence would be if it were true), and divide by how likely the evidence is overall. The surprise it explains: a test that is right 99 percent of the time can still be wrong about most of the people it flags, if what it tests for is rare. A medical test is 99% accurate. You test positive. What are the chances you actually have the disease? Most people say 99%. The real answer depends on how rare the disease is. If 1 in 10,000 people have it, a positive result only gives you about a 1% chance of being sick. The other 99% of positive results are false alarms from healthy people. This is not a trick question. It is Bayes' theorem. Every spam filter, every medical diagnostic, every machine learning model that quantifies uncertainty uses this exact reasoning. You start with a belief. You see evidence. You update. If you build ML systems without understanding this, you will misinterpret model outputs, set bad thresholds, and ship overconfident predictions. Idea 1 · From joint probability to Bayes You already know from Lesson 1.9 that conditional probability is: P ( A and B ) ​ And symmetrically: P ( A and B ) ​ Both expressions share the same numerator: . Set them equal and rearrange: P ( A ∣ B ) ​ = P ( A ∣ B ) ⋅ P ( B ) = P ( B ∣ A ) ⋅ P ( A ) Therefore: = P ( B ) P ( B ∣ A ) ⋅ P ( A ) ​ ​ That is Bayes' theorem. Four quantities, one equation. Idea 2 · The four parts Part Name What it means Posterior Your updated belief about after seeing evidence Likelihood How probable the evidence is if is true Prior Your belief about before seeing any evidence Evidence Total probability of seeing under all possibilities The evidence term acts as a normalizer. You can expand it using the law of total probability: Check your mental model ✗ "P(positive | sick) = 0.99, so P(sick | positive) is about 0.99." ✓ They are different questions with different denominators. With a 1-in-10,000 disease, P(sick | positive) is under 1 percent. Swapping them is called the prosecutor's fallacy. ✗ "Naive Bayes only works when the features really are independent." ✓ Words are not independent, and Naive Bayes still classifies text well: it often gets the ranking of classes right even when its probabilities are off. ✗ "MAP and MLE are unrelated methods." ✓ MAP is MLE plus a prior. With a flat prior they give the same answer; Laplace smoothing is MAP with a particular prior on word probabilities. Idea 3 · Medical test example A disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. The test is 99% accurate (catches 99% of sick people, gives false positives 1% of the time). P ( positive ∣ sick ) P ( positive ∣ healthy ) P ( positive ) P ( sick ∣ positive ) ​ = 0.0001 (prior: disease is rare) = 0.99 (likelihood: test catches it) = 0.01 (false positive rate) = P ( positive ∣ sick ) ⋅ P ( sick ) + P ( positive ∣ healthy ) ⋅ P ( healthy ) = 0.99 ⋅ 0.0001 + 0.01 ⋅ 0.9999 = 0.000099 + 0.009999 = 0.010098 = P ( positive ∣ sick ) ⋅ P ( sick ) / P ( positive ) = 0.99 ⋅ 0.0001/0.010098 = 0.0098 = 0.98% ​ Less than 1%. The prior dominates. When a condition is rare, even accurate tests produce mostly false positives. This is why doctors order confirmation tests. See it drawn The same 99-percent-accurate test, for diseases of every prevalence from 1 in a million to 1 in 2. The posterior only becomes trustworthy once the condition is reasonably common. They take a second, independent test with the same accuracy and it is also positive. What is the probability now, and after a third positive? (Solution P1.) Idea 4 · Spam filter example You receive an email containing the word "lottery". Is it spam? P ( "lottery" ∣ spam ) P ( "lottery" ∣ not spam ) P ( "lottery" ) P ( spam ∣ "lottery" ) ​ = 0.3 (30% of email is spam) = 0.05 (5% of spam emails contain "lottery") = 0.001 (0.1% of legitimate emails contain "lottery") = 0.05 ⋅ 0.3 + 0.001 ⋅ 0.7 = 0.015 + 0.0007 = 0.0157 = 0.05 ⋅ 0.3/0.0157 = 0.955 = 95.5% ​ One word shifts the probability from 30% to 95.5%. A real spam filter applies Bayes across hundreds of words simultaneously. Idea 5 · Naive Bayes: independence assumption Naive Bayes extends this to multiple features by assuming all features are conditionally independent given the class: ​ , feature 2 ​ , … , feature n ​ ) = P ( feature 1 ​ , feature 2 ​ , … , feature n ​ ) P ( class ) ⋅ P ( feature 1 ​ ∣ class ) ⋅ P ( feature 2 ​ ∣ class ) ⋯ P ( feature n ​ ∣ class ) ​ The "naive" part is the independence assumption. In text, word occurrences are not independent ("New" and "York" are correlated). But the assumption works surprisingly well in practice because the classifier only needs to rank classes, not produce calibrated probabilities. Since the denominator is the same for all classes, you can skip it and just compare numerators: ∏ ​ P ( feature i ​ ∣ class ) Pick the class with the highest score. Idea 6 · Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) How do you get from training data? Count. number of spam emails containing "free" ​ This is MLE: choose the parameter values that make the observed data most likely. You are maximizing the likelihood function, which for discrete counts reduces to relative frequency. Problem: if a word never appears in spam during training, MLE gives it probability zero. One unseen word kills the entire product. Fix this with Laplace smoothing: count ( word , class ) + 1 ​ Adding 1 to every count ensures no probability is ever zero. A word that never appeared in any training message is not in the vocabulary. predict skips it, because it gives no evidence for either class. Worked example Worked by hand In Step 3's training data the five spam messages contain 21 words, and "free" appears 5 times. The vocabulary, across all twelve messages, has 44 distinct words. MLE says P("free" | spam) = 5/21 ≈ 0.238. With Laplace smoothing it is (5 + 1) / (21 + 44) = 6/65 ≈ 0.0923 , the top spam word Step 4 prints. A word seen 0 times in spam gets 1/65 instead of 0. Idea 7 · Maximum a posteriori (MAP) MLE asks: what parameters maximize ? MAP asks: what parameters maximize ? By Bayes' theorem: MAP adds a prior over the parameters themselves. If you believe parameters should be small, you encode that as a prior that penalizes large values. This is identical to L2 regularization in ML. The "ridge" penalty in ridge regression is literally a Gaussian prior on the weights. Estimation Optimizes ML equivalent MLE Unregularized training MAP L2 / L1 regularization Idea 8 · Bayesian vs frequentist: the practical difference Frequentists treat parameters as fixed unknowns. They ask: "If I repeated this experiment many times, what would happen?" Bayesians treat parameters as distributions. They ask: "Given what I have observed, what do I believe about the parameters?" For building ML systems, the practical difference: Aspect Frequentist Bayesian Output Point estimate Distribution over values Uncertainty Confidence intervals (about procedure) Credible intervals (about parameter) Small data Can overfit Prior acts as regularization Computation Usually faster Often requires sampling (MCMC) Most production ML is frequentist (SGD, point estimates). Bayesian methods shine when you need calibrated uncertainty (medical decisions, safety-critical systems) or when data is scarce (few-shot learning, cold start). Idea 9 · Why Bayesian thinking matters for ML The connection is deeper than analogy: Priors are regularization. A Gaussian prior on weights is L2 regularization. A Laplace prior is L1. Every time you add a regularization term, you are making a Bayesian statement about what parameter values you expect. Posteriors are uncertainty. A single predicted probability tells you nothing about how confident the model is in that estimate. Bayesian methods give you a distribution: "I think is between 0.8 and 0.95." Bayes updates are online learning. Today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. When your model sees new data, it updates its beliefs incrementally instead of retraining from scratch. Model comparison is Bayesian. Bayesian information criterion (BIC), marginal likelihood, and Bayes factors all use Bayesian reasoning to choose between models without overfitting. Conjugate Priors When the prior and posterior belong to the same family of distributions, the prior is called "conjugate." This makes Bayesian updating algebraically clean -- you get a closed-form posterior without numerical integration. With conjugate priors, you just update two numbers. The Beta distribution is the most common conjugate prior in practice. represents your belief about a probability parameter. The mean is . Sequential Bayesian Updating Bayesian inference is naturally sequential. Today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. This is how real systems learn incrementally without reprocessing all historical data. Concrete example: estimating whether a coin is fair. Day 1: No data yet. Start with -- a uniform prior. You have no opinion. - Prior mean: 0.5 - Prior is flat across [0, 1] Day 2: Observe 7 heads, 3 tails. - Posterior mean: - Evidence suggests the coin is biased toward heads Day 3: Observe 5 more heads, 5 more tails. Use yesterday's posterior as today's prior. - Posterior mean: - The balanced new data pulled the estimate back toward 0.5 The order of observations does not matter. updated with all 12 heads and 8 tails at once gives -- the same result. Sequential updating and batch updating are mathematically equivalent. But sequential updating lets you make decisions at each step without storing raw data. This is the foundation of online learning in production ML systems. Thompson sampling for bandits, incremental recommendation systems, and streaming anomaly detectors all use this pattern. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Training a neural network is nothing more than finding the bottom of a valley. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Gradient descent "Go downhill" Update weights by subtracting the gradient scaled by the learning rate. The most basic optimizer. Learning rate "Step size" A scalar that controls how far each update moves the weights. Too large causes divergence. Too small wastes compute. Momentum "Keep rolling" Accumulate past gradients into a velocity vector. Dampens oscillations and accelerates movement through consistent directions. SGD "Random sampling" Stochastic gradient descent. Compute gradient on a random subset instead of the full dataset. Almost always means mini-batch SGD in practice. Mini-batch "A chunk of data" A small subset of training data (32-256 samples) used to estimate the gradient. Balances speed and gradient accuracy. Adam "The default optimizer" Adaptive Moment Estimation. Tracks per-weight running averages of gradients and squared gradients to give each weight its own learning rate. Bias correction "Fix the cold start" Adam's first and second moments are initialized to zero. Bias correction divides by $(1 - \beta^t)$ to compensate during early steps. Learning rate schedule "Change lr over time" A function that adjusts the learning rate during training. Large steps early, small steps late. Convex function "One valley" A function where any local minimum is the global minimum. Gradient descent always finds it. Neural network losses are not convex. Saddle point "Flat but not a minimum" A point where the gradient is zero but it is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others. Common in high dimensions. Loss landscape "The terrain" The loss function plotted over weight space. Visualized by slicing along two random directions. Convergence "Getting there" The optimizer has reached a point where further steps do not meaningfully reduce the loss. The problem In plain words first An optimiser is the rule that turns a gradient into a step. Plain gradient descent steps straight downhill by a fixed fraction of the slope. Momentum remembers recent steps, so it speeds up along a long valley and stops zigzagging across it. Adam also keeps a running size of each weight's gradients and divides by it, so every weight takes steps of a similar size however steep its own slope is. The learning rate still sets the scale for all of them. You have a loss function. It tells you how wrong your model is. You have gradients. They tell you which direction makes the loss worse. Now you need a strategy for walking downhill. The naive approach is simple: move opposite the gradient. Scale the step by some number called the learning rate. Repeat. This is gradient descent, and it works. But "works" has caveats. Too large a learning rate and you overshoot the valley entirely, bouncing between walls. Too small and you crawl toward the answer over thousands of unnecessary steps. Hit a saddle point and you stop moving even though you have not found a minimum. Every optimizer in deep learning is an answer to the same question: how do you get to the bottom of the valley faster and more reliably? Idea 1 · What optimization means Optimization is finding the input values that minimize (or maximize) a function. In machine learning, the function is the loss. The inputs are the model's weights. Training is optimization. Copy Idea 2 · Gradient descent (vanilla) The simplest optimizer. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Move each weight in the opposite direction of its gradient. Scale the step by the learning rate. That is the entire algorithm. One line. Idea 3 · Learning rate: the most important hyperparameter The learning rate controls step size. It determines everything about convergence. There is no formula for the right learning rate. You find it by experiment. Common starting points: 0.001 for Adam, 0.01 for SGD with momentum. Idea 4 · SGD vs batch vs mini-batch Vanilla gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire dataset before taking one step. This is called batch gradient descent. It is stable but slow. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) computes the gradient on a single random sample and steps immediately. It is noisy but fast. Mini-batch gradient descent splits the difference. Compute the gradient over a small batch (32, 64, 128, 256 samples), then step. This is what everyone actually uses. Variant Batch size Gradient quality Speed per step Noise Batch GD Entire dataset Exact Slow None SGD 1 sample Very noisy Fast High Mini-batch 32-256 Good estimate Balanced Moderate The noise in SGD and mini-batch is not a bug. It helps escape shallow local minima and saddle points. Check your mental model ✗ "A larger learning rate just trains faster." ✓ Up to a point. On this lesson's Rosenbrock valley, plain gradient descent does better at 0.002 than at 0.0005, worse at 0.003, and at 0.005 it overflows within 7 steps. ✗ "SGD's noise is a flaw that bigger batches remove." ✓ Bigger batches reduce it, but some noise helps escape saddle points and sharp minima; batch size is a trade-off, not a quality dial. ✗ "Adam's step is the learning rate times the gradient." ✓ It is the learning rate times the gradient divided by its recent size . On the first step that ratio is ±1, so each weight moves by about the learning rate whatever its gradient is. Idea 5 · Momentum: the ball rolling downhill Vanilla gradient descent only looks at the current gradient. If the gradient zigzags (common in narrow valleys), progress is slow. Momentum fixes this by accumulating past gradients into a velocity term. w ​ = β ⋅ v + gradient = w − lr ⋅ v ​ The analogy: a ball rolling downhill. It does not stop and restart at every bump. It builds speed in consistent directions and dampens oscillations. beta (typically 0.9) controls how much history to keep. Higher beta means more momentum, smoother paths, but slower response to direction changes. Idea 6 · Adam: adaptive learning rates Different weights need different learning rates. A weight that rarely gets large gradients should take bigger steps when it finally does. A weight that gets huge gradients constantly should take smaller steps. Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) tracks two things per weight: First moment ( ): running average of gradients (like momentum) Second moment ( ): running average of squared gradients (gradient magnitude) v m ^ v ^ w ​ = β 1 ​ ⋅ m + ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) ⋅ gradient = β 2 ​ ⋅ v + ( 1 − β 2 ​ ) ⋅ gradient 2 = m / ( 1 − β 1 t ​ ) bias correction = v / ( 1 − β 2 t ​ ) bias correction = w − lr ⋅ m ^ / ( v ^ ​ + ϵ ) ​ The division by sqrt(v_hat) is the key insight. Weights with large gradients get divided by a large number (small effective step). Weights with small gradients get divided by a small number (large effective step). Each weight gets its own adaptive learning rate. Default hyperparameters: lr=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8 . These defaults work well for most problems. Predict before you run At the start point (−1, 1) the Rosenbrock gradient is [−4, 0] . With lr = 0.01 , how far does Adam's first step move x ? How far would plain gradient descent with the same lr move it? (Solution P1.) Idea 7 · Learning rate schedules A fixed learning rate is a compromise. Early in training, you want large steps to make fast progress. Late in training, you want small steps to fine-tune near the minimum. Common schedules: Schedule Formula Use case Step decay every epochs Simple, manual control Exponential decay ​ ⋅ decay t Smooth reduction Cosine annealing ​ + 0.5 ⋅ ( lr m a x ​ − lr m i n ​ ) ⋅ ( 1 + cos ( π t / T )) Transformers, modern training Warmup + decay Linear ramp up, then decay Large models, prevents early instability Idea 8 · Convex vs non-convex A convex function has no bad local minima: every local minimum is a global minimum. For a smooth convex function that has a minimum, gradient descent with a small enough learning rate converges to it. A quadratic like is convex, and its minimum is unique. Neural network loss functions are non-convex. They have many local minima, saddle points, and flat regions. In practice, local minima in high-dimensional neural networks are rarely a problem. Most local minima have loss values close to the global minimum. Saddle points (flat in some directions, curved in others) are the real obstacle. Momentum and noise from mini-batches help escape them. Idea 9 · Loss landscape visualization The loss is a function of all weights. For a model with 1 million weights, the loss landscape lives in 1,000,001-dimensional space. We visualize it by picking two random directions in weight space and plotting the loss along those directions, producing a 2D surface. Sharp minima generalize poorly. Flat minima generalize well. This is one reason SGD with momentum often outperforms Adam on final test accuracy: its noise prevents settling into sharp minima. Recap What to keep from this lesson Gradient descent: w ← w − lr · gradient ; the learning rate is the most important setting. Mini-batches trade gradient accuracy for many more steps; their noise is useful. Momentum accumulates past gradients, damping zigzags and speeding along valleys. Adam divides each weight's step by the recent size of its gradients, with bias correction for the first steps. Start with Adam at 0.001; use schedules for long runs; lower the rate when training is unstable. Solutions Solution P1 · Adam's first step Adam moves x by exactly 0.01 . After bias correction, m̂ = −4 and v̂ = 16 on the first step, so the step is 0.01 × (−4)/√16 = −0.01 in the update, x goes from −1 to −0.99, and y (gradient 0) does not move. Plain gradient descent at lr = 0.01 would move x by 0.01 × 4 = 0.04 , four times as far, because its step scales with the gradient. (Without bias correction Adam's first step would be about 0.032: m and v both start at 0 and are too small, by different amounts.) Solution B1 · Overflow in seven steps The GD run overflows: x passes a million within 7 steps and the loss becomes inf or nan . The valley walls are steep: at the start point the largest curvature (the top eigenvalue of the Hessian, Lesson 1.6) is about 1,000, and plain gradient descent is stable only when the learning rate is below 2 divided by that curvature, about 0.002. That is exactly where the runs change behaviour: 0.002 converges, 0.003 and 0.004 stall, and at 0.005 each step across the valley overshoots further than the last. Adam is protected because it divides by the gradient's size, which is why it tolerates a learning rate (0.01) that kills plain gradient descent. Use it: the same idea with real libraries In practice, use PyTorch or JAX optimizers. They handle parameter groups, weight decay, gradient clipping, and GPU acceleration. Copy Rules of thumb: Start with Adam (lr=0.001). It works for most problems without tuning. Switch to SGD with momentum (lr=0.01, momentum=0.9) when you need the best final accuracy and can afford more tuning. Use AdamW (Adam with decoupled weight decay) for transformers. Always use a learning rate schedule for training runs longer than a few epochs. If training is unstable, reduce the learning rate. If training is too slow, increase it. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) AdamW is the default. Almost every published LLM and vision recipe trains with AdamW (Adam with decoupled weight decay), warmup and a decaying learning rate (Lessons 3.9 and 3.13). Muon in production training. The Muon optimizer orthogonalises each weight matrix's update; Moonshot AI trained the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi K2 with a variant (MuonClip), and PyTorch includes torch.optim.Muon since version 2.9. Second-order ideas, approximately. Shampoo-style preconditioned optimizers are used at scale at Google and Meta; the curvature ideas in this lesson are why they can converge in fewer steps. Explain the mechanism You minimize the Rosenbrock function from the point (-1, 1). Plain gradient descent creeps along the curved valley and needs thousands of steps. The same run with momentum arrives much sooner. Explain what the valley does to plain descent and what momentum changes. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. In a narrow valley the gradient points across the valley, not along it, so each plain step jumps from one wall to the other and makes little progress toward the minimum. Momentum keeps a velocity that sums past gradients. The across components flip sign and cancel, the along component keeps its sign and builds up, so the path is smooth and fast. The function. The function is (1 - x)^2 + 100 (y - x^2)^2. Its minimum is at (1, 1), at the bottom of a curved valley. The factor 100 makes the valley walls steep and the floor almost flat, so the gradient is large across the valley and small along it. Plain descent. The update is w = w - lr times gradient. The step size is set by the learning rate alone. A learning rate large enough to move along the floor overshoots across the walls, and a learning rate small enough to stay inside the walls crawls along the floor. The lesson runs this with a learning rate of 0.0005 for 5000 steps and still sees slow progress. Momentum. Copy The velocity is an exponential sum of past gradients. Components that flip sign at each step cancel inside the sum. Components with a stable sign add up and the ball rolls faster along the floor. The lesson uses beta equal to 0.9, which keeps about the last ten gradients in play. A larger beta gives more smoothing and a slower response when the valley turns. Where this leads. Adam goes one step further and also divides each weight's step by the running size of its gradients, so each weight gets its own step size. "Raise the learning rate until plain descent moves faster." A larger step jumps further across the valley and diverges before it speeds up the along direction. "Momentum is a bigger learning rate." The velocity grows only where gradients keep their sign and cancels where they flip, which a scalar learning rate cannot do. "The valley is a local minimum, so the optimizer is stuck." (level 3) How does this zigzag show up in a real training run? Expected: the loss drops fast and then plateaus while the weights oscillate; a smaller learning rate or momentum smooths it. (level 4) Why does Adam help on the same valley beyond what momentum does? a0109: Course home / Phase 1 · Mathematics for Machine Learning Entropy, Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence: Information Theory Lesson 1.13 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Compute entropy, cross-entropy, and KL divergence from scratch and explain their relationship Derive why minimizing cross-entropy loss is equivalent to maximizing log-likelihood Calculate mutual information between features and a target to rank feature importance Explain perplexity as the effective vocabulary size a language model chooses from Before you start Needs : Lesson 1.9 (Probability) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Information theory measures surprise. Loss functions are built on it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Information content "Surprise" The number of bits (or nats) needed to encode an event: $-\log(p)$ Entropy "Randomness" The average surprise across all outcomes of a distribution. Measures irreducible uncertainty. Cross-entropy "The loss function" Average surprise when using model distribution $Q$ to encode events from true distribution $P$. KL divergence "Distance between distributions" Extra bits wasted by using $Q$ instead of $P$. Equals cross-entropy minus entropy. Not symmetric. Mutual information "How related are X and Y" Reduction in uncertainty about $X$ from knowing $Y$. Zero means independent. Softmax "Turn logits into probabilities" Exponentiate and normalize. Maps any real-valued vector to a valid probability distribution. Perplexity "How confused the model is" Exponential of cross-entropy. The effective vocabulary size the model is choosing from at each step. Bits "Shannon's unit" Information measured with log base 2. One bit resolves one fair coin flip. Nats "ML's unit" Information measured with natural log. Used by PyTorch and TensorFlow by default. Negative log-likelihood "NLL loss" Identical to cross-entropy loss for one-hot labels. Minimizing it maximizes the probability of correct predictions. The problem In plain words first Surprise is how unexpected an outcome is: −log of its probability, so a certain event surprises you 0 and a one-in-a-million event a lot. Entropy is the average surprise of a distribution, how uncertain it is. Cross-entropy is the average surprise when reality follows one distribution but you predicted with another; it is the loss every classifier and language model is trained with. KL divergence is the extra surprise caused by predicting wrong, cross-entropy minus entropy. You call CrossEntropyLoss() in every classification model you train. You see "perplexity" in every language model paper. You read about KL divergence in VAEs, distillation, and RLHF. These are not disconnected concepts. They are all the same idea wearing different hats. Information theory gives you the language to reason about uncertainty, compression, and prediction. Claude Shannon invented it in 1948 to solve communication problems. Turns out, training a neural network is a communication problem: the model is trying to transmit the correct label through a noisy channel of learned weights. This lesson builds every formula from scratch so you see where they come from and why they work. Idea 1 · Information Content (Surprise) When something unlikely happens, it carries more information. A coin landing heads? Not surprising. A lottery win? Very surprising. The information content of an event with probability is: Using log base 2 gives you bits. Using natural log gives you nats. Same idea, different units. Copy Certain events carry zero information. You already knew they would happen. Idea 2 · Entropy (Average Surprise) Entropy is the expected surprise across all possible outcomes of a distribution. ∑ ​ p ( x ) lo g ( p ( x )) A fair coin has maximum entropy for a binary variable: 1 bit. A biased coin (99% heads) has low entropy: 0.08 bits. You already know what will happen, so each flip tells you almost nothing. Explain the mechanism Your classifier trains on a cross-entropy loss. A reviewer asks why you do not train on the KL divergence between the labels and the predictions instead. Explain how the two quantities relate and what would change, if anything, in training. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Cross-entropy of P and Q equals the entropy of P plus the KL divergence from P to Q. The labels fix P, so their entropy is a constant during training, and the two objectives have the same gradient. With one-hot labels the entropy is zero and the two numbers are equal: minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class. The three quantities. Copy Entropy is the average surprise of P under its own code. Cross-entropy is the average surprise when events from P are coded with Q. KL is the extra surprise, the bits wasted by coding with Q instead of P. Why the optimizer cannot tell them apart. The model controls Q. The labels fix P, so H(P) is a constant for each sample. The gradient of a constant is zero, so the gradient of H(P, Q) and the gradient of KL(P||Q) with respect to the model are the same. With a one-hot label the sum has one nonzero term, H(P) is 0, and the loss is minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class. When the two numbers differ. The values differ when the target has positive entropy. Label smoothing turns a hard target into a soft one, and a teacher's softmax in distillation is soft from the start. Then cross-entropy cannot go below H(P), while KL reaches 0 at a perfect match. The gradients are still equal, so the choice changes the number you log, not the model you get. Two facts to say out loud. KL is not symmetric. KL(P||Q) and KL(Q||P) weight the log ratio by different distributions, so it is not a distance. The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is the predicted probability minus the target. That clean form is why it pairs with softmax. Plausible wrong answers. "They are different objectives and give different models." They differ by the entropy of the labels, which does not depend on the model, so the gradients are equal. "Cross-entropy is a distance between two distributions." It is not symmetric, and it is not zero when the distributions match; it equals the entropy of P at a match. "KL is smaller, so it is the better loss." KL is cross-entropy minus a constant. The optimizer sees the same slope. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is KL not a distance? Expected: it is not symmetric; each direction weights the log ratio by a different distribution. (level 3) With label smoothing the loss never reaches zero. Why? Expected: the soft target has positive entropy, and cross-entropy is at least the entropy of the target; KL would reach zero at a perfect match. (level 3) Differentiate the loss by each logit. What form do you get? Expected: the predicted probability minus the target, for each class. (level 4) In distillation the target is a teacher's softmax. Which of the two numbers do you log? Expected: KL, because the teacher's entropy is a constant offset per sample that hides how close the student is; the gradient is the same either way. Where it is taught. On average the model is as uncertain as a uniform pick over the whole vocabulary. A trained model should sit far below V. The mean alone does not prove that the model learned nothing, because other per-token predictions can give the same average, so check per-token predictions and the data. The definition. Perplexity reads as the effective number of equally likely choices the model is torn between at each step. A perplexity of 50 means the model is, on average, as confused as if it had to pick uniformly from 50 tokens. The estimate. The loss is ln V. The exponential of ln V is V. In plain words first The idea in one line High-dimensional data has structure. You find it by looking from the right angle. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Curse of dimensionality "Too many features" Distances, volumes, and data density all behave counterintuitively as dimensions grow. Models need exponentially more data to compensate. PCA "Reduce dimensions" Rotate your coordinate system so the axes align with the directions of maximum variance, then drop the low-variance axes. Principal component "An important direction" An eigenvector of the covariance matrix. The direction in feature space along which the data varies most. Explained variance ratio "How much info this component has" The fraction of total variance captured by one principal component. Sum the top $k$ ratios to see how much $k$ components preserve. Covariance matrix "How features correlate" A symmetric matrix where entry $(i,j)$ measures how feature $i$ and feature $j$ move together. Diagonal entries are individual variances. t-SNE "That cluster plot" A nonlinear method that maps high-dimensional data to 2D by preserving pairwise neighborhood probabilities. Good for visualization, not for preprocessing. UMAP "Faster t-SNE" A nonlinear method based on topological data analysis. Preserves both local and some global structure. Scales better than t-SNE. Perplexity "A t-SNE knob" Controls the effective number of neighbors each point considers. Low perplexity focuses on very local structure. High perplexity captures broader patterns. Manifold "The surface the data lives on" A lower-dimensional surface embedded in a higher-dimensional space. A sheet of paper crumpled in 3D is a 2D manifold. The problem In plain words first A 28 × 28 image is a point in 784 dimensions, and most of those dimensions carry little information. Dimensionality reduction finds a few new axes that keep what matters. PCA keeps the directions in which the data varies most, using the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix from Lesson 1.4; it is linear and fast. t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear: they place points so that neighbours stay neighbours, which makes clusters visible in 2D but distorts distances. You have a dataset with 784 features per sample. Maybe it is pixel values of handwritten digits. Maybe it is gene expression levels. Maybe it is user behavior signals. You cannot visualize 784 dimensions. You cannot plot them. You cannot even think about them. But most of those 784 features are redundant. The actual information lives on a much smaller surface. A handwritten "7" does not need 784 independent numbers to describe it. It needs a few: the angle of the stroke, the length of the crossbar, how much it leans. The rest is noise. Dimensionality reduction finds that smaller surface. It takes your 784-dimensional data and compresses it to 2, 10, or 50 dimensions while keeping the structure that matters. Idea 1 · The curse of dimensionality High-dimensional spaces are unintuitive. Three things break as dimensions grow. Distance becomes meaningless. In high dimensions, the distance between any two random points converges to the same value. If every point is roughly the same distance from every other point, nearest-neighbor search stops working. Copy Volume concentrates in corners. A unit hypercube in dimensions has corners. In 100 dimensions, nearly all the volume is in the corners, far from the center. Data points spread to the edges and your models starve for data in the interior. You need exponentially more data. To maintain the same density of samples in a space, going from 2D to 20D means you need times more data. You never have enough. Reducing dimensions brings the data density back to something workable. Idea 2 · PCA: find the directions that matter Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds the axes along which your data varies the most. It rotates your coordinate system so the first axis captures the most variance, the second captures the next most, and so on. The algorithm: Copy Why eigendecomposition? The covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semi-definite. Its eigenvectors are orthogonal directions in feature space. The eigenvalues tell you how much variance each direction captures. The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points along the direction of maximum variance. Before PCA: Data cloud is spread diagonally across both x and y axes After PCA: Coordinate system is rotated so PC1 aligns with the direction of maximum variance (elongated spread) and PC2 aligns with the direction of minimum variance (narrow spread) Dimensionality reduction: Dropping PC2 projects the data onto PC1, losing very little information Idea 3 · Explained variance ratio Each principal component captures a fraction of the total variance. The explained variance ratio tells you how much. Copy When the cumulative explained variance reaches 0.95, you know that many components capture 95% of the information. Everything after that is mostly noise. Idea 4 · Choosing the number of components Three strategies: Threshold. Keep enough components to explain 90-95% of the variance. Elbow method. Plot explained variance per component. Look for a sharp drop-off. Downstream performance. Use PCA as preprocessing. Sweep and measure your model's accuracy. The best is wherever accuracy plateaus. Check your mental model ✗ "More principal components always give a better downstream model." ✓ In the run at the end of this lesson, logistic regression is most accurate with 50 components and gets worse at 100 and 200: later components carry mostly noise, and more inputs mean more weights to fit on 4,000 images. ✗ "PCA finds the directions that best separate the classes." ✓ It never looks at the labels. It finds the directions of largest variance, which may or may not be the ones that matter for the task. ✗ "Distances and cluster sizes in a t-SNE plot mean something." ✓ t-SNE preserves who is near whom. The gaps between clusters and their sizes are largely artefacts of the method and its perplexity setting. Idea 5 · t-SNE: preserve neighborhoods t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is designed for visualization. It maps high-dimensional data to 2D (or 3D) while preserving which points are near each other. The intuition: in the original space, compute a probability distribution over pairs of points based on their distances. Near points get high probability. Far points get low probability. Then find a 2D arrangement where the same probability distribution holds. Points that were neighbors in 784 dimensions stay neighbors in 2D. Key properties of t-SNE: - Non-linear. It can unfold complex manifolds that PCA cannot. - Stochastic. Different runs produce different layouts. - Perplexity parameter controls how many neighbors to consider (typical range: 5-50). - Distances between clusters in the output are not meaningful. Only the clusters themselves are. - Slow on large datasets. ) by default. Idea 6 · UMAP: faster, better global structure Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) works similarly to t-SNE but with two advantages: - Faster. It uses approximate nearest-neighbor graphs instead of computing all pairwise distances. - Better global structure. The relative positions of clusters in the output tend to be more meaningful than in t-SNE. UMAP builds a weighted graph in high-dimensional space (the "fuzzy topological representation") and then finds a low-dimensional layout that preserves this graph as well as possible. Key parameters: - n_neighbors : how many neighbors define local structure (similar to perplexity). Higher values preserve more global structure. - min_dist : how tightly points pack together in the output. Lower values create denser clusters. In plain words first The idea in one line SVD is the Swiss Army knife of linear algebra. Every matrix has one. Every data scientist needs one. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means SVD "Factor any matrix" Decompose $A$ into $U \Sigma V^T$ where $U$ and $V$ are orthogonal and $\Sigma$ is diagonal with non-negative entries. Works for any matrix of any shape. Singular value "How important this component is" The $i$-th diagonal entry of $\Sigma$. Measures how much the matrix stretches along the i-th principal direction. Always non-negative, sorted in decreasing order. Left singular vector "Output direction" A column of $U$. The direction in output space that the $i$-th right singular vector maps to (after scaling by $\sigma_i$). Right singular vector "Input direction" A column of $V$. The direction in input space that the matrix maps to the $i$-th left singular vector (after scaling by $\sigma_i$). Truncated SVD "Low-rank approximation" Keep only the top $k$ singular values and their vectors. Produces the provably best $\text{rank-}k$ approximation to the original matrix (Eckart-Young theorem). Rank "True dimensionality" The number of non-zero singular values. Tells you how many independent directions the matrix actually uses. Pseudoinverse "Generalized inverse" $V \Sigma^+ U^T$. Inverts non-zero singular values, leaves zeros as zeros. Solves least-squares problems for non-square or singular matrices. Condition number "How sensitive to errors" $\sigma_{\max} / \sigma_{\min}$. A large condition number means small input changes cause large output changes. SVD reveals this directly. Latent factor "Hidden variable" A dimension in the low-rank space discovered by SVD. In recommendations, a latent factor might correspond to genre preference. In NLP, it might correspond to a topic. Frobenius norm "Total matrix size" Square root of the sum of squared entries. Equals the square root of the sum of squared singular values. Used to measure approximation error. Eckart-Young theorem "SVD gives the best compression" For any target rank $k$, the truncated SVD minimizes the approximation error over all possible $\text{rank-}k$ matrices. Power iteration "Find the biggest eigenvector" Repeatedly multiply a random vector by the matrix and normalize. Converges to the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue. The building block of many SVD algorithms. The problem In plain words first The singular value decomposition (SVD) splits any matrix into three simple steps: a rotation, a stretch along each axis, and another rotation. The stretch factors, the singular values , come sorted from largest to smallest, and each one says how much of the matrix lives in that direction. Keep the few largest and drop the rest and you get the best possible smaller approximation of the matrix, which is how SVD compresses images, removes noise and powers PCA and LoRA. You have a 1000x2000 matrix. Maybe it is user-movie ratings. Maybe it is a document-term frequency table. Maybe it is the pixel values of an image. You need to compress it, denoise it, find hidden structure in it, or solve a least-squares system with it. Eigendecomposition only works on square matrices. Even then, it requires the matrix to have a full set of linearly independent eigenvectors. SVD works on any matrix. Any shape. Any rank. No conditions. It decomposes the matrix into three factors that reveal the geometry of what the matrix does to space. It is the most general and most useful factorization in all of linear algebra. Idea 1 · What SVD does geometrically Every matrix, regardless of shape, performs three operations in sequence: rotate, scale, rotate. SVD makes this decomposition explicit. (any) ​ A ​ = m × m (rotate) ​ U ​ ⋅ m × n (scale) ​ Σ ​ ⋅ n × n (rotate) ​ V T ​ Given any matrix , SVD factors it into: - rotates vectors in the input space ( -dimensional) - scales along each axis (stretches or compresses) - rotates the result into the output space ( -dimensional) Think of it this way. You hand SVD a matrix. It tells you: "This matrix takes a sphere of inputs, first rotates it by , then stretches it into an ellipsoid by , then rotates the ellipsoid by ." The singular values are the lengths of the ellipsoid's axes. Idea 2 · The full decomposition For a matrix with shape : ​ A = U ⋅ Σ ⋅ V T where: U is m × m , orthogonal ( U T U = I ) Σ is m × n , diagonal (singular values on the diagonal) V is n × n , orthogonal ( V T V = I ) The singular values σ 1 ​ ≥ σ 2 ​ ≥ ⋯ ≥ σ r ​ > 0 where r = rank ( A ) ​ The columns of are called left singular vectors. The columns of are called right singular vectors. The diagonal entries of are called singular values. They are always non-negative and conventionally sorted in decreasing order. Idea 3 · Left singular vectors, singular values, right singular vectors Each component of the SVD has a distinct geometric meaning. Right singular vectors (columns of ): These form an orthonormal basis for the input space ( ). They are the directions in input space that the matrix maps to orthogonal directions in output space. Think of them as the natural coordinate system for the domain. Singular values (diagonal of ): These are the scaling factors. The i-th singular value tells you how much the matrix stretches vectors along the i-th right singular vector. A singular value of zero means the matrix crushes that direction entirely. Left singular vectors (columns of ): These form an orthonormal basis for the output space ( ). The i-th left singular vector is the direction in output space where the i-th right singular vector lands (after scaling). The relationship between them: Copy This gives you a coordinate-by-coordinate picture of what any matrix does. Idea 4 · Outer product form The SVD can be written as a sum of rank-1 matrices: Copy This form is the foundation of low-rank approximation. Each term adds one layer of structure. The first term captures the single most important pattern. The second captures the next most important. And so on. Truncating this sum gives you the best possible approximation at any given rank. Rank-2 approx: Rank- k approx: ​ A 1 ​ = σ 1 ​ u 1 ​ v 1 T ​ (captures the dominant pattern) A 2 ​ = σ 1 ​ u 1 ​ v 1 T ​ + σ 2 ​ u 2 ​ v 2 T ​ (captures the two most important patterns) A k ​ = sum of top k terms (optimal by the Eckart-Young theorem) ​ Idea 5 · Relationship to eigendecomposition SVD and eigendecomposition are deeply connected. The singular values and vectors of come directly from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A and . Copy This connection tells you three things: 1. Singular values are always real and non-negative (they are square roots of eigenvalues of a positive semi-definite matrix). 2. You could compute SVD via eigendecomposition of A , but this squares the condition number and loses numerical precision. Dedicated SVD algorithms avoid this. 3. When is square and symmetric positive semi-definite, SVD and eigendecomposition are the same thing. Check your mental model ✗ "SVD only works on square or symmetric matrices." ✓ It works on every matrix, any shape and any rank. That is its advantage over eigendecomposition. ✗ "Keeping the top k singular values gives a good approximation of any matrix." ✓ It gives the best rank-k approximation, but best can still be bad. Random noise has no structure, so 50 of 200 components still miss 67 percent of it (Step 3). ✗ "To get the pseudoinverse, invert every singular value." ✓ Invert only those above a tolerance. Inverting a singular value that is really 0 but stored as 10⁻¹⁶ multiplies noise by 10¹⁶; the broken exercise shows it. It is provably the best possible approximation of rank . No other matrix is closer to . Error = remaining values ( ​ through ​ ). If singular values decay fast, a small captures most of the matrix. If they decay slowly, the matrix has no low-rank structure. Idea 7 · Image compression with SVD A grayscale image is a matrix of pixel intensities. An 800x600 image has 480,000 values. SVD lets you approximate it with far fewer. Copy The key insight: natural images have rapidly decaying singular values. The first few singular values capture the broad structure (shapes, gradients). The later ones capture fine detail and noise. Truncating at rank 50 often produces an image that looks nearly identical to the original while using 85% less storage. Idea 8 · SVD for recommendation systems The Netflix Prize made this famous. You have a user-movie ratings matrix where most entries are missing. Copy The idea: this ratings matrix has low rank. Users do not have completely independent tastes. There are a handful of latent factors (action vs. drama, old vs. new, cerebral vs. visceral) that explain most preferences. SVD on the (filled-in) ratings matrix decomposes it into: - : user profiles in latent factor space - : importance of each latent factor - : movie profiles in latent factor space A user's predicted rating for a movie is the dot product of their user profile with the movie's profile (weighted by singular values). The low-rank approximation fills in the missing entries. In practice, you use variants like Simon Funk's incremental SVD or ALS (alternating least squares) that handle missing data directly. But the core idea is the same: latent factor decomposition via SVD. Idea 9 · SVD in NLP: Latent Semantic Analysis Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), also called Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI), applies SVD to a term-document matrix. Copy LSA was one of the first successful methods for capturing semantic similarity from raw text. It works because synonymous terms tend to appear in similar documents, so SVD groups them into the same latent dimensions. Modern word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) can be seen as descendants of this idea. Idea 10 · SVD for noise reduction Noisy data has signal concentrated in the top singular values and noise spread across all singular values. Truncating removes the noise floor. Clean signal singular values: Component Magnitude Type ​ Very large Signal ​ Large Signal ​ Medium Signal ​ Near zero Negligible ​ Near zero Negligible Noisy signal singular values (noise adds to all): Component Magnitude Type ​ Very large Signal ​ Large Signal ​ Medium Signal ​ Small Noise ​ Small Noise ​ Small Noise ​ Small Noise This is used in signal processing, scientific measurement, and data cleaning. Any time you have a matrix corrupted by additive noise, truncated SVD is a principled way to separate signal from noise. Idea 11 · Pseudoinverse via SVD The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse generalizes matrix inversion to non-square and singular matrices. SVD makes computing it trivial. Copy The pseudoinverse solves least-squares problems. If has no exact solution (overdetermined system), then b is the least-squares solution (minimizes ).
