In plain words first The idea in one line The square root of -1 is not imaginary. It is the key to rotations, frequencies, and half of signal processing. Terms you'll hear Term What it means Complex number A number $a + bi$ where $a$ is the real part, $b$ is the imaginary part, and $i^2 = -1$ Imaginary unit The number $i$, defined by $i^2 = -1$. Not imaginary in the philosophical sense -- it is a rotation operator Complex plane The 2D plane where the x-axis is real and the y-axis is imaginary. Also called the Argand plane Magnitude (modulus) The distance from the origin: $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. Written as $\lvert z \rvert$ Phase (argument) The angle from the positive real axis: $\mathop{\mathrm{atan2}}(b, a)$. Written as $\arg(z)$ Conjugate The mirror image across the real axis: conjugate of $a + bi$ is $a - bi$ Polar form Expressing $z$ as $r e^{i\theta}$ instead of $a + bi$. Makes multiplication easy Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i \sin\theta$. Connects exponentials to trigonometry Phasor A rotating complex number $e^{i\omega t}$ representing a sinusoidal signal Roots of unity The $N$ complex numbers $e^{2\pi i k/N}$ for $k = 0$ to $N-1$. $N$ equally spaced points on the unit circle DFT Discrete Fourier Transform. Decomposes a signal into complex sinusoidal components using roots of unity RoPE Rotary Position Embedding. Uses complex multiplication to encode relative position in transformer attention The problem In plain words first A complex number is a point on a plane, a + bi , where i is defined by i² = −1 . The useful fact is what multiplication does: multiplying by a complex number of length 1 rotates a point, and multiplying by any complex number rotates and scales it. Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ , packs a rotation by θ into one number. That is why signals are analysed with complex numbers (the Fourier transform) and why transformers encode positions with rotations (RoPE). You open a paper on Fourier transforms and there is i everywhere. You look at transformer positional encodings and see sin and cos at different frequencies -- the real and imaginary parts of complex exponentials. You read about quantum computing and find everything expressed in complex vector spaces. Complex numbers seem abstract. A number system built on the square root of -1 feels like a mathematical trick. But it is not a trick. It is the natural language of rotations and oscillations. Every time something spins, vibrates, or oscillates, complex numbers are the right tool. Without understanding complex numbers, you cannot understand the Discrete Fourier Transform. You cannot understand FFT. You cannot understand how RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) works in modern language models. You cannot understand why sinusoidal positional encodings in the original Transformer paper use the frequencies they do. This lesson builds complex arithmetic from scratch, connects it to geometry, and shows you exactly where complex numbers appear in machine learning. Idea 1 · What is a complex number? The Fourier transform finds how much of each frequency is in it: the spectrum . The direct method (the DFT) costs N² steps; the FFT gets the same answer in about N log N by splitting the work in halves, which is why it runs everywhere from audio apps to speech models. Multiplying spectra is the same as convolving signals, the operation at the heart of CNNs. An audio recording is a sequence of pressure measurements over time. A stock price is a sequence of values over days. An image is a grid of pixel intensities over space. All of these are data in the time domain (or space domain). You see values changing over some index. But many patterns are invisible in the time domain. Is this audio signal a pure tone or a chord? Does this stock price have a weekly cycle? Does this image have a repeating texture? These questions are about frequency content, and the time domain hides it. The Fourier transform converts data from the time domain to the frequency domain. It takes a signal and decomposes it into sine waves of different frequencies. Each sine wave has an amplitude (how strong it is) and a phase (where it starts). The Fourier transform tells you both. This matters for ML because frequency-domain thinking appears everywhere. Convolutional neural networks perform convolution, which is multiplication in the frequency domain. Transformer positional encodings use frequency decomposition to represent position. Audio models (speech recognition, music generation) operate on spectrograms -- frequency representations of sound. Time series models look for periodic patterns. Understanding the Fourier transform gives you the vocabulary to work with all of these. Idea 1 · The DFT definition Given samples , the Discrete Fourier Transform produces frequency coefficients : ∑ N − 1 ​ x [ n ] e − 2 πikn / N for k = 0 , 1 , … , N − 1 Each is a complex number. Its magnitude is proportional to the amplitude of frequency . Without normalization, a real sine of amplitude that falls exactly on bin gives , so divide by to read the amplitude. Its phase tells you the phase offset of that frequency. The key insight: is a rotating phasor at frequency . The DFT computes the correlation between the signal and each of equally-spaced frequencies. If the signal contains energy at frequency , the correlation is large. If not, it is near zero. Idea 2 · What each coefficient means : the DC component. This is the sum of all samples -- proportional to the mean. It represents the constant (zero-frequency) offset of the signal. ∑ N − 1 ​ x [ n ] e 0 = sum of all samples for : positive frequencies. represents frequency cycles per samples. Higher means higher frequency (faster oscillation). : the Nyquist frequency. The highest frequency you can represent with samples. Above this, you get aliasing -- high frequencies masquerading as low ones. for : negative frequencies. For real-valued signals, ​ . The negative frequencies are mirror images of the positive ones. This is why the useful information is in the first coefficients. Idea 3 · Inverse DFT The inverse DFT reconstructs the original signal from its frequency coefficients: 1 ​ k = 0 ∑ N − 1 ​ X [ k ] e 2 πikn / N for n = 0 , 1 , … , N − 1 The only differences from the forward DFT: the sign in the exponent is positive (not negative), and there is a normalization factor. The inverse DFT is perfect reconstruction. No information is lost. You can go from time domain to frequency domain and back without any error. The DFT is a change of basis -- it re-expresses the same information in a different coordinate system. Idea 4 · The FFT: making it fast The DFT as defined above is ) : for each of output coefficients, you sum over input samples. For = 1 million, that is operations. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) computes the same result in . For = 1 million, that is about 20 million operations instead of a trillion. This is what makes frequency analysis practical. The Cooley-Tukey algorithm (the most common FFT) works by divide and conquer: Split the signal into even-indexed and odd-indexed samples. Compute the DFT of each half recursively. Combine the two half-size DFTs using "twiddle factors" . X [ k + N /2 ] where E O ​ = E [ k ] + e − 2 πik / N O [ k ] = E [ k ] − e − 2 πik / N O [ k ] = DFT of even-indexed samples = DFT of odd-indexed samples ​ ​ for k = 0 , … , N /2 − 1 for k = 0 , … , N /2 − 1 ​ The symmetry means each level of recursion does work, and there are ​ ( N ) levels. Library FFTs such as numpy.fft handle any length with mixed-radix algorithms, but they are fastest on lengths with small prime factors. Idea 8 · Windowing The DFT assumes the signal is periodic -- it treats the samples as one period of an infinitely repeating signal. If the signal does not start and end at the same value, this creates a discontinuity at the boundary, which shows up as spurious high-frequency content. This is called spectral leakage. Windowing reduces leakage by tapering the signal to zero at both ends before computing the DFT. Idea 10 · Connection to positional encodings The original Transformer uses sinusoidal positional encodings: PE ( p os , 2 i + 1 ) ​ = sin ( p os /1000 0 2 i / d model ​ ) = cos ( p os /1000 0 2 i / d model ​ ) ​ Each dimension pair oscillates at a different frequency. The key properties this provides: Uniqueness: No two positions have the same encoding. Bounded values: sin and cos are always in . Relative position: The encoding of position can be expressed as a linear function of the encoding at position . The model can learn to attend to relative positions. Idea 11 · Connection to CNNs A convolution layer applies a learned filter (kernel) to the input by sliding it across the signal or image. Mathematically, this is the convolution operation. By the convolution theorem, this is equivalent to: 1. FFT the input 2. FFT the kernel 3. Multiply in frequency domain 4. IFFT the result Standard CNN implementations use direct convolution (faster for small 3x3 kernels). But for large kernels or global convolution, FFT-based approaches are significantly faster. Some architectures (like FNet) replace attention entirely with FFT, achieving competitive accuracy with instead of ) complexity. Idea 12 · Spectrograms and the Short-Time Fourier Transform A single FFT gives you the frequency content of the entire signal, but tells you nothing about when those frequencies occur. A chirp (a signal whose frequency increases over time) and a chord (all frequencies present simultaneously) can have the same magnitude spectrum. The Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) solves this by computing FFTs on overlapping windows of the signal. The result is a spectrogram: a 2D representation with time on one axis and frequency on the other. The intensity at each point shows the energy at that frequency at that time. Copy Spectrograms are the standard input representation for audio ML models. Speech recognition models (Whisper, DeepSpeech) operate on mel-spectrograms -- spectrograms with frequencies mapped to the mel scale, which better matches human pitch perception. Idea 13 · Aliasing If a signal contains frequencies above ​ /2 (the Nyquist frequency), sampling at rate ​ will create aliased copies. A 90 Hz signal sampled at 100 Hz looks identical to a 10 Hz signal. There is no way to distinguish them from the samples alone. Copy This is why analog-to-digital converters include anti-aliasing filters that remove frequencies above Nyquist before sampling. In ML, aliasing appears when downsampling feature maps without proper low-pass filtering -- some architectures address this with anti-aliased pooling layers. The FFT computes the same DFT in O(N log N) by recursive halving. Frequency resolution is the sample rate divided by N; frequencies above half the sample rate alias. Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency. Window before an FFT to limit leakage; use spectrograms (STFT) for signals that change over time. Solutions Solution P1 · The speed-up In operation counts, N / log₂ N = 1,024 / 10 ≈ 100 times. The measured ratio is in that range but not exactly 100 (about 160 on a quiet machine): constant factors differ, the recursive Python FFT pays for list building and function calls, and the DFT pays for creating millions of Complex objects. For N = 1,000,000 the ratio would be about 50,000, the difference between milliseconds and hours. Solution B1 · Odd lengths fall back to the slow path fft splits the signal in half only while the length is even. 1,024 = 2¹⁰ halves all the way down. 1,000 = 2³ × 125 halves three times, then reaches 125 samples, which is odd, and calls the O(N²) dft on eight blocks of 125. The answer is still right, just much slower. Library FFTs handle any length with other factorisations, but powers of two remain the fastest case, which is why audio frames are usually 256, 512 or 1,024 samples. Use it: the same idea with real libraries For real work, use numpy's FFT which is backed by highly optimized C libraries. In plain words first The idea in one line Graphs are the data structure of relationships. If your data has connections, you need graph theory. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Graph "Nodes and edges" A mathematical structure $G=(V,E)$ encoding pairwise relationships Adjacency matrix "The connection table" An $n \times n$ matrix where $A[i][j] = 1$ if nodes $i$ and $j$ are connected Degree "How connected a node is" The number of edges touching a node Laplacian "D minus A" $L = D - A$, the matrix whose eigenvalues reveal graph structure Fiedler value "The algebraic connectivity" The smallest non-zero eigenvalue of $L$, measuring how well-connected the graph is BFS "Level-by-level search" Traversal that visits all neighbors before going deeper, finds shortest paths DFS "Go deep first" Traversal that follows one path to its end before backtracking Message passing "Nodes talk to neighbors" Each node aggregates information from its neighbors, the core of GNNs Spectral clustering "Cluster by eigenvectors" Partition a graph using eigenvectors of its Laplacian Connected component "A separate piece" A maximal subgraph where every node can reach every other node The problem In plain words first A graph is a set of things (nodes) and the connections between them (edges): people and friendships, atoms and bonds, web pages and links. Store it as an adjacency matrix and linear algebra applies: the Laplacian matrix's eigenvalues count the separate pieces of the graph and reveal where it is easiest to cut. Graph neural networks work by message passing : each node repeatedly replaces its features with an average of its neighbours'. Social networks, molecules, knowledge bases, citation networks, road maps -- all are graphs. Traditional ML treats data as flat tables. Each row is independent. Each feature is a column. But when the structure of connections matters, tables fail. Consider a social network. You want to predict what product a user will buy. Their purchase history matters. But their friends' purchase history matters more. The connections carry signal. Or consider a molecule. You want to predict if it binds to a protein. The atoms matter, but what really matters is how atoms are bonded to each other. The structure is the data. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are the fastest-growing area in deep learning. They power drug discovery, social recommendation, fraud detection, and knowledge graph reasoning. Every GNN builds on the same foundation: basic graph theory. You need four things: 1. A way to represent graphs as matrices (so you can multiply them) 2. Traversal algorithms to explore graph structure 3. The Laplacian -- the single most important matrix in spectral graph theory 4. Message passing -- the operation that makes GNNs work Idea 1 · Graphs: Nodes and Edges A graph consists of vertices (nodes) and edges . Each edge connects two nodes. Directed vs undirected. In an undirected graph, edge means connects to AND connects to . In a directed graph (digraph), edge means points to , but not necessarily the reverse. Weighted vs unweighted. In an unweighted graph, edges either exist or they don't. In a weighted graph, each edge has a numerical weight -- a distance, a cost, a strength. Graph type Example Undirected, unweighted Facebook friendship network Directed, unweighted Twitter follow network Undirected, weighted Road map (distances) Directed, weighted Web page links (PageRank scores) Idea 2 · The Adjacency Matrix The adjacency matrix is the core representation. For a graph with nodes: 0 ​ if there is an edge from node i to node j otherwise ​ For undirected graphs, is symmetric: . For weighted graphs, = weight of edge . Example -- a triangle: Copy The adjacency matrix is the input to every GNN. Matrix operations on correspond to operations on the graph. Idea 3 · Degree The degree of a node is the number of edges connected to it. For directed graphs, you have in-degree (edges coming in) and out-degree (edges going out). The degree matrix is diagonal: D [ i ] [ j ] ​ = degree of node i = 0 for i  = j ​ For the triangle example: ( 2 , 2 , 2 ) because every node connects to two others. Degree tells you about node importance. High degree = hub node. The degree distribution of a network reveals its structure. Social networks follow power laws (few hubs, many leaf nodes). Random graphs have Poisson-distributed degrees. Worked example Worked by hand Two groups of four nodes, each group fully connected, joined by one bridge edge between node 3 and node 4. Nodes 0, 1, 2 have degree 3; nodes 3 and 4 have degree 4 (three friends plus the bridge); 5, 6, 7 have degree 3. Total degree 3 × 6 + 4 × 2 = 26, which is twice the 13 edges (6 + 6 + 1), because every edge is counted at both ends. Idea 4 · BFS and DFS The two fundamental graph traversal algorithms. You need both. Breadth-First Search (BFS): Explore all neighbors first, then neighbors' neighbors. Uses a queue (FIFO). Copy BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. The distance from the start to any node equals the BFS level at which that node is first discovered. This is why BFS is used for hop-count distances in social networks. Depth-First Search (DFS): Go as deep as possible before backtracking. Uses a stack (LIFO) or recursion. Copy DFS is useful for: - Finding connected components (run DFS from unvisited nodes) - Cycle detection (back edges in DFS tree) - Topological sorting (reverse DFS finish order) Algorithm Data structure Finds Use case BFS Queue Shortest paths Social network distance, knowledge graph traversal DFS Stack Components, cycles Connectivity, topological sort Idea 5 · The Graph Laplacian . The most important matrix in spectral graph theory. For the triangle: ​ 2 0 0 ​ 0 2 0 ​ 0 0 2 ​ ​ A = ​ 0 1 1 ​ 1 0 1 ​ 1 1 0 ​ ​ L = ​ 2 − 1 − 1 ​ − 1 2 − 1 ​ − 1 − 1 2 ​ ​ The Laplacian has remarkable properties: is positive semi-definite. All eigenvalues are . The number of zero eigenvalues equals the number of connected components. A connected graph has exactly one zero eigenvalue. A graph with 3 disconnected components has three zero eigenvalues. The smallest non-zero eigenvalue (Fiedler value) measures connectivity. A large Fiedler value means the graph is well-connected. A small Fiedler value means the graph has a weak point -- a bottleneck. The eigenvector of the Fiedler value (Fiedler vector) reveals the best split. Nodes with positive values go in one group, nodes with negative values go in the other. This is spectral clustering. Idea 6 · Spectral Properties The eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix and Laplacian reveal structural properties without any traversal. Spectral clustering works like this: 1. Compute the Laplacian 2. Find the smallest eigenvectors of (skip the first, which is all-ones for connected graphs) 3. Use those eigenvectors as new coordinates for each node 4. Run -means on those coordinates Why does this work? The eigenvectors of encode the "smoothest" functions on the graph. Nodes that are well-connected get similar eigenvector values. Nodes separated by a bottleneck get different values. The eigenvectors naturally separate clusters. Random walk connection. The normalized Laplacian relates to random walks on the graph. The stationary distribution of a random walk is proportional to node degree. The mixing time (how fast the walk converges) depends on the spectral gap. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Randomness with structure. The math behind random walks, Markov chains, and diffusion models. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Random walk "Coin-flip movement" A process where position changes by random increments at each step Markov property "Memoryless" The future depends only on the present state, not on the history Transition matrix "The probability table" $P[i][j]$ = probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ Stationary distribution "The long-run average" The distribution $\pi$ where $\pi P = \pi$ -- the chain's equilibrium Brownian motion "Random jiggling" The continuous-time limit of a random walk, $B(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t)$ Langevin dynamics "Gradient descent with noise" Update rule that combines deterministic gradient and random perturbation MCMC "Walking toward the target" Constructing a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the one you want Metropolis-Hastings "Propose and accept/reject" MCMC algorithm that uses acceptance ratios to ensure convergence Temperature "The randomness knob" Parameter controlling the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation Diffusion process "Noise in, noise out" Forward: gradually add noise. Reverse: gradually remove it. Generates data. The problem In plain words first A stochastic process is a quantity that changes over time with some randomness: a random walk, the weather from day to day, the next word in a sentence. In a Markov chain the next state depends only on the current one, through a table of transition probabilities. Run such a chain long enough and it forgets where it started, settling into a stationary distribution . Language models, MCMC samplers and diffusion models are all built on this idea. Many AI systems involve randomness that evolves over time. Not static randomness -- structured, sequential randomness where each step depends on what came before. Language models generate tokens one at a time. Each token depends on the previous context. The model outputs a probability distribution, samples from it, and moves on. That is a stochastic process. Diffusion models add noise to an image step by step until it becomes pure static. Then they reverse the process, denoising step by step until a new image emerges. The forward process is a Markov chain. The reverse process is a learned Markov chain running backward. Reinforcement learning agents take actions in an environment. Each action leads to a new state with some probability. The agent follows a random policy in a random world. The whole thing is a Markov decision process. MCMC sampling -- the backbone of Bayesian inference -- constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior you want to sample from. All of these build on four foundational ideas: 1. Random walks -- the simplest stochastic process 2. Markov chains -- structured randomness with a transition matrix 3. Langevin dynamics -- gradient descent with noise 4. Metropolis-Hastings -- sampling from any distribution Idea 1 · Random Walks Start at position 0. At each step, flip a fair coin. Heads: move right (+1). Tails: move left (-1). After steps, your position is the sum of random values. The expected position is 0 (the walk is unbiased). But the expected distance from the origin grows as ​ . This is counterintuitive. The walk is fair -- no drift in either direction. But over time, it wanders further and further from where it started. The standard deviation after steps is ​ . Copy In 2D , the walk moves up, down, left, or right with equal probability. The same ​ scaling applies to the distance from the origin. The path traces a fractal-like pattern. Why ​ ? Each step is +1 or -1 with equal probability. After steps, the position ​ = X 1 ​ + X 2 ​ + ⋯ + X n ​ where each ​ is . The variance of each step is 1, and the steps are independent, so ( S n ​ ) = n . Standard deviation = ​ . By the central limit theorem, ​ / n ​ converges to a standard normal distribution. This ​ scaling shows up everywhere in ML. SGD noise scales as 1/sqrt(batch_size). Embedding dimensions scale as ​ . The square root is the signature of independent random additions. Connection to Brownian motion. Take a random walk with step size ​ and steps per unit time. As goes to infinity, the walk converges to Brownian motion -- a continuous-time process where is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance . Brownian motion is the mathematical foundation of diffusion. It models the random jiggling of particles in a fluid, the fluctuations of stock prices, and -- crucially -- the noise process in diffusion models. Gambler's ruin. A random walker starting at position , with absorbing barriers at 0 and . What is the probability of reaching before 0? For a fair walk: . This is surprisingly simple and elegant. It connects to the theory of martingales -- the fair random walk is a martingale (expected future value = current value). Idea 2 · Markov Chains A Markov chain is a system that transitions between states according to fixed probabilities. The key property: the next state depends only on the current state, not on the history. ​ = j ∣ X t ​ = i , X t − 1 ​ = … ) = P ( X t + 1 ​ = j ∣ X t ​ = i ) This is the Markov property. It means you can describe the entire dynamics with a transition matrix : Each row of sums to 1 (you must go somewhere). Example -- Weather: Copy Start in any state. After many transitions, the distribution of states converges to the stationary distribution , where . This is the left eigenvector of with eigenvalue 1. For the weather chain, the stationary distribution is [0.55, 0.18, 0.27] -- over the long run, it is sunny 55% of the time regardless of the starting state. Computing the stationary distribution. There are two approaches: Power method : multiply any initial distribution by repeatedly. After enough iterations, it converges. Eigenvalue method : find the left eigenvector of with eigenvalue 1. This is the eigenvector of with eigenvalue 1. Both approaches require the chain to satisfy convergence conditions. Convergence conditions. A Markov chain converges to a unique stationary distribution if it is: - Irreducible : every state is reachable from every other state - Aperiodic : the chain does not cycle with a fixed period Most chains you encounter in ML satisfy both conditions. Absorbing states. A state is absorbing if once you enter it, you never leave ( ). Absorbing Markov chains model processes with terminal states -- a game that ends, a customer who churns, a token sequence that hits the end-of-text token. Mixing time. How many steps until the chain is "close" to the stationary distribution? Formally, the number of steps until the total variation distance from stationarity drops below some threshold. Fast mixing = few steps needed. For a reversible chain, the spectral gap of (1 minus the largest eigenvalue magnitude other than the eigenvalue 1) controls the mixing time. Larger gap = faster mixing. Worked example Worked by hand Take the chain from Use it, with transition matrix rows [0.7, 0.1, 0.2] , [0.3, 0.4, 0.3] , [0.4, 0.2, 0.4] . Idea 6 · MCMC: Markov Chain Monte Carlo Sometimes you need to sample from a distribution that you can evaluate (up to a constant) but cannot sample from directly. Bayesian posteriors are the classic example -- you know the likelihood times the prior, but the normalizing constant is intractable. Metropolis-Hastings constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is : Start at some position Propose a new position from a proposal distribution ∣ x ) Compute acceptance ratio: ) Q ( x ∣ x ′ ) / ( p ( x ) Q ( x ′ ∣ x )) Accept with probability . Otherwise stay at . Repeat. If is symmetric (e.g., ∣ x ) = Q ( x ∣ x ′ ) = N ( x , σ 2 ) ), the ratio simplifies to ) / p ( x ) . You only need the ratio of probabilities -- the normalizing constant cancels. The chain is guaranteed to converge to under mild conditions. But convergence can be slow if the proposal is too small (random walk) or too large (high rejection). Tuning the proposal is the art of MCMC. Why it works. The acceptance ratio ensures detailed balance: the probability of being at and moving to equals the probability of being at and moving to . Detailed balance implies that is the stationary distribution of the chain. So after enough steps, the samples come from . Practical considerations: - Burn-in : discard the first samples. The chain needs time to reach the stationary distribution from its starting point. - Thinning : keep every -th sample to reduce autocorrelation. - Multiple chains : run several chains from different starting points. If they converge to the same distribution, you have evidence of convergence. - Acceptance rate : for Gaussian proposals in dimensions, the optimal acceptance rate is about 23% (Roberts & Rosenthal, 2001). Too high means the chain barely moves. Too low means it rejects everything. a0201: Course home / Phase 2 · Machine Learning Algorithms Machine Learning: What It Is and How It Works Lesson 2.1 45 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the difference between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning and identify which type applies to a given problem Implement a nearest centroid classifier from scratch and evaluate it against a random baseline Distinguish between classification and regression tasks and select the appropriate loss function for each Evaluate whether a given business problem is suitable for ML or better solved with deterministic rules Before you start Needs : Phase 1 (Mathematics for Machine Learning) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Machine learning is teaching computers to find patterns in data instead of writing rules by hand. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Model "The AI" A mathematical function with learnable parameters that maps inputs to outputs Training "Teaching the AI" Running an optimization algorithm to adjust model parameters so predictions match known outputs Feature "An input column" A measurable property of the data that the model uses to make predictions Label "The answer" The known output for a training example, used to compute the error signal Hyperparameter "A setting you tweak" A parameter set before training that controls the learning process (learning rate, number of layers) Loss function "How wrong the model is" A function that measures the gap between predicted and actual outputs, which training tries to minimize Overfitting "It memorized the test" The model learned training-specific noise instead of general patterns, so it fails on new data Underfitting "It didn't learn anything" The model is too simple to capture the real patterns in the data Generalization "It works on new data" The model's ability to make accurate predictions on data it was not trained on Cross-validation "Testing on different chunks" Repeatedly splitting data into train/test folds and averaging results, giving a more robust performance estimate Regularization "Keeping weights small" Adding a penalty term to the loss function that discourages overly complex models Data drift "The world changed" The statistical distribution of incoming data shifts over time, degrading model performance The problem In plain words first Ordinary programming means writing the rules yourself. Machine learning means showing a program examples with the right answers and letting it find the rules: the training data goes in, a model comes out, and you judge the model only on examples it has never seen (the test set ). Everything in this phase is a variation on that loop, plus the discipline of comparing against a dumb baseline so you know the model learned something. You want to build a spam filter. The traditional approach: sit down and write hundreds of rules. "If the email contains 'FREE MONEY', mark it spam. If it has more than 3 exclamation marks, mark it spam." You spend weeks writing rules. Then spammers change their wording. Your rules break. You write more rules. The cycle never ends. Machine learning flips this. Instead of writing rules, you give the computer thousands of labeled emails ("spam" or "not spam") and let it figure out the rules on its own. The computer finds patterns you never would have thought of. When spammers change tactics, you retrain on new data instead of rewriting code. This shift from "programming rules" to "learning from data" is the core of machine learning. Every recommendation engine, voice assistant, self-driving car, and language model works this way. Idea 1 · Learning From Data, Not Rules Traditional programming and machine learning solve problems in opposite directions. Traditional programming: you write the rules. The program applies them to data to produce output. Machine learning: you provide data and expected outputs. The algorithm discovers the rules. The "model" that comes out of training IS the rules, encoded as numbers (weights, parameters). It generalizes from examples it has seen to make predictions on data it has never seen. Idea 2 · The Three Types of Machine Learning Supervised Learning : You have input-output pairs. The model learns to map inputs to outputs. - "Here are 10,000 photos labeled cat or dog. Learn to tell them apart." - "Here are house features and prices. Learn to predict the price." Unsupervised Learning : You have inputs only. No labels. The model finds structure on its own. - "Here are 10,000 customer purchase histories. Find natural groupings." - "Here are 1,000 dimensional data points. Reduce to 2 dimensions while keeping structure." Reinforcement Learning : An agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards or penalties. It learns a strategy (policy) to maximize total reward. - "Play this game. +1 for winning, -1 for losing. Figure out a strategy." - "Control this robot arm. +1 for picking up the object, -0.01 for each second wasted." Most of what you will build in practice uses supervised learning. Unsupervised learning is common for preprocessing and exploration. Reinforcement learning powers game AI, robotics, and RLHF for language models. Idea 3 · Beyond the Big Three The three categories above are clean, but real-world ML often blurs the lines. Semi-supervised learning uses a small set of labeled data and a large set of unlabeled data. You might have 100 labeled medical images and 100,000 unlabeled ones. Techniques include: Label propagation: Build a graph connecting similar data points. Labels spread from labeled nodes to unlabeled neighbors through the graph. Pseudo-labeling: Train a model on the labeled data, use it to predict labels for unlabeled data, then retrain on everything. The model bootstraps its own training set. Consistency regularization: The model should give the same prediction for an input and a slightly perturbed version of that input. This works even without labels. Self-supervised learning creates supervision from the data itself. No human labels needed at all. The model creates its own prediction task from the structure of the data. Masked language modeling (BERT): Hide 15% of words in a sentence, train the model to predict the missing words. The "labels" come from the original text. Contrastive learning (SimCLR): Take an image, create two augmented versions. Train the model to recognize they came from the same image while distinguishing them from augmented versions of other images. Next-token prediction (GPT): Predict the next word given all previous words. Every text document becomes a training example. These are not separate categories from the big three. They are strategies that combine supervised and unsupervised ideas. Self-supervised learning is technically supervised (the model predicts something), but the labels are generated automatically, not by humans. Idea 4 · Classification vs Regression These are the two main supervised learning tasks. Aspect Classification Regression Output Discrete categories Continuous numbers Example "Is this email spam?" "What will the house price be?" Output space {cat, dog, bird} Any real number Loss function Cross-entropy, accuracy Mean squared error, MAE Decision Boundaries between classes A curve that fits the data Classification answers "which category?" Regression answers "how much?" Some problems can be framed either way. Predicting if a stock goes up or down is classification. Predicting the exact price is regression. Check your mental model ✗ "High accuracy on the training data means the model is good." ✓ A model can memorise its training data. Only data it has never seen tells you how it will do in use. ✗ "Predicting a number is regression and predicting a label is classification, so a model of probabilities is regression." ✓ Logistic regression outputs a probability and is used for classification. The task type depends on what you finally predict, not on the number the model computes. ✗ "A fancier algorithm always beats a simple one." ✓ The No Free Lunch theorem says no algorithm wins on every problem. Start simple, and add complexity only when the simple model's mistakes justify it. Idea 5 · The ML Workflow Every machine learning project follows the same pipeline, regardless of the algorithm. Collect Data : Gather raw data. More data is almost always better, but quality matters more than quantity. Clean & Explore : Handle missing values, remove duplicates, visualize distributions, spot anomalies. This step often takes 60-80% of total project time. Feature Engineering : Transform raw data into features the model can use. Turn dates into day-of-week. Normalize numerical columns. Encode categorical variables. Good features matter more than fancy algorithms. Split Data : Divide into training, validation, and test sets. The model trains on training data, you tune hyperparameters on validation data, and you report final performance on test data. Train Model : Feed training data into an algorithm. The algorithm adjusts internal parameters to minimize a loss function. Evaluate : Measure performance on validation/test data. If performance is not acceptable, go back and try different features, algorithms, or hyperparameters. Deploy : Put the model into production where it makes predictions on new data. Monitor : Track performance over time. Data distributions change (data drift), and models degrade. When performance drops, retrain. Idea 6 · Training, Validation, and Test Splits This is the most important concept beginners get wrong. You must evaluate your model on data it has never seen during training. Otherwise you are measuring memorization, not learning. Split Purpose When used Typical size Training Model learns from this data During training 60-80% Validation Tune hyperparameters, compare models After each training run 10-20% Test Final unbiased performance estimate Once, at the very end 10-20% The test set is sacred. You look at it exactly once. If you keep adjusting your model based on test performance, you are effectively training on the test set and your reported numbers are meaningless. For small datasets, use k-fold cross-validation: split data into parts, train on parts, validate on the remaining part, rotate, and average results. Idea 7 · Overfitting vs Underfitting Underfitting : The model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data. A straight line trying to fit a curved relationship. Training error is high. Test error is high. Overfitting : The model is too complex and memorizes the training data, including its noise. A wiggly curve that passes through every training point but fails on new data. Training error is low. Test error is high. Good fit : The model captures real patterns without memorizing noise. Training error and test error are both reasonably low. Signs of overfitting: - Training accuracy is much higher than validation accuracy - The model performs well on training data but poorly on new data - Adding more training data improves performance (the model was memorizing, not learning) Fixes for overfitting: - Get more training data - Reduce model complexity (fewer parameters, simpler architecture) - Regularization (add a penalty for large weights) - Dropout (randomly zero out neurons during training) - Early stopping (stop training when validation error starts increasing) Fixes for underfitting: - Use a more complex model - Add more features - Reduce regularization - Train longer Predict before you run The two classes below are bell-shaped clouds centred at (1, 1) and (−1, −1). The nearest-centroid classifier draws a straight line halfway between their means. Roughly what test accuracy do you expect: near 100 percent, around 85, or around 50? (Solution P1.) Idea 8 · The Bias-Variance Tradeoff This is the mathematical framework behind overfitting and underfitting. Bias : Error from wrong assumptions in the model. A linear model has high bias when the true relationship is nonlinear. High bias leads to underfitting. Variance : Error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training data. A model with high variance gives very different predictions when trained on different subsets of data. High variance leads to overfitting. Model complexity Bias Variance Result Too low (linear model for curved data) High Low Underfitting Just right Medium Medium Good generalization Too high (degree-20 polynomial for 10 points) Low High Overfitting + Variance + Irreducible noise You cannot reduce irreducible noise (it is randomness in the data itself). You want to find the sweet spot where + variance is minimized. Idea 9 · No Free Lunch Theorem There is no single algorithm that works best for every problem. An algorithm that performs well on one class of problems will perform poorly on another. This is why data scientists try multiple algorithms and compare results. In practice, the choice depends on: - How much data you have - How many features there are - Whether the relationship is linear or nonlinear - Whether you need interpretability - How much compute you can afford Idea 10 · When NOT to Use Machine Learning ML is powerful but not always the right tool. Before reaching for a model, ask whether you actually need one. Do not use ML when: Rules are simple and well-defined. Tax calculation, sorting algorithms, unit conversions. If you can write the logic in a few if-statements, a model adds complexity for no benefit. You have no data or very little data. ML needs examples to learn from. With 10 data points, you cannot train anything meaningful. Collect data first. The cost of being wrong is catastrophic and you need guaranteed correctness. Medical dosage calculation, nuclear reactor control, cryptographic verification. ML models are probabilistic. They will sometimes be wrong. If "sometimes wrong" is unacceptable, use deterministic methods. A lookup table or heuristic solves the problem. If a simple threshold or table covers 99% of cases, adding ML increases maintenance cost without meaningful improvement. You cannot explain the decision and explainability is required. Regulated industries (lending, insurance, criminal justice) sometimes require that every decision be fully explainable. Some ML models are interpretable (linear regression, small decision trees). Most are not. The problem changes faster than you can retrain. If the rules change daily and retraining takes a week, the model is always stale. Given labelled examples ​ , y i ​ ) , a family of models and a loss , training picks ​ = ar g f ∈ F min ​ n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ ℓ ( f ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) (the empirical risk ). What we care about is the error on new data from the same source, , which we can only estimate on examples the model never saw: the test set. The generalisation gap is the difference between the two. How precise is a test score? An accuracy measured on independent test examples has standard error ( 1 − a ^ ) / m ​ so a 95% interval is about ± 2 SE . Two models whose scores differ by less than that are not clearly different. Bias and variance. For squared error, the expected test error at a point splits into noise (irreducible), bias² (the model family cannot represent the truth: underfitting) and variance (the fitted model changes a lot with the training sample: overfitting). Lesson 2.15 derives it. Worked example How big a test set? By hand A classifier scores 90% accuracy. On 100 test examples: ​ = 0.03 , so the truth is plausibly anywhere from 84% to 96%. To tell a 90% model from a 91% one you need the interval narrower than one point, which takes several thousand test examples. Ten times the precision costs a hundred times the data. Step 1 · Nearest Centroid Classifier from Scratch The code in code/ml_intro.py implements a nearest centroid classifier from scratch, the simplest possible ML algorithm. It demonstrates the core idea: learn from data, then predict on new data. The nearest centroid classifier computes the center (mean) of each class in the training data. To predict, it assigns each new point to the class whose center is closest. Copy That is the entire algorithm. Fit computes two means. Predict computes distances. No gradient descent, no iteration, no hyperparameters. Step 2 · Train on Synthetic Data We generate a 2D classification dataset with two classes that overlap slightly. The centroid classifier draws a linear decision boundary between the class centers. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Step 3 · Compare Against a Baseline Every ML model should be compared against a trivial baseline. Here, the baseline predicts a random class. If your ML model does not beat random guessing, something is wrong. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The centroid classifier should get around 90%+ accuracy on this clean dataset. Random baseline gets around 50%. Reading this output The random baseline scored 0.65 on these 40 test points, well above its expected 0.5: with so few test points luck matters a lot, which is itself a lesson about small test sets. A better baseline for imbalanced data is "always predict the most common class", and every result in this course should beat it. Build · Why This Matters The nearest centroid classifier is trivially simple. It has no hyperparameters, no iteration, no gradient descent. Yet it captures the fundamental ML pattern: Learn a representation from training data (the centroids) Predict on new data using that representation (nearest distance) Evaluate against a baseline (random guessing) Every ML algorithm, from logistic regression to transformers, follows this same three-step pattern. The representation gets more complex, but the workflow stays the same. Step 4 · What the Centroid Classifier Cannot Do The nearest centroid classifier assumes each class forms a single blob. It draws linear decision boundaries. It fails when: Classes have multiple clusters (e.g., the digit "1" can be written in several different ways) The decision boundary is nonlinear (e.g., one class wraps around another) Features have very different scales (distance is dominated by the largest-scale feature) These limitations motivate every other algorithm you will learn. K-nearest neighbors handles multiple clusters. Decision trees handle nonlinear boundaries. Feature scaling fixes the scale problem. Each lesson builds on the limitations of the previous one. Split data into train, validation and test; judge the model only on data it never trained on. Always compare with a baseline; a model that cannot beat it has learned nothing useful. Underfitting is too simple a model, overfitting is memorising noise; the bias-variance trade-off sits between them. Simple models fail in predictable ways, and each failure motivates a later algorithm. Solutions Solution P1 · Two overlapping clouds Around 85 percent : the run gets 0.825 on this split. The clouds overlap, because points from each are spread with standard deviation 1 around centres only about 2.8 apart, so some points from each class sit on the wrong side of any line. Distances are now dominated by the noise feature, whose values are around 100 times larger than the two useful ones, so "nearest centroid" mostly measures noise. Standardising every feature (subtract its training mean, divide by its training standard deviation) restores about 0.85. Short answer. I ask whether a short rule already reaches the goal, whether labels exist or can be collected, whether anyone will act on the prediction, whether the data at decision time holds the signal, and whether one error is acceptable. A model loses when a few conditions stay correct and explain themselves, when there are no labels, or when the cost of building and running the system exceeds the value of the better decisions. A model wins when the rule has grown long and fragile, because a learned model is easier to update than a complex heuristic. The cases against a model. Condition Why a rule wins The logic fits in a few conditions and stays correct Cheaper to run, test and explain No labels and no practical way to collect them Nothing to learn from Nobody acts on the prediction A better score changes nothing The decision-time data does not contain the signal The model cannot see what matters One error is unacceptable and no person checks the output A probabilistic system will be wrong sometimes The system costs more than the better decisions are worth Negative return The problem changes faster than retraining The model is always stale A lookup table or a threshold that covers 99% of cases is the right system, and adding a model raises maintenance cost for little gain. The cases for a model. The rules guide quoted in the design lesson says not to fear launching without machine learning, and also to prefer a model over a complex heuristic. The crossing point is when the rule has many branches, breaks on new cases, and nobody can say why it decides as it does. A learned model is retrained; a long rule is rewritten. How I would run the ticket case. Ask what the escalation decision is, who makes it, and when the features exist. Build the rule the support team already uses, even if it lives in a spreadsheet, and measure it. Set the minimum lift a model must show over that rule before any training. Only then collect labels and train, and compare against the rule with the same metric. The rule is also the safe default when the model service fails, so it is built first either way. Plausible wrong answers. "A model always beats a rule given enough data." The rule can win when the features carry weak signal, and the lift must be measured, not assumed. "Collect data later; ship the model first." Without labels there is nothing to train on and nothing to evaluate against. "The heuristic baseline is just a sanity check." It is the real competitor and the safe default for failures. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Where do labels for ticket escalation come from, and what is their delay? Expected: from past escalation decisions or outcomes, which arrive after the ticket closes; the delay sets how fresh the training data can be. (level 2) The team has no escalation history at all. What do you build first? Expected: the rule, with logging of the decision and its inputs, so labels start to accumulate. (level 2) A regulator requires that every escalation decision be explainable. What changes? Expected: either keep the rule or restrict the model to interpretable forms such as a small tree or a linear model. Where it is taught. The introduction to machine learning gives the decision flowchart for when not to use a model, and the ML system design lesson lists the cases where a rule wins and sets the minimum lift. Sources and further reading An Introduction to Statistical Learning - free textbook covering all classical ML methods with practical examples Google's Machine Learning Crash Course - concise visual introduction to ML concepts Scikit-learn User Guide - the practical reference for implementing ML in Python Check your understanding Q1 In supervised learning, what does the model receive during training? A Input-output pairs where the correct answer is provided B A set of rules written by a human expert C A reward signal for each action taken D Only input data with no labels Supervised learning trains on input-output pairs (labeled data). The model learns to map inputs to known correct outputs. Q2 What is the purpose of splitting data into training and test sets? A To have backup data in case the training data is lost B To evaluate whether the model generalizes to data it has never seen during training C To make training faster by using less data D To balance the classes in the dataset The test set measures generalization. If you evaluate on training data, you measure memorization, not learning. Q3 A model gets 98% accuracy on training data but 55% on test data. What is this an example of? A Data drift: the test distribution changed B Underfitting: the model is too simple C Overfitting: the model memorized training noise instead of learning general patterns D Good generalization: the model learned the true patterns A large gap between training accuracy (high) and test accuracy (low) is the hallmark of overfitting. The model memorized the training data. Q4 An e-commerce site wants to group customers into segments based on purchase behavior without any predefined labels. Which type of ML is this? A Unsupervised learning (clustering) B Supervised learning (regression) C Supervised learning (classification) D Reinforcement learning Finding natural groupings in data without predefined labels is clustering, which is a form of unsupervised learning. Q5 Which scenario is NOT a good use case for machine learning? A Detecting fraudulent transactions in a stream of millions of payments B Predicting customer churn from historical behavior data C Classifying images of skin lesions as benign or malignant D Converting temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit Celsius to Fahrenheit is a fixed formula (F = 9/5 * C + 32). Simple, well-defined rules do not need ML. ML adds complexity with no benefit. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in RLHF Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preferences, then optimise against it Lesson 10.10 BERT The 2018 encoder-only model trained by filling in masked words Lesson 7.13 Why this came about For decades, making a computer do something clever meant writing down the rules yourself. That works for tax calculations, but fails for tasks where nobody can write the rules: recognising a handwritten 7, telling an angry email from a polite one, translating a sentence. In 1959 Arthur Samuel, who had built a checkers program at IBM that improved by playing against itself, described machine learning as giving computers "the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed". The idea took decades to pay off at scale, because it needs lots of data and lots of computing power. Today it is how almost all of modern AI is built, including every large language model . In plain words first Learning from examples, like a new employee Imagine a new support agent on their first day. Nobody hands them a complete rulebook for spotting urgent tickets, because nobody could write one. Instead, they read hundreds of past tickets that experienced colleagues have already marked "urgent" or "not urgent", and gradually get a feel for it. Machine learning does the same: you show the computer many examples together with the right answers , and a training procedure adjusts a model until its answers match. Then you use the model on tickets it has never seen. Step 1 · Writing the rules by hand Here is the traditional approach: a person decides that tickets with certain words are urgent. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The rule handles the first two tickets and the last one correctly. It misses the leaking parcel, which is the most urgent ticket of all, because it uses none of the listed words. It raises a false alarm on a polite question that happens to contain the word "urgent". You could keep adding words and exceptions, but people phrase things in endless ways. The rule list grows, conflicts, and still misses cases. This is exactly the kind of task where hand-written rules break down. Traditional programming: a person writes the rules, and the computer applies them to data to get answers. Machine learning: you give the computer data together with the right answers, and it finds the rules (the model) itself. Step 2 · Learning a rule from examples Now the machine learning approach, at its very simplest. Suppose you want to predict whether a delivery will be late , and you have records of past deliveries: the distance in kilometres, and whether it was late (1) or on time (0). Instead of guessing a rule, let the computer search for the rule that makes the fewest mistakes on the past data. Copy What you should see Copy That search is the learning. The rule "late if more than 9 km" was not written by a person; it was found from the data. It still makes 2 mistakes (the 7 km delivery that was late, and the 13 km one that was not), because real data is noisy and one number cannot explain everything. Now use the learned rule on new deliveries: Copy What you should see Copy Every machine learning method you will meet, up to the largest language model, follows this same pattern. What changes is how flexible the rule is (one threshold here, billions of numbers in an LLM ) and how cleverly the search is done (trying every value here, gradient descent in Lesson 2.4 ). Step 3 · The vocabulary These words are used everywhere in AI, so it is worth getting them exactly right. Word Meaning In the example above Example (or sample, row) one record to learn from one past delivery Feature (or input) a number describing the example the distance, 7 km Label (or target, answer) the right answer for that example late = 1 Dataset all the examples together the 14 past deliveries Model the rule, with some adjustable numbers "late if km > threshold" Parameter (or weight) an adjustable number inside the model the threshold Training (or fitting) searching for parameter values that fit the data trying thresholds 0 to 15 Loss a number measuring how wrong the model is the count of mistakes Inference (or prediction) using the trained model on new examples 17 km → late Two of these deserve a closer look. Features must be numbers. A model only does arithmetic, so everything about an example has to become numbers first. Choosing and building good features by hand is called feature engineering : Copy What you should see Copy The "rush hour" feature did not exist in the raw data; someone who understands deliveries created it because it probably matters. Deep learning (the Neural networks and deep learning section) changed this: neural networks learn useful features by themselves from raw inputs such as pixels or text. That is a large part of why they took over. Training and inference are separate phases. Training is slow and done once (or occasionally); inference is fast and done every time the model is used. A language model is trained once over months, at enormous cost, then answers millions of questions using fixed parameters. When you chat with an LLM, it is doing inference: it is not learning from your conversation. Step 4 · Four ways to learn Four ways a model can learn. Supervised: from examples with the right answer. Unsupervised: finds structure with no answers. Self-supervised: makes its own answers from the data, which is how language models are pretrained. Reinforcement: learns from rewards for its actions. Supervised learning : every example comes with the right answer, and the model learns to map inputs to answers. If the answer is a number (delivery time in minutes), it is called regression ( Lesson 2.4 ). If it is a category (late or on time, urgent or not), it is classification ( Lesson 2.6 ). Unsupervised learning : there are no answers; the model finds structure, such as groups of similar customers or unusual transactions ( Lesson 2.11 ). Self-supervised learning : the answers are hidden inside the data itself, so no person has to label anything. This is how language models learn. Any sentence becomes a set of fill-in-the-next-word questions: Copy What you should see Copy One six-word sentence gives five training examples, each with a free label. The internet has trillions of words, which is why language models can be trained on so much data: nobody had to label it. Lesson 10.6 shows this at full scale. Reinforcement learning : the model (called an agent here) takes actions and receives rewards , and learns to choose actions that lead to more reward. It is used for games and robots, and, in a form called RLHF later · 10.10 , to teach chat assistants to give answers people prefer ( Lesson 10.10 ). Step 5 · The workflow of a real project The machine learning workflow. Most of the effort goes into the data and the evaluation, not the training step. After deployment, you monitor the model and go round the loop again when the world changes. Define the problem. What exactly do you predict, and what will you do with the prediction? "Flag tickets likely to need a reply within the hour" is a problem; "use AI on tickets" is not. Collect data. Examples with labels. Often the hardest step: labels may need people to create them, and they must be correct. Prepare it. Clean errors, turn everything into features, and split the data so that some is kept aside for testing ( Lesson 2.16 ). Train. Usually the shortest step: a few lines of code with a library. Evaluate. Measure the model on data it never saw during training, with a measure that matches what matters ( Lesson 2.14 ). Deploy. Put it where it gets used. Monitor. The world changes (new products, new slang, a new city), and a model trained on last year's data can quietly get worse. A common saying is "garbage in, garbage out": a sophisticated model trained on poor or mislabelled data will learn the wrong thing very precisely. Most of a real project's time goes into steps 2, 3 and 5. Step 6 · Where generative AI fits You now have the frame for everything that follows. A large language model is: a model with billions of parameters , trained by self-supervised learning on a huge dataset of text, where the label for each position is simply the next word, with a loss that measures how surprised the model is by the real next word (the cross-entropy of Lesson 1.10 ), then fine-tuned with supervised examples and reinforcement learning to behave like an assistant (the From language model to assistant section), and finally used for inference : predicting one word at a time, which is what you saw in Lesson 0.2 . The next five lessons teach the classic pieces (fitting a model, measuring it, avoiding fooling yourself) on small problems where you can see every number. The same ideas carry straight over to neural networks and language models. Check your mental model ✗ "Machine learning means the computer understands the problem." ✓ It means a procedure adjusted some numbers until the model's answers matched the examples. Whether that reflects real understanding is a separate, harder question. ✗ "A chatbot learns from every conversation I have with it." ✓ During a chat it does inference with fixed parameters. Some products store your conversations and may use them in a later training run, but the model does not change while it talks to you. ✗ "More complicated models are always better." ✓ The threshold rule above is easy to explain and check. Lesson 2.16 shows how flexible models can fit noise and do worse on new data. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 2, change the label of the 13 km delivery from 0 to 1. Which threshold will be best now, and how many mistakes will it make? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Extend the learner in Step 2 to use a second rule shape, "late if km > threshold or raining", using a raining list of your own. Does adding the feature reduce the mistakes? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it For each task, say whether it is regression, classification, unsupervised or self-supervised learning: (a) predicting tomorrow's sales in rupees; (b) sorting emails into "billing", "delivery" and "other"; (c) grouping customers by shopping habits with no predefined groups; (d) training a model to fill in a masked word in a sentence. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · One label changed The best threshold is still 9, now with only 1 mistake. With the 13 km delivery late, every delivery over 9 km is late, so the only error left is the 7 km delivery. A lower threshold such as 6 would fix that one but get the 8 and 9 km deliveries wrong (2 mistakes). Solution M1 · Adding a second feature Copy With these made-up rain values, the 7 km late delivery is explained by rain, so the best threshold (9) now makes only 1 mistake. A useful extra feature lets the model explain more of the data. Whether it helps on new data is what Lesson 2.16 teaches you to check. Solution X1 · Naming the type (a) regression (the answer is a number); (b) classification (the answer is one of three categories); (c) unsupervised learning (clustering, no answers given); (d) self-supervised learning (the hidden word is the label, taken from the text itself). This is how BERT later · 7.13 -style models are pretrained ( Lesson 7.13 ). Recap Hand-written rules break down when nobody can state the rules; machine learning finds them from examples. Training searches for parameter values that make the model fit labelled examples; inference uses the trained model on new data. Features are the numbers that describe an example; labels are the right answers. Supervised learning uses given answers (regression for numbers, classification for categories); unsupervised finds structure; self-supervised makes labels from the data itself; reinforcement learns from rewards. Language models are trained self-supervised to predict the next word, then refined with supervised and reinforcement learning. Check your understanding Q1 A model is trained to predict the price of a used car in rupees. What kind of task is this? A Regression B Classification C Unsupervised learning D Reinforcement learning The answer is a number, so it is regression. Q2 How do language models get labels for pretraining without people labelling text? A They use reinforcement learning from the start B The next word in real text is the label, so the labels come free with the data C They cluster text into topics D They copy labels from search engines This is self-supervised learning: the data contains its own answers. Q3 You are chatting with a deployed language model. Which phase is it in? A Training B Inference C Labelling D Feature engineering It uses fixed, already-trained parameters to predict; it is not updating them. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, Julia, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Linear regression draws the best straight line through your data. It is the "hello world" of machine learning. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Linear regression "Draw a line through data" Find weight $w$ and bias $b$ that minimize the sum of squared differences between $wx+b$ and actual $y$ values Cost function "How bad the model is" A function that maps model parameters to a single number measuring prediction error, which optimization minimizes Mean squared error "Average of squared errors" $\frac{1}{n} \sum (\text{predicted} - \text{actual})^2$, penalizing large errors disproportionately Gradient descent "Walk downhill" Iteratively adjust parameters in the direction that reduces the cost function, using partial derivatives Learning rate "Step size" A scalar that controls how much parameters change per gradient descent step Normal equation "Solve it directly" The closed-form solution $w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ that gives optimal weights without iteration R-squared "How good the fit is" The fraction of variance in $y$ explained by the model, ranging from negative infinity to 1.0 Feature scaling "Make features comparable" Transforming features to similar ranges (e.g., zero mean, unit variance) so gradient descent converges faster Regularization "Penalize complexity" Adding a term to the cost function that shrinks weights, preventing overfitting Ridge regression "L2 regularization" Linear regression with a penalty of $\lambda \sum w_i^2$ added to MSE Polynomial regression "Fitting curves with linear math" Linear regression on polynomial features ($x, x^2, x^3, \ldots$), still linear in the weights Overfitting "Memorizing training data" Using a model so complex that it fits noise in training data and fails on new data The problem In plain words first Linear regression fits a straight line (or, with many inputs, a flat surface) through data so it can predict a number: prediction = w · x + b . "Best" means the line with the smallest mean squared error , the average of the squared gaps between predictions and true values. You can find it two ways: walk downhill on the error with gradient descent , or solve for it directly with the normal equation . Both should land in the same place. You have data: house sizes and their sale prices. You want to predict the price of a new house given its size. You could eyeball it on a scatter plot, but you need a formula. You need a line that best fits the data so you can plug in any size and get a price prediction. Linear regression gives you that line. More importantly, it introduces the entire ML training loop: define a model, define a cost function, optimize the parameters. Every ML algorithm follows this same pattern. Master it here with the simplest case, and you will recognize it everywhere. This is not just for simple problems. Linear regression is used in production systems for demand forecasting, A/B test analysis, financial modeling, and as a baseline for every regression task. Idea 1 · The Model Linear regression assumes a linear relationship between input ( ) and output ( ): w (weight/slope): how much changes when increases by 1 b (bias/intercept): the value of when For multiple inputs (features), this extends to: ​ x 1 ​ + w 2 ​ x 2 ​ + ⋯ + w n ​ x n ​ + b Or in vector form: x + b The goal: find the values of and that make the predicted as close as possible to the actual across all training examples. Idea 2 · The Cost Function (Mean Squared Error) How do you measure "as close as possible"? You need a single number that captures how wrong your predictions are. The most common choice is Mean Squared Error (MSE): 1 ​ ∑ ( y predicted ​ − y actual ​ ) 2 Why squared? Two reasons. First, it penalizes large errors more than small errors (an error of 10 is 100x worse than an error of 1, not 10x). Second, the squared function is smooth and differentiable everywhere, which makes optimization straightforward. The cost function creates a surface. For a single weight and bias , the MSE surface looks like a bowl (a convex paraboloid). The bottom of the bowl is where MSE is minimized. Training means finding that bottom. Worked example Worked by hand Three points: (1, 5), (2, 7), (3, 12). Try the line y = 3x + 1 : predictions 4, 7, 10, errors −1, 0, −2, squared 1, 0, 4, so MSE = 5/3 ≈ 1.67 . Try y = 3.5x + 1 : predictions 4.5, 8, 11.5, errors −0.5, 1, −0.5, squared 0.25, 1, 0.25, MSE = 1.5/3 = 0.5 . The second line is better, and gradient descent finds the best one by repeatedly nudging w and b in the direction that lowers this number. Idea 3 · Gradient Descent Gradient descent finds the bottom of the bowl by taking steps downhill. The gradients tell you two things: which direction to move each parameter, and how much to move. For MSE with ​ = w x + b : ∂ MSE ​ ∂ b ∂ MSE ​ ​ = n 2 ​ ∑ ( y ^ ​ − y ) x = n 2 ​ ∑ ( y ^ ​ − y ) ​ The update rule: b ​ = w − learning_rate ⋅ ∂ w ∂ MSE ​ = b − learning_rate ⋅ ∂ b ∂ MSE ​ ​ The learning rate controls step size. Too large: you overshoot the minimum and diverge. Too small: training takes forever. Typical starting values: 0.01, 0.001, or 0.0001. Idea 4 · The Normal Equation (Closed-Form Solution) For linear regression specifically, there is a direct formula that gives the optimal weights without any iteration: X ) − 1 X T y This inverts a matrix to solve for in one step. It works perfectly for small datasets. For large datasets (millions of rows or thousands of features), gradient descent is preferred because matrix inversion is ) in the number of features. Check your mental model ✗ "Gradient descent and the normal equation can give different best lines." ✓ For linear regression the error surface is a single bowl, so they share one minimum. If they disagree, gradient descent has not finished: see the reading box in Step 2. ✗ "Squared error is just a convention; absolute error would work the same." ✓ Squaring punishes big misses much more, makes the cost smooth (so gradients exist everywhere) and gives the closed-form solution. Absolute error is more robust to outliers but has neither of the last two properties. ✗ "R² = 0.95 means 95 percent of predictions are correct." ✓ It means the model explains 95 percent of the variance of y around its mean. Predictions can still be off by a lot in absolute terms. Idea 5 · Multiple Linear Regression With multiple features, the model becomes: ​ x 1 ​ + w 2 ​ x 2 ​ + ⋯ + w n ​ x n ​ + b Everything works the same: MSE is the cost function, gradient descent updates all weights simultaneously. The only difference is that you are fitting a hyperplane instead of a line. Feature scaling matters here. If one feature ranges from 0 to 1 and another ranges from 0 to 1,000,000, gradient descent will struggle because the cost surface becomes elongated. Standardize features (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) before training. Idea 6 · Polynomial Regression What if the relationship is not linear? You can still use linear regression by creating polynomial features: ​ x + w 2 ​ x 2 + w 3 ​ x 3 + b This is still "linear" regression because the model is linear in the weights ( ​ , w 2 ​ , w 3 ​ ). You are just using nonlinear features of . Higher-degree polynomials can fit more complex curves but risk overfitting. A degree-10 polynomial will pass through every point in a 10-point dataset but predict poorly on new data. Idea 7 · R-Squared Score MSE tells you how wrong you are, but the number depends on the scale of . R-squared ( ) gives a scale-independent measure: ​ = 1 − sum of squared deviations from mean sum of squared residuals ​ = 1 − S S tot ​ S S res ​ ​ ​ = 1.0 : perfect predictions = 0.0 : the model is no better than predicting the mean every time < 0.0 : the model is worse than predicting the mean Idea 8 · Regularization Preview (Ridge Regression) When you have many features, the model can overfit by assigning large weights. Ridge regression (L2 regularization) adds a penalty: 2 ​ The penalty term discourages large weights. The hyperparameter controls the tradeoff: higher means smaller weights and more regularization. This is covered in depth in a later lesson. For now, know that it exists and why it helps. Solutions Solution P1 · Just below the edge 0.03 converges (its cost first jumps to about 495, then falls steadily); 0.035 blows up. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A regression report shows a negative R-squared on the test set. A teammate says the metric code must be broken, because R-squared lives between 0 and 1. How do you answer? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. R-squared is one minus the ratio of the residual sum of squares to the total sum of squares around the mean. It is 1 for a perfect fit, 0 for a model that only predicts the mean, and below zero when the model does worse than that constant. A negative value is a real result, and it says the fitted model hurts on this data. The formula. Copy The total sum of squares is the error of the simplest model: predict the mean every time. When the model's residuals are larger than that, the ratio is above 1 and the metric goes negative. There is no lower bound. How it happens on a test set. The model was fit on the training set. On the test set, a model that overfit the training data, or data whose distribution moved, can give predictions that are further from the targets than the test mean. The evaluation lesson prints a mean baseline next to the model for this reason, and a model must beat it. That baseline uses the mean of the training targets. It scores near 0 only when the test mean is close to the training mean, and below 0 when the two means differ. What to do with the number. Compare with the training R-squared. A high training value and a negative test value points at overfitting or a shift between the two sets. Check the split. A time series shuffled before the split, or a scaler fit on all the data, gives a very different pair of numbers. Report RMSE and MAE next to it. RMSE is in the units of the target. R-squared is a scale free fraction of the variance. Each answers a different question. Plausible wrong answers. "R-squared cannot be negative, so the code has a bug." The formula has no lower bound. A model that predicts worse than the mean gives a negative value. "Negative means the slope is negative." R-squared compares residuals with the variance around the mean. It carries no sign of a slope. "Clip it to zero in the report." That hides the fact that the mean would beat the model. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What value does a model that predicts the training mean get on the test set? Expected: near 0 when the test mean is close to the training mean, because the residual and total sums are almost the same; below 0 when the two means differ. (level 2) Training R-squared is high and the test value is negative. What does the gap say? Expected: the model fit the training data and does not transfer; suspect overfitting or a shift between the sets. (level 2) Why report R-squared next to RMSE? Expected: RMSE is in the units of the target and shows the size of a typical error; R-squared is a fraction of variance and has no units. (level 3) The target has a heavy tail. What else do you check? Expected: MAE next to MSE, because squared errors let a few outliers dominate both MSE and R-squared. Where it is taught. The linear regression lesson defines R-squared, and the model evaluation lesson compares a model with the mean baseline. A The number of features used by the model B The size of each parameter update step C The ratio of training to test data D How many epochs the model trains for The learning rate is a scalar that controls how much weights change per gradient descent step. Too large causes divergence, too small causes slow convergence. Q2 What does R-squared = 0 mean for a regression model? A The model has negative error B The model has not been trained yet C The model is no better than always predicting the mean of the target D The model makes perfect predictions R-squared = 0 means the model explains none of the variance in the target. It performs exactly as well as simply predicting the mean every time. Q3 Why is feature scaling important for gradient descent in multiple linear regression? A It guarantees the model will find the global minimum B It reduces the number of features needed C It prevents the cost surface from being elongated, allowing faster convergence D It makes the model more interpretable When features have very different scales, the cost surface becomes elongated. Gradient descent takes many more steps to converge. Standardizing features makes the surface more spherical. Q4 The normal equation gives optimal weights directly.
