First explained in Lesson 10.10; the hands-on workshop is Lessons 7.25 to 11.17 Lesson 10.10 Why this came about Fitting a straight line to measurements is one of the oldest ideas in data analysis. Around 1805 to 1809, Adrien-Marie Legendre and Carl Friedrich Gauss independently published the method of least squares : choose the line that makes the sum of squared errors as small as possible. Gauss used it to predict where the asteroid Ceres would reappear after it passed behind the Sun, and he was right. Two hundred years later the same recipe (a model, a squared-error loss, and an optimiser) is still the backbone of machine learning ; only the models have grown. In plain words first A recipe with two dials A delivery company wants to tell customers how long their order will take. A sensible guess is "a fixed time to pack the order, plus some minutes per kilometre". That is a linear model with two dials: the slope w (minutes per km) and the intercept b (fixed minutes). Training means turning the two dials until the predictions match past deliveries as closely as possible. "As closely as possible" needs a precise score, the loss , and turning the dials needs a method, gradient descent , the walk downhill you met in Lesson 1.7 . Step 1 · The data and the model Here are 17 past deliveries: the distance, and how many minutes each one took. Copy What you should see Copy The model is just a formula. km is the feature , minutes is the label , and w and b are the parameters . Because predict uses NumPy arithmetic, it works on a whole array of distances at once, which the next step uses. Before reading on, try fitting the line yourself. Drag the sliders until the line passes close to the dots, and watch the error number fall. Fit a line by hand, then let gradient descent do it Each dot is a past delivery. Move the slope and intercept to make the line pass close to the dots, and watch the error. Then press gradient descent. Step 2 · The loss: one number for "how wrong" For each delivery, the error (or residual ) is the prediction minus the truth. Some errors are positive, some negative, so you cannot simply add them up (they would cancel). The standard fix is to square each error, which makes them all positive and punishes big misses much more than small ones, then average. That is the mean squared error , or MSE . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first delivery (1.5 km) took 11.9 minutes, but the guess predicts 2 × 1.5 + 15 = 18 minutes, so the error is +6.1 (the model was 6.1 minutes too slow). The MSE is in "squared minutes", which is hard to picture. Its square root, about 4.3 minutes here, is the typical size of an error. That square root is called the RMSE ( Lesson 2.14 ). Lower is better. The guess w=2, b=15 is much better than w=1, b=25 . Training's job is to find the w and b with the lowest MSE of all. Step 3 · Gradient descent, from scratch You need the slope of the MSE with respect to each parameter. Using the chain rule from Lesson 1.7 (the square becomes "2 × error", times the slope of the prediction with respect to that parameter), they come out as: slope with respect to w : 2 × average(error × km) slope with respect to b : 2 × average(error) You do not need to derive these; libraries compute them for you ( Lesson 3.6 ). Read them as common sense: if the errors are mostly positive (predictions too high), both slopes are positive, so gradient descent lowers w and b . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output After one step the slope w is already near 2.5, but the intercept b has barely moved from 0. From step 10 to step 500, w slowly comes down while b slowly climbs. The two dials trade off: a line with a too-small intercept compensates with a too-steep slope. It takes about 2,000 steps to settle at w ≈ 2.5, b ≈ 8.6 and MSE ≈ 8.33. The model has learned: "about 8.6 minutes to pack, plus 2.5 minutes per km". These five lines (predict, error, gradient, update, repeat) are the training loop of every neural network in this course, including the language model you train in Lesson 7.22 . Only the model and the way the gradient is computed change. Why is it so slow? Try a slightly bigger learning rate to speed it up: Copy What you should see Copy At 0.011 the loss grows with every step instead of shrinking: training diverges . So the learning rate cannot go above about 0.01, yet at that size b crawls. The cause is that the two parameters live on very different scales: km goes up to 18, so a small change in w moves the predictions a lot, while a change in b moves them by only that amount. Step 4 · Feature scaling: making the valley round Why feature scaling helps gradient descent. With one input in kilometres (values up to 18) and the intercept on a scale of 1, the loss valley is a long thin trough, and steps zig-zag. After scaling both to similar ranges, the valley is round and steps head straight for the bottom. The fix is to put the feature on a standard scale before training: subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation (its typical spread). This is called standardisation (or z-scoring), and the scaled values sit roughly between −2 and +2. Copy What you should see Copy With scaling, 100 steps reach the same best MSE (8.33) that took 2,000 steps before, and the same line, once translated back into kilometres. The scaled w (about 12.1) means "minutes per standard deviation of distance", and the scaled b (about 29.9) is simply the average delivery time. Scaling features is standard practice whenever you train with gradient descent. Neural networks build the same idea into the network itself with normalisation layers ( Lesson 3.12 ), and every transformer block in the Transformers, step by step section contains them. Tip Fit the scaler on training data only The mean and standard deviation must be computed from the training data, then reused unchanged on any new data. Computing them from all the data, test set later · 2.16 included, leaks information about the test set into training ( Lesson 2.16 ). Step 5 · The same model in scikit-learn In practice you rarely write the loop for a linear model. scikit-learn (imported as sklearn ) is the standard Python library for classic machine learning, and every model in it has the same two main methods: fit (train) and predict (inference). Copy What you should see Copy The same answer as gradient descent, found instantly: for a linear model with squared error there is an exact formula for the best parameters (the least-squares solution, see the box below), and sklearn uses it. The reshape(-1, 1) turns the 17 distances into a table of 17 rows and 1 column (the -1 means "work out this size for me"); sklearn always expects features in this rows-by-columns shape, with the label as a separate 1-D array. Step 6 · More features, and what the parameters mean Real predictions use more than one feature. With several, the model becomes w1 × feature1 + w2 × feature2 + ... + b , still a sum of feature-times-weight. Here are 200 simulated deliveries where the true rule is "6 minutes, plus 2.4 per km, plus 1.5 per item, plus 7 if it rains", with random noise added: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The model recovered the hidden rule closely (2.45 vs 2.4 per km, 1.38 vs 1.5 per item, 6.71 vs 7 for rain) from noisy data alone. Each weight has a plain meaning: "holding the other features fixed, one more item adds about 1.4 minutes". This interpretability is the great strength of linear models, and why they are still widely used in business and science. np.column_stack puts the three arrays side by side as columns. True / False become 1/0 automatically. The two predictions differ by exactly the rain weight (36.5 − 29.8 = 6.7 minutes). Watch out A linear model can only draw straight lines If the true relationship curves (say, deliveries slow sharply beyond 15 km), a linear model will be systematically wrong at the ends. You can add curved features yourself, such as km ** 2 , and Lesson 2.16 does exactly that and shows how it can go too far. Neural networks (the Neural networks and deep learning section) learn curved relationships without you having to design those features. Some points will always sit off the line. ✗ "If gradient descent is slow, increase the learning rate." ✓ Only up to a limit, then it diverges. When parameters are on very different scales, scale the features instead. ✗ "The weight for rain is 6.71, so rain causes 6.71 extra minutes." ✓ It is an association learned from data. If rainy days are also busy days, part of that effect may be busyness. Weights describe the data, not necessarily cause and effect. This is why, for large models, a good starting point matters ( Lesson 3.12 ), and why fine-tuning later · 10.10 a pretrained model is much cheaper than training from scratch ( Lesson 10.10 ). Mean squared error averages the squared errors; training looks for the parameters that minimise it. The training loop (predict, compute the error, compute the gradient, step downhill, repeat) is the same one used for neural networks. Features on very different scales make gradient descent slow; standardising them makes the valley round and training fast. scikit-learn's fit and predict handle classic models in two lines; linear weights are easy to interpret, but describe association, not cause. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, Julia, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Logistic regression bends a straight line into an S-curve to answer yes-or-no questions with probabilities. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Logistic regression "Regression for classification" A linear model followed by a sigmoid function that outputs class probabilities Sigmoid function "The S-curve" The function $1/(1+e^{-z})$ that maps any real number to the range (0, 1) Binary cross-entropy "Log loss" The loss function $-[y \log(p) + (1-y) \log(1-p)]$ that penalizes confident wrong predictions severely Decision boundary "The dividing line" The surface where the model's output probability equals 0.5, separating predicted classes Softmax "Multi-class sigmoid" A function that converts a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1 Precision "How many selected are relevant" $TP / (TP + FP)$, the fraction of positive predictions that are actually positive Recall "How many relevant are selected" $TP / (TP + FN)$, the fraction of actual positives that the model correctly identifies F1 score "Balanced accuracy" The harmonic mean of precision and recall: $2PR / (P+R)$ Confusion matrix "The error breakdown" A table showing TP, TN, FP, FN counts for each class pair Threshold "The cutoff" The probability value above which the model predicts class 1 (default 0.5, tunable) One-hot encoding "Binary columns for categories" Representing class $k$ as a vector of zeros with a 1 at position $k$ Categorical cross-entropy "Multi-class log loss" The extension of binary cross-entropy to $k$ classes using one-hot encoded labels The problem In plain words first Logistic regression answers yes-or-no questions with a probability. It computes the same weighted sum as linear regression, z = w · x + b , then squeezes it through the sigmoid function, which turns any number into one between 0 and 1. Training minimises cross-entropy , which punishes confident wrong answers heavily. The set of points where the probability is exactly 0.5 is a straight line (a flat surface in more dimensions): the decision boundary . You want to predict whether a tumor is malignant or benign given its size. You try linear regression. It outputs numbers like 0.3 or 1.7 or -0.5. What do those mean? Is 1.7 "very malignant"? Is -0.5 "very benign"? Linear regression outputs unbounded numbers. Classification needs bounded probabilities between 0 and 1, and a clear decision: yes or no. Logistic regression solves this. It takes the same linear combination ( ) and passes it through the sigmoid function, which squashes any number into the range (0, 1). The output is a probability. You set a threshold (usually 0.5) and make a decision. This is one of the most widely used algorithms in practice. Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification algorithm, not a regression algorithm. The name comes from the logistic (sigmoid) function it uses. Idea 1 · Why Linear Regression Fails for Classification Imagine predicting pass/fail (1/0) based on study hours. Linear regression fits a line through the data: Copy A linear fit might produce predictions like -0.2 at hour 1 and 1.3 at hour 10. These values are not probabilities. They go below 0 and above 1. Worse, a single outlier (someone who studied 50 hours) would drag the entire line, changing predictions for everyone. Classification needs a function that: - Outputs values between 0 and 1 (probabilities) - Creates a sharp transition (a decision boundary) - Is not distorted by outliers far from the boundary Idea 2 · The Sigmoid Function The sigmoid function does exactly this: 1 ​ Properties: - When is large and positive, approaches 1 - When is large and negative, approaches 0 - When , - The output is always between 0 and 1 - The function is smooth and differentiable everywhere The derivative has a convenient form: ( z ) = σ ( z ) ( 1 − σ ( z )) . This makes gradient computation efficient. Worked example Worked by hand sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) . At z = 0 it is 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.5 . At z = 2 it is 1 / (1 + 0.135) = 0.881 ; at z = −2 it is 0.119 , the mirror image. With the model trained in Step 2, the point [3.5, 3.5] gives z = 0.9886 × 3.5 + 0.7629 × 3.5 − 5.9623 = 0.168, so the probability is sigmoid(0.168) = 0.542 : just on the class-1 side, as Step 4 prints. Idea 3 · Logistic Regression = Linear Model + Sigmoid The model computes (same as linear regression), then applies sigmoid: The output is interpreted as , the probability that the input belongs to class 1. The decision boundary is where , which makes sigmoid output exactly 0.5. Idea 4 · Binary Cross-Entropy Loss You cannot use MSE for logistic regression. MSE with a sigmoid creates a non-convex cost surface with many local minima. Instead, use binary cross-entropy (log loss): 1 ​ ∑ ( y lo g ( p ) + ( 1 − y ) lo g ( 1 − p ) ) Why this works: - When and is close to 1: , so loss is near 0 (correct, low cost) - When and is close to 0: approaches negative infinity, so loss is huge (wrong, high cost) - When and is close to 0: , so loss is near 0 (correct, low cost) - When and is close to 1: approaches negative infinity, so loss is huge (wrong, high cost) This loss function is convex for logistic regression, so every local minimum is a global minimum and gradient descent cannot get stuck in a bad one. On perfectly separable data the loss keeps falling as the weights grow, so no finite minimum exists; L2 regularization fixes that and makes the minimum unique. Check your mental model ✗ "Mean squared error would work just as well for classification." ✓ Through a sigmoid, MSE's gradient vanishes for confident mistakes. At z = −5 with a true label of 1, the cross-entropy gradient is −0.993 and the MSE gradient is −0.0066, about 150 times smaller, so the worst errors barely get corrected. ✗ "The predicted probability is how sure the model is that it is right." ✓ It is the model's estimate of P(class 1). Whether 0.8 really means "right 80 percent of the time" is calibration, which needs checking. ✗ "Logistic regression draws curved boundaries because the sigmoid is curved." ✓ The boundary is where w · x + b = 0, a straight line. Explain the mechanism You fit a logistic regression with gradient descent on a small dataset where one line separates the two classes with no errors. The loss falls at every epoch, the weights grow at every epoch, and the run never settles. A colleague proposes a squared error loss instead, because it has a clear bottom. What is happening, and what do you do? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. On separable data the log loss has no finite minimum: scaling the weights up pushes every probability closer to its label and the loss closer to zero, so descent walks forever. Squared error through a sigmoid is a worse trade, because that cost surface is not convex and has flat regions where the gradient dies. Keep the log loss and add an L2 penalty, which gives one finite, unique minimum. Why the log loss is the right loss. The model is a linear score z = w x + b passed through a sigmoid, and the binary cross-entropy is minus the mean of y log p plus (1 - y) log (1 - p). For this model the loss is convex, so every local minimum is the global one and gradient descent cannot stop in a bad valley. The gradient has the same clean form as in linear regression, the mean of (p - y) times x, with p the sigmoid output instead of the raw score. What separable data does to it. When a line classifies every point correctly, multiplying w and b by a constant above 1 leaves the line in place and moves every probability toward 0 or 1. Each such step lowers the loss, so no finite w is the minimizer. In the run you see the loss fall, the weights grow, the probabilities saturate, and the sigmoid clamp in the code start to matter. The decision boundary itself has stopped changing. Why squared error does not help. Squared error on a sigmoid output is not convex. It has local minima, and where the sigmoid saturates its gradient is near zero, so a confident wrong prediction gets almost no correction. The lesson's reason to avoid it for classification is exactly this shape. The fix. Add an L2 penalty, lambda times the sum of squared weights, to the loss. Its gradient, two lambda times w, pulls every weight back toward zero at each step. The pull grows with the weights and the pull of the data loss shrinks as the probabilities saturate, so they balance at a finite point, and the minimum is unique. The library implementation in the lesson applies regularization by default for this reason. Plausible wrong answers. "The falling loss means the model is still improving, let it run." The boundary stopped improving; only the confidence grows, until the weights overflow or every probability saturates. "Switch to squared error for a well-defined minimum." That surface is not convex with a sigmoid output, so descent can stop in a poor local minimum, and the gradient vanishes where the sigmoid saturates. "Add early stopping and call it solved." Stopping fixes the run time but leaves the weights wherever the clock ran out; a penalty gives a defined answer that does not depend on the epoch count. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is the cross-entropy convex for this model while squared error is not? Expected: the log of the sigmoid combines with the linear score into a convex function; squaring the gap between a sigmoid and a label creates flat regions and several local minima. (level 3) What does the decision boundary do while the weights grow? Expected: the line w x + b = 0 barely moves; only the steepness of the sigmoid across it grows, so predictions become overconfident. (level 4) How does the L2 penalty change each gradient step? Expected: it adds a term proportional to w to the gradient, so each step also shrinks the weights, and the shrinking balances the pull toward larger weights at a finite point. (level 4) The data is nearly separable instead. Does the problem go away? Expected: a finite minimum exists, but the weights are large and the probabilities overconfident; the penalty still helps calibration, and a validation loss shows it. Where it is taught. The logistic regression lesson explains why the log loss is convex and why separable data has no finite minimizer, and the linear regression lesson introduces the L2 penalty. Weigh a trade-off A binary classifier reports 95 percent accuracy on a dataset where 95 percent of the rows are negative. The product owner is happy. You are not. Which numbers do you ask for, and how do you choose the decision threshold for this product? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A model that always says negative also gets that accuracy, so the number proves nothing. Ask for the confusion matrix, then precision, recall and F1 at the current threshold, and the AUC-ROC for the ranking. Move the threshold from the default of 0.5 toward the error that costs the product more: raise it when a false positive is expensive, lower it when a missed positive is expensive. The four counts. Predicted positive Predicted negative Actually positive true positive false negative Actually negative false positive true negative Precision is true positives over all predicted positives. Recall is true positives over all actual positives. F1 is their harmonic mean. Accuracy mixes the two error types with the class sizes, so on imbalanced data it tracks the majority class. What the threshold does. The model outputs a probability. The decision compares it with a threshold. A higher threshold predicts positive less often: precision rises and recall falls. A lower threshold does the reverse. The lesson on logistic regression sweeps thresholds of 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.7 on one model and prints the four metrics at each, which is the table to show the product owner. Which way to move. When a false positive costs more, such as a filter that blocks a real message, favor precision and raise the threshold. When a false negative costs more, such as a screen that misses a disease, favor recall and lower the threshold. When neither clearly dominates, report F1, and show the precision and recall behind it. The threshold-free view. AUC-ROC plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every threshold. It measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives: 0.5 is a random ranking, 1.0 is a perfect one. Use it to compare models, then pick the threshold from the product's costs. Plausible wrong answers. "Accuracy is 95 percent, so the model is good." The always-negative model gets the same number. Accuracy hides the minority class. "Keep the threshold at 0.5 because that is where the sigmoid crosses." The default is only the point where the model is unsure. The product's costs decide the cut. "Pick the threshold that gives the best test F1." That fits the test set. Choose it on validation data and report the test score once. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What precision and recall does the always-negative model get? Expected: recall is 0, because it finds no positives, and precision is undefined or set to 0 because it predicts none. (level 2) Why is F1 a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean? Expected: the harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide a near-zero recall behind a high precision. (level 3) How do you keep the threshold choice honest? Expected: pick it on the validation set, not the test set, and report the test metrics at that fixed threshold once. (level 3) When is AUC-ROC the wrong summary? Expected: when the positive class is rare and the product cares about the precision of the top predictions; a precision-recall curve shows that part of the picture. Where it is taught. The logistic regression lesson builds the metrics and sweeps the threshold, and the model evaluation lesson adds AUC-ROC and the imbalance example. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in PyTorch The most widely used Python library for building and training neural networks Lesson 3.16 Why this came about Many real questions have yes/no answers: will this customer cancel, is this transaction fraud, is this email spam. Statisticians needed a model that outputs a probability rather than an unbounded number. The logistic function (an S-shaped curve) had been used since the 1830s to model population growth, and in 1958 the statistician David Cox showed how to use it for yes/no outcomes: logistic regression . It became the workhorse of medicine, credit scoring and online advertising, and it is still the first model to try for a new classification problem. Its multi-class version, with softmax , sits at the very end of every language model. In plain words first A score, squashed into a probability Think of a doctor's checklist that adds up points: +2 for high blood pressure, +3 for smoking, −1 for regular exercise. The total is a score : higher means more risk, but the number itself is not a probability. Logistic regression computes exactly such a weighted score from the features (like linear regression), then passes it through the sigmoid , a squashing function that turns any score into a number between 0 and 1. Training adjusts the points so the probabilities match what actually happened. Step 1 · Why not just fit a line? Take the deliveries from Lesson 2.2 : distance, and whether each was late (1) or on time (0). A straight line through those 0s and 1s would predict values like −0.2 for short trips and 1.3 for long ones. Neither is a probability. You want an output that is always between 0 and 1, rises with distance, and flattens out at the ends: near 0 for very short trips, near 1 for very long ones. The sigmoid function squashes any score into a probability between 0 and 1. A score of 0 becomes 0.5; large positive scores approach 1 and large negative ones approach 0. Logistic regression is a straight-line score passed through a sigmoid. Copy What you should see Copy The model is now two steps: score z = w × km + b , then probability p = sigmoid(z) . The score is called the logit , the same word you met for the raw numbers before softmax in Lesson 1.10 . A probability above 0.5 means the score is positive. Step 2 · The loss: binary cross-entropy For yes/no labels, the right loss is the surprise you met in Lesson 1.10 : the negative log of the probability the model gave to what actually happened . If the delivery was late, the loss is −log(p) ; if it was on time, −log(1 − p) . Averaged over all examples, this is called binary cross-entropy (or log loss ). Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p) is a compact way to pick the right term: when y is 1 only the first part counts, when y is 0 only the second. Confidently right (0.99) costs almost nothing. Unsure (0.5) costs 0.69. Confidently wrong (0.01 for something that happened) costs 4.6, nearly seven times as much. The loss punishes overconfidence. This is exactly the loss a language model is trained with; there, the "yes" is "the real next token" out of tens of thousands of options (Step 5). Only the prediction (now with a sigmoid) and the loss changed, and conveniently the gradient comes out very simple: the slope of the loss with respect to the score is just p − y , "the probability minus the truth". Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The loss starts at 0.69, which is what you get by saying 0.5 for everything ( w = b = 0 ), and falls to about 0.44. The trained model gives a 4 km delivery a 7% chance of being late, 8 km 33%, and 12 km 75%. Unlike the threshold rule of Lesson 2.2 , it says how sure it is. The 50% point, about 9.6 km, is the decision boundary : predicting "late" when p > 0.5 means predicting late beyond 9.6 km, close to the threshold of 9 that Lesson 2.2 found by brute force. Training on raw kilometres needed thousands of steps, for the same reason as in Lesson 2.4 . Standardising km would make it much faster. Each row sums to 1. predict simply picks the class with the higher probability, which for two classes means "late if P(late) > 0.5". Lesson 2.14 shows why 0.5 is often the wrong threshold. The weights are smaller than the hidden rule's (0.38 vs 0.45, 1.46 vs 2.0). Part of that is noise in 300 random examples, and part is that sklearn's LogisticRegression adds a small penalty on large weights by default, called regularisation ( Lesson 2.16 ). With two features the boundary is a line in the (km, rain) plane; with more, a flat surface. That is why logistic regression is called a linear classifier . Debugging exercise A colleague computes bce and gets nan , with a warning divide by zero encountered in log . The model's predictions include exactly 0.0 and 1.0. Why does this happen, and how do libraries avoid it? (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · At the boundary, and doubled weights At about 9.6 km the score w × km + b is 0, so the probability is 0.5. Doubling both w and b doubles every score, so the boundary stays at 9.6 km (where the score is still 0), but the curve becomes steeper: probabilities move away from 0.5 faster on each side. The model becomes more confident without changing its decisions. Scaling scores up or down like this is exactly what temperature does to a language model's logits ( Lesson 7.19 ). Solution M1 · A feature with no real effect The rain weight comes out close to 0 (about −0.10 with this seed; noise decides its exact value and sign), and the two boundaries end up close together, about 10.9 km dry and 11.1 km in rain. The model correctly learns that rain no longer matters. With fewer examples, noise could make an irrelevant feature look important, which is one reason to check models on held-out data. Solution D1 · log of zero np.log(0) is minus infinity, and 0 × log(0) is nan . A model's sigmoid can round to exactly 0.0 or 1.0 in floating point when scores are very large. Libraries avoid it by clipping probabilities to a tiny range such as [1e-15, 1 - 1e-15] , or better, by computing the loss directly from the score (the logit) with a numerically stable formula. PyTorch later · 3.16 's BCEWithLogitsLoss and cross_entropy take logits for exactly this reason ( Lesson 3.16 ). Recap Logistic regression computes a weighted score, then squashes it with the sigmoid into a probability between 0 and 1. It is trained with binary cross-entropy, the average surprise at the true labels, which strongly punishes confident mistakes. Its gradient is simply (probability − truth) times the features, so the training loop is the same as for linear regression. The decision boundary is where the score is 0 (probability 0.5); it is a line or flat surface, so the model is a linear classifier. With many classes, one score per class goes through softmax; a language model's final layer is exactly this, over its whole vocabulary. Same size, but with duplicates The problem In plain words first A decision tree is a flowchart of yes-or-no questions about the features: "is age above 40?", then "is income above 50,000?", until it reaches a leaf that makes a prediction. Training picks, at each step, the question that best separates the classes, measured by Gini impurity or entropy . A single deep tree memorises its training data; a random forest averages many trees, each grown on a different random sample, and is much harder to fool. You have tabular data. Rows are samples, columns are features, and there is a target column you want to predict. You could throw a neural network at it. But for tabular data, tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosted trees) consistently outperform deep learning. Kaggle competitions on structured data are dominated by XGBoost and LightGBM, not transformers. Why? Trees handle mixed feature types (numeric and categorical) without preprocessing. They handle nonlinear relationships without feature engineering. They are interpretable: you can look at the tree and see exactly why a prediction was made. And random forests, which average many trees, are highly resistant to overfitting on moderate-sized datasets. This lesson builds decision trees from scratch using recursive splitting, then builds a random forest on top. You will implement the math behind split criteria (Gini impurity, entropy, information gain) and understand why an ensemble of weak learners becomes a strong one. Idea 1 · What a decision tree does A decision tree partitions the feature space into rectangular regions by asking a sequence of yes/no questions. Each internal node tests a feature against a threshold. Each leaf node makes a prediction. To classify a new data point, you start at the root and follow the branches until you reach a leaf. The tree is built top-down by choosing, at each node, the feature and threshold that best separate the data. "Best" is defined by a split criterion. Idea 2 · Split criteria: measuring impurity At each node, we have a set of samples. We want to split them so that the resulting child nodes are as "pure" as possible, meaning each child contains mostly one class. Gini impurity measures the probability that a randomly chosen sample would be misclassified if it were labeled according to the class distribution at that node. ∑ ​ p k 2 ​ where p k ​ is the proportion of class k in set S . For a pure node (all one class), Gini = 0. For a binary split with 50/50 classes, Gini = 0.5. Lower is better. Copy Entropy measures the information content (disorder) in a node. Covered in Phase 1 Lesson 09. ∑ ​ p k ​ lo g 2 ​ ( p k ​ ) For a pure node, entropy = 0. For a 50/50 binary split, entropy = 1.0. Lower is better. Copy Information gain is the reduction in impurity (entropy or Gini) after a split. ​ I G ( S , feature , threshold ) = Impurity ( S ) − weighted_avg ( Impurity ( S left ​ ) , Impurity ( S right ​ )) where the weights are the proportions of samples in each child. ​ The greedy algorithm at each node: try every feature and every possible threshold. Pick the (feature, threshold) pair that maximizes information gain. Worked example Worked by hand A node with 5 positives and 5 negatives has Gini impurity 1 − (0.5² + 0.5²) = 0.5 , the maximum for two classes. A split sends [4 positive, 1 negative] left and [1, 4] right; each side has Gini 1 − (0.8² + 0.2²) = 0.32 . The weighted average is 0.32, so the information gain is 0.5 − 0.32 = 0.18 . The lesson's gini_impurity and information_gain return exactly these numbers; with entropy the same split gains 0.278 bits from a starting entropy of 1.0. Idea 3 · How splitting works For a dataset with features and samples at the current node: For each feature ( to ): - Sort the samples by feature - Try every midpoint between consecutive distinct values as a threshold - Compute the information gain for each threshold Select the feature and threshold with the highest information gain Split the data into left (feature <= threshold) and right (feature > threshold) Recurse on each child This greedy approach does not guarantee the globally optimal tree. Finding the optimal tree is NP-hard. But greedy splitting works well in practice. Idea 4 · Stopping conditions Without stopping conditions, the tree grows until every leaf is pure or no split can separate its samples, often down to a single sample per leaf. This perfectly memorizes the training data and generalizes terribly. Pre-pruning stops the tree before it fully grows: - Maximum depth: stop splitting when the tree reaches a set depth - Minimum samples per leaf: stop if a node has fewer than samples - Minimum information gain: stop if the best split improves impurity by less than a threshold - Maximum leaf nodes: limit the total number of leaves Post-pruning grows the full tree, then trims it back: - Cost-complexity pruning (used by scikit-learn): adds a penalty proportional to the number of leaves. Increase the penalty to get smaller trees - Reduced error pruning: remove a subtree if the validation error does not increase Pre-pruning is simpler and faster. Post-pruning often produces better trees because it does not prematurely stop splits that might lead to useful further splits. On the moons data below it scores 0.86 on test data, worse than a depth-2 tree. ✗ "Trees need scaled features, like distance-based models." ✓ A split only asks whether a value is above a threshold, so multiplying a feature by 1,000 changes nothing. That is one reason trees are easy to use on tabular data. ✗ "A random forest is many copies of the same tree." ✓ Each tree sees a different bootstrap sample and a random subset of features at every split, so the trees make different mistakes, and averaging cancels many of them. Idea 5 · Decision trees for regression For regression, the leaf prediction is the mean of the target values in that leaf. The split criterion changes too: Variance reduction replaces information gain: ​ ) , Var ( S right ​ )) Pick the split that reduces variance the most. The tree partitions the input space into regions, and predicts a constant (the mean) in each region. Idea 6 · Random forests: the power of ensembles A single decision tree is high variance. Small changes in the data can produce completely different trees. Random forests fix this by averaging many trees. Two sources of randomness make the trees diverse: Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample, a random sample with replacement from the training data. About 63% of the original samples appear in each bootstrap (the rest are out-of-bag samples that can be used for validation). Feature randomization: At each split, only a random subset of features is considered. For classification, the default is ​ ​ . For regression, ​ /3 . This prevents all trees from splitting on the same dominant feature. The key insight: averaging many decorrelated trees reduces variance without increasing bias. Each individual tree may be mediocre. The ensemble is strong. Idea 7 · Feature importance Random forests naturally provide feature importance scores. The most common method: Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI): For each feature, sum the total reduction in impurity across all trees and all nodes where that feature is used. Features that produce bigger impurity reductions at earlier splits are more important. ​ ) = nodes where feature j ​ is used ∑ ​ n total samples ​ n samples at node ​ ​ ⋅ impurity_decrease This is fast (computed during training) but biased toward high-cardinality features and features with many possible split points. Permutation importance is the alternative: shuffle one feature's values and measure how much the model's accuracy drops. More reliable but slower. The tree tries every feature and threshold and keeps the split with the largest drop from the parent's impurity to the weighted impurity of the two children. The two numbers. Copy Gini is the chance that a random sample at the node is labeled wrong when you label it by the node's class distribution. Entropy is the average surprise of the labels at the node. Both are 0 for a pure node. For a two class node with equal shares, Gini is 0.5 and entropy is 1.0 bit. How the tree uses them. The information gain of a split is the parent's impurity minus the weighted average of the children's impurity, where each child is weighted by its share of the samples. The algorithm is greedy: at each node it sorts each feature, tries every midpoint between distinct values as a threshold, and keeps the pair with the highest gain. Then it recurses into both children. Greedy splitting does not find the best tree, because that problem is NP-hard, but it works well in practice. Gini or entropy. On most data the two criteria pick the same splits and give trees of about the same depth. Gini has no logarithm, so it is a little cheaper to compute. Entropy connects the split to information theory: the split that minimizes the conditional entropy of the label given the feature is the split that removes the most uncertainty. Plausible wrong answers. "Gini is 0.6 times 0.4." That product is half of the two class Gini. The formula is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, which gives 0.48 here. "Entropy of a 6 to 4 node is 1 bit because there are two classes." One bit is the maximum, reached only at equal shares. Unequal shares give less, 0.971 bits here. "Pick the split with the lowest child impurity, and the parent does not matter." The parent's impurity is the same for every candidate split at that node, so the ranking is the same, but the gain is what the tree stores and reports as feature importance. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What is the gain of a split that puts all the cats on one side and all the dogs on the other? Expected: the children are pure, so their impurity is 0 and the gain equals the parent's impurity, 0.48 for Gini. (level 2) Why weight the children by their sample share? Expected: a pure child with one sample should not count as much as a mixed child with the rest of the data. (level 3) How does the tree turn a continuous feature into candidate thresholds? Expected: sort the values and try the midpoint between each pair of distinct neighbors. (level 3) What stops the recursion before every leaf holds one sample? Expected: pre-pruning limits such as a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples per leaf, or a minimum gain, or post-pruning after the full tree is grown. Where it is taught. The decision trees lesson computes both criteria for this node, and the information theory lesson defines entropy and conditional entropy. Debug a failure A random forest's feature importance puts a user id column near the top of the list. The column is an integer with a different value in almost every row. The team wants to build a product rule around it. What do you tell them, and how do you check? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The default importance is the mean decrease in impurity, summed over every split that used the feature. A column that is distinct on nearly every row offers a huge number of candidate thresholds, so trees split on it to carve out small pure groups by chance, and those impurity drops add up on the training data. Run a permutation importance check instead: shuffle the column on held-out data, measure the drop in accuracy, and expect close to zero for an id. What the default number measures. Copy The number is a by-product of training, so it costs nothing, and it is biased in two ways the lesson names: toward features with many distinct values, and toward features with many possible split points. An id column is the extreme case of both. Each tree can find a threshold that isolates a handful of rows with the same label, the gain looks real on the bootstrap sample, and nothing in the formula asks whether it transfers. The check that does ask. The permutation method shuffles one feature's values on data the model did not train on and measures how much the score drops. A feature the model needs produces a large drop. A feature that only absorbed training noise produces none. It costs one evaluation per feature per repeat, which is slower than the default, but it answers the question the team is asking. The lesson sets this exact case as an exercise: a high cardinality noise feature that the impurity method ranks high and the permutation method does not. What to tell the team. The ranking they saw does not mean the id predicts anything. Run the permutation check on a validation set with several shuffles and average. Retrain without the id and compare validation scores. If the score holds, the id carried nothing. If the permutation check also scores the id high, treat it as leakage: ids that correlate with the target through time or data source will not hold in production, and no product rule should rest on them. Plausible wrong answers. "The forest found the id useful, so it is useful." The impurity sum counts splits that fit training noise; a column with many distinct values collects them. "Drop every integer column to be safe." Integers such as counts carry real signal. Test the one column with a permutation. "The two importance methods always agree." The lesson's exercise builds a case where the impurity method ranks a noise feature highly and the permutation method does not. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why do many distinct values make it easy for a tree to find a good-looking split? Expected: more thresholds mean more chances that one of them separates a few rows by luck; the gain is real on the training sample and absent on new data. (level 3) Permutation importance for the id is near zero and the validation score is fine. What does that say? Expected: the id carried no signal the model depends on; it absorbed training noise, and the other features do the work. (level 4) The permutation importance of the id is large as well. What now? Expected: suspect leakage; the id tracks the target through time or source, and that link breaks in production. (level 4) How do you compute permutation importance so it is not optimistic? Expected: on held-out data, shuffle only the one column, repeat several times and average, and keep every other column fixed. Where it is taught. The decision trees lesson defines both importance measures and names the bias of the impurity method. Q2 What is the main advantage of tree-based models over neural networks for tabular data? A Trees train faster on GPU hardware B Trees handle mixed feature types, require less preprocessing, and are more interpretable C Trees can process images and text natively D Trees always have lower bias than neural networks Trees natively handle numeric and categorical features without encoding, require minimal preprocessing, and produce interpretable rules. A To reduce the depth of individual trees B To ensure each tree sees every data point at least once C To speed up training by reducing the dataset size D To create diverse, decorrelated trees so that averaging reduces variance without increasing bias Both sources of randomness make the trees diverse. Without feature randomization, all trees would split on the same dominant feature. Diversity is what makes averaging effective at reducing variance. Q4 A node contains 8 dogs and 2 cats. What is its Gini impurity? A 0.20 B 0.50 C 0.32 D 0.0 Gini = 1 - (0.8^2 + 0.2^2) = 1 - (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32. The node is mostly dogs but not pure, so Gini is between 0 (pure) and 0.5 (max for binary). Q5 MDI (Mean Decrease in Impurity) feature importance is biased toward which type of feature? A Binary features with only two values B Features with low variance C High-cardinality features with many possible split points D Features that are highly correlated with the target MDI is biased toward high-cardinality features because they offer more possible split points, giving them more chances to reduce impurity by luck. Only the points touching the margin, the support vectors , decide where it goes; move any other point and nothing changes. The C setting decides how much to tolerate points inside the margin, and the kernel trick lets the same method draw curved boundaries by measuring similarity in a richer space without ever computing that space. You have two classes of data points and need to draw a line (or hyperplane) separating them. Infinitely many lines could work. Which one should you pick? The one with the biggest margin. The margin is the distance between the decision boundary and the nearest data points on each side. A wider margin means the classifier is more confident and generalizes better to unseen data. This intuition leads to Support Vector Machines, one of the most mathematically elegant algorithms in ML. SVMs were the dominant classification method before deep learning and remain the best choice for small datasets, high-dimensional data, and problems where you need a principled, well-understood model with theoretical guarantees. SVMs connect directly to Phase 1: the optimization is convex ( Lesson 2.24 ), the margin is measured with norms ( Lesson 2.20 ), and the kernel trick exploits dot products to handle nonlinear boundaries without ever computing in the high-dimensional space. Idea 1 · The maximum margin classifier Given linearly separable data with labels ​ ∈ { − 1 , + 1 } and feature vectors ​ , we want a hyperplane x + b = 0 that separates the classes. The distance from a point ​ to the hyperplane is: ∣ w T x i ​ + b ∣ ​ For a correctly classified point: ​ ( w T x i ​ + b ) > 0 . The margin is twice the distance from the hyperplane to the nearest point on either side. The optimization problem: subject to ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 ​ (the margin width) y i ​ ( w T x i ​ + b ) ≥ 1 for all i ​ Equivalently (minimizing is easier to optimize): subject to ​ 2 1 ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 y i ​ ( w T x i ​ + b ) ≥ 1 for all i ​ This is a convex quadratic program. They are the only points that determine the decision boundary. Move or remove any non-support-vector point, and the boundary does not change. Idea 2 · Support vectors: the critical few Most training points are irrelevant. Only the support vectors matter. This is why SVMs are memory-efficient at prediction time: you only need to store the support vectors, not the entire training set. Norms and distances) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Store everything. Predict by looking at your neighbors. The simplest algorithm that actually works. Terms you'll hear Term What it actually means K-nearest neighbors Non-parametric algorithm that predicts by finding the K closest training points to a query Lazy learning No computation at training time. All work happens at prediction time. KNN is the canonical example Eager learning Heavy computation at training time to build a compact model. Most ML algorithms are eager Curse of dimensionality In high dimensions, distances converge and neighborhoods expand to cover most of the space, making KNN ineffective KD-tree Binary tree that recursively partitions space along feature axes. $O(\log n)$ queries in low dimensions Ball tree Tree of nested hyperspheres. Works better than KD-trees in moderate dimensions (up to ~50) Weighted KNN Neighbors weighted inversely by distance. Closer neighbors have more influence on the prediction Feature scaling Normalizing features to comparable ranges. Required for distance-based methods like KNN Majority vote Classification by counting which class is most common among K neighbors Brute force search Computing distance to every training point. $O(n \cdot d)$ per query. Exact but slow for large $n$ Approximate nearest neighbor Algorithms (HNSW, LSH, IVF) that find approximately nearest points much faster than exact search Voronoi diagram The partition of space where each region contains all points closer to one training point than any other. $K=1$ KNN produces Voronoi boundaries The problem In plain words first K-nearest neighbours has no training step: it stores every example. To classify a new point it finds the k closest stored points and lets them vote. Everything depends on two choices: k (one neighbour copies noise; very many neighbours blur the classes together) and the distance (which needs features on comparable scales). The same idea, at scale, is what a vector database does when it retrieves documents for RAG. You have a dataset. A new data point arrives. You need to classify it or predict its value. Instead of learning parameters from the data (like linear regression or SVMs), you just find the K training points closest to the new point and let them vote. This is K-nearest neighbors. There is no training phase. No parameters to learn. No loss function to minimize. You store the entire training set and compute distances at prediction time. It sounds too simple to work. But KNN is surprisingly competitive for many problems, especially with small to medium datasets, and understanding it deeply reveals fundamental concepts: the choice of distance metric (connecting to Phase 1 Lesson 2.20 ), the curse of dimensionality, and the difference between lazy and eager learning. KNN also shows up everywhere in modern AI, just under different names. Vector databases do KNN search over embeddings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds the K nearest document chunks. Recommendation systems find similar users or items. The algorithm is the same. The scale and the data structures are different. Idea 1 · How KNN works Given a dataset of labeled points and a new query point: Compute the distance from the query to every point in the dataset Sort by distance Take the K closest points For classification: majority vote among the K neighbors For regression: average (or weighted average) of the K neighbors' values That is the entire algorithm. No fitting. No gradient descent. No epochs. Idea 2 · Choosing K K is the single hyperparameter. It controls the bias-variance trade-off: K Behavior Decision boundary follows every point. But a neighbor at distance 0.1 should matter more than one at distance 5.0. Distance-weighted KNN weights each neighbor inversely by distance: ​ weight i ​ = distance i ​ + ϵ 1 ​ For classification: weighted vote For regression: weighted average = ∑ i ​ w i ​ ∑ i ​ w i ​ y i ​ ​ ​ The prevents division by zero when a query point exactly matches a training point. Weighted KNN is less sensitive to the choice of K because distant neighbors contribute very little regardless. Idea 5 · The curse of dimensionality KNN performance degrades in high dimensions. This is not a vague concern. It is a mathematical fact. Problem 1: distances converge. As dimensionality increases, the ratio of the maximum distance to the minimum distance approaches 1. All points become equally "far" from the query. Copy Problem 2: volume explodes. To capture K neighbors within a fixed fraction of the data, you need to extend your search radius to cover a much larger fraction of the feature space. The "neighborhood" in high dimensions encompasses most of the space. Problem 3: corners dominate. In a unit hypercube in d dimensions, most of the volume is concentrated near the corners, not the center. A sphere inscribed in the cube contains a vanishing fraction of the volume as d grows. Practical consequence: KNN works well up to about 20-50 features. Beyond that, you need dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP, t-SNE) before applying KNN, or you need to use tree-based search structures that exploit the data's intrinsic lower dimensionality. That is per query. For large datasets, this is too slow. A KD-tree recursively partitions the space along feature axes. At each level, it splits along one dimension at the median value. To find the nearest neighbor, traverse the tree to the leaf containing the query, then backtrack and check neighboring partitions only if they could contain closer points. Average query time: for low dimensions. But KD-trees degrade to in high dimensions ( ) because the backtracking eliminates fewer and fewer branches. Idea 7 · Ball trees: better for moderate dimensions Ball trees partition data into nested hyperspheres instead of axis-aligned boxes. Each node defines a ball (center + radius) that contains all points in that subtree. Advantages over KD-trees: - Work better in moderate dimensions (up to ~50) - Handle non-axis-aligned structure - Tighter bounding volumes mean more branches are pruned during search Both KD-trees and ball trees are exact algorithms. For truly large-scale search (millions of points, hundreds of dimensions), approximate nearest neighbor methods (HNSW, IVF, product quantization) are used instead. These are covered in Phase 1 Lesson 14. Idea 8 · Lazy learning vs eager learning KNN is a lazy learner: it does no work at training time and all work at prediction time. Most other algorithms (linear regression, SVMs, neural networks) are eager learners: they do heavy computation at training time to build a compact model, then predictions are fast. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line No labels, no teacher. The algorithm finds structure on its own. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Clustering "Grouping similar things" Partitioning data into subsets where within-group similarity exceeds between-group similarity, measured by a specific distance metric Centroid "The center of a cluster" The mean of all points assigned to a cluster; used by K-Means as the cluster representative Inertia "How tight the clusters are" Sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned centroid; lower is tighter Silhouette score "How well-separated clusters are" For each point, $(b - a) / \max(a, b)$ where $a$ is mean intra-cluster distance and $b$ is mean nearest-cluster distance Core point "A point in a dense region" A point with at least min_samples neighbors within eps distance, in DBSCAN EM algorithm "Soft K-Means" Expectation-Maximization: iteratively compute membership probabilities (E-step) and update distribution parameters (M-step) Dendrogram "A tree of clusters" A tree diagram showing the order and distance at which clusters were merged in hierarchical clustering Anomaly "An outlier" A data point that does not conform to the expected pattern, identified as noise by DBSCAN or low-probability by GMM The problem In plain words first Clustering finds groups in data that has no labels. K-means places k centres and repeatedly moves each one to the middle of the points nearest to it; it assumes round, similar-sized groups. DBSCAN grows clusters from dense regions and labels isolated points as noise; it finds any shape but needs a sensible distance threshold. Gaussian mixtures give each point a probability of belonging to each cluster. Without labels there is no accuracy to check, so you judge clusters with measures like inertia and the silhouette score, and with your eyes. Every ML lesson so far has assumed labeled data: "here is an input, here is the correct output." In the real world, labels are expensive. A hospital has millions of patient records but no one has manually tagged each one with a disease category. An e-commerce site has millions of user sessions but no one has hand-labeled customer segments. A security team has network logs but nobody has flagged every anomaly. Unsupervised learning finds patterns without being told what to look for. It groups similar data points, discovers hidden structures, and surfaces anomalies. If supervised learning is learning from a textbook with an answer key, unsupervised learning is staring at raw data until the patterns reveal themselves. The catch: without labels, you cannot directly measure "right" or "wrong." You need different tools to evaluate whether the structure your algorithm found is meaningful. Idea 1 · Clustering: Grouping Similar Things Together Clustering assigns each data point to a group (cluster) so that points within the same group are more similar to each other than to points in other groups. The question is always: what does "similar" mean? Idea 2 · K-Means: The Workhorse K-Means partitions data into exactly K clusters. Each cluster has a centroid (its center of mass), and every point belongs to the nearest centroid. Lloyd's algorithm: Pick K random points as initial centroids Assign each data point to the nearest centroid Recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points Repeat steps 2-3 until assignments stop changing The objective function (inertia) measures the total squared distance from each point to its assigned centroid. K-Means minimizes this, but only finds a local minimum. Different initializations can give different results. Worked example Worked by hand Points 1, 2, 9, 10 on a line, k = 2, starting centres 1 and 2. Assign: 1 goes to centre 1; 2, 9 and 10 go to centre 2. Update: centres become 1 and (2 + 9 + 10) / 3 = 7. Assign again: 1 and 2 are closer to 1; 9 and 10 to 7. Update: centres 1.5 and 9.5. Assign: nothing changes, so K-means has converged, with inertia (sum of squared distances to centres) 0.25 × 4 = 1.0 . Idea 3 · Choosing K Two standard methods: Elbow method: Run K-Means for . Plot inertia vs K. Look for the "elbow" where adding more clusters stops reducing inertia significantly. Silhouette score: For each point, measure how similar it is to its own cluster ( ) versus the nearest other cluster ( ). The silhouette coefficient is , ranging from -1 (wrong cluster) to +1 (well-clustered). Average across all points for a global score. Idea 4 · DBSCAN: Density-Based Clustering K-Means assumes clusters are spherical and requires you to pick K upfront. DBSCAN makes neither assumption. It finds clusters as dense regions separated by sparse regions. Two parameters: - eps : the radius of a neighborhood - min_samples : the minimum number of points needed to form a dense region Three types of points: - Core point : has at least min_samples points within eps distance - Border point : within eps of a core point but not itself a core point - Noise point : neither core nor border. These are outliers. DBSCAN connects core points that are within eps of each other into the same cluster. Border points join the cluster of a nearby core point. Noise points belong to no cluster. Strengths: finds clusters of any shape, automatically determines the number of clusters, identifies outliers. Weakness: struggles with clusters of varying densities. Check your mental model ✗ "K-means finds the best clustering." ✓ It finds a local optimum that depends on the starting centres. In the broken exercise, one seed out of eight gets twice the inertia of the others. Libraries run several starts ( n_init ) and keep the best. ✗ "The elbow plot tells you the true number of clusters." ✓ Inertia always falls as k grows; the elbow is a judgement call and often unclear. Silhouette scores and domain knowledge help decide. ✗ "DBSCAN needs no parameters because you do not choose k." ✓ It needs eps and min_samples , and is very sensitive to eps : on the moons below, 0.1 shatters the data into 16 clusters plus 68 "noise" points, and 0.25 merges everything into one. Idea 5 · Hierarchical Clustering Builds a tree (dendrogram) of nested clusters. Agglomerative (bottom-up): 1. Start with each point as its own cluster 2. Merge the two closest clusters 3. Repeat until only one cluster remains 4. Cut the dendrogram at the desired level to get K clusters The "closeness" between clusters can be measured as: - Single linkage : minimum distance between any two points in the two clusters - Complete linkage : maximum distance between any two points - Average linkage : average distance between all pairs - Ward's method : the merge that causes the smallest increase in total within-cluster variance Idea 6 · Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) K-Means gives hard assignments: each point belongs to exactly one cluster. GMM gives soft assignments: each point has a probability of belonging to each cluster. GMM assumes the data is generated from a mixture of K Gaussian distributions, each with its own mean and covariance. The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm alternates between: E-step : compute the probability that each point belongs to each Gaussian M-step : update the mean, covariance, and mixing weight of each Gaussian to maximize the likelihood of the data GMM can model elliptical clusters (not just spherical like K-Means) and naturally handles overlapping clusters. Idea 7 · When to Use Which Method Best for Avoid when K-Means Large datasets, spherical clusters, known K Irregular shapes, outliers present DBSCAN Unknown K, arbitrary shapes, outlier detection Varying densities, very high dimensions Hierarchical Small datasets, need dendrogram, unknown K Large datasets ( ) memory) GMM Overlapping clusters, soft assignments needed Very large datasets, too many dimensions Idea 8 · Anomaly Detection with Clustering Clustering naturally supports anomaly detection: - K-Means : points far from any centroid are anomalies - DBSCAN : noise points are anomalies by definition - GMM : points with low probability under all Gaussians are anomalies The same idea as a formula K-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) ∑ n ​ ∥ x i ​ − μ c ( i ) ​ ∥ 2 by alternating two steps that can each only lower : assign every point to its nearest centroid, then move every centroid to the mean of its points (the mean minimises the sum of squared distances). There are finitely many assignments, so it stops, but at a local minimum that depends on the start; k-means++ seeding and several restarts guard against bad ones. Each iteration costs . Silhouette. For a point with mean distance to its own cluster and to the nearest other cluster, ; the average over all points scores a clustering without labels. DBSCAN. A point is a core point if at least min_samples points lie within distance ; clusters are core points connected through such neighbourhoods plus the points they reach; everything else is noise. No to choose, any shape, but one for the whole dataset. Gaussian mixtures (EM). The E-step computes responsibilities ​ = π k ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) / ∑ j ​ π j ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ j ​ , Σ j ​ ) ; the M-step re-estimates ​ , μ k ​ , Σ k ​ as responsibility-weighted averages. K-means is the limit of equal, tiny, round covariances, where responsibilities become hard 0/1 assignments. Hint 1 Broadcast to get every difference at the same time. X[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :] has shape (n, k, d) . Hint 2 Sum the squared differences over the last axis to get a distance matrix of shape (n, k) . np.argmin(..., axis=1) returns the first index of the smallest value, so it follows the tie rule. Hint 3 In update , start from a float copy of the old centroids. Then replace centroid j with X[assignments == j].mean(axis=0) only when that selection has at least one row. Hint 4 In kmeans , keep the old assignments in a variable. Compare them with the new ones with np.array_equal . The counter is the number of update steps, so a stop after the first update gives 1. Reference solution and notes Copy Why it stops The inertia is the sum of the squared distances from each point to its centroid. The assignment step cannot increase it, because each point picks its nearest centroid. The update step cannot increase it, because the mean is the point with the smallest sum of squared distances to a set. There is only a finite number of ways to assign the points. So the run must stop, often after a few passes. A local minimum The stop does not give the best clusters. The line example in the problem stops with one cluster at 0, one at 1.5 and one at 13.25. A better answer puts one centroid near 11 and one at 20. The start centroids decide the result. The lesson picks random points as the start. K-means++ picks start points that are far apart, and libraries run several starts and keep the one with the lowest inertia. Empty clusters A centroid can lose all its points. The mean of no points is not defined, and numpy returns NaN. Keeping the old centroid is the simplest rule. The lesson moves the centroid to a random point. Some libraries move it to the point that is farthest from its centroid. Where this goes next The assignment step is the pairwise distance matrix and an argmin. Vector quantization, product quantization for vector search, and the codebooks of some audio and image tokenizers use the same two steps. Ship it This lesson produces working implementations of K-Means, DBSCAN, and GMM from scratch. The clustering code can be reused as a foundation for more advanced unsupervised methods. outputs/skill-clustering-guide.md Copy Exercises Implement K-Means++ initialization: instead of picking random centroids, pick the first randomly and each subsequent centroid with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest existing centroid. Compare convergence speed to random initialization. Add hierarchical agglomerative clustering to the code. Implement Ward's linkage and produce a dendrogram (as a nested list of merges). Cut it at different levels and compare to K-Means results. Build a simple anomaly detection pipeline: run DBSCAN and GMM on the same data, flag points that both methods agree are outliers (noise in DBSCAN, low probability in GMM). A Unsupervised learning has no labeled outputs -- the algorithm finds structure on its own B Unsupervised learning always produces better results C Unsupervised learning uses more data D Unsupervised learning only works with text data In unsupervised learning, there are no labels. The algorithm discovers patterns, groupings, or structure in the data without being told what the correct output should be. Q2 What does K-Means require you to specify before training? A The number of clusters K B The exact cluster centers C The distance metric to use D The labels for each data point K-Means requires the number of clusters K as input. It then iteratively assigns points to the nearest centroid and recomputes centroids until convergence. Q3 K-Means fails on two interlocking half-moon shapes but DBSCAN succeeds. Why? A DBSCAN always outperforms K-Means on every dataset B DBSCAN uses more data than K-Means C DBSCAN finds clusters based on density, so it can discover arbitrary shapes, while K-Means assumes spherical clusters D K-Means cannot handle 2D data K-Means assigns points to the nearest centroid, producing spherical (convex) clusters. DBSCAN grows clusters from dense regions, discovering any shape as long as the cluster is connected by density. Q4 What is the silhouette score measuring? A The total number of clusters found B How similar each point is to its own cluster compared to the nearest other cluster C The speed of the clustering algorithm D The percentage of outliers in the data Silhouette score = (b - a) / max(a, b), where a is mean intra-cluster distance and b is mean nearest-cluster distance. It ranges from -1 (wrong cluster) to +1 (well-clustered). Q5 How does a Gaussian Mixture Model differ from K-Means in its cluster assignments? A GMM uses hard assignments where each point belongs to exactly one cluster B GMM gives soft (probabilistic) assignments where each point has a probability of belonging to each cluster C GMM only works with one-dimensional data D GMM does not use centroids at all K-Means assigns each point to exactly one cluster (hard). GMM computes the probability that each point belongs to each Gaussian component (soft), and can model elliptical, overlapping clusters.
