Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Vector search Finding text by meaning: embed the query and return the stored passages whose vectors are closest Lesson 14.26 Embedding A learned vector that stands for a word, token, product or anything else Lesson 3.19 RLHF Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preferences, then optimise against it Lesson 10.10 Reasoning model A model that works through a problem in hidden thinking tokens before it answers Lesson 10.14 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.37 Why this came about Logistic regression draws straight lines; real data often follows rules like "late if it is long and at rush hour". Researchers in the 1960s to 1980s (notably Leo Breiman and Ross Quinlan) built decision trees that learn such if-then rules directly. Single trees overfit, so Breiman's random forests (2001) averaged hundreds of them, and Jerome Friedman's gradient boosting (1999 to 2001) built trees that correct each other's errors. Boosted trees, in libraries like XGBoost (2014) and LightGBM (2017), still win most competitions on spreadsheet-style data today. Alongside these, methods for data without labels (clustering, compression) and for learning from rewards grew into fields of their own. This lesson is a guided tour, so you know what exists and when to reach for it. In plain words first A toolbox, not a ladder It is tempting to think of AI methods as a ladder, with language models at the top making everything below obsolete. A better picture is a toolbox. A spreadsheet of past orders with a yes/no column to predict is a job for boosted trees: they train in seconds on a laptop and are often more accurate than anything else for that shape of data. Grouping customers with no labels is a job for clustering. Reading and writing language is the job for a language model. Knowing which tool fits is a large part of building good AI systems, including agents, which often call classic models as tools. Step 1 · Decision trees: learned if-then rules A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions about the features. Training picks, at each step, the question that best separates the examples (for instance, the one that makes the groups below as close as possible to all-late or all-on-time), then repeats inside each group. Here are 600 simulated deliveries with three features: Copy What you should see Copy A decision tree learned from 450 simulated deliveries: a flowchart of yes/no questions. Each question splits the examples so that the groups below are as pure as possible. Follow the branches for a new delivery to reach a prediction. Reading this output Each |--- line is a question; indentation shows which branch you are on. weights: [133.00, 11.00] means 133 on-time and 11 late training deliveries ended up in that leaf, so its prediction is class 0 (on time). The tree found the hidden rule from data alone: first split on distance near 9 km, then ask about rain for short trips and rush hour for long ones. A linear model cannot express "rain matters for short trips but not long ones" without hand-made features; a tree learns it directly. raining <= 0.50 is how the tree writes "not raining", because it only knows numbers (0 or 1). You can read the whole model. That makes trees popular where decisions must be explained, such as credit and medicine. Let the tree grow deeper and watch Lesson 2.16 happen again: Copy What you should see Copy An unlimited tree carves the training data into 132 tiny leaves, many holding just one or two deliveries, and memorises the noise: training accuracy 0.95, test accuracy down to 0.68. max_depth is the tree's regularisation dial, chosen on validation data. Step 2 · Many trees: forests and boosting Two ways to combine many trees. A random forest trains many trees independently on random samples and lets them vote. Gradient boosting trains trees one after another, each one fixing the errors the previous ones still make. A single deep tree is unstable: change a few training examples and it can change completely. Combining many trees, called an ensemble , fixes this: Random forest : train hundreds of trees, each on a random sample of the examples and considering a random subset of features at each question, then let them vote. Their individual mistakes are partly random, so they cancel out. Gradient boosting : train small trees one after another; each new tree is fitted to the errors the trees so far still make. The prediction is the sum of all the trees' contributions. This is gradient descent again, but each "step" is a whole tree. Both appear in the head-to-head comparison in Step 6. In practice, for data that fits in a spreadsheet (rows of customers, orders, transactions, sensor readings), gradient boosted trees are usually the strongest first choice , ahead of neural networks. scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier and the separate libraries XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost implement it. Step 3 · Nearest neighbours: "you are like the things you are close to" The simplest classifier of all does no training. To label a new example, find the k labelled examples closest to it and take a vote: k-nearest neighbours (kNN). Here it is with the snack vectors of Lesson 1.2 ([sweet, salty]): Copy What you should see Copy np.linalg.norm(a - b) is the straight-line distance between two vectors. Chikki (peanut brittle) is closest to the sweet snacks, so it is classed as sweet. This is the same operation as the vector search later · 14.26 at the heart of retrieval ( Lesson 14.26 ): turn every document chunk into a vector (an embedding later · 3.19 ), turn the question into a vector, and fetch the nearest chunks. Real systems use cosine similarity rather than distance, and special indexes ( Lesson 14.29 ) to search millions of vectors without comparing against every one. Step 4 · Learning without labels: clusters and compression k-means clustering groups examples into k clusters, with no labels at all. It starts with k random centres, then repeats two steps: assign each example to its nearest centre; move each centre to the average of its examples. Here are 150 customers described by orders per month and average basket value. We secretly made them as three kinds (40 occasional big spenders, 60 frequent small shoppers, 50 in between), but k-means is not told. Copy What you should see Copy k-means on 150 customers, with no labels given. Left: on raw numbers, the basket value (hundreds of rupees) swamps the order count, so the groups are cut by basket size alone. Right: after scaling both features, k-means finds the three real kinds of customer. Crosses mark the cluster centres. Reading this output On raw numbers, distances are dominated by the basket value (differences of hundreds of rupees) while order counts (differences of a few orders) barely count. The clusters come out the wrong sizes, cut by basket size alone. After StandardScaler (the standardisation of Lesson 2.4 ) both features count equally, and the cluster sizes come close to the true 40, 60 and 50. The centres describe three customer types a marketing team can act on. n_init=10 runs k-means ten times from different random starts and keeps the best, because a bad start can give poor clusters. inverse_transform turns the centres back into orders and rupees. Distance-based methods (kNN, k-means) almost always need scaled features. How do you choose k when you do not know it? A common check is the elbow : run k-means for several k and look at the total squared distance from points to their centres (called inertia ), which always falls as k grows. Look for where it stops falling fast. Copy What you should see Copy The big drops stop after 3 (95 to 24.5, then only to 17): three clusters is a sensible answer. Real data is rarely this clear, and the choice also depends on what is useful to the business. PCA (principal component analysis) is the other classic unsupervised tool: it compresses many features into a few new ones, the directions in which the data varies most. It is used to visualise high-dimensional data and to remove redundant features. Copy What you should see Copy PCA squashes each 64-pixel digit image down to 2 numbers, keeping the directions along which the images vary most. Each dot is one real image from scikit-learn's digits dataset (30 each of four digits). Without being told the labels, PCA already places most images of the same digit near each other. Two numbers keep only 28.5% of the variation in 64 pixels, yet the picture already separates the digits quite well. Ten keep almost three-quarters. You will use PCA in Lesson 5.7 to draw word embeddings (hundreds of numbers each) on a flat page. Step 5 · Learning from rewards Reinforcement learning: an agent takes an action in an environment, sees the new situation and a reward, and adjusts so that actions which led to reward become more likely. RLHF ( Lesson 10.10 ) uses this loop with human preference as the reward. In reinforcement learning , nobody gives the right answers. An agent tries actions, receives rewards, and gradually prefers actions that pay off. It must balance exploring (trying options to learn about them) and exploiting (using the best option found so far). The smallest version is the multi-armed bandit : here, a dispatcher choosing among three delivery routes whose on-time rates it does not know. The loop of reinforcement learning. The agent takes an action; the environment answers with an observation of the new situation and a reward; the agent adjusts so that rewards add up to more over time. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The agent's estimates end close to the hidden rates for the routes it tried often, and it used the best route (index 1, 75%) for 855 of 1,000 deliveries, while still occasionally checking the others. It achieved 730 on-time deliveries. Always using the best route would give about 750; picking at random about 633. The small gap to 750 is the cost of exploring. estimate += (reward - estimate) / tries is a running average: it nudges the estimate towards each new reward by a shrinking amount. Notice the shape: "estimate plus step size times error", like a gradient descent step. Full reinforcement learning adds situations (the best action depends on the state of the world) and delayed rewards (a chess move pays off twenty moves later). It mastered Go in 2016 (AlphaGo). For language models, it is how assistants are tuned to give answers people prefer ( RLHF later · 10.10 ), and how reasoning models later · 10.14 learn to work through problems, rewarded when their final answer is correct (Lessons 10.10 and 10.14 ). That shared interface is scikit-learn's great strength: trying five models costs five lines. A single tree (0.838) is clearly the weakest; a forest of 200 trees (0.982) fixes most of its mistakes. There is no best model in general, which is why you compare on validation data. A small neural network (scikit-learn's MLPClassifier , one hidden layer of 64) gets about 0.976 on this split. Neural networks' real advantage shows on large, raw data such as photos, sound and text (the Neural networks and deep learning section). The classic model is cheaper, faster, consistent, and measurable with the methods of Lesson 2.14 . Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A good feature is worth a thousand data points. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Feature engineering "Making new columns" Transforming raw data into representations that expose patterns to the model Standardization "Making it normal" Subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation so the feature has mean=0 and std=1 One-hot encoding "Making dummy variables" Creating one binary column per category, where exactly one column is 1 for each row Target encoding "Using the answer to encode" Replacing each category with the average target value for that category, with smoothing to prevent overfitting TF-IDF "Fancy word counts" Term Frequency times Inverse Document Frequency: words weighted by how distinctive they are across the corpus Imputation "Filling in blanks" Replacing missing values with estimated values (mean, median, mode, or model-predicted) Feature selection "Throwing out bad columns" Removing features that add noise or redundancy, keeping only those with signal about the target Mutual information "How much one thing tells you about another" A measure of the reduction in uncertainty about variable Y gained by observing variable X Data leakage "Accidentally cheating" Using information during training that would not be available at prediction time, giving falsely optimistic results The problem In plain words first A model only sees numbers, and it only learns what those numbers make easy to see. Feature engineering turns raw columns into useful inputs: putting numbers on comparable scales, turning categories into numbers, turning text into word counts, filling in missing values, and combining columns into new ones. It often matters more than the choice of model. Its main danger is leakage : accidentally letting information about the answer, or about the test set, into the features. You have a dataset. You pick an algorithm. You train it. The results are mediocre. You try a fancier algorithm. Still mediocre. You spend a week tuning hyperparameters. Marginal improvement. Then someone transforms the raw data into better features and a simple logistic regression beats your tuned gradient-boosted ensemble. This happens constantly. In classical ML, the representation of the data matters more than the choice of algorithm. A house price model with "square footage" and "number of bedrooms" will beat a model with "address as a raw string" no matter how sophisticated the learner is. The algorithm can only work with what you give it. Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw data into representations that make patterns easier for models to find. Feature selection is the process of throwing away features that add noise without adding signal. Together, they are the highest-leverage activity in classical ML. Idea 1 · The Feature Pipeline Idea 2 · Numerical Features Raw numbers are rarely model-ready. Common transforms: Scaling: Put features on the same range so distance-based algorithms (K-Means, KNN, SVM) treat all features equally. Min-max scaling maps to [0, 1]. Standardization (z-score) maps to mean=0, std=1. Log transform: Compresses right-skewed distributions (income, population, word counts). Turns multiplicative relationships into additive ones. Binning: Converts continuous values into categories. Useful when the relationship between feature and target is non-linear but step-wise (e.g., age groups). Polynomial features: Creates , , ​ x 2 ​ terms. Lets linear models capture non-linear relationships at the cost of more features. Worked example Worked by hand Scale the values [1, 2, 3, 100]. Min-max maps the smallest to 0 and the largest to 1: (x − 1) / 99 gives [0, 0.010, 0.020, 1.0], so the three ordinary values are squeezed into the bottom 2 percent. Standardising subtracts the mean (26.5) and divides by the standard deviation (42.4): [−0.60, −0.58, −0.55, 1.73]. The outlier still stands out, but the others are no longer crushed together. The lesson's min_max_scale and standardize return exactly these values. Idea 3 · Categorical Features Models need numbers. Categories need encoding. One-hot encoding: Creates a binary column for each category. "color = red/blue/green" becomes three columns: is_red, is_blue, is_green. Works well for low-cardinality features but explodes with many categories. Label encoding: Maps each category to an integer: red=0, blue=1, green=2. Introduces false ordering (the model might think green > blue > red). Only appropriate for tree-based models that split on individual values. Target encoding: Replaces each category with the mean of the target variable for that category. Powerful but dangerous: high risk of data leakage. Must be computed only on training data and applied to test data. Check your mental model ✗ "Label encoding (red = 0, green = 1, blue = 2) is fine for any model." ✓ Linear and distance-based models then treat blue as "twice green". Use one-hot encoding for unordered categories; trees cope with label codes better. ✗ "Always log-transform prices and incomes." ✓ Log helps right-skewed values with a long tail. The lesson's synthetic house prices are symmetric (skewness about 0), and taking their log makes them strongly skewed (about −5). Look at the distribution first. ✗ "Fill missing values with the column mean and move on." ✓ Missingness is often informative (an unrecorded age may mean an old record). Add a "was missing" indicator column alongside the filled value, as the lesson's add_missing_indicator does. Idea 4 · Text Features Count vectorizer: Counts how many times each word appears in a document. "the cat sat on the mat" becomes {the: 2, cat: 1, sat: 1, on: 1, mat: 1}. TF-IDF: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency. Weighs words by how unique they are across documents. Common words like "the" get low weight. Rare, distinctive words get high weight. IDF ( word ) TF-IDF ​ = total words in doc count(word in doc) ​ = lo g docs containing word total docs ​ = TF ⋅ IDF ​ Idea 5 · Missing Values Real data has holes. Strategies: Drop rows: Only when missing data is rare and random Mean/median imputation: Simple, keeps the center of the feature (median is more robust to outliers), but shrinks its variance and piles every filled value onto one spike, so the distribution shape changes Mode imputation: For categorical features Indicator column: Add a binary column "was_this_missing" before imputing. The fact that data is missing can itself be informative Forward/backward fill: For time series data See it drawn Where a log transform earns its place: 2,000 incomes drawn from a skewed (log-normal) distribution, before and after np.log . The long right tail, which would let a few huge values dominate a linear model, becomes a symmetric bell. Show the code that draws this Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Skewness measures asymmetry: 0 for a symmetric bell, positive for a long right tail. The raw incomes have 1.83, a strong right tail; after the log it is , essentially symmetric, because a log-normal variable is by definition one whose log is normal. A linear model fitted to the raw values would spend most of its effort on the few largest incomes; on the log scale every doubling of income is one equal step. Idea 6 · Feature Interaction Sometimes the relationship is in the combination. "Height" and "weight" alone are less predictive than . Feature interactions multiply the feature space, so use domain knowledge to pick the right ones. Idea 7 · Feature Selection More features is not always better. Irrelevant features add noise, increase training time, and can cause overfitting. Filter methods (pre-model): - Correlation: remove features highly correlated with each other (redundant) - Mutual information: measures how much knowing a feature reduces uncertainty about the target - Variance threshold: remove features that barely vary Wrapper methods (model-based): - L1 regularization (Lasso): drives irrelevant feature weights to exactly zero - Recursive feature elimination: train, remove least important feature, repeat Why selection matters: A model with 10 good features will usually outperform a model with 10 good features and 90 noisy ones. The noisy features give the model opportunities to overfit on training data patterns that do not generalize. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A model is only as good as the way you measure it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Overfitting "Memorizing the training data" The model captures noise in the training data, performing well on training but poorly on unseen data Cross-validation "Testing on different subsets" Systematically rotating which portion of data is used for validation, averaging results across all rotations Precision "How many predicted positives are correct" $TP / (TP + FP)$: the fraction of positive predictions that are actually positive Recall "How many actual positives we found" $TP / (TP + FN)$: the fraction of actual positives that were correctly identified AUC-ROC "How well the model separates classes" The area under the curve of true positive rate vs false positive rate across all thresholds, from 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect) R-squared "How much variance is explained" $1 - (\text{sum of squared residuals} / \text{total sum of squares})$: the fraction of target variance captured by the model Data leakage "The model cheated" Using information during training that would not be available at prediction time, leading to optimistic evaluation Learning curve "How performance changes with more data" A plot of training and validation scores vs training set size, revealing underfitting or overfitting Stratified split "Keeping class ratios balanced" Splitting data so each subset has the same proportion of each class as the full dataset The problem In plain words first Evaluation answers one question honestly: how well will this model do on data it has never seen? That needs data the model never trained on (a test set , or the rotating hold-out of cross-validation ) and a metric that matches what you care about. Accuracy alone misleads when one class is rare; precision, recall, F1 and the area under the ROC or precision-recall curve describe which mistakes the model makes. And every time you use the test set to make a choice, it becomes a little less honest. You trained a model. It gets 95% accuracy on your data. Is it good? Maybe. Maybe not. If 95% of your data belongs to one class, a model that always predicts that class gets 95% accuracy while being completely useless. If you evaluated on the same data you trained on, the 95% number is meaningless because the model just memorized the answers. If your dataset has a time component and you randomly shuffled before splitting, your model might be using future data to predict the past. Model evaluation is where most ML projects go wrong. The wrong metric makes a bad model look good. The wrong split lets a model cheat. The wrong comparison makes you pick the worse model. Getting evaluation right is not optional. It is the difference between a model that works in production and one that fails the moment it sees real data. Idea 1 · Train, Validation, Test Three splits, three purposes: Training set : the model learns from this data. It sees these examples during training. Validation set : used to tune hyperparameters and select between models. The model never trains on this data, but your decisions are influenced by it. Test set : touched exactly once, at the very end, to report final performance. If you look at test performance and then go back to change your model, it is no longer a test set. It has become a second validation set. The test set is your hold-out guarantee that the reported performance reflects how the model will do on truly unseen data. Idea 2 · K-Fold Cross-Validation With small datasets, a single train/validation split wastes data and gives noisy estimates. K-fold cross-validation uses all the data for both training and validation: Split data into equal-sized folds For each fold, train on folds and validate on the remaining fold Average the validation scores or are standard choices. Every data point gets used for validation exactly once. The average score is a more stable estimate than any single split. Stratified K-fold : preserves the class distribution in each fold. If your dataset is 70% class A and 30% class B, each fold will have roughly the same ratio. This is important for imbalanced datasets where a random split might put all minority samples in one fold. Idea 3 · Classification Metrics Confusion matrix : the foundation. For binary classification: Predicted Positive Predicted Negative Actually Positive True Positive (TP) False Negative (FN) Actually Negative False Positive (FP) True Negative (TN) From this matrix, all other metrics follow: Accuracy = . Fraction of correct predictions. Misleading when classes are imbalanced. Precision = . Of all things predicted positive, how many actually were? Use when false positives are costly (e.g., spam filter marking real email as spam). Recall (sensitivity) = . Of all actual positives, how many did we catch? Use when false negatives are costly (e.g., cancer screening missing a tumor). F1 score = . Harmonic mean of precision and recall. Balances both when neither clearly dominates. AUC-ROC : Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. Plots true positive rate vs false positive rate at various classification thresholds. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing, AUC = 1.0 means perfect separation. Threshold-independent: it measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives, regardless of the cutoff you pick. Worked example Worked by hand The lesson's demo gets TP = 24, TN = 25, FP = 3, FN = 8 on 60 validation points. Accuracy = (24 + 25) / 60 = 0.817 . Precision = 24 / (24 + 3) = 0.889 : of the points it called positive, 89 percent were. Recall = 24 / (24 + 8) = 0.750 : it found 75 percent of the real positives. F1 = 2 × 0.889 × 0.750 / (0.889 + 0.750) = 0.814 , the harmonic mean, which is dragged towards the weaker of the two. Predict before you run 3.4 percent of transactions are fraud. A model that always says "not fraud" has what accuracy, and what recall? (Solution P1.) Idea 4 · Regression Metrics MSE (Mean Squared Error) = ​ − y pred ​ ) 2 ) . Penalizes large errors quadratically. Sensitive to outliers. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) = ​ . Same units as the target variable. Easier to interpret than MSE. MAE (Mean Absolute Error) = ​ − y pred ​ ∣) . Treats all errors linearly. More robust to outliers than MSE. R-squared = ​ / S S tot ​ , where ​ = ∑ ( y true ​ − y pred ​ ) 2 and ​ = ∑ ( y true ​ − y mean ​ ) 2 . Fraction of variance explained by the model. = 1.0 is perfect. = 0.0 means the model is no better than always predicting the mean. can be negative if the model is worse than the mean. Idea 5 · Learning Curves Plot training and validation scores as a function of training set size: High bias (underfitting) : both curves converge to a low score. Adding more data will not help. You need a more complex model. High variance (overfitting) : training score is high but validation score is much lower. The gap between them is large. Adding more data should help. Idea 6 · Validation Curves Plot training and validation scores as a function of a hyperparameter: At low complexity: both scores are low (underfitting) At the right complexity: both scores are high and close together At high complexity: training score stays high but validation score drops (overfitting) The optimal hyperparameter value is where the validation score peaks. Idea 7 · Common Evaluation Mistakes Data leakage : information from the test set leaks into training. Examples: fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting, including future data in time series prediction, using a feature that is derived from the target. Always split first, then preprocess. Class imbalance : 99% of transactions are legitimate, 1% are fraud. A model that always predicts "legitimate" gets 99% accuracy. Use precision, recall, F1, or AUC-ROC instead. Wrong metric : optimizing accuracy when you should optimize recall (medical diagnosis), or optimizing RMSE when your data has heavy outliers (use MAE instead). Not using stratified splits : with imbalanced data, a random split might put very few minority samples in the validation fold, giving unstable estimates. Testing too often : every time you look at test performance and adjust, you overfit to the test set. The test set is single-use. The same idea as a formula From the confusion matrix. Average precision (area under the PR curve) has a random baseline equal to the positive rate, so on rare classes it shows what the ROC hides. Split into folds, train on and score the held-out one, times; report the mean and the spread of the scores. Stratified folds keep the class balance in each. Every tuning decision made by looking at a score turns that data into training data; only a final, untouched test set gives an unbiased estimate. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Two variants of a classifier differ by one hyperparameter. On one held-out split, variant B beats variant A by a small margin, and the team wants to ship B. Design the evaluation that decides whether B is better, and say what you would report. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. One split gives one noisy number, so the gap could be chance. Run k-fold cross-validation with the same folds for both variants, keep the per-fold differences, and test whether their mean is far from zero with a paired t-statistic. Report the mean and spread of each variant's fold scores, the mean difference and the statistic, and keep the test set out of the comparison. Why one split is not enough. A single split depends on which rows landed in each part. A different seed gives a different gap, and nothing in one number says how large that swing is. Folds show the spread. The design. Hold the test set out before anything else. It is for the final report, once. Build K folds on the training data. The lesson uses K equal to 5 and names 5 or 10 as the standard choices. Stratify when the classes are imbalanced, so every fold keeps the class ratio. Train and score both variants on the same folds, so the two scores in each fold are a pair. Pairing removes the fold-to-fold variation from the difference. Compute the per-fold differences, their mean and their standard deviation, and the paired t-statistic: mean difference divided by the standard deviation over the square root of K. The lesson's threshold for 5 folds is a t-statistic whose magnitude exceeds 2.78, for significance at p below 0.05 with 4 degrees of freedom. If the hyperparameter was chosen on these folds, wrap the whole thing in nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks the value, an outer loop measures it. Repeat with a few fold seeds and check the conclusion holds. What to report. Each variant's mean fold score with its spread. The mean difference, the statistic and the fold count. The effect size in product terms, so the team can weigh it against the cost of the change. One test set number for the variant you ship, measured once at the end. Caveats to say out loud. The folds share training rows, so the t-test is an approximation, not a clean independent sample. A significant difference can still be too small to matter. And a comparison made on the test set turns it into a validation set, which is the mistake the design is built to prevent. Plausible wrong answers. "One held-out split is enough if it is large." A single split still depends on which rows landed where; folds show the spread. "Compare the two mean scores and pick the higher one." Without the per-fold pairing and the spread, a gap smaller than the fold noise looks like a win. "Use the test set to break the tie." The test set is single use; a choice made on it turns it into a validation set. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why must both variants use the same folds? Expected: pairing removes the fold-to-fold variation from the difference, so the test asks only about the variants. (level 4) What does an absolute t above 2.78 mean with five folds? Expected: with 4 degrees of freedom the mean difference is unlikely to be zero at the 5 percent level, so the gap is probably real. (level 4) How do you avoid tuning on the folds you report? Expected: nested cross-validation; the inner loop picks the hyperparameter and the outer loop measures it, so the reported folds never saw the choice. (level 4) The difference is significant and tiny. Do you ship B? Expected: weigh the effect size against the cost of the change; significance says the sign is reliable, not that it matters. Short answer. The scaler saw the test rows, so the mean and standard deviation carried information from the test set into training. That is data leakage, and it makes the reported score optimistic. Split first, fit every preprocessing step on the training rows only, and apply the fitted transform to the other two sets. What leaked. Standardization subtracts a mean and divides by a standard deviation. Both are statistics of the rows the scaler saw. When those rows include the test set, the training data has been shaped by the test data. The evaluation lesson names this as its first example of leakage, next to two others that hide behind the same habit: future rows in a time series that was shuffled before the split, and a feature computed from the target. The three sets and their jobs. Set Share Job Training 60-70 percent the model fits these rows Validation 15-20 percent choose hyperparameters and models Test 15-20 percent report the final score, once The test set is a hold-out guarantee. After you look at its score and change the model, it is a second validation set, and its score no longer predicts unseen data. A pipeline that holds. Split before any statistic is computed. For a time series, split by time. Fit the scaler, the encoder and any imputation on the training rows. Transform the other rows with those fitted values. Inside cross-validation, repeat the fit inside each training fold. A transform fit on all rows before the folds leaks across every fold. Use a stratified split when the classes are imbalanced, so each fold keeps the class ratio. Check for duplicate rows across the splits. Touch the test set once, at the end. Plausible wrong answers. "Scaling is a harmless transform, so the order does not matter." The mean and standard deviation are statistics of the data. Fitting them on test rows moves test information into training. "A leak this small cannot move the score much." The size is unknown until you remove it, and other leaks, such as a target-derived feature, hide behind the same habit. "Run the test set after each change to be safe." Each look and change fits the test set, and the number stops predicting production. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) How does the same fault appear inside k-fold cross-validation? Expected: a transform fit on all rows before the folds leaks across every fold; fit it inside each training fold. (level 2) Why does reading the test score many times also inflate it? Expected: each change after a look fits the test set, so it becomes a second validation set. (level 3) The data has a time axis. What changes in the split? Expected: split by time, so the model never trains on rows after the ones it predicts; a shuffled split lets future rows into training. (level 4) How do you tune hyperparameters and still report an honest number? Expected: nested cross-validation with an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for the estimate, or a validation set for tuning and a test set used once. Where it is taught. A The test set is too small for reliable estimates B Adjusting the model based on test results effectively trains on the test set, making reported performance meaningless C Hyperparameters cannot be changed after training D The test set always has different features than the training set Every time you adjust your model based on test performance, you leak test information into your modeling decisions. A Exactly once B 5 times C It depends on the random seed D Never -- all data is used for training In K-fold CV, data is split into K equal folds. Each fold is used as the validation set exactly once while the remaining K-1 folds are used for training. Q4 A learning curve shows training score = 0.95 and validation score = 0.60 that does not improve with more data. What should you try? A Increase the learning rate B Use a simpler model or add regularization to reduce variance (overfitting) C Remove the validation set to give the model more training data D Collect more training data A large gap between training (high) and validation (low) scores is high variance (overfitting). Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Hallucination A fluent statement that is not supported by the model's input or by fact Lesson 10.32 Test set Examples used once, at the end, to report an honest result Lesson 2.16 Why this came about The words come from older fields. Precision and recall were defined for library and document retrieval in the 1950s and 1960s, when people asked how many of the documents a search returned were relevant, and how many of the relevant documents it found. The ROC curve ("receiver operating characteristic") comes from radar engineering in the Second World War, where operators had to set how sensitive to be: too sensitive and every flock of birds looked like a plane; not sensitive enough and real planes were missed. Machine learning inherited both, because a classifier faces exactly the same trade-off. In plain words first Two ways to be wrong A smoke alarm can fail in two ways. It can stay silent during a real fire (a miss ), or it can go off when you burn toast (a false alarm ). You can make it more sensitive (fewer misses, more false alarms) or less sensitive (the reverse), but not improve both just by turning a dial. Which way you set it depends on the costs: a missed fire is far worse than a burnt-toast alarm. Measuring a classifier means counting each kind of mistake separately, then setting the dial for your situation. Step 1 · The data: a model's scores for 24 tickets A model (like the ones in Lesson 2.6 ) has scored 24 support tickets with the probability that each is urgent. You also know the truth: which tickets really were urgent. Copy What you should see Copy 87.5% sounds good. But is it? Before trusting any number, compare it with a baseline , the simplest possible approach: Copy What you should see Copy A model that does nothing useful at all scores 62.5%, because most tickets are not urgent. Accuracy mixes up the two kinds of mistake and hides which one is happening. You need to count them separately. Step 2 · The confusion matrix Every prediction falls into one of four boxes: predicted urgent predicted not urgent really urgent true positive (TP): caught it false negative (FN): a miss really not urgent false positive (FP): a false alarm true negative (TN): correctly ignored "Positive" just means "the class we are looking for" (urgent), not "good". Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output & means "and" for arrays: (predicted == 1) & (truth == 1) is True where both hold. .sum() counts the Trues. Precision 0.8: when the model raises a flag, it is right 8 times out of 10. Low precision means many false alarms, which waste people's time and teach them to ignore the flags. Recall 0.889: the model catches 8 of the 9 urgent tickets. Low recall means misses, which here means an angry customer waiting. F1 combines the two into one number (their harmonic mean , which is low if either one is low). Use it when you need a single score and care about both kinds of mistake. The baseline has recall 0: it never catches anything. Its 62.5% accuracy hid that completely. scikit-learn computes all of these, and prints a summary per class: Copy What you should see Copy The matrix puts class 0 first, so its layout is [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]] . The report gives precision and recall for each class, and "support" is how many examples of that class there are. "Macro avg" averages the classes equally; "weighted avg" weights them by support. Step 3 · Choosing the threshold The 0.5 threshold was a default, not a decision. Move it and see the trade-off: Choose a threshold, trade precision for recall Circles are tickets that really were urgent, squares are ones that were not, placed by the model's score. Everything right of the line is flagged urgent. Green is a correct flag, red is a mistake, grey is correctly left alone. Which threshold is right depends on what each mistake costs. Suppose a missed urgent ticket costs 10 (an escalation, a lost customer) and a false alarm costs 1 (a few minutes of someone's time): Copy What you should see Copy Here the threshold 0.4 is cheapest: it catches every urgent ticket at the price of 3 false alarms. With the default 0.5, the single miss costs more than all of those alarms. In a different business (say, flagging transactions for a manual check that costs real money) the costs, and so the best threshold, would be different. Choose the threshold from costs, on validation data, never on the final test data ( Lesson 2.16 ). Step 4 · When one class is rare Imbalance makes accuracy useless. Imagine 10,000 card payments of which 10 are fraud: Copy What you should see Copy 99.9% accurate and completely useless. For rare classes, report precision and recall (or the precision–recall curve) for the rare class, and always state the baseline. The same trap appears in AI products: "our assistant answers 95% of questions correctly" means little if 95% of questions are trivially easy. Step 5 · A threshold-free score: ROC AUC Sometimes you want to compare two models before anyone has chosen a threshold. The ROC curve plots recall (called the true positive rate ) against the false-alarm rate ( false positive rate ) as the threshold sweeps from 1 down to 0. The area under it, AUC , has a plain meaning: the probability that a randomly chosen urgent ticket gets a higher score than a randomly chosen non-urgent one. Copy What you should see Copy An AUC of 1.0 means every urgent ticket outscores every non-urgent one (a threshold exists that makes no mistakes). 0.5 means the scores are no better than random. 0.94 is good. AUC tells you how well the model ranks ; it does not tell you whether the probabilities themselves are trustworthy, or which threshold to use. Step 6 · Measuring regression models For models that predict numbers, like the delivery-time model of Lesson 2.4 , there are three common measures: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output MAE (mean absolute error): the average size of an error, in the original units. "Predictions are off by about 2.4 minutes on average." The easiest to explain to anyone. RMSE (root mean squared error): the square root of the MSE . Also in minutes, but larger than MAE because squaring gives more weight to big misses. Use it when a few big errors are especially bad. R² ("R squared"): how much better than the baseline of always predicting the average, on a scale where 1 is perfect and 0 is no better than the average. 0.946 means the model explains about 95% of the variation in delivery times. The baseline MAE is about 11 minutes, so the model cuts the typical error more than fourfold. These numbers are measured on the same data the model was trained on, which flatters it. Lesson 2.16 fixes that. a0210: Course home / Phase 2 · Machine Learning Algorithms The Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Underfitting and Overfitting Lesson 2.15 75 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Derive the bias-variance decomposition of expected prediction error and explain the role of irreducible noise Diagnose whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance using training and test error patterns Explain how regularization techniques (L1, L2, dropout, early stopping) trade bias for variance Implement experiments that visualize the bias-variance tradeoff across models of increasing complexity Before you start Needs : Lessons 2.1 to 2.13 (ML basics, regression, classification, evaluation) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Every model error comes from one of three sources: bias, variance, or noise. You can only control the first two. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Bias "The model is too simple" Systematic error from wrong assumptions. The gap between the average model prediction and truth. Variance "The model is overfitting" Error from sensitivity to training data. How much predictions change across different training sets. Irreducible error "Noise in the data" Error from randomness in the true data-generating process. No model can eliminate it. Underfitting "Not learning enough" Model has high bias. It misses the real pattern even on training data. Overfitting "Memorizing the data" Model has high variance. It fits noise in training data that does not generalize. Regularization "Constraining the model" Adding a penalty to reduce model complexity, trading bias for lower variance. Double descent "More parameters can help" Test error decreases again when model capacity far exceeds the interpolation threshold. Model complexity "How flexible the model is" The capacity of a model to fit arbitrary patterns. Controlled by architecture, features, or regularization. The problem In plain words first A model's error on new data has three sources. Bias : the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so it is wrong in the same way whatever data you train it on. Variance : the model is so flexible that it chases the particular noise in its training set, so it changes a lot from one training set to another. Noise : randomness in the data that no model can remove. Making a model more flexible lowers bias and raises variance; the sweet spot is in between. You trained a model. It has some error on test data. Where does that error come from? If your model is too simple (linear regression on a curved dataset), it will consistently miss the true pattern. That is bias. If your model is too complex (degree-20 polynomial on 15 data points), it will fit the training data perfectly but give wildly different predictions on new data. That is variance. You cannot minimize both at the same time for a fixed model capacity. Push bias down and variance goes up. Push variance down and bias goes up. Understanding this tradeoff is the single most useful diagnostic skill in machine learning. It tells you whether to make your model more complex or less complex, whether to get more data or engineer better features, whether to regularize more or less. Idea 1 · Bias: Systematic Error Bias measures how far off your model's average prediction is from the true value. If you trained the same model on many different training sets drawn from the same distribution and averaged the predictions, bias is the gap between that average and the truth. High bias means the model is too rigid to capture the real pattern. A straight line fit to a parabola will always miss the curve, no matter how much data you give it. This is underfitting. Copy Idea 2 · Variance: Sensitivity to Training Data Variance measures how much your predictions change when you train on different subsets of data. If small changes in the training set cause large changes in the model, variance is high. High variance means the model is fitting noise in the training data, not the underlying signal. A degree-20 polynomial will thread through every training point but oscillate wildly between them. This is overfitting. Copy Idea 3 · The Decomposition For any point , the expected prediction error under squared loss decomposes exactly: ​ Expected Error = Bias 2 + Variance + Irreducible Noise where: Bias 2 = ( E [ f ^ ​ ( x )] − f ( x ) ) 2 Variance = E [( f ^ ​ ( x ) − E [ f ^ ​ ( x )] ) 2 ] Noise = E [( y − f ( x ) ) 2 ] ( σ 2 ) ​ is the true function ​ ( x ) is your model's prediction is the expectation over different training sets is the observed label (true function plus noise) The noise term is irreducible. No model can do better than on noisy data. Your job is to find the right balance between and variance. Check your mental model ✗ "High training error means high variance." ✓ High training error is bias: the model cannot even fit what it has seen. High variance shows as low training error with much higher validation error. ✗ "More data fixes everything." ✓ More data reduces variance. It does nothing for bias: a straight line stays wrong on a curve however many points you give it, as the degree-1 learning curve shows. ✗ "Bigger models always overfit." ✓ In classical models, yes, past a point. Very large neural networks show double descent: past the point where they can fit the training data exactly, test error can fall again. Idea 4 · Model Complexity vs Error The classic U-shaped curve: Complexity Bias Variance Total Error Too low HIGH LOW HIGH (underfitting) Just right MODERATE MODERATE LOWEST Too high LOW HIGH HIGH (overfitting) Idea 5 · Regularization as Bias-Variance Control Regularization deliberately increases bias to reduce variance. It constrains the model so it cannot chase noise. L2 (Ridge): Shrinks all weights toward zero. Keeps all features but reduces their influence. L1 (Lasso): Pushes some weights exactly to zero. Performs feature selection. Dropout: Randomly disables neurons during training. Forces redundant representations. Early stopping: Stops training before the model fully fits the training data. The regularization strength (lambda, dropout rate, number of epochs) directly controls where you sit on the bias-variance curve. More regularization means more bias, less variance. Idea 6 · Double Descent: The Modern Perspective Classical theory says: after the sweet spot, more complexity always hurts. But research since 2019 has shown something unexpected. If you keep increasing model capacity far past the interpolation threshold (where the model has enough parameters to perfectly fit training data), test error can decrease again. This "double descent" phenomenon explains why massively overparameterized neural networks (with far more parameters than training examples) still generalize well. The classical bias-variance tradeoff is not wrong, but it is incomplete for the modern regime. Key observations about double descent: - It happens in linear models, decision trees, and neural networks - More data can actually hurt in the interpolation region (sample-wise double descent) - More training epochs can cause it too (epoch-wise double descent) - Regularization smooths out the peak but does not eliminate it Why does this happen? At the interpolation threshold, the model has just enough capacity to fit all training points. It is forced into a very specific solution that threads through every point, and small perturbations in the data cause large changes in the fit. This is where variance peaks. Past the threshold, the model has many possible solutions that fit the data perfectly. The learning algorithm (e.g., gradient descent with implicit regularization) tends to pick the simplest one among them. This implicit bias toward simple solutions is why overparameterized models generalize. Regime Parameters vs Samples Behavior Underparameterized Classical tradeoff applies Interpolation threshold Variance peaks, test error spikes Overparameterized Implicit regularization kicks in, test error drops For practical purposes: if you are using neural networks or large tree ensembles, do not stop at the interpolation threshold. Either stay well below it (with explicit regularization) or go well past it. The worst place to be is right at the threshold. Idea 7 · Diagnosing Your Model Symptom Diagnosis Fix High train error, high test error Bias More features, complex model, less regularization Low train error, high test error Variance More data, regularization, simpler model, dropout Low train error, low test error Good fit Ship it Train error decreasing, test error increasing Overfitting in progress Early stopping Idea 8 · Practical Strategies When bias is the problem: - Add polynomial or interaction features - Use a more flexible model (tree ensemble instead of linear) - Reduce regularization strength - Train longer (if not yet converged) When variance is the problem: - Get more training data - Use bagging (random forests) - Increase regularization (higher lambda, more dropout) - Feature selection (remove noisy features) - Use cross-validation to detect it early Idea 9 · Ensemble Methods and Variance Reduction Ensemble methods are the most practical tool for fighting variance. Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) trains multiple models on different bootstrap samples of the training data, then averages their predictions. Each individual model has high variance, but the average has much lower variance. Random forests are bagging applied to decision trees. Why it works mathematically: if you average independent predictions, each with variance , the variance of the average is / N . The models are not truly independent (they all see similar data), so the reduction is less than , but it is still substantial. Boosting reduces bias by building models sequentially, where each new model focuses on the errors of the ensemble so far. Gradient boosting and AdaBoost are the main examples. Boosting can overfit if you add too many models, so you need early stopping or regularization. Method Primary Effect Bias Change Variance Change Bagging Reduces variance No change Decreases Boosting Reduces bias Decreases Can increase Stacking Reduces both Depends on meta-learner Depends on base models Dropout Implicit bagging Slight increase Decreases Practical rule: if your base model has high variance (deep trees, high-degree polynomials), use bagging. If your base model has high bias (shallow stumps, simple linear models), use boosting. Idea 10 · Learning Curves Learning curves plot training and validation error as a function of training set size. They are the most practical diagnostic tool you have. Unlike a single train/test comparison, learning curves show you the trajectory of your model and tell you whether more data will help. How to read them: Scenario Training Error Validation Error Gap What It Means What to Do High bias High High Small Model cannot capture the pattern More features, complex model, less regularization High variance Low High Large Model memorizes training data More data, regularization, simpler model Good fit Moderate Moderate Small Model generalizes well Ship it High variance, improving Low Decreasing with more data Shrinking Variance problem that data can fix Collect more data High bias, flat High High and flat Small and flat More data will NOT help Change model architecture The critical insight: if both curves have plateaued and the gap is small but both errors are high, more data is useless. You need a better model. If the gap is large and still shrinking, more data will help. Idea 11 · How to Generate Learning Curves There are two approaches: Approach 1: Vary training set size, fixed model. Hold the model and hyperparameters constant. Train on increasingly large subsets of the training data. Measure training error and validation error at each size. This is the standard learning curve. Approach 2: Vary model complexity, fixed data. Hold the data constant. Sweep a complexity parameter (polynomial degree, tree depth, number of layers). Measure training error and validation error at each complexity. This is a validation curve and shows the bias-variance tradeoff directly. Both approaches complement each other. The first tells you if more data will help. The second tells you if a different model will help. Run both before making decisions about your next step. The same idea as a formula The decomposition. At high alpha, the penalty is so strong that the model effectively becomes a near-constant function. Bias dominates. The optimal alpha sits between these extremes. In practice, regularization is the preferred way to control the tradeoff because it allows fine-grained control without changing the feature set. Too flexible: high variance, a large gap between them. More data cuts variance; more features or capacity cut bias; regularisation and ensembles cut variance. Use learning and validation curves to diagnose, then change the right thing. Solutions Solution P1 · The U-curve Degree 3 has the lowest total error, about 0.14 (bias² 0.077, variance 0.059). Degrees 1 and 2 are biased (bias² about 0.48: a line or parabola cannot follow the wave). Degree 5 has almost no bias (0.003) but triple the variance (0.22). Degree 8 has by far the highest variance, about 21: with 30 points, a degree-8 polynomial swings wildly wherever data is sparse. Solution B1 · Variance explodes at the edges At degree 12 the average variance is in the hundreds of thousands, and almost all of it comes from the edges. Near −3 and 3 there are few training points, and a high-degree polynomial is free to shoot off to huge values between and beyond them; in the middle, where points are dense, the variance is far smaller. This is why high-degree polynomial features are dangerous unless regularised, and why models extrapolate badly outside their training range. Use it: the same idea with real libraries sklearn provides learning_curve and validation_curve to automate these diagnostics without writing bootstrap loops. Validation Curve: Sweep Model Complexity Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output With 200 points and a little ridge penalty, the best validation error comes at a high degree, about 13, and it is 0.244, essentially the noise level (the data's noise has variance 0.5² = 0.25, which no model can beat). That seems to contradict the bootstrap experiment, where degree 8 was a disaster. It does not: there each fit saw only 30 points with no regularisation. More data and a ridge penalty both cut variance, which is what lets a flexible model work. This gives you the bias-variance tradeoff curve directly. Where the validation score is worst relative to train score, variance dominates. Where both are bad, bias dominates. Learning Curve: Sweep Training Set Size Copy Plot train_mse and val_mse against train_sizes . The shape tells you everything about your model. Cross-Validation with Regularization Sweep Copy What you should see Copy Copy This sweeps regularization strength for a fixed model complexity. You will see the same bias-variance tradeoff: low alpha means high variance, high alpha means high bias. Putting It All Together: A Complete Diagnostic Workflow In practice, you run these diagnostics in sequence: Train your model. Compute train and test error. If both are high: you have a bias problem. Skip to step 4. If train is low but test is high: you have a variance problem. Generate a learning curve to see if more data will help. If not, regularize. Generate a validation curve sweeping your main complexity parameter. Find the sweet spot. At the sweet spot, generate a learning curve. If the gap is still large, you need more data or regularization. Try Ridge/Lasso with different alpha values using cross_val_score . Pick the alpha where cross-validated error is lowest. This takes 10-15 minutes of compute for most tabular datasets and saves hours of guessing. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Large models break the simple picture. Very large networks can fit training data perfectly and still generalise; in practice, teams control variance with more data, data augmentation, weight decay and early stopping rather than smaller models. Learning curves are the everyday tool. Plotting training and validation loss against data size or steps (in Weights & Biases, MLflow or TensorBoard) is how practitioners decide between more data, more capacity and more regularisation. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A team keeps growing a model. Test error falls, then spikes as the parameter count approaches the number of training rows, then falls again as they keep going. The classical U-shaped curve predicts the spike but not the second fall. Explain what the curve shows, and give the team a rule about model size. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The spike sits at the interpolation threshold, where the model has just enough capacity to fit every training row and is forced into one specific, noise-sensitive solution, so variance peaks. Past it, many solutions fit the training data and gradient descent's implicit regularization picks a simple one, so error falls again. That is double descent. The rule: stay well below the threshold with explicit regularization, or go well past it; the worst place to sit is on it. The classical picture. Expected error is squared bias plus variance plus irreducible noise. As capacity grows, bias falls and variance rises, and the sum has one minimum. The classical rule was that more capacity past that point always hurts. The three regimes. Regime Parameters against rows Behavior Underparameterized far fewer the classical trade-off applies Interpolation threshold about equal variance peaks, test error spikes Overparameterized far more implicit regularization, test error falls At the threshold the model can just barely thread every training point, and a small change in the data moves the fit a lot. Past it, the training data no longer pins down one solution, and the learning algorithm chooses among the many that fit. Gradient descent tends to pick a simple one, and that bias toward simplicity is why heavily overparameterized networks generalize. What the lesson adds. The pattern appears in linear models, decision trees and neural networks. More data can hurt near the threshold, because adding rows moves the threshold under a fixed model. That is the sample-wise form. Training longer can produce the same curve over epochs. Regularization smooths and lowers the peak but does not remove it. The rule for the team. Measure where the threshold is: training error reaches zero and test error peaks at about the same size. Then size the model far from it on one side or the other. Below it, use explicit regularization and the classical diagnostics. Above it, keep going and verify with learning curves rather than with the classical intuition. Plausible wrong answers. "The second fall is a measurement error." It appears in linear models, trees and networks, and in both the sample-wise and epoch-wise forms. "Make the model as big as the budget allows and stop thinking about it." Bigger past the threshold works, but sitting on the threshold is the worst outcome; size the model deliberately away from it. "Regularization removes the problem." It smooths and lowers the peak; it does not remove it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How do you recognize the threshold in a training log? Expected: training error reaches zero and test error is at its worst at about the same model size or epoch. (level 4) Why can adding data hurt in this regime? Expected: more rows move the threshold; a fixed model that was past it can land on it, which is the sample-wise form. (level 4) What does regularization do to the peak? Expected: it smooths and lowers the peak but does not remove it. (level 4) Does this make the bias-variance trade-off wrong? Expected: no; it holds below the threshold and is incomplete above it, where the implicit bias of the optimizer takes over. Where it is taught. The bias-variance lesson derives the decomposition and describes double descent and its three regimes. Which error component dominates? A Bias: the model is too rigid to capture the true nonlinear pattern B Variance: the model changes too much with different training data C Irreducible noise: the data is too noisy D None: the model should fit perfectly A linear model cannot capture a quadratic curve no matter how much data it sees. This systematic error from wrong model assumptions is bias. The model underfits. Q2 The bias-variance decomposition of expected error has three terms. Which one cannot be reduced by any model? A All three can be reduced to zero B Variance C Irreducible noise (sigma squared) D Bias squared Irreducible noise comes from randomness in the data itself (measurement error, missing variables). No model can predict noise. Expected error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise. Q3 Adding L2 regularization to a model increases bias and decreases variance. Why is this useful? A The reduction in variance can outweigh the increase in bias, lowering total error B It makes the model faster to train C L2 regularization eliminates irreducible noise D It always improves both training and test accuracy Regularization trades a small increase in bias for a larger decrease in variance. When a model is overfitting (high variance), this tradeoff reduces total error even though bias goes up slightly. Q4 A model has training error = 2% and test error = 25%. What is the most likely diagnosis? A High irreducible noise: the data is too noisy B High bias (underfitting): the model is too simple C High variance (overfitting): the model memorized training data and fails to generalize D The model is perfectly calibrated Low training error + high test error + large gap = high variance (overfitting). The model fits training-specific noise. Remedies: regularize, reduce complexity, get more data. Q5 You train the same model architecture on 50 different random training subsets and observe that predictions vary wildly between them. What does this indicate? A High irreducible noise: the target variable is random B High bias: the model consistently misses the true pattern C The learning rate is too high D High variance: the model is sensitive to which specific training data it sees Variance measures how much predictions change when trained on different data subsets. Wildly different predictions across subsets is the definition of high variance. Mark complete and continue Mark as not done Previous 2.14 · Is it any good? Depth : Core, for everyone. This is the lesson that separates models that work in a notebook from models that work for real. Time : about 60 minutes. Next : Lesson 2.11 tours the rest of the classic machine learning toolbox. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Overfitting Doing well on the training data and badly on new data, because the model memorised Training Underfitting Doing badly even on the training data, because the model is too simple or undertrained Training Training set The examples the model learns from Splits Validation set Examples held back to make choices during development Splits Test set Examples used once, at the end, to report an honest result Splits Early stopping Ending training when the validation loss stops improving Training Hyperparameters Settings you choose before training, such as the learning rate Tuning Cross-validation Rotating which part of the data is held out, and averaging the results Small datasets Data leakage Information from the test data reaching the model during training, which inflates results Evaluation Distribution shift Production data differing from the data the model was trained and tested on Monitoring Knowledge cutoff The date after which a model has seen no training data Why retrieval exists Mentioned here, taught later 2 Deep learning, Evals and evaluation sets This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Deep learning Machine learning done with neural networks that have many layers Lesson 3.4 Evals and evaluation sets Evals are repeatable tests that measure how well a model or system does a task; an evaluation set is the fixed list of test cases with known good answers. Introduced in Lesson 11.22, first built in Lesson 14.27, and covered in depth in Lessons 14.117 and 14.118 Lesson 11.22 Why this came about Early statisticians noticed that a formula with enough adjustable numbers could fit any data perfectly, including pure noise, and still predict nothing. The mathematician John von Neumann reportedly joked, "With four parameters I can fit an elephant, and with five I can make him wiggle his trunk." The fix that machine learning settled on is simple and strict: judge a model only on data it did not learn from. Holding out data, cross-validation (developed by statisticians in the 1970s) and regularisation all follow from that one rule. It matters even more for large language models , whose billions of parameters could memorise a great deal. In plain words first Memorising the answers versus learning the subject A student who memorises last year's exam answers can score 100% on last year's exam and fail this year's. A student who understood the subject does well on both. A model can do the same: with enough flexibility, it can memorise the training examples, noise and all, instead of learning the pattern behind them. You only find out by testing it on questions it has never seen. That is why data is split, and why the test questions must stay secret until the end. Step 1 · See it happen Below, 12 training points (filled) follow a gentle S-shaped pattern with some noise. Another 12 points from the same pattern (hollow) are kept aside as validation data. The model is a polynomial curve: degree 1 is a straight line, and each extra degree adds a parameter and lets the curve bend once more. Drag the degree up slowly. Too simple, just right, too flexible Fit a curve through 12 training points (filled) and check it on 12 new points it never saw (hollow). Raise the degree: training error keeps falling, but validation error turns back up. The classic picture of what you just saw in the slider. As a model gets more flexible (left to right), its loss on the training data keeps falling, but its loss on new data falls only up to a point and then rises. Left of the dashed line the model is underfitting ; right of it, overfitting . Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . The same experiment in code, with NumPy 's polyfit (fit a polynomial of a given degree by least squares) and polyval (evaluate it): Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Training error only ever goes down as the degree rises. At degree 11 (12 parameters for 12 points) it is 0.0000: the curve passes through every training point exactly. Validation error goes down, then up. It is lowest around degree 3 to 4, and at degree 11 it explodes to about 288,000, because between and beyond the training points the curve swings wildly. Degree 0 (a flat line) is underfitting : too simple, bad on both. Degrees 3 to 4 are a good fit. Degree 7 and above is overfitting : excellent on the data it memorised, poor on anything new. The gap between training error and validation error is the warning sign. A small training error on its own tells you nothing. Step 2 · Three splits, three jobs Split the data before you start. Train on the training set , use the validation set to choose between models and settings, and touch the test set only once at the end, to get an honest estimate of performance on new data. Training set : the only data fit ever sees. Validation set (or development set ): used to compare models and choose settings, such as the polynomial degree above or the threshold in Lesson 2.14 . You look at it many times. Test set : used once, at the very end, to report how well the chosen model will do on new data. Why a separate test set? Because every time you pick the model that scores best on validation data, you are fitting a little to the validation set's quirks. After many choices, its score becomes optimistic. The untouched test set gives an honest final number. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output 25% of the remaining 240 is 60, so the split is 180 / 60 / 60. random_state=0 fixes the shuffle so the split is the same every run. Change it and the numbers move. Validation accuracy (0.90) is much higher than test accuracy (0.767) for the same model. Nothing is wrong: with only 60 examples, the score depends a lot on which 60 you happen to get. One lucky or unlucky split can mislead you, which is the problem Step 4 solves. Tip Split by time when the future matters If the model will predict the future (next month's demand, tomorrow's fraud), do not shuffle: train on older data and test on newer data. Shuffling lets the model peek at the future and makes the test score too optimistic. Step 3 · Fighting overfitting There are four main remedies, and you will meet all of them again in deep learning later · 3.4 . A simpler model : fewer parameters, as when you chose degree 4 over degree 11. More data : with 1,000 training points instead of 12, even a degree-9 curve has nowhere to wiggle. Regularisation : keep the flexible model, but add a penalty to the loss for large weights, so the model only uses large weights when the data really demands it. Early stopping : in gradient descent , stop training when the validation error stops improving ( Lesson 3.16 ). Regularisation is worth seeing. Ridge regression adds alpha × (sum of squared weights) to the squared error. Here is the degree-9 polynomial with different penalty strengths: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output PolynomialFeatures(9) turns each x into the columns x, x², …, x⁹ so that a linear model can fit a curve; make_pipeline chains it with the model, so fit and predict run both steps. model[-1] is the last step, the linear model, whose coef_ holds the weights. No penalty : weights up to about 265, and a validation error of 0.31. Huge weights that nearly cancel each other are how a curve wiggles through every point. A small penalty (0.0001 to 0.01) shrinks the weights to a few units and cuts the validation error more than tenfold, to about 0.025, not far from the best simple model's 0.017. The flexible model behaves like a simpler one. Too strong a penalty (10) squashes the weights so much that the model underfits again. The penalty strength is itself a setting you choose on validation data. Settings like alpha , the polynomial degree, or the learning rate are called hyperparameters : you choose them, training does not learn them. Choosing them is what the validation set is for. Step 4 · Cross-validation: a steadier score from limited data Step 2 showed that a single validation split of 60 examples can be noisy. Cross-validation reuses the data: split it into k parts (often 5), train k times with a different part held out each time, and average. Five-fold cross-validation: split the training data into five parts. Train five times, each time holding out a different part for validation, and average the five scores. Every example gets used for validation exactly once. Copy What you should see Copy The five scores range from 0.872 to 0.942 depending on which fifth was held out. Reporting "0.915 ± 0.027" is far more honest than any single one of them. Cross-validation costs k times the training time, so it is common for small and medium datasets and rare for large neural networks, where one big held-out set is used instead. Step 5 · Leakage: when the test is secretly easy Data leakage means information that would not be available at prediction time slips into the features or into training. The model looks brilliant in testing and fails in real use. Here is a classic: the company sends an apology coupon after a late delivery, and someone includes "coupon sent" as a feature. Copy What you should see Copy Perfect accuracy, and a huge weight on the coupon. But at the moment you need the prediction (before the delivery), no coupon exists yet. In real use this model is worthless. Ask of every feature: would I know this at the moment I make the prediction? Other common leaks: Preprocessing on all the data : computing the mean and standard deviation for scaling ( Lesson 2.4 ) over training and test data. Fit every preprocessing step on the training set only; a sklearn pipeline does this for you. Duplicates across splits : the same customer, document or near-identical image in both training and test sets. The model has seen the answer. Split by customer or by document, not by row. The future in the past : shuffling time-ordered data (the tip above). Benchmark contamination in language models: if a public test set's questions were on the internet, they may be in the model's training data, so a high benchmark score can partly be memory ( Lesson 10.16 ). Step 6 · Distribution shift: when the world moves Even without leakage, a model only knows the world its training data came from. When the data it meets in use differs, called distribution shift , performance drops, often silently. A delivery-time model trained in the dry season meets the monsoon. A fraud model trained before a new payment method launched meets fraud patterns it has never seen. A language model trained on text up to a knowledge cutoff date is asked about events after it, and may answer confidently and wrongly. This is one big reason for retrieval (the Retrieval (RAG) section): give the model current facts at question time instead of relying on its training. The remedy is the "monitor" step of the workflow ( Lesson 2.2 ): keep measuring the model on recent real data, and retrain when it drifts. Watch out You can overfit with prompts too The same trap applies when you build with LLMs and never train anything. If you tweak a prompt fifty times until it scores perfectly on the same twenty test questions, you have fitted the prompt to those twenty questions. Keep a separate set of questions you only run at the end, exactly like a test set. The same idea as a formula ridge (L2) regularisation: loss = MSE + α Σⱼ wⱼ² lasso (L1) regularisation: loss = MSE + α Σⱼ |wⱼ|, which pushes some weights to exactly 0 k-fold cross-validation score = (1/k) Σ score on fold i, after training on the other k − 1 folds expected error on new data ≈ bias² (too simple) + variance (too sensitive to the particular sample) + irreducible noise Check your mental model ✗ "My training error is nearly zero, so the model is excellent." ✓ It may have memorised the data. Only error on held-out data tells you about new data. ✗ "It is fine to look at the test set as long as I don't train on it." ✓ Choosing models or settings because of their test score leaks it into your decisions. Use validation data for choices, and the test set once. ✗ "Bigger models always overfit more." ✓ Usually more flexible means more risk, but with enough data and regularisation, very large neural networks generalise well. Data size and regularisation matter as much as model size. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 1, the degree-11 curve passes through all 12 training points.
