a0216: Course home / Phase 2 · Machine Learning Algorithms Anomaly and Outlier Detection Lesson 2.22 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Implement Z-score, IQR, and Isolation Forest anomaly detection methods from scratch Distinguish between point, contextual, and collective anomalies and select the appropriate detection method for each Explain why anomaly detection is framed as modeling normal data rather than classifying anomalies Compare unsupervised anomaly detection with supervised classification and evaluate the tradeoff between novel anomaly coverage and precision Before you start Needs : Lessons 2.1 to 2.13 Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Normal is easy to define. Abnormal is whatever doesn't fit. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Anomaly "Outlier, unusual point" A data point that deviates significantly from the expected pattern of normal data Point anomaly "A single weird value" An individual observation that is unusual regardless of context Contextual anomaly "Normal value, wrong context" An observation that is unusual given its context (time, location, etc.) but might be normal in another context Isolation Forest "Random splits to find outliers" An ensemble of random trees that isolates anomalies with fewer splits than normal points Local Outlier Factor "Compare density to neighbors" A method that flags points whose local density is much lower than their neighbors' density Z-score "Standard deviations from mean" $(x - \text{mean}) / \text{std}$, measuring how far a point is from the center in units of standard deviation IQR "Interquartile range" $Q3 - Q1$, measuring the spread of the middle 50% of data, used for robust outlier detection Contamination "Expected fraction of anomalies" A hyperparameter telling the detector what proportion of the data it should flag as anomalous Precision@k "Of the top k flags, how many are real" Precision computed on only the $k$ most suspicious points, useful for imbalanced anomaly detection AUPRC "Area under precision-recall curve" A metric that summarizes precision-recall performance across all thresholds, better than AUROC for imbalanced data The problem In plain words first An anomaly detector learns what normal looks like and gives every new point a score for how badly it fits. You need almost no examples of the rare bad events, which is the point: fraud and failures are rare and keep changing shape. The hard parts are choosing how to describe "normal" (a bell curve? dense regions?) and choosing the score threshold, which is a business decision about false alarms against missed events. A credit card is used in New York at 2pm, then in Tokyo at 2:05pm. A factory sensor reads 150 degrees when the normal range is 80-120. A server sends 50,000 requests per second when the daily average is 200. These are anomalies. Finding them matters. Fraud costs billions. Equipment failures cost downtime. Network intrusions cost data. The challenge: you rarely have labeled examples of anomalies. Fraud makes up 0.1% of transactions. Equipment failures happen a few times per year. You cannot train a standard classifier because there is almost nothing in the "anomaly" class to learn from. Even if you have some labels, the anomalies you have seen are not the only types you will encounter. Tomorrow's fraud scheme looks different from today's. Anomaly detection flips the problem. Instead of learning what is abnormal, learn what is normal. Anything that deviates from normal is suspicious. This works without labels, adapts to new types of anomalies, and scales to massive datasets. Idea 1 · Types of Anomalies Not all anomalies are the same: Point anomalies. A single data point that is unusual regardless of context. A temperature reading of 500 degrees. A transaction of $50,000 from an account that normally spends $50. Contextual anomalies. A data point that is unusual given its context. A temperature of 90 degrees is normal in summer, anomalous in winter. Same value, different context. Collective anomalies. A sequence of data points that is unusual as a group, even though each individual point might be normal. Five login failures is normal. Fifty in a row is a brute-force attack. Most methods detect point anomalies. Contextual anomalies need time or location features. Collective anomalies need sequence-aware methods. Idea 2 · The Unsupervised Framing In standard classification, you have labels for both classes. In anomaly detection, you typically have one of three situations: Fully unsupervised. No labels at all. You fit the detector on all data and hope anomalies are rare enough not to corrupt the "normal" model. Semi-supervised. You have a clean dataset of normal data only. You fit on this clean set and score everything else. This is the strongest setup when possible. Weakly supervised. You have a few labeled anomalies. Use them for evaluation, not training. Train unsupervised, then measure precision/recall on the labeled subset. The key insight: anomaly detection is fundamentally different from classification. You are modeling the distribution of normal data, not the decision boundary between two classes. Idea 3 · Supervised vs Unsupervised: The Tradeoff If you do have labeled anomalies, should you use them for training (supervised classification) or for evaluation only (unsupervised detection)? Supervised (treat as classification): - Catches the exact types of anomalies you have seen before - Higher precision on known anomaly types - Misses novel anomaly types entirely - Requires retraining when new anomaly types emerge - Needs enough anomaly examples (often too few) Unsupervised (model normal, flag deviations): - Catches any deviation from normal, including novel types - Does not require labeled anomalies - Higher false positive rate (not everything unusual is bad) - More robust to distribution shift In practice, the best systems combine both: unsupervised detection for broad coverage, supervised models for known high-priority anomaly types, and human review for ambiguous cases. Idea 4 · Z-Score Method The simplest approach. Compute the mean and standard deviation of each feature. Flag any point more than standard deviations from the mean. Copy The default threshold is 3.0 (99.7% of normal data falls within 3 standard deviations for a Gaussian distribution). Strengths: Simple. Fast. Interpretable ("this value is 4.5 standard deviations from normal"). Weaknesses: Assumes data is normally distributed. Sensitive to outliers in the training data (the outliers shift the mean and inflate the std, making them harder to detect). Fails on multimodal distributions. When it works well: Single-feature monitoring where data is roughly bell-shaped. Server response times, manufacturing tolerances, sensor readings with stable baselines. When it fails: Multi-cluster data (two office locations with different baseline temperatures), skewed data (transaction amounts where $1000 is rare but not anomalous), data with outliers in the training set. Idea 5 · IQR Method More robust than Z-score. Uses the interquartile range instead of mean and standard deviation. Copy The default factor is 1.5. Strengths: Robust to outliers (percentiles are not affected by extreme values). Works on skewed distributions. No normality assumption. Weaknesses: Univariate only (applies per feature independently). Cannot detect anomalies that are unusual only when features are considered together (a point might be normal in each feature individually but anomalous in the joint space). Practical note: The 1.5 factor in IQR corresponds to the whiskers in a box plot. Points outside the whiskers are potential outliers. Using 3.0 instead of 1.5 makes the detector more conservative (fewer flags, fewer false positives). The right factor depends on your tolerance for false alarms. Worked example Six readings, one outlier A sensor reports 10, 11, 9, 10, 10, 50 . Z-score. The mean is 16.67 and the standard deviation 14.92, so the 50 scores (50 − 16.67) ÷ 14.92 = 2.23 : not flagged at 3. The outlier dragged the mean up and inflated the spread it is measured against. In fact, with points no z-score can ever exceed ​ , which is 2.24 for six points, so a threshold of 3 can never fire. IQR. Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 10.75 (NumPy's percentile interpolates), so IQR = 0.75 and the upper fence is 10.75 + 1.5 × 0.75 = 11.875 . The 50 is far outside: flagged. Percentiles barely notice one extreme value. Check your mental model ✗ "Z-score at 3 always flags about 0.3 percent of the data." ✓ Only for bell-shaped data with no outliers in it. Outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide themselves, and on tiny samples a z of 3 is impossible. ✗ "A point that is normal on every feature is normal." ✓ Per-feature methods (z-score, IQR) miss points that sit between clusters or off a diagonal. Isolation Forest and LOF look at the features jointly. ✗ "High AUROC means the detector is ready." ✓ With very few anomalies, AUROC can be high while the top of the list is still full of false alarms. Look at precision at the number of alerts you can actually review. Idea 6 · Isolation Forest The key insight: anomalies are few and different. In a random partitioning of the data, anomalies are easier to isolate -- they need fewer random splits to be separated from the rest. How it works: 1. Build many random trees (an isolation forest) 2. At each node, pick a random feature and a random split value between the feature's min and max 3. Keep splitting until every point is isolated (in its own leaf) 4. Anomalies have shorter average path lengths across all trees Why it works: Normal points live in dense regions. Many random splits are needed to isolate one from its neighbors. Anomalies live in sparse regions. One or two random splits are enough to isolate them. The anomaly score is based on the average path length across all trees, normalized by the expected path length of a random binary search tree: Where c(n) is the expected path length for samples. Score near 1 means anomaly. Score near 0.5 means normal. Score near 0 means very normal (deep in dense clusters). Strengths: No distribution assumptions. Works in high dimensions. Scales well (sublinear in sample size because each tree uses a subsample). Handles mixed feature types. Weaknesses: Struggles with anomalies in dense regions (masking effect). Random splitting is less effective when many features are irrelevant. Key hyperparameters: - n_estimators : Number of trees. 100 is usually enough. More trees give more stable scores but slower computation. - max_samples : Number of samples per tree. 256 is the default in the original paper. Smaller values make individual trees less accurate but increase diversity. The subsampling is what makes Isolation Forest fast -- each tree sees a small fraction of the data. - contamination : Expected fraction of anomalies. Used only for setting the threshold. Does not affect the scores themselves. Idea 7 · Local Outlier Factor (LOF) LOF compares the local density around a point to the density around its neighbors. A point in a sparse region surrounded by dense regions is anomalous. How it works: 1. For each point, find its nearest neighbors 2. Compute the local reachability density (how dense is the neighborhood) 3. Compare each point's density to its neighbors' densities 4. If a point has much lower density than its neighbors, it is an outlier LOF score: - LOF close to 1.0 means similar density as neighbors (normal) - LOF greater than 1.0 means lower density than neighbors (potentially anomalous) - LOF much greater than 1.0 (e.g., 2.0+) means significantly lower density (likely anomaly) The "local" part is critical. Consider a dataset with two clusters: a dense cluster of 1000 points and a sparse cluster of 50 points. A point on the edge of the sparse cluster is not globally unusual -- it has 50 neighbors. But it is locally unusual if its immediate neighbors are denser than it is. LOF captures this nuance that global methods miss. Strengths: Detects local anomalies (points that are unusual in their neighborhood, even if they are not globally unusual). Works on clusters of different densities. Weaknesses: Slow on large datasets ( ) for naive implementation). Sensitive to the choice of . Does not work well in very high dimensions (curse of dimensionality affects distance calculations). Predict before you run On the three-cluster data (600 normal points in three clusters, 20 anomalies scattered around them), rank z-score, Isolation Forest and LOF by precision@20: of the 20 highest-scoring points, how many are real anomalies? (Solution P1; the comparison runs under "Build · Demo Scenarios".) Idea 8 · Comparison Method Assumptions Speed Handles High Dims Detects Local Anomalies Z-score Normal distribution Very fast Yes (per feature) No IQR None (per feature) Very fast Yes (per feature) No Isolation Forest None Fast Yes Partially LOF Distance is meaningful Slow Poorly Yes Idea 9 · Evaluation Challenges Evaluating anomaly detectors is harder than evaluating classifiers: Extreme class imbalance. With 0.1% anomalies, predicting "normal" for everything gives 99.9% accuracy. Accuracy is useless. AUROC is misleading. With heavy imbalance, AUROC can look good even when the model misses most anomalies at practical thresholds. Better metrics: Precision@k (of the top flagged items, how many are real anomalies), AUPRC (area under precision-recall curve), and recall at a fixed false positive rate. Idea 10 · Anomaly Detection Pipeline In practice, anomaly detection follows this workflow: Collect baseline data. Ideally, a period where you know there are no (or very few) anomalies. Feature engineering. Raw features plus derived features (rolling statistics, time features, ratios). Train the detector. Fit on the baseline data. The model learns what "normal" looks like. Score new data. Each new observation gets an anomaly score. Threshold selection. Choose the score cutoff. This is a business decision: higher threshold means fewer false alarms but more missed anomalies. Alert and investigate. Flagged points go to human review or automated response. Feedback collection. Record whether flagged items were true anomalies or false alarms. Use this data to evaluate the detector and tune the threshold over time. The pipeline is never "done." Data distributions shift, new anomaly types emerge, and thresholds need adjustment. Treat anomaly detection as a living system, not a one-time model. The same idea as a formula Z-score. Flag when . For normal data that flags 0.27% of points by chance; the anomalies themselves inflate (masking), so robust versions use the median and the median absolute deviation instead. IQR rule. Flag values below ​ − 1.5 IQR or above ​ + 1.5 IQR , with ​ − Q 1 ​ . For normal data the fences sit at and catch about 0.7%; quartiles barely move when a few extreme values are added. Isolation forest. Random splits isolate an unusual point in few steps. With the path length to isolate in a random tree built on points, the score is , c ( n ) = 2 H ( n − 1 ) − n 2 ( n − 1 ) ​ where is the harmonic number and the average path length in such a tree: near 1 means anomalous, around 0.5 means normal. Local outlier factor compares a point's local density with its neighbours': inside a cluster, well above 1 for a point in a sparser region than its neighbours, which catches outliers next to dense clusters that a global threshold misses. Evaluation. With few labelled anomalies, use precision at the top flagged and the PR curve; at a 1% anomaly rate, a detector that flags nothing is 99% accurate. Shorter paths mean more anomalous. The IsolationForest class wraps multiple trees: Copy The normalization factor c(n) ( _c_factor in the code) is the expected path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree with elements. It equals 2 * H(n-1) - 2*(n-1)/n where H is the harmonic number. The code uses the standard approximation H(i) ≈ ln(i) + 0.5772 (Euler's constant), as the original Isolation Forest paper does. This normalization ensures scores are comparable across datasets of different sizes. Reading this output Reading the scores In practice the scores do not spread over the whole 0 to 1 range. Autoencoder Approach (Preview) Autoencoders are neural networks that learn to compress and reconstruct data. Train on normal data. At test time, anomalies have high reconstruction error because the network learned to reconstruct normal patterns only. Ensemble Anomaly Detection Just as ensemble methods improve classification ( Lesson 2.17 ), combining multiple anomaly detectors improves detection. The simplest approach: Run multiple detectors (Z-score, IQR, Isolation Forest, LOF) Normalize each detector's scores to [0, 1] Average the normalized scores Flag points above the threshold on the average score This reduces false positives because different methods have different failure modes. A point flagged by all four methods is almost certainly anomalous. A point flagged by only one might be a quirk of that method. More sophisticated ensembles weight each detector by its estimated reliability (measured on a validation set with known anomalies, if available). Production Considerations Threshold drift. As data distribution shifts, a fixed threshold becomes outdated. Monitor the distribution of anomaly scores and adjust periodically. Alert fatigue. Too many false alarms and operators stop paying attention. Start with a high threshold (fewer, more reliable alerts) and lower it as trust builds. Ensemble approach. In production, combine multiple detectors. Flag a point only if multiple methods agree it is anomalous. This reduces false positives significantly. Feature engineering. Raw features are rarely enough. Add rolling statistics, ratios, time-since-last-event, and domain-specific features. A good feature set matters more than the choice of detector. Feedback loop. When operators investigate flagged items and confirm or dismiss them, feed this back into the system. Accumulate labeled data over time to evaluate and improve the detector. Recap What to keep from this lesson Model normal and score deviations; you rarely have enough labelled anomalies to classify them. Z-score is simple but fooled by skew, several clusters and outliers in its own training data; IQR is robust but still one feature at a time. Isolation Forest isolates rare points in few random splits; LOF compares each point's density with its neighbours'. Evaluate with precision@k or average precision, never accuracy. The threshold is a cost decision: false alarms against missed events. Solutions Solution P1 · Density wins on clusters LOF is best with 0.85 (17 of the top 20 are real anomalies), the from-scratch Isolation Forest next with 0.75, and z-score last with 0.50 . Z-score measures distance from the overall mean of all three clusters, so points between the clusters, near that mean, look perfectly ordinary, while the edges of the outer clusters look extreme. LOF judges each point against its own neighbourhood, which is exactly what this data needs. Solution B1 · Outliers hide themselves With 20 copies every one has z ≈ 5.3 and all 20 are flagged. With 100 copies the standard deviation swells from about 1 to 2.47 and the mean moves up, so each 8.0 now has z ≈ 2.93 , and none is flagged. The outliers have become part of "normal". A robust z-score that uses the median and the median absolute deviation (scaled by 1.4826) still gives them about 7.3. Better still, fit the detector on a period you know is clean. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Isolation Forest remains the workhorse. It is the usual first unsupervised detector for transactions, logs and sensor data; PyOD collects dozens of detectors behind one API. Anomaly detection as a platform feature. Snowflake's ANOMALY_DETECTION function, BigQuery ML's ML.DETECT_ANOMALIES and observability tools (Datadog, Grafana) run detection on metrics without custom models. Embeddings for unstructured data. Distance from normal examples in an embedding space flags unusual images, documents or support tickets. A Supervised classification is always less accurate B Labeled anomalies are extremely rare, and novel anomaly types differ from previously seen ones C Anomaly detection only works on time series data D Anomaly detection does not require any data Anomalies are rare (often <0.1% of data), so there are too few labeled examples to train a classifier. Q3 The Z-score method flags points more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. When does this approach fail? A When there are exactly 3 anomalies in the dataset B When the data is perfectly normally distributed C When the features are standardized D When the data is multimodal, skewed, or when outliers in the training data inflate the mean and std Z-score assumes a single Gaussian distribution. It fails on multimodal data (multiple clusters), skewed distributions, and when outliers in training data shift the mean/std, making real anomalies harder to detect. A It isolates points using random splits; anomalies require fewer splits to isolate because they are few and different B It only works on text data C It uses neural networks instead of trees D It computes distances to every other point in the dataset Isolation Forest randomly partitions data with tree splits. Anomalies, being rare and different, end up isolated (in their own leaf) with fewer splits. Short average path length = more anomalous. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line When 99% of your data is "normal," accuracy is a lie. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Class imbalance "One class has way more samples" The distribution of classes in the dataset is significantly skewed, causing models to favor the majority class SMOTE "Synthetic oversampling" Creates new minority samples by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest minority neighbors Class weights "Making errors on rare classes more expensive" Multiplying the loss function by class-specific weights so the model penalizes minority misclassification more heavily Threshold tuning "Moving the decision boundary" Changing the probability cutoff for classification from the default 0.5 to a value that optimizes the desired metric Precision-recall tradeoff "You cannot have both" Lowering the threshold catches more positives (higher recall) but also flags more false positives (lower precision), and vice versa AUPRC "Area under the PR curve" Summarizes the precision-recall curve into a single number; more informative than AUC-ROC when classes are heavily imbalanced Matthews Correlation Coefficient "The balanced metric" A correlation between predicted and actual labels that produces a high score only when the model performs well on both classes Cost-sensitive learning "Different mistakes cost different amounts" Incorporating real-world misclassification costs into the training objective so the model optimizes for total cost, not error count Random oversampling "Duplicate the minority" Repeating minority class samples to balance class counts; simple but risks overfitting to duplicated points The problem In plain words first When one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy by ignoring it. Three things fix that. Measure with metrics that look at the rare class (precision, recall, F1, MCC, average precision). Train so that rare-class mistakes count more (class weights, oversampling, SMOTE, undersampling). Decide with a threshold chosen for your costs rather than the default 0.5. The third is often the one that matters most. You build a fraud detection model. It gets 99.9% accuracy. You celebrate. Then you realize it predicts "not fraud" for every single transaction. This is not a bug. It is the rational thing to do when only 0.1% of transactions are fraudulent. The model learns that always guessing the majority class minimizes overall error. It is technically correct and completely useless. This happens everywhere real classification matters. Disease diagnosis: 1% positive rate. Network intrusion: 0.01% attacks. Manufacturing defects: 0.5% defective. Spam filtering: 20% spam. Churn prediction: 5% churners. The more consequential the minority class, the rarer it tends to be. Accuracy fails because it treats all correct predictions equally. Correctly labeling a legitimate transaction and correctly catching fraud both count as one point of accuracy. But catching fraud is the entire reason the model exists. We need metrics, techniques, and training strategies that force the model to pay attention to the rare but important class. Idea 1 · Why Accuracy Fails Consider a dataset with 1000 samples: 990 negative, 10 positive. A model that always predicts negative: Predicted Positive Predicted Negative Actually Positive 0 (TP) 10 (FN) Actually Negative 0 (FP) 990 (TN) The model catches zero fraud. Zero disease. Zero defects. But accuracy says 99%. This is why accuracy is dangerous for imbalanced problems. Idea 2 · Better Metrics Precision = . Of everything flagged as positive, how many actually are? High precision means few false alarms. Recall = . Of everything actually positive, how many did we catch? High recall means few missed positives. F1 Score = . The harmonic mean. Penalizes extreme imbalance between precision and recall more than the arithmetic mean would. F-beta Score = ) ⋅ precision ⋅ recall / ( β 2 ⋅ precision + recall ) . When , recall matters more. When , precision matters more. F2 is common in fraud detection (missing fraud is worse than a false alarm). AUPRC (Area Under Precision-Recall Curve). Like AUC-ROC but more informative for imbalanced data. A random classifier has AUPRC equal to the positive class rate (not 0.5 like ROC). This makes improvements easier to see. Matthews Correlation Coefficient = ​ . Ranges from -1 to +1. Only gives a high score when the model does well on both classes. Balanced even when classes are very different sizes. For the "always predict negative" model above: (undefined, often set to 0), , , . These metrics correctly identify the model as worthless. Worked example The metrics on a real confusion matrix In Step 7 the untreated model, on 200 test samples with 14 positives, catches 9 positives with no false alarms: TP = 9, FP = 0, FN = 5, TN = 186. Accuracy = (9 + 186) ÷ 200 = 0.975 . Predicting "negative" for everything would already score 186 + 0 = 0.930. Precision = 9 ÷ 9 = 1.0 ; recall = 9 ÷ 14 = 0.643 . F1 = 2 × 9 ÷ (2 × 9 + 0 + 5) = 18 ÷ 23 = 0.783 . MCC = (9 × 186 − 0 × 5) ÷ √(9 × 14 × 186 × 191) = 1674 ÷ 2115.7 = 0.791 . Accuracy calls this model nearly perfect; recall says it misses a third of the positives. Idea 3 · The Imbalanced Data Pipeline Idea 4 · SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique Random oversampling duplicates existing minority samples. This works but risks overfitting because the model sees identical points repeatedly. SMOTE creates new synthetic minority samples that are plausible but not copies. The algorithm: For each minority sample , find its nearest neighbors among other minority samples Pick one neighbor at random Create a new sample on the line segment between and that neighbor The formula: new_sample = x + random(0, 1) * (neighbor - x) This interpolates between real minority points, creating samples in the same region of feature space without just copying existing data. Worked example One synthetic point Take ​ = ( 1.0 , 2.0 ) and its neighbour ​ = ( 1.5 , 2.5 ) , and draw . The new point is ​ + 0.4 ( x 2 ​ − x 1 ​ ) = ( 1.0 + 0.2 , 2.0 + 0.2 ) = ( 1.2 , 2.2 ) : 40 percent of the way along the segment between two real minority points. Idea 5 · Sampling Strategies Compared Random Oversampling : duplicate minority samples to match majority count. - Pros: simple, no information loss - Cons: exact duplicates cause overfitting, increases training time Random Undersampling : remove majority samples to match minority count. - Pros: fast training, simple - Cons: throws away potentially useful majority data, higher variance SMOTE : create synthetic minority samples via interpolation. - Pros: generates new data points, reduces overfitting compared to random oversampling - Cons: can create noisy samples near the decision boundary, does not account for majority class distribution Strategy Data Changed Risk When to Use Oversample Minority duplicated Overfitting Small datasets, moderate imbalance Undersample Majority removed Information loss Large datasets, want fast training SMOTE Synthetic minority added Boundary noise Moderate imbalance, enough minority samples for k-NN Idea 6 · Class Weights Instead of changing the data, change how the model treats errors. Assign higher weight to misclassifying the minority class. For a binary problem with 950 negative and 50 positive samples: - Weight for negative class = ​ / ( 2 ⋅ n negative ​ ) = 1000/ ( 2 ⋅ 950 ) = 0.526 - Weight for positive class = ​ / ( 2 ⋅ n positive ​ ) = 1000/ ( 2 ⋅ 50 ) = 10.0 The positive class gets 19x the weight. Misclassifying one positive sample costs as much as misclassifying 19 negative samples. The model is forced to pay attention to the minority class. In logistic regression, this modifies the loss function: ​ ⋅ [ y i ​ lo g ( p i ​ ) + ( 1 − y i ​ ) lo g ( 1 − p i ​ )] ) where ​ depends on the class of sample . Class weights are mathematically equivalent to oversampling in expectation, but without creating new data points. This makes them faster and avoids the overfitting risk of duplicated samples. Idea 7 · Threshold Tuning Most classifiers output a probability. The default threshold is 0.5: if , predict positive. But 0.5 is arbitrary. When classes are imbalanced, the optimal threshold is usually much lower. The process: 1. Train a model 2. Get predicted probabilities on the validation set 3. Sweep thresholds from 0.0 to 1.0 4. Compute F1 (or your chosen metric) at each threshold 5. Pick the threshold that maximizes your metric A model might output for a fraudulent transaction. At threshold 0.5, this is classified as not fraud. At threshold 0.10, it is correctly caught. The probability calibration matters less than the ranking -- as long as fraud gets higher probabilities than non-fraud, there exists a threshold that separates them. Sources and further reading SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (Chawla et al., 2002) -- the original SMOTE paper, still the most cited work on imbalanced learning Learning from Imbalanced Data (He & Garcia, 2009) -- comprehensive survey covering sampling, cost-sensitive, and algorithmic approaches imbalanced-learn documentation -- Python library with SMOTE variants, undersampling strategies, and pipeline integration The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015) -- when and why to prefer PR curves over ROC curves for imbalanced problems Check your understanding Q1 A fraud detection dataset has 99.9% legitimate transactions and 0.1% fraud. A model predicts 'legitimate' for every transaction. What is its accuracy? A 99.9% B 0.1% C 50% D 100% Accuracy = 999/1000 = 99.9%. The model catches zero fraud but looks great by accuracy. This is exactly why accuracy is dangerous for imbalanced datasets. Q2 Which metric would correctly identify the always-predict-negative model as useless? A Accuracy (99.9%) B True negative rate (100%) C Recall (0%) or F1 score (0%) D Specificity (100%) Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 0/total_positives = 0%. F1 = 2*0*0/(0+0) = 0. Both correctly show the model catches nothing in the positive class. Accuracy hides this failure. Q3 How does SMOTE generate synthetic minority samples? A By flipping the labels of majority class samples B By interpolating between a minority sample and one of its K nearest minority neighbors C By randomly generating points anywhere in the feature space D By duplicating existing minority samples exactly SMOTE picks a minority point, selects one of its K nearest minority neighbors, and creates a new point on the line segment between them: new = x + rand(0,1) * (neighbor - x). This produces plausible, non-duplicate samples. Q4 You lower the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 on an imbalanced dataset. What happens to precision and recall? A Both precision and recall increase B Precision increases but recall decreases C Recall increases (more positives caught) but precision decreases (more false positives) D Neither changes -- threshold only affects speed Lowering the threshold means more samples are predicted positive. This catches more true positives (recall up) but also adds more false positives (precision down). Threshold tuning trades precision for recall. Q5 Why is AUPRC (Area Under Precision-Recall Curve) more informative than AUC-ROC for highly imbalanced datasets? A AUC-ROC cannot be computed for imbalanced data B AUPRC does not require a threshold C AUPRC is always higher than AUC-ROC D A random classifier has AUPRC equal to the positive class rate (e.g., 0.001), making improvements visible, while AUC-ROC starts at 0.5 regardless of imbalance For imbalanced data, AUC-ROC can look deceptively good because the large number of true negatives inflates the true negative rate. AUPRC's baseline equals the positive rate, making real improvements in detecting the minority class much more apparent. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line More features is not better. The right features is better. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Filter method "Score features independently" A feature selection approach that ranks features using a statistical measure without training a model, evaluating each feature in isolation Wrapper method "Use the model to pick features" A feature selection approach that evaluates feature subsets by training a model and using its performance as the selection criterion Embedded method "The model selects features during training" Feature selection that happens as part of model fitting, such as L1 regularization driving weights to zero Mutual information "How much one variable tells you about another" A measure of the reduction in uncertainty about $Y$ given knowledge of $X$, capturing both linear and nonlinear dependencies Recursive Feature Elimination "Train, rank, prune, repeat" An iterative wrapper method that trains a model, removes the least important feature(s), and repeats until a target count is reached L1 / Lasso regularization "Penalty that kills features" Adding the sum of absolute weight values to the loss function, which drives unimportant feature weights to exactly zero Variance threshold "Remove constant features" Dropping features whose variance across samples falls below a specified threshold, filtering out features that carry no information Feature importance "Which features matter most" A score indicating how much each feature contributes to model predictions, computed from split gains (trees) or coefficient magnitudes (linear) Permutation importance "Shuffle and measure the damage" Evaluating feature importance by randomly shuffling each feature's values and measuring the resulting drop in model performance Curse of dimensionality "Too many features, not enough data" The phenomenon where adding features increases the volume of the feature space exponentially, making data sparse and distances meaningless The problem In plain words first Feature selection keeps the columns that carry information about the target and drops the rest. Fewer, better columns mean less overfitting, faster training and a model you can explain. There are three ways to choose: score each column on its own (filters), try subsets with a model (wrappers such as RFE), or let the model ignore columns while it trains (embedded: L1 penalties, tree importances). All of them must be chosen on training data only, or they leak. You have 500 features. Your model trains slowly, overfits constantly, and nobody can explain what it learned. You add more features hoping to improve performance. It gets worse. This is the curse of dimensionality in action. As the number of features grows, the volume of the feature space explodes. Data points become sparse. Distances between points converge. The model needs exponentially more data to find real patterns. Noise features drown out signal features. Overfitting becomes the default. Feature selection is the antidote. Strip away the noise. Remove the redundancy. Keep the features that carry actual information about the target. The result: faster training, better generalization, and models you can actually explain. The goal is not to use all available information. It is to use the right information. Idea 1 · Three Categories of Feature Selection Every feature selection method falls into one of three categories: Filter methods score each feature independently using a statistical measure. They do not use a model. Fast, but they miss feature interactions. Wrapper methods train a model to evaluate feature subsets. They use model performance as the score. Better results, but expensive because they retrain the model many times. Embedded methods select features as part of model training. L1 regularization drives weights to zero. Decision trees split on the most useful features. Selection happens during fitting, not as a separate step. Idea 2 · Variance Threshold The simplest filter. If a feature barely varies across samples, it carries almost no information. Consider a feature that is 0.0 for 999 out of 1000 samples. Its variance is near zero. No model can use it to distinguish between classes. Remove it. ) Set a threshold (e.g., 0.01). Drop every feature with variance below it. This removes constant or near-constant features without looking at the target variable at all. When to use it: as a preprocessing step before other methods. It catches obviously useless features at near-zero cost. Limitation: a feature can have high variance and still be pure noise. Variance threshold is necessary but not sufficient. Idea 3 · Mutual Information Mutual information measures how much knowing the value of feature reduces uncertainty about target . ∑ ​ y ∑ ​ p ( x , y ) ⋅ lo g p ( x ) ⋅ p ( y ) p ( x , y ) ​ If and are independent, , so the log term is zero and . The more tells you about , the higher the mutual information. Key advantage over correlation: mutual information captures nonlinear relationships. A feature might have zero correlation with the target but high mutual information because the relationship is quadratic or periodic. For continuous features, discretize into bins first (histogram-based estimation). The number of bins affects the estimate -- too few bins lose information, too many bins add noise. A common choice: ​ bins or Sturges' rule ( ​ n ). The most a feature can tell you about a fair yes/no target is nats, when it predicts it perfectly. Idea 4 · Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) RFE is a wrapper method. It uses a model's own feature importance to iteratively prune: Train the model with all features Rank features by importance (coefficients for linear models, impurity reduction for trees) Remove the least important feature(s) Repeat until the desired number of features remains RFE considers feature interactions because the model sees all remaining features together. Removing one feature changes the importance of others. This makes it more thorough than filter methods. The cost: you train the model times. With 500 features and a target of 10, that is 490 training runs. For expensive models, this is slow. You can speed it up by removing multiple features per step (e.g., remove the bottom 10% each round). Idea 5 · L1 (Lasso) Regularization L1 regularization adds the absolute value of weights to the loss function: ​ ∣ The alpha parameter controls how aggressively features are pruned. Higher alpha means more weights go to exactly zero. Why exactly zero? The L1 penalty creates a diamond-shaped constraint region in weight space. The optimal solution tends to land at a corner of this diamond, where one or more weights are zero. L2 regularization (ridge) creates a circular constraint where weights shrink but rarely hit zero. This is embedded feature selection: the model learns during training which features to ignore. Features with zero weight are effectively removed. Advantages: single training run, handles correlated features (picks one and zeros the others), built into most linear model implementations. Limitation: only works for linear models. Cannot capture nonlinear feature importance. Idea 6 · Tree-Based Feature Importance Decision trees and their ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) naturally rank features. Every split reduces impurity (Gini or entropy for classification, variance for regression). Features that produce larger impurity reductions are more important. For a random forest with trees: ​ ) = T 1 ​ all trees ∑ ​ all nodes splitting on feature j ​ ∑ ​ ( n_samples ⋅ impurity_decrease ) This gives a normalized importance score for each feature. It handles nonlinear relationships and feature interactions automatically. Caution: tree-based importance is biased toward features with many unique values (high cardinality). A random ID column will appear important because it perfectly splits every sample. Use permutation importance as a sanity check. Idea 7 · Permutation Importance A model-agnostic method: Train the model and record baseline performance on validation data For each feature: shuffle its values randomly, measure the drop in performance The bigger the drop, the more important the feature If shuffling a feature does not hurt performance, the model does not depend on it. If performance collapses, that feature is critical. Permutation importance avoids the cardinality bias of tree-based importance. But it is slow: one full evaluation per feature, repeated multiple times for stability. Recap What to keep from this lesson Filters score columns one at a time; wrappers search subsets with a model; embedded methods select while training. Mutual information catches non-linear links, but noisy estimates make weak features hard to separate from noise. Correlated copies split importance and make selections unstable. Impurity importance favours columns with many values; check with permutation importance on held-out data. Select inside the cross-validation loop, never on the whole dataset first. Solutions Solution P1 · Distance drowns in noise k-NN falls from 0.916 to 0.790 with 10 noise columns, 0.676 with 50, 0.562 with 200 and 0.518 (a coin toss) with 1,000. Logistic regression holds 0.936 with 10, 0.894 with 50, then drops to 0.794 and 0.602. Distances in k-NN weigh every column equally, so noise columns swamp the three that matter; logistic regression can give noise small weights, until there are more noise columns than training rows. Solution B1 · Selection leakage Selecting on all the data gives a cross-validated accuracy of 0.85 on labels that are pure coin flips. Inside a pipeline it is 0.40 , around chance (0.5). With 2,000 features, some fit 100 random labels well by luck; choosing them with the test folds' labels bakes that luck into every fold. Any step that looks at the labels (selection, target encoding, SMOTE, tuning) belongs inside the cross-validation loop. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) SHAP-based selection. SHAP values from gradient-boosted trees ( shap.TreeExplainer ) are the common way to rank and prune features in production tabular models, alongside permutation importance in scikit-learn. Selection inside the pipeline. SelectFromModel and SequentialFeatureSelector in a scikit-learn pipeline keep selection inside cross-validation, avoiding the leakage this lesson warns about. Sources: SHAP , scikit-learn feature selection , permutation importance . A Models have a hard limit on the number of features they can accept B More features always improve model accuracy C More features make the model run out of memory D Irrelevant features add noise, increase overfitting risk, and dilute the signal from useful features Irrelevant features give the model opportunities to overfit on noise in the training data. They increase dimensionality, making the data sparser and distances less meaningful (curse of dimensionality). Q2 What is the key difference between filter and wrapper feature selection methods? A Filter methods score features using statistics without a model; wrapper methods train a model to evaluate feature subsets B Filter methods are always more accurate than wrapper methods C Wrapper methods can only select one feature at a time D Filter methods use a model to evaluate features; wrapper methods use statistics Filter methods (variance threshold, mutual information, correlation) score features with statistical measures. Wrapper methods (RFE, forward selection) train models repeatedly to evaluate different feature subsets. Q3 Mutual information can detect relationships that Pearson correlation cannot. What kind? A Relationships that require more than 1000 data points B Nonlinear relationships such as quadratic or periodic dependencies C Linear relationships between continuous features D Relationships between categorical features only Pearson correlation only measures linear association. A quadratic relationship (y = x^2) has zero correlation but high mutual information. MI captures any statistical dependency between variables. Q4 L1 (Lasso) regularization performs feature selection as part of training. How? A It removes features with low variance before training starts B It ranks features by correlation with the target C It drives the weights of irrelevant features to exactly zero, effectively eliminating them from the model D It trains separate models for each feature L1 regularization adds |w| penalty to the loss. The geometry of the L1 constraint (diamond shape) causes some weight solutions to land exactly at zero, producing sparse models that automatically select features. Q5 RFE removes the least important feature and retrains. Why is this better than just removing all low-importance features at once? A It is not better -- removing all at once is always preferred B Feature importances change as features are removed, so iterative removal accounts for interactions between features C Removing one at a time is only necessary for neural networks D RFE uses a different importance metric than single-step removal Feature importances are relative. When a correlated feature is removed, the importance of its counterpart may increase. Iterative removal lets the model reassess importances at each step, capturing these interactions. a0219: Course home / Phase 2 · Machine Learning Algorithms ML System Design: From Problem to Production Model Lesson 2.25 110 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Frame a business problem as an ML task with a prediction, a decision that uses it, and a reason why rules are not enough Separate offline, online, business, and guardrail metrics, and compare every model against trivial and heuristic baselines Estimate the daily cost, latency, and staleness of batch and online inference from traffic numbers Choose a rollout pattern (shadow, canary, A/B test) and a safe default for each failure mode Identify feedback loops in which the model changes the data that trains its next version Write an ML design document and score it against a fixed checklist Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.13 (Model Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and More) and 13 (Scikit-learn ML Pipelines) Type : Build. Time : about 110 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A model is one part of a system. The design decides what the model predicts, who acts on it, what it costs, and what happens when it fails. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it means ML task "Build a churn model" A prediction target, an entity, a horizon, and the decision that uses the prediction Offline metric "The model score" A metric computed on held-out past data before launch Online metric "Live numbers" A metric measured on real traffic while the model runs Business metric "The goal" The company outcome that the decision must change, measured with an experiment Guardrail metric "Do no harm" A metric that must not get worse when the new model launches Baseline "The dumb model" A trivial, heuristic, or current-system predictor that the model must beat by a set margin Batch inference "Precomputed scores" A scheduled job scores every entity and stores the results for lookup Online inference "Real-time model" The model scores each request when it arrives Shadow deployment "Dark launch" The new model scores live traffic, and nobody uses its output Canary release "Slow rollout" The new model decides for a small, growing share of traffic, with a rollback ready Feedback loop "The model trains itself" The model's decisions change the data that trains its next version The problem In plain words first Before training anything, write down what the model predicts, who acts on the prediction, how you will know the action got better, which simple rule it has to beat, how fresh and fast the predictions must be, and what happens when something breaks. Those decisions, not the algorithm, decide whether a model gets used. This lesson turns each one into a number or a checklist item you can test. A subscription company asks for "a churn model". A data scientist trains a gradient-boosted classifier and reports an AUC of 0.91. Three months later, nobody uses it. The reasons have nothing to do with the algorithm. Nobody decided which action a score starts. The scores arrive once a week, but the retention team calls customers every day. The label came from a cancellations table that also stored the cancellation reason, so one feature contained the answer. Nobody compared the model with the rule the support team already used: call anyone idle for two weeks. Each of these failures happened before training started. They are design failures, and a one-page design document asks about each of them. This lesson teaches the decisions in that document. You build a toolkit that prices batch and online serving, compares a model with its baselines, and scores a design document against a checklist. Idea 1 · From a business goal to an ML task A business goal is not an ML task. You turn it into one with four questions: What exactly does the model predict, and for which entity (user, payment, store, item)? Which decision uses the prediction, and who or what makes that decision? When is the prediction needed, and which data exists at that moment? How will you know that the decision got better? Business goal Prediction Decision that uses it ML task Reduce churn Probability that a user cancels in the next 30 days Send a save offer to the top 5 percent each night Binary classification Cut fraud losses Probability that a payment is fraud Approve, review, or block within 100 ms Binary classification Keep shelves stocked Units sold per store per day next week Order quantity for each store Forecasting Show relevant items Relevance score for a (user, item) pair Order of items in the feed Ranking The second column needs the most care. "Predict churn" leaves the horizon, the entity, and the action open. "Predict whether this user cancels in the next 30 days, so that tonight's job can pick who gets an offer" fixes all three. Idea 2 · When not to use ML Rule #1 in Google's Rules of Machine Learning says not to be afraid to launch a product without machine learning. Machine learning needs data, and a simple heuristic often gets you part of the way. Do not use ML in these cases: A short rule reaches the goal and stays correct. A rule is cheaper to run, test, and explain. You have no labels and no practical way to collect them. Nobody acts on the prediction, so a better prediction changes nothing. The data that exists at prediction time does not contain the signal. One error is unacceptable and no person can check the output. Building and running the system costs more than the better decisions are worth. When a rule gets long and fragile, ML starts to pay off. Rule #3 of the same guide prefers ML over a complex heuristic, because a learned model is easier to update and maintain. Idea 3 · Three layers of metrics You measure an ML system at three layers, plus a set of limits: Layer When you can measure it Churn example Offline metric Before launch, on held-out past data F1 at the offer threshold, precision in the top 5 percent Online metric During launch, on live traffic Offer acceptance rate, share of users scored, score distribution Business metric Weeks after launch, with an experiment 30-day churn rate in the treated group versus a holdout group Guardrail metric All the time Offer cost per saved user, unsubscribe rate, p99 latency The layers often disagree. An offline metric scores past data, and the past did not contain your model. An online metric depends on how people react to the decision. A business metric moves slowly and carries noise from everything else in the company. Pick the offline metric that matches the decision. If the job contacts the top 5 percent of users, measure precision in the top 5 percent. AUC averages over every threshold, including thresholds that you never use. Rule #2 of the same guide says to design and implement metrics first, before you decide what the ML system will do. Idea 4 · Baselines A metric value means nothing alone. An F1 of 0.56 is good if the best alternative reaches 0.30 and poor if a rule reaches 0.60. Compare every model with three kinds of baseline: Trivial baseline. Always predict the majority class, or always predict the training mean. We used this check in the model evaluation lesson. Heuristic baseline. A rule from domain knowledge, or a one-feature threshold that you fit on the training data. Current system. Whatever makes the decision today, even when it is a person with a spreadsheet. The lift is the model score minus the score of the strongest baseline. Set a minimum lift before you look at the results, and make it large enough to pay for the extra system. The trivial baseline is usually weak. The heuristic baseline is the hard one to beat. Check your mental model ✗ "An AUC of 0.91 means the model is ready." ✓ AUC averages over every threshold. If the job contacts the top 5 percent, measure precision in the top 5 percent, and compare it with a rule on the same metric. ✗ "Beating the majority-class baseline proves the model works." ✓ On F1 the majority baseline scores 0 because it never predicts churn, so anything beats it. The fitted one-feature rule (0.500 in Step 5) is the real competitor. ✗ "A better offline score means a better business result." ✓ Offline data never contained your model's decisions. Only an experiment with a holdout group measures the business metric. Idea 5 · Data and label requirements Answer these questions before you train: Label source. Which table or event defines the label, and who owns it? Label delay. How long after the prediction does the true outcome arrive? Fraud chargebacks can arrive weeks after the payment. Churn labels arrive at the end of the 30-day horizon. Label quality. Who assigns the label, and how often is it wrong? Availability at prediction time. Does every feature exist at the moment of the prediction? A feature that the system writes after the outcome leaks the label into training. Volume per class. How many positive examples exist? Two hundred positives limit you to simple models. Time split. Hold out the most recent period. We split data by time in the time-series lesson for the same reason. Idea 6 · Latency, throughput, and cost budgets Three numbers bound every serving design: Latency budget. The p99 latency is the time that 99 of 100 requests stay under. A payment check can need 50 ms. A nightly report can take hours. Peak throughput. Size the system for the busiest minute, not for the daily average. Peak QPS is often several times the average. Cost budget. Express it as dollars per day or dollars per 1000 predictions, so that you can compare designs. Little's law connects the first two. The number of requests in progress equals throughput times latency. At 400 requests per second and 50 ms each, 20 requests are in progress at any moment. Worked example Pricing the feed ranking by hand The feed has 5,000,000 items to score, 2,000,000 requests a day, a peak of 120 requests per second and a freshness limit of 2 hours. With this lesson's prices: Batch. A run takes 1 hour, so runs must start every 2 − 1 = 1 hour: 24 runs a day, 5,000,000 × 24 = 120 million predictions. At $0.40 per million that is $48.00, plus 2 million lookups at $0.25 per million, $0.50: $48.50 a day . Online. 120 ÷ 200 requests per replica rounds up to 1, but the minimum is 2 replicas for availability: 2 × $0.50 × 24 hours = $24.00 a day . Online wins, because the short freshness limit forces 24 full re-scorings a day. Little's law gives the load on those replicas: 120 requests per second × 0.035 s = about 4 requests in progress at the peak. Predict before you run Relax the feed's freshness limit from 2 hours to 4 hours. Which mode does choose_serving pick now, and at what daily cost? At what freshness limit do the two modes cost the same? (Solution P1.) Idea 7 · Batch inference versus online inference There are two basic ways to serve predictions: Batch inference. A scheduled job scores every entity and writes the scores to a table or a key-value store. The application reads the stored score at request time. Online inference. The application sends the features to a model service at request time and waits for the score. Property Batch Online Freshness As old as the last run, plus the run time Uses the data of the request Request latency One key-value read, a few ms Feature fetch plus model time Cost driver Number of entities times runs per day Replicas sized for peak QPS New entities No score until the next run Scored on the first request When it breaks Old scores stay readable Requests fail or time out The toolkit in this lesson prices both. Batch cost grows with the number of entities and with the number of runs per day. A shorter staleness limit means more runs. Online cost grows with peak traffic, because you pay for idle replicas between peaks. A batch job that takes one hour cannot meet a staleness limit under one hour at any price. A hybrid design is common. A nightly batch job scores known users, and an online path scores new users and requests that need fresh data. See it drawn Daily cost of each serving mode for the feed-ranking workload as the freshness limit changes. Batch gets cheaper as the limit grows, because it re-scores all five million items less often; online costs the same at any limit. The system logs its predictions and never uses them. You compare latency, error rate, and prediction distribution with the current model. Canary. The new model makes real decisions for a small share of traffic, often 1 to 5 percent. You widen the share in steps and roll back when a guardrail breaks. A/B test. A random split of users sees each model. You measure the business metric with a statistical test, and you need enough traffic and enough time to see the difference. Every stage needs a rollback that takes minutes. Keep the old model version deployed and switch traffic with configuration. Idea 9 · Feedback loops A feedback loop exists when the model's decisions change the data that trains its next version. Sculley et al. list direct and hidden feedback loops among the main sources of technical debt in ML systems. Three common cases: Interventions hide the label. A churn model sends offers, and the offers keep some users. Next month, high-risk users look loyal, and the retrained model learns that their features do not predict churn. Blocked actions have no outcome. A fraud model blocks a payment, so that payment never gets a chargeback label. Retrained models see fewer fraud examples from the blocked region. Exposure limits feedback. A ranking model shows its top items, so only those items collect clicks. The fixes share one idea: keep some data that the model did not influence. Hold out a small random group that never gets the intervention. Give a small share of traffic a random decision. Log the score and the decision with each example, so that later training can tell influenced data from clean data. Worked example Why the holdout matters Suppose 1,000 users a month would churn without help and the save offer keeps 30 percent of those who get it. If every high-risk user gets the offer, next month's data shows only 700 churners among them, and the high-risk features look less predictive than they are. Retrain on that data and the model gets worse at finding the very users the offer saved. A 5 percent random holdout that never gets offers keeps a clean sample: there the true churn rate of high-risk users stays visible, and comparing holdout with treated users also measures the offer's real effect. Idea 10 · Failure modes and safe defaults Every part of the system fails sooner or later. Decide the default action for each failure in the design, not during the incident: Failure Result without a plan Safe default Model service times out The request fails Use the heuristic baseline Nightly batch job fails Scores go missing or get old Serve the last good scores for a fixed time, then the rule Feature is missing or out of range The model scores bad input Use the documented default value and log the event New entity with no history No score exists Use the rule or the population average Score distribution moves suddenly Wrong decisions at scale Pause automatic actions and alert a person The heuristic baseline from your metric section is also the default for most failures, so build it first. Design how it reaches users: the stages, how users are assigned, what you measure at each stage, and when it rolls back automatically. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run it in shadow first, on all traffic, logging its answers without showing them, and compare quality metrics with the current prompt. Then route a small share of users to it, 10% in the lesson, and widen in steps to 25%, 50% and 100% while the metrics hold. Assign by a deterministic hash of the user id so each user sees one version, and roll back automatically when the new version's error rate reaches twice the old one over a window of requests. Shadow mode. The new prompt runs on 100% of traffic but only its logs are kept. Nobody sees its output. This gives a full comparison of latency, cost per request, guardrail block rate and quality scores against the current version, and users never see a shadow answer. Shadow calls can share the provider quota with live calls, so give them a separate quota or key; otherwise a quota limit can slow or fail live requests. It is the same first stage that the ML design lesson calls shadow deployment for a model. Percentage rollout. Route 10% of traffic to the new version. If quality holds, raise it to 25%, then 50%, then 100%. If quality drops, switch back at once. Both versions stay deployed and the switch is configuration, so a rollback takes minutes, which is the lesson's rule for every stage. Deterministic assignment. Hash the user id combined with the name of the experiment and take it modulo 100. Buckets below the traffic share get the variant, the rest get the control. A user then sees the same version across requests inside one experiment, and the assignment can be recomputed later from the log. Random assignment per request mixes versions inside one conversation and makes the comparison noisy. What to measure. Per prompt version: latency percentiles, user ratings where they exist, error rate, guardrail block rate and cost per request. The eval logger records the template name and version with every request, so the metrics split by version without extra plumbing. Automatic rollback. The lesson's exercise sets the rule: when a new version shows 2x the error rate of the previous version over 100 requests, revert automatically. The window matters; a handful of requests is noise, and waiting for thousands lets a bad prompt run too long. A note on the business metric. Shadow and canary protect the user. Whether the new prompt improves the outcome that matters, such as task completion, needs a randomized split with enough traffic and time, which is the A/B stage from the ML design lesson. Plausible wrong answers. "Ship to everyone and watch the dashboard." A regression then hits every user before the dashboard moves. "Assign per request at random for a cleaner statistic." Users see both versions in one conversation and the logged metrics mix them. "Shadow mode is enough; skip the canary." Shadow mode never shows the output to a user, so it cannot measure user reaction. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why hash the user id and not pick randomly per request? Expected: a user then gets one consistent version across a session and the assignment is reproducible from the log. (level 2) What does shadow mode not tell you? Expected: how users react to the new answers; it only compares logged outputs and system metrics. (level 3) The new prompt costs more per request but scores higher. Who decides? Expected: a guardrail on cost per request decides whether it can ship at all; the quality gain against the cost is then a product decision with both numbers on the table. (level 3) How do you keep the control and the variant from sharing a cache entry? Expected: include the prompt version in the cache key, otherwise a hit returns the other version's answer and the comparison is corrupted. Where it is taught. Price batch and online serving with the lesson's cost model, pick one, and say what would flip the choice. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. With a one-hour batch job and a two-hour staleness limit, the job must run every hour, which the lesson's cost model prices at 24.0 runs per day over 5,000,000 items for $48.50 a day. Two online replicas sized for 120 peak QPS cost $24.00 a day and serve the freshest data. Online wins here; the choice flips when the freshness limit relaxes enough to cut the runs, or when peak traffic grows enough to need many replicas. How each plan is priced. Property Batch Online Freshness As old as the last run plus the run time The data of the request Request latency One key-value read, a few milliseconds Feature fetch plus model time, 35 ms in the model Cost driver Entities times runs per day Replicas sized for peak QPS, minimum of two New entities No score until the next run Scored on the first request When it breaks Old scores stay readable Requests fail or time out Batch must finish inside the staleness limit, so the time between runs is the limit minus the job time. Each run scores every entity whether or not anyone asks. Online pays for idle replicas between peaks, with a floor of two for availability. The arithmetic for this workload. The staleness limit of two hours minus a one-hour job leaves one hour between runs, so 24.0 runs per day. Every run scores all 5,000,000 items. That is why the batch plan costs $48.50 a day while the online plan sits at its two-replica floor of $24.00, since 120 peak QPS fits inside the capacity of two replicas. What flips it. A longer staleness limit cuts runs and batch cost in proportion; the nightly churn job in the same lesson costs under a dollar. A staleness limit shorter than one batch job makes batch infeasible at any price. A much higher peak needs more replicas and raises online cost linearly with peak traffic. A latency budget below the online path's model time rules online out, and a hybrid serves known items from a store and new items online. What the decision is not about. Freshness and cost decide; model quality does not change between the two plans. The failure modes differ: a broken batch job leaves old but readable scores, while a broken online service fails requests, so the online design needs a default such as the last stored score or the heuristic. Plausible wrong answers. "Batch is always cheaper." Batch cost scales with runs per day times entities; a tight freshness limit makes it the expensive plan. "Online is always fresher, so always better." Fresher costs replicas, and a nightly process cannot use freshness it does not read. "Pick by model accuracy." Accuracy is the same in both plans; the choice is about freshness, latency and cost. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is the online plan at its minimum here? Expected: two replicas is the availability floor, and 120 peak QPS fits inside what two replicas handle, so traffic does not drive the count. (level 2) The job takes longer than the staleness limit. What does the planner return? Expected: infeasible; no schedule satisfies the limit, so the budgets or the job must change. (level 3) Design the hybrid. Expected: batch scores known items on the relaxed schedule, online scores new items and requests that need fresh data; price it as the sum of a cheaper batch plan and a small online tier. (level 3) Which design document check does this feed? Expected: the serving-fit check, which prices the chosen mode against the staleness, latency and cost budgets and fails a mode that misses any of them. Where it is taught. Defend a design You are the reviewer for ML design documents before any training starts. A team hands you a document for a payment fraud check that proposes batch scoring, where one job takes an hour, with a three-minute staleness limit, reports an offline AUC, lists a majority-class baseline, and has no rollout section. Walk me through your review: the sections you expect, which gaps block, how you score it, and what you tell the team. Level 4 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The document needs nine sections, and six items block a review because each one makes the system unsafe or useless: the decision that uses the prediction, a business metric, a heuristic or current-system baseline, confirmation that every feature exists at prediction time, a shadow or canary stage with a rollback, and a default action for every failure. This document fails at least three of them: the only baseline is trivial, there is no rollout and no rollback, and the serving choice fails the fit check because batch cannot meet a limit of three minutes when one job takes an hour. I send it back with the blocking list first, and I ask for precision at the decision threshold instead of AUC. The nine sections. Section Question it answers Blocking item Problem What is predicted, which decision uses it, why rules are not enough The decision Metrics Offline, online, business and guardrail metrics The business metric Baselines Trivial, heuristic and current-system baselines A heuristic or current baseline Data Label source, delay, feature availability at prediction time No leakage Budgets and serving Latency, peak QPS, cost, staleness, and the mode that fits None Rollout Shadow, canary, A/B and the rollback Shadow or canary plus rollback Feedback loops How the model's decisions alter its later training data None Failure modes The default action for each failure A default for every failure Monitoring What is watched after launch None Scoring. Each checklist item has a weight, a blocking flag and a check. Blocking items weigh 2. The score is the sum of passed weights over the total, and the verdict is ready for review only when the score reaches 0.85 and no blocking item fails. A document can score high on the non-blocking items and still be sent back on one blocker; that is the point of the flag. The serving fit check. This check reuses the cost model. It reads the workload numbers from the document, prices the chosen mode, and fails when that mode misses the staleness limit, the latency budget or the daily cost budget. A batch job that takes an hour cannot meet a limit of three minutes at any price, so a document that says batch with that limit fails the check. For a payment decision made at request time the fit is online, and the document must state the peak QPS and the p99 budget that size it. What I tell the team. Blockers first: name the action that each score starts; add the rule the fraud team uses today as the heuristic baseline and set the minimum lift; add shadow and canary stages with a configuration rollback; write a default for a timeout, a missing feature, a new card and a sudden score shift. Then the serving section: switch to online, give the budgets, price it. Then the metric: AUC averages thresholds nobody uses; report precision and recall at the approve, review and block thresholds, and name the business metric and the guardrails. Last the feedback loop and the monitoring, which are not blocking but will decide the second quarter. Why the review happens before training. Every failure in the churn story at the start of the design lesson happened before training: no decision, stale cadence, a leaked feature, no comparison with the existing rule. A one-page document asks about each, and the review costs a day where the failures cost a quarter. Plausible wrong answers. "A strong offline metric compensates for a missing rollout." A model with no shadow stage and no rollback reaches users with no way back; that is why rollout blocks. "Score the document and pass it at a high enough total." One failed blocker fails the review regardless of the total. "Serving mode is an implementation detail for later." The fit check shows batch cannot meet the limit at all, which changes the architecture and the cost. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask.
