Expected: it is the trivial one and usually weak; the heuristic or current system is the real competitor and the one the lift is measured against. (level 4) Why does the serving fit check belong in a document review rather than in load testing? Expected: it is arithmetic on stated budgets and prices, so it catches an infeasible design before a line of serving code exists. (level 4) The document proposes a hybrid serving mode. What does the checker do and what do you do? Expected: the lesson's cost model has no hybrid plan, so the check fails until a hybrid plan is added; ask the team to price the batch and the online parts and add the plan. (level 4) What is the one non-blocking section you would still refuse to skip for a fraud system? Expected: feedback loops, because blocked payments never get a label and the model drifts toward its own decisions without a clean sample. Where it is taught. The ML system design lesson defines the design document, its six blocking items, the score threshold and the serving fit check. Defend a design Three systems retrain monthly on their own production data: a churn model that sends save offers, a fraud model that blocks payments, and a ranking model that orders a feed. Each one gets a little worse after every retrain. Explain the shared cause, design the data layer that prevents it, and say what each training row must carry for the fix to work. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each model's decisions change the data that trains its next version, which is a feedback loop. Offers keep users who would have churned, so high-risk users look loyal; blocked payments never get a chargeback, so fraud disappears from the blocked region; the feed shows only its top items, so only those collect clicks. The fix is to keep data the model did not influence: a random holdout that never receives the intervention, a small share of random decisions, and a log that stores the score and the decision with every row, joined to features as of the decision time so training can separate influenced from clean data. Three shapes of the same loop. System How the decision hides the label What the retrain learns Churn offers Offers retain some at-risk users Their features do not predict churn Fraud blocks A blocked payment has no outcome The blocked region looks safe Feed ranking Only shown items can be clicked The current top items are the only good ones The loop is listed among the main sources of technical debt in production ML systems because it is silent: every retrain looks fine on its own held-out data, which is also influenced. The data layer. A random holdout group that never receives the intervention. Its outcomes are the clean estimate of the base rate and the clean labels for training. A small share of random decisions on live traffic, for example payments that are not blocked or items shown out of order, so the blocked and unshown regions keep producing labels. The share is sized as the smallest that keeps enough labels from those regions. Logging of the score, the decision and the assignment with every row at decision time. Features joined as of the decision time, with the point-in-time rule from the feature store, so that a row's inputs are what the model saw and not a later snapshot that already reflects the outcome. What a training row carries. The entity and the decision time, the features as of that time, the model score, the decision taken, the group it belonged to, the label and the label time. With those fields training can select clean rows, weight influenced rows, or model the decision as a feature. Without the decision and the group, influenced and clean rows are indistinguishable and the loop is invisible. Why the feature store is part of it. A naive join on the entity returns the newest feature snapshot for every label, which copies the outcome into the input. The same mistake inside a feedback loop is worse: the newest snapshot also reflects the intervention. The as-of join with a TTL makes each row describe the moment of the decision, and the created timestamp check keeps a backfill from reading data that arrived later. Measuring the fix. The holdout gives the business metric: the outcome in the treated group against the holdout group. It also gives the retrain test: evaluate the new model on holdout rows only, so the score is not inflated by the model's own decisions. A model that improves on influenced data and not on the holdout has learned the loop. Plausible wrong answers. "More training data fixes a drifting model." The new data is influenced; more of it entrenches the loop. "A random train and test split shows the real performance." Both halves are influenced; only a holdout that never saw the intervention is clean. "Log the decision later from the outcome table." The decision and the assignment must be recorded at decision time, with the features as of that time, or the join leaks the outcome. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a time split alone not enough here? Expected: the recent period is also influenced by the deployed model; time ordering prevents future leakage but not intervention bias. (level 4) The random non-blocking share costs real fraud. How do you argue for it? Expected: as the price of clean labels against the cost of a model that drifts blind; size it to the minimum that keeps enough labeled fraud from the blocked region. (level 4) How does the exposure loop in ranking differ from the other two? Expected: the label is never collected rather than hidden; random exposure of lower-ranked items is the only way to learn their click rate. (level 4) A retrain evaluated on the holdout is worse than on the full set. Which number do you trust? Expected: the holdout; the full set rewards the model for agreeing with its own past decisions. Where it is taught. The ML system design lesson names the three feedback loops and the shared fix, and the feature store lesson gives the as-of join that keeps each training row at the decision time. Defend a design A payment service must approve, review or block each payment within 100 ms, at 400 requests per second at peak. Fraud labels arrive as chargebacks weeks later. Design the system: the task, the serving mode and its sizing, the data and label plan, the rollout, the failure defaults, and the two things that will quietly break it after launch. Level 3 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The task is binary classification of fraud probability with two thresholds that split the score into approve, review and block, served online because the decision needs the data of the request. At 400 requests a second and 50 ms per request about 20 requests are in flight at any moment, so the service is small, and the budget leaves room for a feature fetch plus the model. Chargeback labels come weeks after the payment, so training uses a time split and features that exist at payment time, and the rollout goes shadow, then canary on a small share, with the heuristic rule as the default on timeout. The two quiet failures are the feedback loop, where blocked payments never get a label, and concept drift, where the same basket changes its fraud risk and only outcome monitors see it. Task and decision. Question Answer Prediction, per entity Probability that this payment is fraud Decision Approve, send to review, or block, inside 100 ms When, with what data At the request, with the payment, the card history and the device Success Fraud losses down with the approval rate as a guardrail Serving and sizing. Batch cannot serve this: the staleness limit is zero because the payment did not exist a minute ago. Online inference fetches features and runs the model inside the budget. Little's law sizes it: throughput times latency is the number in progress, so 400 requests a second at 50 ms each is 20 requests in flight, far below what two replicas handle. The p99, not the mean, must stay under the budget; a p99 of 100 ms means 99 of 100 requests finish in time. Data and labels. Chargebacks arrive weeks after the payment, so the outcome of recent traffic is unknown. Train on a time split with the most recent labeled period held out. Every feature must exist at payment time; anything written after the outcome, such as a dispute flag, leaks the label. Rollout. Shadow: score live payments and log, never act; compare latency, error rate and score distribution with the current rule. Canary: act on a small share, often 1 to 5 percent, widen in steps, roll back by configuration when a guardrail moves. Then measure losses against a holdout. Failure defaults. Model times out: apply the heuristic baseline the team already uses. A feature is missing or out of range: use its documented default and log it. A new card with no history: the rule or the population average. The score distribution moves suddenly: pause automatic blocks and page a person. The two quiet failures. The feedback loop. A blocked payment never gets a chargeback, so the retrained model sees fewer fraud examples from the region it blocks and slowly learns that region is safe. Give a small random share of payments a non-blocking decision and log the score and the action with every row, so later training can tell influenced data from clean data. Concept drift. Fraudsters change tactics, and payments that were safe start to charge back. Inputs look the same, so input monitors stay quiet; only the outcome monitor sees it, and only after the label delay. Prior drift, such as the fraud rate doubling during an attack, shows up earlier in the prediction monitor as a moving positive rate. Monitoring. System health at once, inputs and predictions at once, outcomes joined as chargebacks arrive and computed on the labeled part only. Alert policy with effect sizes, a corrected alpha and persistence, so the on-call person reads the alerts. Plausible wrong answers. "Precompute fraud scores nightly for every card." The payment did not exist last night; the decision needs request-time data. "Retrain weekly on all blocked and approved payments." Blocked payments have no outcome, so the training set drifts toward the model's own decisions. "Watch feature drift and you will see the fraudsters change." Concept drift leaves inputs unchanged; only outcomes show it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does a time split matter more here than a random split? Expected: a random split leaks future tactics into training and overstates performance on the next month's fraud. (level 3) The review queue grows after launch. Which guardrail caught it and what do you adjust? Expected: the review rate guardrail; move the review threshold, not the model. (level 4) The random non-blocking share costs real fraud losses. How do you size it? Expected: as the smallest share that keeps enough labeled fraud examples from the blocked region to retrain; price it as the cost of clean data against the cost of a model that drifts blind. (level 4) Retraining on the last quarter's labels after a tactic change makes the model worse. Why? Expected: concept drift; most of the labels still describe the old relation, so new labels must be collected before retraining helps. Where it is taught. The ML system design lesson gives the latency budget, Little's law, the rollout stages and the feedback loop, and the model monitoring lesson explains the drift kinds and the label delay. Explain the mechanism A data scientist reports a churn classifier with an AUC of 0.91. Three months after launch, nobody on the retention team uses the scores. The algorithm was fine. Name the design decisions that were missing, and say which metric should have been reported instead. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The failures happened before training: nobody named the action a score starts, the scores arrived weekly while the team called customers daily, a feature leaked the label through the cancellation reason, and nobody compared the model with the rule the team already used. AUC averages over every threshold including ones never used; the decision was to contact the top 5 percent each night, so the right offline number was precision in that top 5 percent, paired with online, business and guardrail metrics. Four layers of metrics. Layer When measured Churn example Offline Before launch, on held-out past data Precision in the top 5 percent at the offer threshold Online During launch, on live traffic Offer acceptance rate, share of users scored Business Weeks later, with an experiment 30-day churn in the treated group versus a holdout Guardrail All the time Offer cost per saved user, unsubscribe rate, p99 latency The layers disagree often. The offline score comes from a past that did not contain the model. The online metric depends on how people react to the decision. The business metric moves slowly and carries noise from everything else in the company. The guardrails must not get worse. Pick the offline metric from the decision. The job contacts a fixed share of users, so the metric is the precision of that share. AUC ranks every pair of users, most of which never reach the decision. The rules guide quoted in the lesson puts it first: design the metrics before deciding what the system does. Baselines. An F1 of 0.56 is good against a best alternative of 0.30 and poor against a rule that reaches 0.60. Three baselines are needed: the trivial one, a heuristic such as the idle-days rule the support team used, and the current system. The lift is measured against the strongest one, and a minimum lift is set before the results are seen. The other three failures. Freshness: weekly scores for a daily process means the team acted on stale numbers. Leakage: a feature written after the outcome contained the answer, so the offline score was inflated. Decision: a score with no action attached cannot change a business metric. Plausible wrong answers. "A higher AUC would have fixed adoption." Adoption failed on freshness, action and trust, not on ranking quality. "Business metrics are enough; skip the offline one." The business metric arrives weeks later and is noisy; the offline metric gates the launch. "Guardrails are a product concern, not a model concern." A model that moves a guardrail the wrong way is rolled back no matter its offline score. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why is a 30-day churn label slow to evaluate? Expected: the label arrives at the end of the horizon, so the business metric lags the launch by at least that long. (level 2) Which guardrail would catch a model that saves users at any price? Expected: offer cost per saved user. (level 2) The heuristic baseline beats the model by a small margin. What ships? Expected: the rule, because it is cheaper to run and explain, unless the model clears the minimum lift. Where it is taught. The ML system design lesson opens with the churn model that nobody used and defines the four metric layers and the baselines. In plain words first The idea in one line A deployed model fails without an error message. It keeps returning scores while the world moves away from its training data, and only monitoring shows the gap. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it means Data drift "The data changed" A change in the distribution of inputs, predictions, or labels compared with a reference window Covariate drift "New kinds of users" P(x) changes while P(y \| x) stays the same Prior drift "More positives than before" P(y) changes while P(x \| y) stays the same, also called label shift Concept drift "The rules of the game changed" P(y \| x) changes, so the same input now has a different correct answer Reference window "The baseline data" A fixed sample, often the training data, that every current window is compared with PSI "The stability score" A symmetric sum over bins of (current share minus reference share) times the log of their ratio KS statistic "The KS test" The largest gap between two empirical cumulative distribution functions Cramér's V "Effect size for categories" The chi-square statistic scaled to the range 0 to 1 Label delay "Ground truth comes later" The time between a prediction and the arrival of its true outcome Alert fatigue "Too many pages" People ignore alerts because most of them were false alarms The problem In plain words first A model in production can go wrong silently: it keeps answering, but the world has moved. Monitoring compares recent data with a reference sample. Input monitors (PSI, KS, chi-square) warn early but only see changes in the inputs. Outcome monitors (accuracy once the true labels arrive) see every kind of change, but late. An alert policy decides which differences are worth waking someone for. A payment-risk model goes live with 95 percent accuracy. Two months later, a marketing campaign brings in app users with larger baskets. Four months later, fraudsters change their tactics, and payments that used to be safe start to turn into chargebacks. The model service returns HTTP 200 for every request during all of this. The latency is normal, and the logs show no errors. The first sign of trouble is a finance report about chargebacks, weeks after the damage. Software monitoring checks whether a service answers. Model monitoring checks whether the answers are still right, and whether the data still looks like the data that trained the model. This lesson builds the statistics, the windows, and the alert policy for that second job. You run them on a synthetic stream with two injected changes and watch which monitor reacts to which change. Idea 1 · What to monitor Monitor four layers. The first three give early warnings. Only the fourth measures correctness, and it arrives late. Layer Signals Available Question it answers System health p50 and p99 latency, error rate, throughput, memory At once Does the service answer? Inputs Distribution of each feature, missing-value rate, schema, new categories At once Does live data look like training data? Predictions Score distribution, positive rate, share of default answers At once Does the model behave as before? Outcomes Accuracy, precision, calibration, business metric After the label delay Is the model still right? Input monitoring is the main subject of this lesson, because it works before labels arrive. It has a limit that the demo shows: some changes leave the inputs untouched. Idea 2 · Three kinds of drift Write the joint distribution of inputs x and labels y in two ways: Each kind of drift changes a different factor: Drift What changes What stays Payment example Which monitor sees it Covariate drift P(x) P(y \| x) More app users with larger baskets Input monitors Prior drift P(y) P(x \| y) The fraud rate doubles during an attack, and fraud looks the same Prediction and outcome monitors Concept drift P(y \| x) Can stay The same basket now has a different fraud risk Outcome monitors only Gama et al. call a change in P(y | x) real concept drift. They call a change in P(x) that leaves P(y | x) alone virtual drift. Their survey also sorts drift by how it happens over time: sudden, incremental, gradual, or as a concept that comes back. Covariate drift does not always hurt. If the model learned P(y | x) well, it stays right for each input. It can still lose accuracy when traffic moves into regions with little training data or close to the decision boundary. Check your mental model ✗ "If the inputs look the same, the model is fine." ✓ In Step 6 the concept drift at event 6500 leaves every input monitor quiet, while accuracy falls from 0.946 to about 0.77. Only outcome monitoring catches it. ✗ "Input drift means retrain now." ✓ During the covariate drift (events 3000 to 5000) PSI reaches 0.88, yet accuracy stays between 0.90 and 0.94, because the rule linking amount to fraud did not change. ✗ "A tiny p-value means a big change." ✓ With a million events per window, a shift of 0.02 standard deviations gives KS D = 0.007 and p ≈ 5 × 10⁻²⁴. Judge the size of the change (D, PSI, Cramér's V), not just its p-value. Idea 3 · Delayed labels The outcome arrives after the prediction. The delay depends on the problem: Problem When the label arrives Ad click Seconds Churn in the next 30 days 30 days Card fraud When the chargeback arrives, often weeks later Loan default Months or years During the delay, you have inputs and predictions but no outcomes. Monitor the inputs and predictions, join the labels when they arrive, and compute outcome metrics on the labeled part only. The demo uses a label delay of 500 events, so the outcome monitor always looks 500 events into the past. Idea 4 · Reference and current windows Every drift test compares two samples: Reference window. The training data, or a period of production that you checked by hand. It stays fixed until you retrain. Current window. The most recent events, either the last N events or the last T hours. A sliding window moves forward by a step smaller than its size, so consecutive windows overlap. A tumbling window moves by its full size. Window size is a trade-off. A small window reacts quickly but scores noise as drift. A large window is stable but reports a change late. Seasonality breaks naive windows. Monday traffic differs from Saturday traffic in many products. Make the reference cover a full cycle, or compare each window with the same period in an earlier cycle. Idea 5 · Population Stability Index PSI comes from credit scoring. Cut the reference values into bins, usually ten bins at the reference deciles, so that each bin holds 10 percent of the reference. Count the share of current values in each bin. Then add up one term per bin: ∑ ​ ( current_share − reference_share ) ⋅ ln ( reference_share current_share ​ ) A bin with a share of zero makes the log infinite, so clip every share to a small value such as 0.0001. PSI is symmetric. It equals the KL divergence from current to reference plus the KL divergence from reference to current. Practitioners read PSI with fixed bands: below 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.25 is a moderate shift, and above 0.25 is a significant shift. Treat these bands as a convention, not a test. PSI grows with the number of bins and shrinks with sample size. In the demo, windows of 500 events with no drift score between 0.01 and 0.04. Worked example PSI with four bins The reference is cut into four bins of 25 percent each. The current window puts 15, 20, 30 and 35 percent of its values into them: Bin Reference Current (current − reference) × ln(current ÷ reference) 1 0.25 0.15 (−0.10) × ln 0.6 = 0.0511 2 0.25 0.20 (−0.05) × ln 0.8 = 0.0112 3 0.25 0.30 (+0.05) × ln 1.2 = 0.0091 4 0.25 0.35 (+0.10) × ln 1.4 = 0.0336 PSI = 0.105 , just inside the "moderate shift" band. Every term is positive: a bin that loses share and a bin that gains share both add to the score. Predict before you run Draw a reference of 2,000 values and a current window from the same normal distribution, so there is no drift at all, and compute PSI with ten decile bins. Repeat 200 times. What is the typical PSI for windows of 100, 500 and 5,000 values? (Solution P1.) Idea 6 · Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic The two-sample KS statistic D is the largest vertical gap between the two empirical cumulative distribution functions: max ​ ∣ F reference ​ ( x ) − F current ​ ( x ) ∣ D is 0 for identical samples and 1 for samples that do not overlap. It needs no bins. The p-value comes from the Kolmogorov distribution with the effective sample size n * m / (n + m) . With large samples, the p-value goes to zero for a gap that nobody cares about. A shift of 0.02 standard deviations is "significant" with a million events per window. Use D itself as an effect size, and alert only when both D and the p-value pass their thresholds. Idea 7 · Chi-square test for categorical features For a categorical feature, such as the payment channel, build a table with two rows (reference, current) and one column per category. The expected count in each cell comes from the row and column totals: chi2 ​ = row_total [ r ] ⋅ column_total [ c ] / grand_total = cells ∑ ​ ( observed − expected ) 2 / expected ​ The test has k - 1 degrees of freedom for k categories. A category that appears only in the current window adds a large term, so the test reacts to new values. Cramér's V is the effect size. For a table with two rows, it equals the square root of chi2 / grand_total . Worked example The chi-square table from "Use it" Reference channel counts are 1000, 700, 300 (app, store, web) and current counts 140, 290, 70; the grand total is 2,500. The expected current count for app is 500 × 1140 ÷ 2500 = 228, but only 140 arrived: that cell alone adds (140 − 228)² ÷ 228 = 34.0. All six cells together give χ² = 96.2 with 2 degrees of freedom, p ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻²¹, and Cramér's V = √(96.2 ÷ 2500) = 0.196 : a real shift in the channel mix. Idea 8 · Alert thresholds and false alarms Each test has a false-alarm rate alpha when nothing changed. Monitoring runs many tests. With 50 features checked every hour at alpha = 0.05 , you expect about 60 false alarms per day when nothing changed. People stop reading alerts long before that. Four rules keep the alert rate useful: Correct for multiple tests. The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests. The demo uses a family alpha of 0.01 over two tests, so each test uses 0.005. Require an effect size. Alert only when PSI, D , or Cramér's V also passes a threshold. Require persistence. Alert only after k consecutive drift windows. The demo uses k = 2 . Separate warnings from alerts. A warning goes to a dashboard. An alert goes to a person. The demo shows rule 2 at work. One clean window has a chi-square p-value of 0.0009, below the per-test alpha . Its Cramér's V is below 0.1, so the policy logs a warning, not an alert. Idea 9 · Retraining triggers There are three common triggers for retraining: Schedule. Retrain every week or month. This is simple, but it retrains when nothing changed and waits when something did. Drift. Retrain when input drift on important features stays above the threshold. Performance. Retrain when an outcome metric drops below the reference value minus a tolerance. The kind of drift decides what retraining can do: Drift Useful action Covariate drift, accuracy stable Often none. Keep watching the outcome metric. Covariate drift into regions with little data Retrain on recent data that includes those regions Prior drift Recalibrate the scores or move the decision threshold Concept drift Collect new labels first. Retraining on old labels teaches the old concept again. After retraining, test the new model on the most recent labeled data. Roll it out with the shadow and canary stages from the system design lesson. Then reset the reference window to the new training data. The same idea as a formula Population stability index. Over 200 random pairs of samples, the KS p-values differed from scipy's by up to 18 percent of scipy's value. The largest gaps were at very small p-values. The gap comes from the method. Our code uses the limiting Kolmogorov distribution. By default, ks_2samp uses an exact method when both samples have at most 10,000 values. Its asymptotic mode uses a finite-sample distribution with the rounded effective sample size. With two categories, chi2_contingency applies Yates' continuity correction by default, so the statistics differ there. Monitoring libraries. Several open-source libraries package these tests with reports and dashboards: Evidently picks a drift test per column. For a reference with 1000 rows or fewer, it uses the KS test for numeric columns and the chi-square test for categorical columns. For larger data, it uses the Wasserstein distance and the Jensen-Shannon divergence with a threshold of 0.1. PSI is one of the other methods that you can select. NannyML estimates model performance before labels arrive. Its Confidence-based Performance Estimation (CBPE) uses the model's predicted probabilities, which must be well calibrated. The NannyML documentation states that CBPE handles covariate shift but does not cope with concept drift. The demo stream shows why: only labels revealed the concept drift. TensorFlow Data Validation compares consecutive spans of data. It uses the L-infinity distance for categorical features and an approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence for numeric features. It also compares training data with serving data, which the feature store lesson covers. The from-scratch code shows what every one of these tools computes. The tools add storage, scheduling, dashboards, and many more tests. For LLM applications, the LLM observability lesson in the infrastructure phase covers tracing and evaluation tools. The ideas in this lesson still apply to the inputs and outputs of those systems. Recap What to keep from this lesson Monitor four layers: system, inputs, predictions, outcomes. Only outcomes measure correctness, and they arrive late. Covariate drift changes , prior drift , concept drift ; only outcome monitors see pure concept drift. PSI and KS D measure how far a numeric feature moved; chi-square and Cramér's V do the same for categories. Small windows react fast and raise false alarms; large windows are calm and late. Alert on effect size plus significance, correct for many tests, and require persistence. Concept drift needs new labels before retraining. Solutions Solution P1 · PSI depends on window size With no drift at all, PSI averages about 0.098 for windows of 100 (one window in twenty reaches 0.18), 0.023 for windows of 500 and 0.006 for windows of 5,000. Small windows put sampling noise into every bin, and PSI adds it all up as "shift". The 0.1 and 0.25 bands only make sense for a fixed window size; calibrate yours by computing PSI on clean windows first. Solution B1 · Fast and jumpy The windows of 100 react sooner: the amount alert comes at 3150 instead of 3500, and the accuracy alert at 7100 instead of 7500. But the clean period before 3000 now shows amount warnings in 7 of 19 windows, the channel alert switches on and off three times during the drift, and accuracy alerts fire at 4200, 5350 and 5500, when the labelling rule had not changed. Each of those would have paged someone for nothing. Choose the window from the delay you can afford and the false-alarm rate you can tolerate, measured on clean data. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Open monitoring tools. Evidently computes drift reports and tests for tabular and text data, NannyML estimates performance before labels arrive, and Arize Phoenix and Langfuse trace and evaluate LLM applications. Monitoring built into platforms. SageMaker Model Monitor, Vertex AI Model Monitoring, Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring and Snowflake ML Observability track drift and performance of deployed models. LLM apps need different signals. Production teams log prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and user feedback, and run scheduled evaluations on samples of real traffic. Sources: Evidently , NannyML , Arize Phoenix , Langfuse , SageMaker Model Monitor . Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A payment model's accuracy, measured as labels arrive, fell from 0.946 to between 0.76 and 0.79. The feature monitors and the score distribution stayed quiet the whole time. The team proposes retraining on the last quarter of labeled data tonight. What happened, why did the monitors miss it, and is the proposal right? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The relation between inputs and labels changed while the inputs themselves did not, which is concept drift. Input and prediction monitors compare distributions of features and scores, so a change in the conditional label distribution is invisible to them, and only the outcome monitor can see it, after the label delay. Retraining tonight on the last quarter is the wrong move: most of those labels still describe the old relation, so the model relearns it; collect labels from after the change first, then retrain on them. Three kinds of drift. Drift What changes Which monitor sees it Covariate The input distribution Input monitors Prior The label rate Prediction and outcome monitors Concept The label given the input Outcome monitors only Covariate drift moves features and often leaves accuracy alone. Prior drift moves the positive rate. Concept drift changes which answer is right for the same input, so nothing upstream of the label moves. What the demo shows. The lesson's stream injects both kinds. During the covariate segment the PSI and the KS statistic alert on the amount feature while accuracy stays between 0.89 and 0.95. During the concept segment the inputs are identical to the reference, both input monitors stay at their clean values, and accuracy falls from 0.946 to the 0.76 to 0.79 range. The accuracy alert fires 1000 events after the change, and the label delay of 500 events accounts for half of that lag. Why the lag. The outcome monitor always looks one label delay into the past, because it can only score the events whose outcome has arrived. The persistence rule, which requires consecutive drift windows before an alert, adds the rest. Both are deliberate: without them the alert rate is unusable. Why the retraining proposal is wrong. Retraining answers covariate drift into regions with little data. Concept drift needs labels from after the change. A quarter of labels where the change happened late in the window teaches mostly the old concept. The right sequence is: confirm the change point from the outcome monitor, gather enough labels past it, retrain on those, test on the most recent labeled slice, roll out through shadow and canary, and reset the reference window to the new training data. What to do tonight. Route more cases to review if the business impact is large, as a temporary measure while labels from after the change arrive. A threshold move is the lesson's action for prior drift. For concept drift it helps only when the boundary moved on the same score, and it cannot restore a risk order that changed. Keep the model; replace it only with labels that describe the new relation. Plausible wrong answers. "The feature monitors are broken; nothing changed in the inputs." They worked as designed; the inputs did not change, the labels did. "Retrain on everything so the model sees the new pattern." The old labels outnumber the new ones and the model relearns the old relation. "Shorten the windows to catch it faster." Smaller windows add noise and false alarms; the lag here comes from the label delay, which windows cannot remove. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which signal could you add that reacts before the labels? Expected: none for pure concept drift; a proxy such as a review queue outcome or a faster partial label is the only earlier signal. (level 3) How does a performance estimator that uses predicted probabilities behave here? Expected: it assumes the calibration still holds, so it misses concept drift; the lesson notes that such estimators handle covariate shift and not concept drift. (level 4) How do you choose how many post-change labels are enough? Expected: enough to test the retrained model on a recent held-out slice with a tolerance you set in advance; the test on recent labels is the gate, not a count. (level 4) After retraining, the input monitors start to alert on the clean reference. Why? Expected: the reference window was not reset to the new training data, so it compares live traffic with an old distribution. Where it is taught. The model monitoring lesson runs the stream with injected covariate and concept drift and shows which monitor reacts to each. Defend a design A payment risk model scores every transaction. Labels arrive weeks later as chargebacks. Design the monitoring: what you watch, how you compare windows, which statistics you compute, and how you keep the alert rate low enough that people read the alerts. Level 2 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Monitor four layers: system health, input distributions, prediction distributions, and outcomes once labels arrive. Compare a fixed reference window with sliding current windows, with the Population Stability Index and the two-sample KS statistic for numeric features and a chi-square test with Cramér's V for categorical ones. Alert only when a corrected p-value and an effect size both pass and the condition persists for consecutive windows, and send warnings to a dashboard rather than to a person. Four layers. Layer Signals Available Question System health p50 and p99 latency, error rate, throughput At once Does the service answer? Inputs Feature distributions, missing rates, schema, new categories At once Does live data look like training data? Predictions Score distribution, positive rate, share of default answers At once Does the model behave as before? Outcomes Accuracy, precision, calibration, business metric After the label delay Is the model still right? Only the last layer measures correctness and it arrives late, so the first three are the early warning. Windows. The reference is the training data or a hand-checked production period, fixed until retraining. The current window is the last N events or the last T hours, sliding by a step smaller than its size. A small window reacts quickly and scores noise as drift; a large window is stable but late. Seasonality breaks naive windows, so the reference covers a full cycle or each window is compared with the same period of an earlier cycle. The lesson's demo uses windows of 500 events that move by 250, with labels 500 events late. Statistics. PSI over ten reference-decile bins, with shares clipped to a small value so no bin is empty; conventional bands read below 0.1 as stable and above 0.25 as a significant shift, with the caveat that PSI grows with bins and shrinks with sample size. KS statistic D as the effect size for numeric features, with its p-value from the effective sample size; with large samples the p-value alone flags gaps nobody cares about. Chi-square with Cramér's V for categorical features, which also reacts to a category that appears only in the current window. With few events in a cell the p-value is not reliable, so pool rare categories into one bin before the test. Alert policy. With 50 features checked every hour at an alpha of 0.05, about 60 false alarms a day arrive when nothing changed. Four rules keep the rate useful: correct for multiple tests, so a family alpha of 0.01 over two tests gives 0.005 each; require an effect size; require persistence over consecutive drift windows, two in the demo; and separate dashboard warnings from alerts to a person. What retraining does. Covariate drift with stable accuracy often needs no action. Covariate drift into regions with little data calls for retraining on recent data. Prior drift calls for recalibration or a new threshold. Concept drift needs new labels first, because retraining on old labels teaches the old concept again. Plausible wrong answers. "Alert on any p-value below 0.05." With many features and hourly checks that is dozens of false alarms a day and people stop reading. "Watch accuracy; it is the only metric that matters." Accuracy arrives after the label delay; input and prediction monitors give the early warning. "Retrain on a schedule and skip monitoring." A schedule retrains when nothing changed and waits when something did. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why fix the reference window instead of sliding it too? Expected: a sliding reference follows the drift and hides it; the reference changes only at retraining. (level 2) A clean window shows a tiny chi-square p-value. Why is it a warning and not an alert? Expected: the effect size is below threshold, so the policy logs a warning; the p-value alone is not enough. (level 3) Labels arrive 500 events late. How does the outcome monitor handle that? Expected: it joins labels as they arrive and computes metrics on the labeled part, always looking that far into the past. (level 3) Which drift stays invisible to this whole design except the last layer? Expected: concept drift, where the inputs do not change and only outcomes reveal the new relation. Where it is taught. The model monitoring lesson gives the four layers, the windows, the three statistics and the alert policy. Time : about 100 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A feature has one definition and two readers. Training reads its history as of each label time, and serving reads its latest value. When the two readers disagree, the model sees inputs that it never trained on. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it means Feature store "A database for features" A system that computes features from one set of definitions and serves them to training and to serving Offline store "The training data" Full feature history with event timestamps, read by training jobs and backfills Online store "The feature cache" The latest value per entity, read by the serving path in milliseconds Entity "The ID" The key that a feature describes, such as a user or a card Event timestamp "When it happened" The time at which a feature value became true Point-in-time join "An as-of join" A join that pairs each label with the latest feature row at or before the label time TTL "Expiry" The maximum age of a feature value before a reader treats it as missing Materialization "Syncing to online" The job that copies the latest feature values from the offline store to the online store Backfill "Computing history" Running a feature definition at past dates to create its history Training-serving skew "It worked offline" A difference between the features or behavior in training and in serving The problem In plain words first A feature such as "days since the last purchase" is read twice: by training, which needs its value as it was at each past label time, and by serving, which needs its value now . If the two reads use different code, different defaults, different freshness, or if training accidentally reads values from after the label time, the model is tested on inputs unlike the ones it learned from. A feature store prevents this with one registry of definitions, a point-in-time join for training, and an online store for serving. A team builds a churn model. Each label says whether a user made no purchase in the 30 days after a label day. The team joins the labels to the user feature table on user_id and trains a rule on days_since_last_purchase . Offline accuracy is 0.948. On live traffic, the model does worse than an older and simpler version. The feature table held the newest value for each user, from weeks after the label days. A user whose last purchase was on day 115 showed 60 idle days in the day 175 snapshot, so the feature contained the answer. Meanwhile, another team wrote the serving features again in a different service. Their 30-day window included one extra day, and their default for a new user was -1 instead of 365. Both defects have the same cause. Training and serving computed "the same feature" in two different ways. This lesson builds the pieces of a feature store from scratch. You write a registry, a backfill, a point-in-time join, an online store with a TTL, and a skew check. The demo reproduces both defects with numbers. Idea 1 · Two readers of the same feature Training and serving ask for features in different shapes: Property Training (offline) Serving (online) Question "What was the value for each of 10 million (entity, time) pairs?" "What is the value for this one entity now?" Time Many points in the past The present Volume Millions of rows per job One row per request Latency Minutes are fine A few milliseconds Storage Offline store: full history with timestamps, in columnar files or a warehouse Online store: the latest value per entity, in a key-value database A feature store keeps both stores filled from one set of feature definitions. Materialization is the job that copies the latest values from the offline store to the online store. Idea 2 · Entities, timestamps, and TTL Four terms describe every feature row: Entity. The key that a feature describes, such as user_id or card_id . Event timestamp. The time at which the value became true. A purchase count "as of day 14" has the event timestamp day 14. Created timestamp. The time at which the system wrote the row. A backfill that runs today writes rows with old event timestamps and a new created timestamp. TTL (time to live). The maximum age of a value. A value older than the TTL counts as missing, so the reader uses the default. A group of features with the same entity, source, and TTL is often called a feature view. Idea 3 · Point-in-time correct joins A training row pairs a label with the feature values that existed at the label time. The point-in-time join does this for each label: Find the feature rows of the same entity. Keep the rows whose event timestamp is at or before the label timestamp. Take the latest of those rows. Drop it if the label timestamp minus its event timestamp is more than the TTL. Here is one user, a label at day 16, and weekly feature rows: Feature row day purchases_30d Point-in-time join Naive join on user_id 7 4 14 3 Selected 21 1 Future 28 0 Future Selected The label asks whether the user buys anything in days 17 to 46. The day 28 row already counts the quiet days after the label day. It shows 0 purchases because the user stopped buying, which is the event that the label measures. The naive join copies the answer into the input. We split data by time in the time-series lesson for the same reason. A point-in-time join applies that rule to every row instead of to one split point. Check your mental model ✗ "Higher offline accuracy means the training data is fine." ✓ The naive join scores 0.948 offline against 0.893 for the point-in-time join, then 0.763 against 0.876 on new data. A leak makes offline numbers better and production worse. ✗ "Joining on the entity ID is enough." ✓ An entity has many rows over time. Without the time condition, every label gets the newest row, which in the demo came from after the label day for 100 percent of rows. ✗ "Fresher serving features are always better." ✓ The model learned from weekly snapshots up to six days old. Fresh values differ from what training saw on 83 percent of requests for days_since_last_purchase ; consistency matters more than freshness. Idea 4 · Causes of training-serving skew Google's Rules of Machine Learning define training-serving skew as a difference between performance during training and performance during serving. They name three causes: different data handling in the two pipelines, a change in the data between training and serving, and a feedback loop. In feature pipelines, four concrete causes appear again and again: Cause What happens Example from the demo Two code paths Training and serving compute the feature with different code The serving window includes day now - 30 , and the training window does not Stale features The value that serving reads has a different age from the value that training used Training reads weekly snapshots, and a new service computes fresh values Different defaults The two paths fill a missing value differently Training uses 365 for "no purchase yet", and serving uses -1 Time travel Training reads a value from after the label time The naive join reads the newest snapshot for every label Rule #32 of the same guide says to reuse code between the training pipeline and the serving pipeline whenever possible. A feature store follows that rule with one definition that both paths call. Worked example Two small differences, one big effect On day 145 the registry's 30-day window covers days 116 to 145 ( e.day > as_of - 30 ). The second code path uses now - 30 <= e.day <= now , days 115 to 145: 31 days. A purchase on day 115 counts in serving and not in training. The default matters more. For a user with no purchases yet, training fills days_since_last_purchase with 365 and the second path with −1. The point-in-time rule predicts churn when idle days exceed 19, so every new user flips: 365 says "churn", −1 says "stays". Twenty new users in the request log, twenty wrong answers, and no error anywhere. Idea 5 · A feature registry The registry is the catalog of feature definitions. Each entry holds a name, an entity, a source, a transformation, a window, a default value, a TTL, an owner, a version, and a description. Two rules keep it safe: Both paths read the definition from the registry. No service keeps a private copy of the transformation. A change to a definition creates a new version. The old version stays, so old models keep the feature that they trained on. Idea 6 · Backfills A new feature has no history, but training needs its value at every old label time. A backfill runs the definition at each past date and writes one row per entity and date. Each run reads only the events with timestamps at or before its date. Backfills cost compute that grows with the number of entities times the number of dates. They also bring a subtle leak. A backfill that runs today writes rows with old event timestamps, but it can read data that arrived late or was corrected later. A strict point-in-time join also checks that the created timestamp is at or before the label time. Idea 7 · Detecting skew Rule #29 of the same guide says to log the features at serving time and use them in training. Even a small logged sample lets you check consistency. Compare each logged value with the value that the training path produces for the same entity and time. For each feature, report the share of mismatches and the mean absolute difference. To find the cause, compare three pairs: Online store read versus training join. This tests the whole system and should show zero skew. Fresh computation versus training join. This isolates staleness. Second code path versus fresh computation. This isolates code differences, such as windows and defaults. The same idea as a formula Point-in-time join. For a label of entity at time , the training row must use the value the online store would have served at : ) , τ ∗ = max { τ ≤ t } among the feature’s event times for e and the value counts as missing (use the default) if > TTL . A strict join also requires the row's created time to be at or before , so late-arriving or corrected data cannot leak backwards. A plain "latest value" join uses = max { τ } over all time, including the future. Skew. Training–serving skew is any difference between ​ ( e , t ) and ​ ( e , t ) for the same entity and time: different code, different windows, stale values. Measured by logging served features and recomputing them offline, the mismatch rate is 1 ​ ∑ i ​ 1 [ ∣ x i serve ​ − x i offline ​ ∣ > tol ] per feature. Backfill cost grows with entities × dates × features: two million users over 365 days is 730 million rows per feature. Step 1 · Feature definitions and the registry The code in code/main.py uses only the standard library. Time is a whole number of days. A weekly batch job writes feature snapshots on days 7, 14, and so on up to 175. A FeatureDefinition holds the transformation as data: an aggregate, a window, and a default. Its compute method never reads events after as_of . Copy FeatureRegistry.register accepts the same definition twice, but it rejects a different definition with the same name and version. fill_defaults gives both paths the same default for a missing value. A model pins a definition with a reference such as spend_30d@1 . compute and fill_defaults resolve the reference, and a name without @ reads the latest version. A reference with @ and no version number raises ValueError , so a typo cannot read the latest version without a warning. The reference is also the key in each stored row, so the backfill, the online store, and the serving read all use the pinned definition. Recap What to keep from this lesson One registry of feature definitions feeds both training and serving; no private copies of the transformation. Training needs a point-in-time join: the latest row at or before each label time, within the TTL. Skew comes from two code paths, stale features, different defaults and time travel. The TTL must cover the gap between snapshots plus any delay, or serving falls back to defaults. Log serving features and compare them with the training path for the same entity and time. Solutions Solution P1 · Training is fine, serving is not None of the training rows lose their features: the label days 100, 120 and 140 sit 2, 1 and 0 days after the snapshots on days 98, 119 and 140. But on day 145 the newest snapshot is 5 days old, so all 299 day-145 rows expire and get the defaults. With days_since_last_purchase = 365 , the rule (idle > 19) predicts churn for everyone, and accuracy drops from 0.876 to 0.445 , the share of users who really churn. The TTL must be longer than the time between snapshots plus the job delay; training data cannot tell you that. Solution B1 · A week of the future The leaky backfill scores 0.934 offline against 0.893 for the honest one, and moves the rule from 19 to 16 idle days. On day 145, with honest features, it reaches 0.873 against 0.876: the four-point offline gain was never real. A backfill must read only data that existed at each snapshot date; store a created timestamp and filter on it, as Feast's filter_by_created_timestamp does. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Feature stores moved into data platforms. Databricks acquired Tecton in 2025; Databricks (Unity Catalog), Snowflake, Vertex AI and SageMaker all offer built-in feature stores, and Feast is the main open-source option. Real-time features for agents. The same online stores now serve fresh customer context to LLM agents, not only to classic models, which was Databricks' stated reason for the Tecton deal. Fix legacy_serving_features until the third skew check passes. List each change. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Design the feature layer for a churn model. Training needs the value of each feature for millions of user and time pairs. Serving needs the latest value for one user in a few milliseconds. Name the parts, explain how a training row gets its features, and show with the lesson's numbers what goes wrong without the right join. Level 2 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. One registry holds each feature definition with its entity, window, default, TTL and version, and both paths compute from it. An offline store keeps the full history with event timestamps for training and backfills; a materialization job copies the latest value per entity into an online key-value store with a TTL. A training row takes the latest feature row at or before its label time, inside the TTL. Without that point-in-time join the lesson's demo looks better offline, 0.948 against 0.893, and worse on new data, 0.763 against 0.876, because the newest snapshot leaks the answer. The parts. Part Job Registry One definition per feature: entity, source, transformation, window, default, TTL, owner, version Offline store Full history with event timestamps, read by training and backfills Point-in-time join Pairs each label with the latest row at or before the label time, dropped if older than the TTL Materialization Copies the latest values from offline to online Online store Latest value per entity, read in milliseconds, refuses rows older than the TTL Skew check Compares logged serving features with the training path for the same entity and time Two readers, one definition. Training asks "what was the value for each of millions of entity and time pairs". Serving asks "what is the value for this entity now". Both read the same definition from the registry; no service keeps a private copy of the transformation. A change creates a new version, and old models pin the version they trained on. The join. Find the feature rows of the same entity. Keep rows whose event timestamp is at or before the label time. Take the latest of those. Drop it if the label time minus its event time exceeds the TTL. A naive join on the entity alone returns the newest row for every label. For a churn label, the newest snapshot already counts the quiet days after the label day, so the feature contains the answer. The demo fits a rule on both training sets and tests on later labels: the naive join scores 0.948 offline and 0.763 on new data, the point-in-time join scores 0.893 offline and 0.876 on new data, and the leaked feature moved the threshold from 19 to 53 idle days. TTL and defaults. With a TTL of 10 days, a read five days after the last snapshot returns it, and a read 20 days later returns the defaults because the row is too old. The default lives in the registry so both paths fill a missing value the same way. Backfills and created time. A new feature has no history, so a backfill runs the definition at each past date and reads only events at or before that date. A backfill run today can still read data that arrived late, so a strict join also checks the created timestamp. The skew check. Log a sample of served features and compare each value with the training path for the same entity and time. Report the mismatch rate and the mean absolute difference per feature, and flag a feature above 1 percent mismatch. Three comparisons separate the causes: store read against training join for the whole system, fresh computation against training join for staleness, and a second code path against fresh computation for code differences. Plausible wrong answers. "Join labels to the feature table on the user id." That returns the newest value and copies the outcome into the input. "Fresher features are always better at serving time." The model learned the freshness of its training data; a different age is skew. "Snapshots every day remove the problem." Daily snapshots reduce staleness but the join still needs the as-of rule and the TTL. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the leaked model look better offline? Expected: the feature contains the outcome, so the offline split rewards it; on new data the information is not there. (level 2) What does the TTL do in the join, and relative to what time? Expected: it drops a feature row too old for the label; the age is measured from each label time, not from the query time. (level 3) Two teams compute the same feature in two services. Which skew cause is that, and how does the registry remove it? Expected: two code paths; both services call the registry definition instead of their own copy. (level 3) Fresher serving features turn out to hurt. Why? Expected: the model trained on weekly snapshots, so values up to six days old are what it learned; staleness skew runs both ways. Where it is taught. The feature store lesson builds the registry, the point-in-time join, the online store and the skew check, and measures the naive join against the correct one. Debug a failure A churn model scored well offline and does worse than the older, simpler model on live traffic. Serving features are computed by another team's service. You have a sample of logged serving requests. Design the triage: which comparisons you run, in which order, what each one isolates, and what the fix looks like for each cause you find. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Compare the same entity and time across three pairs. The online store read against the training join tests the whole system and should show zero skew when both read one definition. A fresh computation against the training join isolates staleness, and the second team's code path against a fresh computation isolates code differences such as window boundaries and defaults. Each pair gives a mismatch rate and a mean absolute difference per feature, and the fix for every cause is the same shape: one registry definition that both paths call, with logged serving features checked against it. The four causes. Cause What happens Example from the lesson Two code paths Training and serving compute the feature differently The serving window includes one extra day Stale features The served value has a different age than training saw Training read weekly snapshots, serving computes fresh Different defaults The two paths fill a missing value differently Training used 365 for no purchase yet, serving used -1 Time travel Training read a value from after the label time A naive join took the newest snapshot The three comparisons. Online store read against the training join. Both read the same materialized rows from one definition, so every feature should show a mismatch of zero. A nonzero result here means the store or the join itself is wrong. Fresh computation against the training join. This isolates staleness. In the lesson's demo the fresh value differs on most requests: 83.0% mismatch for days since last purchase, 30.5% for the purchase count, 37.1% for spend. Fresher is not better here, because the model learned from values up to six days old. Second code path against fresh computation. This isolates code. The demo shows 12.5% mismatch on both window counts, because the other team's window includes one extra day, and 5.5% mismatch on days since last purchase with a mean difference of 20.07, which comes only from new users where the defaults disagree, -1 against 365. The check needs the same request keys on both sides, and it fails loudly when the keys differ or when there are no requests, because a missing request hides skew and an empty check proves nothing. The fixes. Two code paths: delete the private copy; both services call the registry definition, and a change creates a new version that old models do not pick up. Stale features: match the serving age to the training age, or retrain on the fresher snapshots; a feature's freshness is part of its definition. Different defaults: one default in the registry, applied by one function in both paths. Time travel: the point-in-time join with the TTL, which the demo shows moves offline accuracy from an inflated 0.948 to an honest 0.893 and live accuracy from 0.763 to 0.876. Why the simpler model won live. The older model used features that both paths computed the same way. The new model trusted a feature whose live values came from a different window and a different default, so it saw inputs it never trained on. Plausible wrong answers. "Fresh serving features are always better than training snapshots." The model learned the training freshness; a different age is skew in either direction. "A mismatch rate under a few percent is fine." A small rate with a large mean difference, as with the defaults, still breaks every affected prediction. "Compare offline accuracy with live accuracy and call it drift." Drift is a change over time; skew is a difference between two readers of the same feature at the same time, and the three comparisons tell them apart. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which comparison would you run first with one hour available? Expected: the first one; if the store read matches the training join, the system is consistent and the problem is elsewhere, and if not, every downstream check is moot. (level 3) The defaults differ only for new users. Why does the mismatch rate understate the damage? Expected: the rate is low because new users are few, but the difference per mismatch is huge, so the model's output for every new user is wrong. (level 4) The other team cannot change their service this quarter. What do you do? Expected: log their served features, train the next model on those logged values so training matches serving, and keep the skew check running so the gap is visible. (level 4) How does a created timestamp enter the triage? Expected: a backfill written today can read late-arriving data, so a strict join also drops rows created after the label time; otherwise the training path itself is skewed. Where it is taught. The feature store lesson names the four causes of skew and runs the three comparisons on logged requests. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Turing test Turing's 1950 proposal: a machine passes if a person chatting with it cannot tell it from a human The 1950s Perceptron The first trainable artificial neuron (1958): weighted inputs, a threshold, one output The 1950s AI winter A period when funding and interest in AI collapsed after promises were not met 1970s and late 1980s AlexNet The 2012 deep network that won the ImageNet contest by a wide margin and started the deep learning era 2012 Sequence-to-sequence A model that reads one sequence and writes another, such as a translation 2014 Scaling laws The finding that model quality improves predictably with more data, parameters and compute 2020 Function calling A model replying with a structured request to run a named function, which your code executes 2023 Mentioned here, taught later 13 Machine learning, Transformer, Backpropagation, LSTM, GPU, Word2vec and more This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Machine learning Software that learns a rule from examples instead of being given the rule Lesson 2.2 Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.8 Backpropagation Computing every parameter's gradient by applying the chain rule backwards through the network Lesson 3.6 LSTM A recurrent network with gates that help it remember over longer spans Lesson 5.13 GPU A processor built to do many simple calculations at once, which is what neural networks need Lesson 3.20 Word2vec The 2013 method that learns word vectors by predicting nearby words Lesson 5.7 Instruction tuning Fine-tuning a base model on instructions paired with good responses, so that it follows requests Lesson 10.10 Base model A model that has only been pretrained to continue text, before it is taught to follow instructions Lesson 10.6 Reasoning model A model that works through a problem in hidden thinking tokens before it answers Lesson 10.14 Frontier model The largest, most capable hosted models at a given time Lesson 10.21 EU AI Act The EU's risk-based AI regulation Lesson 15.25 Embedding A learned vector that stands for a word, token, product or anything else Lesson 3.19 Deep learning Machine learning done with neural networks that have many layers Lesson 3.4 Why this came about Every few years someone announces that AI has changed everything, and every few years a technology that was promised turns out to be harder than expected. Knowing the history helps you tell the two apart. It also explains the shape of this course: each chapter of the foundations corresponds to an era, and each era ended because of a limit the next one solved. In plain words first Seventy years in one paragraph For thirty years people tried to make computers intelligent by writing rules by hand. That worked for chess and narrow puzzles but not for messy things like recognizing a face or understanding a sentence, because nobody can write down all the rules. So researchers switched to learning from examples ( machine learning later · 2.2 ). Learning got dramatically better once computers were fast enough and data plentiful enough to train deep neural networks (from 2012). A new design for those networks, the transformer later · 7.8 (2017), could be trained on almost all the text on the internet, producing large language models . Teaching those models to follow instructions (2022) produced assistants; giving them tools and a loop (2023 onward) produced agents . Seventy years of AI in five eras (the scale stretches after 2010, where most of the change happened). Each era ran into a limit that the next one addressed; two periods of disappointment, called AI winters, followed over-promising. Era 1 · Rules and logic (1950s to 1970s) In 1950 Alan Turing asked whether machines could think, and proposed judging them by whether their conversation could be told apart from a person's: the imitation game , now called the Turing test . In 1956 a summer workshop at Dartmouth College coined the phrase artificial intelligence . Early programs proved logic theorems, played checkers and solved algebra problems by search : trying many possibilities quickly. In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt built the perceptron , a machine that learned to recognize simple patterns: the first artificial neuron you will build in Lesson 3.4 . In 1966 ELIZA imitated a therapist with simple pattern-matching rules, and people confided in it anyway: an early lesson that sounding intelligent and being intelligent are different things. The limit. Real-world problems have too many exceptions to write down, and single-layer perceptrons provably could not learn some simple patterns. Funding collapsed in the mid-1970s: the first AI winter . Era 2 · Expert systems (1980s) Companies captured experts' knowledge as thousands of if-then rules ("if the infection is bacterial and the patient is allergic to penicillin, then..."). Some worked well in narrow domains. In 1986 a widely read paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed how to train neural networks with several layers using backpropagation later · 3.6 , the algorithm you will build by hand in Lesson 3.6 . But computers were too slow and datasets too small for it to shine. The limit. Rule systems were expensive to build, brittle when the world changed, and could not learn. The market collapsed in the late 1980s: the second AI winter. Era 3 · Statistical machine learning (mid-1990s to 2012) The field moved from rules to statistics : models that learn patterns from data and report how confident they are. Spam filters, search ranking, product recommendations, credit scoring and fraud detection all came from this era, using methods such as logistic regression , decision trees and support vector machines (the Machine learning from zero section). In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion (mostly by search), and the LSTM later · 5.13 , a neural network that could remember across a sequence, was published ( Lesson 5.13 ). The web made data plentiful; graphics cards ( GPUs later · 3.20 ), built for video games, turned out to be very good at the arithmetic neural networks need. The limit. These models needed people to hand-design the features they learned from ("count the exclamation marks", "is the sender in the address book"). For images, sound and language, nobody could design good enough features. Era 4 · Deep learning (2012 to 2017) In 2012 a neural network called AlexNet , trained on GPUs, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a wide margin. Deep networks learn their own features from raw data, and they keep improving with more data and computing power. Within a few years they led in speech recognition, translation and image recognition. For language, word2vec later · 5.7 (2013) learned a vector of numbers for every word, so that similar words get similar vectors ( Lesson 5.7 ); sequence-to-sequence models (2014) translated whole sentences; and attention (2014) let a model look back at the most relevant words of the input ( Lesson 5.16 ). In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat a world champion at Go. The limit. Language models of this era read text one word at a time, in order. That was slow to train and they lost track of long passages. Era 5 · Transformers, LLMs and agents (2017 to now) In 2017 Google researchers published Attention Is All You Need , introducing the transformer : a network that uses attention everywhere and reads all the words of a passage at once (the Transformers, step by step section). Because it trains efficiently on parallel hardware, it could be scaled up enormously: Year What happened Why it mattered 2018 BERT (Google) and GPT (OpenAI) Pretrain once on lots of text, then adapt to many tasks ( Lesson 7.13 ) 2019 GPT-2 Fluent text generation from next-word prediction alone; the model you ran in Lesson 0.2 2020 GPT-3 , and scaling laws 175 billion parameters; performance improved predictably with size, data and compute ( Lesson 10.6 ). The same year, retrieval-augmented generation was published (the Retrieval (RAG) section) 2022 Instruction tuning later · 10.10 and human feedback , then ChatGPT (November) Base models later · 10.6 were trained to follow instructions and to prefer helpful answers ( Lesson 10.10 ); a chat interface brought them to hundreds of millions of people 2022 Image generators such as Stable Diffusion Generative AI beyond text ( Lesson 10.34 ) 2023 GPT-4 , Claude , Gemini , open-weight Llama models; function calling Much stronger models; models could request tool use, the basis of agents (the Agents from first principles section) 2024 Reasoning models later · 10.14 (OpenAI o1), multimodal models, the Model Context Protocol Models that think step by step before answering ( Lesson 10.14 ); a standard way to connect tools (the Protocols section) 2025 Open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1), coding and research agents in daily work, agent frameworks reach 1.0 Agents moved from demos into real workflows (the Agents from first principles , LangChain and LangGraph and Production engineering and AI system design sections) By 2026, the frontier models later · 10.21 handle text, images and audio, work through long multi-step tasks with tools, and run inside company systems under governance rules such as the EU AI Act later · 15.25 , whose obligations phase in from 2025 ( Lesson 15.25 ). Why the jumps happened: three ingredients together Progress in AI has come when three things improved at the same time: Ingredient 1990s Today Data Thousands to millions of examples Trillions of words of text, billions of images Compute One processor, megaflops Clusters of tens of thousands of GPUs Methods Hand-designed features Networks that learn their own features; transformers that use hardware efficiently The researcher Richard Sutton summed up seventy years of experience in a 2019 essay called The Bitter Lesson : methods that make use of more computing power, such as learning and search, have repeatedly beaten methods that build in human knowledge by hand. It is a debated claim, but it explains why today's systems are trained, not programmed. What history teaches someone building with AI Hype runs ahead of reality. Both AI winters followed promises that were too large. When someone says a technology "will replace" a whole job next year, ask what it can reliably do today, measured how (the Production engineering and AI system design section teaches evaluation). Sounding right is not being right. ELIZA fooled people in 1966; language models can be fluent and wrong today ( Lesson 10.32 ). Always check. Each limit created the next idea. Models without your data led to retrieval; models that cannot act led to tools and agents; agents with real permissions led to security and governance. Every chapter of this course is a step in that chain. The fundamentals last. Products and model names change every few months; next-token prediction, attention, embeddings later · 3.19 , retrieval and evaluation have stayed central for years. That is why this course spends time on them. Check your mental model ✗ "Generative AI appeared suddenly in 2022." ✓ ChatGPT made it visible, but it rests on decades of work: backpropagation (1986), deep learning later · 3.4 (2012), attention (2014), transformers (2017), scaling (2020) and human-feedback training (2022). ✗ "AI progress is steady and always upward." ✓ It has come in bursts, with two long periods of disappointment when promises outran results. ✗ "Better algorithms alone explain the progress." ✓ Data, computing power and methods improved together; none would have been enough alone. Recap Five eras: rules, expert systems, statistical learning, deep learning, transformers and LLMs; each ended at a limit the next one addressed. The big jumps came when data, computing power and methods improved together. Assistants (2022) came from teaching language models to follow instructions; agents (2023 onward) from giving them tools and a loop. Hype cycles are real: judge claims by what is measured today.
