Debug a failure After a few hundred steps at a high learning rate, a ReLU network's loss stops falling. You log the activations after each ReLU, and in two layers more than half of them are exactly zero on every batch. Explain what happened to those units, why they cannot come back on their own, and what you change. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. First confirm that the units are dead and not only sparse: over a large sample, a dead unit is zero on every input. A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input outputs zero and has a derivative of zero, so it receives no gradient and its weights never move again. A large update, driven by the high learning rate, pushed those units' weights and biases far enough negative that no input brings them back. Lower the learning rate, re-initialize the dead units or the dead layers, and move to an activation with a gradient on the negative side, such as a leaky variant or GELU. What a dead unit is. ReLU is max(0, x). Its derivative is 1 for positive inputs and 0 otherwise. A unit whose input is negative on every sample outputs 0, passes 0 gradient to its weights, and nothing else in the loss touches those weights. It is dead for the rest of training. The activation lesson reports that 10 to 40 percent of units can die in a ReLU network in practice. The debugging lesson's threshold is more than half zeros after a ReLU layer: at that point switch the activation or reduce the learning rate. How the high learning rate did it. One oversized step moves a unit's bias or weights far negative. After that step every input lands below zero. The debugging lesson's demo builds the state directly by filling weights with -1.0 and biases with -5.0 and shows a flat loss with most activations at zero. A high learning rate reaches the same state by accident. Telling dead from sparse. Some zeros are normal; ReLU is meant to be sparse. Count, over a large sample, the fraction of inputs on which each unit is positive. Dead means zero on all of them. The activation lesson's detector reports dead, barely alive and healthy units from that count. What to change. Lower the learning rate, and add gradient clipping so one bad batch cannot produce the step again. Re-initialize the incoming weights of the dead units with a Kaiming draw and continue; the rest of the network keeps its progress. This is the debugging lesson's dead neuron resurrector exercise. Switch the activation. A leaky ReLU keeps a small slope on the negative side, so a unit can recover. GELU is smooth and avoids the failure entirely; the activation lesson prefers it over the leaky variant unless there is a specific reason. Check initialization. A Kaiming draw keeps pre-activations centered at the start, so fewer units begin life negative. Plausible wrong answers. "Half zeros is normal sparsity for ReLU." Some zeros are normal; a unit that is zero on every input is dead and contributes nothing, and the lesson flags a layer above half zeros. "Raise the learning rate so the units jump back." The gradient is zero regardless of the rate; no step reaches them. "Switch to sigmoid to avoid zeros." Sigmoid trades dead units for vanishing gradients through depth; a leaky variant or GELU keeps the benefits of ReLU. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the unit stay dead rather than drift back? Expected: zero output gives zero gradient to its weights, and nothing else in the loss touches them. (level 3) How do you tell a dead unit from a sparsely active one? Expected: count the fraction of inputs on which it is positive over a large sample; dead is zero on all, sparse is positive on a small fraction. (level 4) What links the high learning rate to the death? Expected: one large step moves the bias or weights far negative so every input lands below zero; clipping and a smaller rate limit the step. (level 4) Can you revive the dead units without retraining from scratch? Expected: re-initialize their incoming weights with a Kaiming draw and continue; the rest of the network keeps its progress. Where it is taught. The activation functions lesson explains dead units and builds the detector, and the debugging lesson reproduces the failure and sets the threshold. Explain the mechanism A junior engineer removes every activation function from a 10 layer network to make it faster and reports that training still runs and the loss still falls. What did they build, and why will it fail on XOR or on a spiral dataset? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Two linear layers compose into one: W2 (W1 x + b1) + b2 equals (W2 W1) x + (W2 b1 + b2), which is a single matrix and a single bias. Ten linear layers are one linear layer with extra parameters and the same decision boundary, a hyperplane. XOR and a spiral need a curved boundary, so the network cannot fit them at any width or depth. The substitution. Copy Matrix products compose, so a stack of linear maps is one linear map. Repeat the substitution and ten layers fold into one matrix A and one vector c. Depth without a nonlinearity is an illusion: the model has the capacity of a single linear layer, it only costs more to run. What an activation changes. Insert a nonlinear function g between the layers, so that h = g(W1 x + b1). The substitution fails, because W2 g(W1 x + b1) + b2 does not reduce to A x + c. Each extra layer with an activation adds representational capacity. That is what lets a network bend its boundary around a spiral or separate the XOR points. What to add back. The lesson's defaults: ReLU for a plain MLP or a CNN, GELU for a transformer, tanh inside recurrent cells. The output layer is the one place a missing activation is correct: a regression head emits any real number, a binary head uses a sigmoid, and a multi-class head uses a softmax. Why the loss still fell. A stack of linear layers only finds the best linear fit to the data. On XOR or a spiral that fit is close to chance, but it is better than random weights, so the loss moves. A falling loss is not evidence that the model can represent the target. Plausible wrong answers. "Ten layers are deeper, so they represent more." Without a nonlinearity the product of the matrices is one matrix; depth adds nothing. "The biases make it nonlinear." A bias shifts the hyperplane; it does not bend it. "The loss went down, so it is learning fine." It learns the best linear fit, which for XOR or a spiral is near chance. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which layer is allowed to have no activation? Expected: the output layer of a regression model, which must produce any real number. (level 2) Does the deep linear network train faster than one layer? Expected: no; it computes the same function with more parameters and more matrix multiplies. (level 2) Which activation would you add back for a plain MLP and for a transformer? Expected: ReLU for the MLP and GELU for the transformer. (level 3) Why is the collapse not a proof that depth is useless? Expected: with a nonlinearity between layers the substitution fails and each layer adds capacity; deep networks fit the same functions with fewer parameters than wide shallow ones. Where it is taught. The activation functions lesson proves the collapse and gives the default activation for each architecture. Sources and further reading Nair & Hinton, "Rectified Linear Units Improve Restricted Boltzmann Machines" (2010) -- the paper that introduced ReLU and enabled training of deep networks Hendrycks & Gimpel, "Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)" (2016) -- introduced the activation function that became the default for transformers Ramachandran et al., "Searching for Activation Functions" (2017) -- used automated search to discover Swish, showing that activation design can be automated Glorot & Bengio, "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks" (2010) -- the paper that diagnosed vanishing/exploding gradients and proposed Xavier initialization Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, "Deep Learning" Chapter 6.3 (https://www.deeplearningbook.org/) -- rigorous treatment of hidden units and activation functions Check your understanding Q1 Why can't you build a useful deep network using only linear layers (no activation functions)? A Stacking linear layers collapses to a single linear transformation, giving no benefit from depth B Linear layers are too slow C Linear layers can't handle batched data D Linear layers don't have biases y = W2(W1*x + b1) + b2 simplifies to y = Ax + c. No matter how many linear layers you stack, the result is equivalent to one linear layer. Activation functions break this composability. Q2 What is the output range of the ReLU activation function? A (-infinity, infinity) B [0, infinity) C (0, 1) D (-1, 1) ReLU(x) = max(0, x). It outputs 0 for all negative inputs and passes positive inputs unchanged, giving a range of [0, infinity). Q3 What is the 'dead neuron' problem in ReLU networks? A Neurons with zero bias B Neurons that compute too slowly C Neurons whose input is permanently negative, producing zero output and zero gradient forever D Neurons that produce NaN values If a ReLU neuron's weighted input is always negative (due to bad initialization or large negative bias), it outputs 0 with gradient 0. It can never recover because zero gradient means zero update. Q4 Which activation function is the default for hidden layers in modern transformers like GPT and BERT? A Sigmoid B Tanh C GELU D ReLU GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) is the default activation in transformers. It provides smooth gradient flow, avoids dead neurons, and has been shown to outperform ReLU in language models. Q5 Why is softmax used only in the output layer and never in hidden layers? A It only works with two classes B It causes exploding gradients C It converts a vector into a probability distribution (values sum to 1), which is needed for classification output but not for intermediate representations D It's too slow for hidden layers Softmax normalizes a vector so all values are in (0,1) and sum to 1, creating a probability distribution. Hidden layers need to preserve and transform information, not compress it into probabilities. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Your network makes a prediction. The ground truth says otherwise. How wrong is it? That number is the loss. Pick the wrong loss function and your model optimizes for the wrong thing entirely. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Loss function "How wrong the model is" A differentiable function mapping predictions and targets to a scalar that the optimizer minimizes MSE "Average squared error" Mean of squared differences between predictions and targets; penalizes large errors quadratically Cross-entropy "The classification loss" Measures divergence between predicted probability distribution and true distribution using $-\log(p)$ Binary cross-entropy "BCE" Cross-entropy for two classes: $-(y \log(p) + (1-y) \log(1-p))$ Label smoothing "Softening the targets" Replacing hard 0/1 targets with soft values (e.g., 0.1/0.9) to prevent overconfidence and improve generalization Contrastive loss "Pull together, push apart" A loss that learns representations by making similar pairs close and dissimilar pairs far in embedding space InfoNCE "The CLIP/SimCLR loss" Normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy over similarity scores; treats contrastive learning as classification Focal loss "The imbalanced data fix" Cross-entropy weighted by $(1-p_t)^\gamma$ to down-weight easy examples and focus on hard ones Triplet loss "Anchor-positive-negative" Pushes anchor closer to positive than negative by at least a margin in embedding space Temperature "Sharpness knob" A scalar divisor on logits/similarities that controls how peaked the resulting distribution is; lower = sharper The problem In plain words first The loss is the single number the optimiser makes smaller, so it defines what "better" means. For predicting numbers, mean squared error punishes big misses heavily. For predicting classes, cross-entropy scores the probability given to the right answer, and its gradient stays strong exactly when the model is confidently wrong. For learning embeddings without labels, contrastive losses pull matching pairs together and push the rest apart. Change the loss and you change what the model learns. A classifier that predicts 0.5 for everything scores an MSE of 0.25 on balanced classes, the best that any guess blind to the input can do. That is low-looking loss from a useless model, and the warning sign this lesson starts from. The loss function is the only thing your model actually optimizes. Not accuracy. Not F1 score. Not whatever metric you report to your manager. The optimizer takes the gradient of the loss function and adjusts weights to make that number smaller. If the loss function doesn't capture what you care about, the model will find the mathematically cheapest way to satisfy it, and that way is almost never what you wanted. Here is a concrete example. You have a binary classification task. Two classes, 50/50 split. You use MSE as your loss. The model predicts 0.5 for every single input. The average MSE is 0.25, which is the minimum possible without actually learning anything. The model has zero discriminative ability but it has technically minimized your loss function. Switch to cross-entropy and the same model is forced to push predictions toward 0 or 1, because -log(0.5) = 0.693 is a terrible loss, while -log(0.99) = 0.01 rewards confident correct predictions. The choice of loss function is the difference between a model that learns and a model that games the metric. It gets worse. In self-supervised learning, you don't even have labels. Contrastive loss defines the learning signal entirely: what counts as similar, what counts as different, and how hard the model should push them apart. Get contrastive loss wrong and your embeddings collapse to a single point -- every input maps to the same vector. Technically zero loss. Completely worthless. Idea 1 · Mean Squared Error (MSE) The default for regression. Compute the squared difference between prediction and target, average over all samples. 1 ​ ∑ ( y pred ​ − y true ​ ) 2 Why squaring matters: it penalizes large errors quadratically. An error of 2 costs 4x as much as an error of 1. An error of 10 costs 100x. This makes MSE sensitive to outliers -- a single wildly wrong prediction dominates the loss. Real numbers: if your model predicts housing prices and is off by $10,000 on most houses but off by $200,000 on one mansion, MSE will aggressively try to fix that one mansion, potentially hurting performance on the other 99 houses. The gradient of MSE with respect to a prediction is: ​ ∂ MSE ​ = n 2 ​ ( y pred ​ − y true ​ ) Linear in the error. Bigger errors get bigger gradients. This is a feature for regression (large errors need large corrections) and a bug for classification (you want to penalize confident wrong answers exponentially, not linearly). Idea 2 · Cross-Entropy Loss The loss function for classification. Rooted in information theory -- it measures the divergence between the predicted probability distribution and the true distribution. Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE): Where is the true label (0 or 1) and is the predicted probability. Why works: when the true label is 1 and you predict , the loss is . When you predict , the loss is . That 460x difference is why cross-entropy works. It brutally punishes confident wrong predictions while barely penalizing confident correct ones. The gradient tells the same story: ∂ BCE ​ = − p y ​ + 1 − p 1 − y ​ When and is near zero, the gradient is which approaches negative infinity. The model gets an enormous signal to fix its mistake. When is near 1, the gradient is tiny. Already correct, nothing to fix. Categorical Cross-Entropy: For multi-class classification with one-hot encoded targets. ∑ ​ y i ​ lo g ( p i ​ ) Only the true class contributes to the loss (because all other ​ are zero). If there are 10 classes and the correct class gets probability 0.1 (random guessing), the loss is . If the correct class gets probability 0.9, the loss is . The model learns to concentrate probability mass on the right answer. Idea 3 · Why MSE Fails for Classification MSE gradients flatten when predictions are near 0 or 1 (due to sigmoid saturation). Cross-entropy gradients compensate for this -- the cancels the sigmoid's flat regions, giving strong gradients exactly where they are needed most. It only heads for 0 and 1 when the training data can be separated perfectly, which is one reason label smoothing exists. ✗ "Lower contrastive temperature is always better." ✓ A low temperature sharpens the softmax so much that only the hardest negatives matter, and training can become unstable; the best value depends on batch size and data. Idea 4 · Label Smoothing Standard one-hot labels say "this is 100% class 3 and 0% everything else." That's a strong claim. Label smoothing softens it: α ​ With and 10 classes: instead of [0, 0, 1, 0, ...], the target becomes [0.01, 0.01, 0.91, 0.01, ...]. The model targets 0.91 instead of 1.0. Why this works: a model trying to output exactly 1.0 through a softmax needs to push logits to infinity. This causes overconfidence, hurts generalization, and makes the model brittle to distribution shift. Label smoothing caps the target at 0.9 (with ), keeping logits in a reasonable range. Inception-v3 introduced it and the original Transformer used a smoothing of 0.1; large language models are usually pretrained without it. Idea 5 · Contrastive Loss No labels. No classes. Just pairs of inputs and the question: are these similar or different? SimCLR-style contrastive loss (NT-Xent / InfoNCE): Take one image. Create two augmented views of it (crop, rotate, color jitter). These are the "positive pair" -- they should have similar embeddings. Every other image in the batch forms a "negative pair" -- they should have different embeddings. ​ exp ( sim ( z i ​ , z k ​ ) / τ ) exp ( sim ( z i ​ , z j ​ ) / τ ) ​ Where is cosine similarity, ​ and ​ are the positive pair, the sum is over all negatives, and (temperature) controls how sharp the distribution is. Lower temperature = harder negatives = more aggressive separation. Real numbers: batch size 256 means 255 negatives per positive pair. Temperature (the value MoCo uses and CLIP starts from; SimCLR reported 0.1 as best on ImageNet and 0.5 on CIFAR-10). The loss looks like a softmax over similarities -- it wants the positive pair's similarity to be highest among all 256 options. Triplet Loss: Takes three inputs: anchor, positive (same class), negative (different class). The margin (typically 0.2-1.0) enforces a minimum gap between positive and negative distances. If the negative is already far enough away, the loss is zero -- no gradient, no update. This makes training efficient but requires careful triplet mining (choosing hard negatives that are close to the anchor). Focal loss down-weights easy examples: ​ ) γ lo g ( p t ​ ) Where ​ is the predicted probability of the true class and controls the focusing. With , this is standard cross-entropy. With (the default): Easy example ( ​ = 0.9 ): weight = 0.01 . Effectively ignored. Hard example ( ​ = 0.1 ): weight = 0.81 . Full gradient signal. Focal loss was introduced by Lin et al. for object detection, where 99% of candidate regions are background (easy negatives). Without focal loss, the model drowns in easy background examples and never learns to detect objects. With it, the model focuses its capacity on the hard, ambiguous cases that matter. Contrastive losses for embeddings. Embedding models (sentence-transformers, CLIP-style models) are trained with InfoNCE-style losses over in-batch negatives. With two classes split evenly, a constant output of 0.5 gives a squared error of 0.25 on every row, which the lesson calls the minimum MSE a model can reach without learning anything, and the sigmoid's flat regions give MSE almost no gradient near a confident wrong answer. Cross-entropy charges minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class: 0.693 for 0.5, 0.01 for 0.99 and 4.6 for 0.01, so it pushes each prediction toward its label. Switch to binary cross-entropy. Why MSE is content. MSE averages the squared gap between the prediction and the label. Its gradient with respect to a prediction is linear in the gap. The prediction passes through a sigmoid, whose derivative is p(1 - p) and is near zero when p is near 0 or 1. A confident wrong answer, p near 0 for a positive row, sits exactly where the sigmoid is flat, so the update is tiny. A model can lower the loss a little by moving everything toward the middle and then stop, because the gradient has little left to say. Why cross-entropy is not. Binary cross-entropy is minus y log p minus (1 - y) log (1 - p). Its derivative with respect to p is minus y over p plus (1 - y) over (1 - p). For a positive row with p near 0 that is about minus 1 over p, which grows without bound as p falls. The log undoes the sigmoid: the derivative of the loss with respect to the logit is the prediction minus the target, linear in the error and never flat. The lesson's scale: a right answer at 0.99 costs 0.01, a wrong answer at 0.01 costs 4.6, a ratio of about 460. The multi-class version. Categorical cross-entropy on a one-hot target reduces to minus the log of the probability of the true class. A random guess among 10 classes puts probability 0.1 there and costs 2.3; a probability of 0.9 costs 0.105. A loss stuck near 2.3 on a 10 class problem is the multi-class twin of the 0.5 symptom. When the switch does not help. The switch helps only when the inputs carry signal about the label. On balanced data with no predictive features, both losses are lowest at a constant 0.5, so cross-entropy settles there too. Check that a simple model beats the constant before you blame the loss. Where MSE belongs. Regression on real valued targets, where a linear gradient in the error is what you want. For targets with heavy outliers, MAE or a Huber loss are the lesson's alternatives. Plausible wrong answers. "Lower the learning rate so MSE converges properly." The 0.5 output is where MSE is content; a smaller step arrives there more slowly. "MSE and cross-entropy have the same minimizer, so it does not matter." They agree only at a perfect fit. Away from it, MSE's gradient flattens where cross-entropy's grows. "Use accuracy as the loss instead." Accuracy has no useful gradient; the optimizer needs a smooth loss. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Write the derivative of binary cross-entropy with respect to p. Expected: minus y over p plus (1 - y) over (1 - p), which grows without bound when p is near 0 for a positive row. (level 2) Why does a prediction of 0.5 cost 0.693 under cross-entropy? Expected: it is minus the natural log of 0.5. (level 3) After the sigmoid, differentiate cross-entropy by the logit. What do you get? Expected: the prediction minus the target; the log cancels the sigmoid's derivative. (level 3) When is MSE the right loss? Expected: regression on real valued targets; for heavy outliers, MAE or a Huber loss. Where it is taught. The loss functions lesson opens with this failure and derives both gradients. Read the code This function claims to return, for each logit, the derivative of the cross-entropy loss. python def cce_gradient(logits, target_index): probs = softmax(logits) grads = list(probs) grads[target_index] -= 1.0 return grads Explain why three lines are enough. Then describe the gradient vector when the model is sure and right, and when it is sure and wrong. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. For softmax followed by cross-entropy on a one-hot target, the derivative of the loss with respect to logit i is the predicted probability of class i minus the target for class i. The function copies the probabilities and subtracts 1 at the true class, which is that vector. When the model is confident and right, every entry is near zero. When it is confident and wrong, the entry at the true class is near minus 1 and the entry at the class it chose is near plus 1. Why the form is so simple. The loss is minus the log of the probability of the true class, and that probability is exp of the true logit over the sum of exp of all logits. Differentiate with respect to logit i: the log of the denominator contributes plus p_i for every i, and the log of the numerator contributes minus 1 only for the true class. The softmax derivative on its own is a full matrix; combined with the log it collapses to p minus the one-hot target. The lesson's phrase is that softmax and cross-entropy are paired on purpose. Reading the vector. Confident right: p at the true class is near 1, so that entry is near 0, and every other p is near 0. Almost no update. Confident wrong: p at the true class is near 0, so that entry is near minus 1; the chosen class has p near 1 and an entry near plus 1. A large update that lowers the chosen logit and raises the true one. The entries sum to zero, because the probabilities sum to 1 and so does the one-hot target. That is a quick check for a hand-written version. What the three lines rely on. The softmax call must be the stable one, with the largest logit subtracted before the exponential, or large logits give inf. A framework fuses log-softmax and the negative log-likelihood into one loss that takes logits, for the same reason; the lesson's rule is to call that fused loss rather than a softmax followed by a separate log. With label smoothing. Replace the one-hot target by the smoothed vector: with alpha of 0.1 on ten classes the true class gets 0.91 and the others 0.01. The gradient is p minus that vector, so it reaches zero at 0.91, not at 1.0, which keeps the logits from running to infinity. Plausible wrong answers. "The gradient is minus 1 over p at the true class, like binary cross-entropy." That is the derivative with respect to the probability; through the softmax, the derivative with respect to the logit is p minus the target. "Only the true class has a gradient, because only it appears in the loss." Every logit appears in the softmax denominator, so every logit receives its p as gradient. "Divide by the number of classes." The gradient per sample is p minus the target; averaging over a batch divides by the batch size, not the class count. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the gradient vector sum to? Expected: zero; the probabilities sum to 1 and the one-hot target sums to 1. (level 2) Why pair softmax with cross-entropy rather than with squared error? Expected: the log undoes the exponential, so the gradient is linear in the error and never flattens. (level 3) How does the gradient change with label smoothing of 0.1 on ten classes? Expected: the target becomes 0.91 at the true class and 0.01 elsewhere, so the gradient is p minus that vector and reaches zero at 0.91, not at 1.0. (level 3) A framework offers a loss on logits and a loss on log probabilities. Which do you call? Expected: the one on logits, which fuses log-softmax and the negative log-likelihood in one numerically stable step. Where it is taught. The loss functions lesson writes this function and explains why the pairing simplifies. Sources and further reading Lin et al., "Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection" (2017) -- introduced focal loss for handling extreme class imbalance in object detection (RetinaNet) Chen et al., "A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations" (SimCLR, 2020) -- defined the modern contrastive learning pipeline with NT-Xent loss Szegedy et al., "Rethinking the Inception Architecture" (2016) -- introduced label smoothing as a regularization technique, now standard in most large models Hinton et al., "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network" (2015) -- knowledge distillation using soft targets and KL divergence, foundational for model compression Check your understanding Q1 What does the loss function represent in neural network training? A The learning rate schedule B A differentiable measure of how wrong the model's predictions are, which the optimizer minimizes C The number of incorrect predictions D The size of the training dataset The loss function maps predictions and targets to a single scalar that the optimizer minimizes via gradient descent. It must be differentiable so gradients can be computed. Q2 Why is cross-entropy preferred over MSE for classification tasks? A Cross-entropy punishes confident wrong predictions exponentially via -log(p), while MSE gives weak gradients near 0 and 1 B Cross-entropy doesn't require labels C MSE only works for regression D Cross-entropy is faster to compute When a model confidently predicts the wrong class (p near 0 for true class), -log(p) produces a huge loss and strong gradient. MSE produces weak gradients in the same situation because sigmoid is flat near 0 and 1. Q3 What happens if you use MSE loss for binary classification? A Gradients explode B Training diverges immediately C The model trains normally D The model can minimize loss by predicting 0.5 for everything, achieving MSE=0.25 without learning With MSE on a balanced binary dataset, predicting 0.5 for every input gives MSE=0.25 -- the minimum achievable without discrimination. The model satisfies the loss without learning any useful patterns. Q4 What does label smoothing do and why is it useful? A It smooths the learning rate schedule B It replaces hard 0/1 targets with soft values like 0.1/0.9, preventing overconfident predictions and improving generalization C It removes noisy labels from the dataset D It applies a moving average to the loss Label smoothing changes targets from [0,0,1,0] to [0.025,0.025,0.925,0.025] (with alpha=0.1). This prevents the model from pushing logits to infinity to achieve hard targets, reducing overconfidence. Q5 In contrastive loss (InfoNCE), what role does the temperature parameter play? A It controls how sharp the similarity distribution is -- lower temperature means harder separation between positives and negatives B It sets the number of negative samples C It controls the learning rate D It determines the embedding dimension Temperature divides the similarity scores before softmax. Lower temperature (e.g., 0.07) creates a sharper distribution where the model must clearly separate positives from negatives. Higher temperature is more forgiving. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Gradient descent tells you which direction to move. It says nothing about how far or how fast. SGD is a compass. Adam is GPS with traffic data. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Learning rate "Step size" The scalar multiplier on the gradient update; the single most impactful hyperparameter in training SGD "Basic gradient descent" Stochastic gradient descent: update weights by subtracting $\text{lr} \cdot \text{gradient}$, computed on a mini-batch Momentum "Rolling ball analogy" Exponential moving average of past gradients; dampens oscillation and accelerates consistent directions RMSProp "Adaptive learning rate" Divides each parameter's gradient by the running RMS of its recent gradients; equalizes learning rates Adam "The default optimizer" Combines momentum (first moment) and RMSProp (second moment) with bias correction for the initial steps AdamW "Adam done right" Adam with decoupled weight decay; applies regularization directly to weights rather than through the gradient Bias correction "Warmup for running averages" Dividing by $(1 - \beta^t)$ to compensate for the zero-initialization of Adam's moment estimates Weight decay "Shrink the weights" Subtracting a fraction of the weight value at each step; a regularizer that penalizes large weights Learning rate schedule "Changing lr over time" A function that adjusts the learning rate during training; warmup + cosine decay is the modern default Gradient clipping "Capping the gradient norm" Scaling down the gradient vector when its norm exceeds a threshold; prevents exploding gradient updates The problem In plain words first An optimiser turns gradients into weight changes. Plain SGD steps against the gradient by a fixed fraction. Momentum keeps a running velocity, so steady directions speed up and zig-zags cancel. Adam also tracks how large each weight's gradients usually are and divides by that, giving every weight its own step size. AdamW adds weight decay as a separate shrink, so it is not distorted by those per-weight step sizes. The learning rate still matters more than which of these you pick. You computed the gradients. You know that weight #4,721 should decrease by 0.003 to reduce the loss. But 0.003 in what units? Scaled by what? And should you move the same amount on step 1 as on step 1,000? Vanilla gradient descent applies the same learning rate to every parameter on every step: . This creates three problems that make training neural networks painful in practice. First, oscillation. The loss landscape is rarely shaped like a smooth bowl. It's more like a long, narrow valley. The gradient points across the valley (steep direction), not along it (shallow direction). Gradient descent bounces back and forth across the narrow dimension while making tiny progress along the useful one. You've seen this: loss drops fast then plateaus, not because the model converged but because it's oscillating. Second, one learning rate for all parameters is wrong. Some weights need large updates (they're in the early, underfitting stage). Others need tiny updates (they're near their optimal value). A learning rate that works for the former destroys the latter, and vice versa. Third, saddle points. In high dimensions, the loss landscape has vast flat regions where the gradient is near zero. Vanilla SGD crawls through these at the speed of the gradient, which is effectively zero. The model looks stuck. It isn't stuck -- it's in a flat region with useful descent on the other side. But SGD has no mechanism to push through. Adam solves all three. It maintains two running averages per parameter -- the mean gradient (momentum, handles oscillation) and the mean squared gradient (adaptive rate, handles different scales). Combined with bias correction for the first few steps, it gives you a single optimizer that works on 80% of problems with default hyperparameters. This lesson builds it from scratch so you understand exactly when and why it fails on the other 20%. Idea 1 · Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) The simplest optimizer. Compute the gradient on a mini-batch and step in the opposite direction. The "stochastic" means you use a random subset (mini-batch) of data to estimate the gradient, rather than the full dataset. This noise is actually useful -- it helps escape sharp local minima. But the noise also causes oscillation. Learning rate is the only knob. Too high: the loss diverges. Too low: training takes forever. The optimal value depends on the architecture, the data, the batch size, and the current stage of training. For vanilla SGD on modern networks, typical values range from 0.01 to 0.1. But even within a single training run, the ideal learning rate changes. Idea 2 · Momentum The ball-rolling-downhill analogy is overused but accurate. Instead of stepping by the gradient alone, you maintain a velocity that accumulates past gradients. ​ w ​ = β m t − 1 ​ + gradient = w − lr ⋅ m t ​ ​ Beta (typically 0.9) controls how much history to keep. With , the momentum is roughly the average of the last 10 gradients ( ). Why this fixes oscillation: gradients that point in the same direction accumulate. Gradients that flip direction cancel out. In that narrow valley, the "across" component flips sign each step and gets dampened. The "along" component stays consistent and gets amplified. The result is smooth acceleration in the useful direction. Real numbers: SGD alone on a badly conditioned loss landscape might take 10,000 steps. SGD with momentum ( ) typically takes 3,000-5,000 steps on the same problem. The speedup is not marginal. Worked example A long, narrow valley Take 1 ​ ( x 2 + 100 y 2 ) : 100 times steeper across ( ) than along ( ). Momentum lets the consistent gradient build up speed while the alternating gradient cancels. The paths are drawn under Step 5. Idea 3 · RMSProp The first per-parameter adaptive learning rate method that actually worked. Proposed by Hinton in a Coursera lecture (never formally published). ​ w ​ = β s t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β ) ⋅ gradient 2 = w − lr ⋅ s t ​ ​ + ϵ gradient ​ ​ ​ tracks the running average of squared gradients. Parameters with consistently large gradients get divided by a large number (smaller effective learning rate). Parameters with small gradients get divided by a small number (larger effective learning rate). This solves the "one learning rate for all parameters" problem. A weight that's already been getting large updates is probably near its target -- slow it down. A weight that's been getting tiny updates might be undertrained -- speed it up. Epsilon (typically 1e-8) prevents division by zero when a parameter hasn't been updated. Idea 4 · Adam: Momentum + RMSProp Adam combines both ideas. It maintains two exponential moving averages per parameter: ​ v t ​ ​ = β 1 ​ m t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) ⋅ gradient = β 2 ​ v t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 2 ​ ) ⋅ gradient 2 ​ ​ (first moment: mean) (second moment: variance) ​ Bias correction is the key detail most explanations skip. At step 1, ​ = ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) ⋅ gradient . With ​ = 0.9 , that's -- ten times too small. The moving average hasn't warmed up yet. Bias correction compensates: v ^ ​ = 1 − β 1 t ​ m t ​ ​ = 1 − β 2 t ​ v t ​ ​ ​ At step 1 with ​ = 0.9 : = m 1 ​ / ( 1 − 0.9 ) = m 1 ​ /0.1 = the actual gradient. With a learning rate of 0.01 Adam also gets there by epoch 8. That is why Step 5's momentum run overshoots. Idea 5 · AdamW: Weight Decay Done Right L2 regularization adds to the loss. In vanilla SGD, this is equivalent to weight decay (subtracting from the weight at each step). In Adam, this equivalence breaks. The Loshchilov & Hutter insight: when you add L2 to the loss and then Adam processes the gradient, the adaptive learning rate scales the regularization term too. Parameters with large gradient variance get less regularization. Parameters with small variance get more. This is not what you want -- you want uniform regularization regardless of the gradient statistics. AdamW fixes this by applying weight decay directly to the weights, after the Adam update: ​ + ϵ m ^ ​ − lr ⋅ λ w The weight decay term ( ) is not scaled by Adam's adaptive factor. Every parameter gets the same proportional shrinkage. This seems like a minor detail. It's not. AdamW converges to better solutions than Adam + L2 regularization on virtually every task. It's the default optimizer in PyTorch for training transformers, diffusion models, and most modern architectures. BERT, GPT, LLaMA, Stable Diffusion -- all trained with AdamW. Worked example Adam + L2 against AdamW Two weights both start at 1.0, and their gradients are pure noise: standard deviation 1 for the first, 100 for the second. Weight decay should shrink both the same way. After 1,000 steps at lr = 0.01 with decay 0.1: Quiet weight (noise 1) Noisy weight (noise 100) Adam with L2 added to the gradient 0.333 1.006 AdamW (decoupled decay) 0.334 0.319 With L2, the decay term rides inside the gradient, so Adam divides it by the noisy weight's large ​ : that weight is never regularised. AdamW applies the same shrink to both. Idea 6 · Learning Rate: The Most Important Hyperparameter If you tune one hyperparameter, tune the learning rate. A 10x change in learning rate matters more than any architectural decision you'll make. Common defaults: SGD: lr = 0.01 to 0.1 Adam/AdamW: lr = 1e-4 to 3e-4 Fine-tuning pretrained models: lr = 1e-5 to 5e-5 Learning rate warmup: linear ramp over first 1-10% of steps Idea 7 · Optimizer Comparison Idea 8 · When Each Optimizer Wins The same idea as a formula With gradient ​ at step and learning rate : Optimiser Update SGD ​ Momentum ​ ; RMSProp 2 ​ ; ​ / ( s ​ + ϵ ) Adam ​ m + ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) g t ​ , ​ v + ( 1 − β 2 ​ ) g t 2 ​ ; / ( v ^ ​ + ϵ ) AdamW Adam's step, plus applied separately with Adam's bias corrections = m / ( 1 − β 1 t ​ ) , = v / ( 1 − β 2 t ​ ) . Typical values: ; ​ = 0.9 , ​ = 0.999 (0.95 for large language models), . Effective step sizes. Momentum with a steady gradient reaches , a step times SGD's at . Adam's step per weight is roughly whatever the gradient's scale, so its learning rates (around to ) are not comparable with SGD's. Why AdamW. Adding to the gradient inside Adam divides the decay by ​ , so weights with large gradients are barely regularised. AdamW's separate decay shrinks every weight by the same fraction per step. Memory. Adam stores and : two extra numbers per parameter. With fp32 weights, gradients and states, training costs about 16 bytes per parameter, 112 GB for a 7-billion-parameter model before activations. Recap What to keep from this lesson SGD steps against the gradient; its learning rate is capped by the steepest direction. Momentum averages gradients, cancelling zig-zags and speeding up steady directions; its effective step is about lr ÷ (1 − β). Adam divides each weight's step by its typical gradient size, with bias correction for the zero start. AdamW decays weights directly, so noisy weights are regularised like quiet ones. Tune the learning rate first; compare optimisers only at their own best learning rates. Solutions Solution P1 · Plain SGD, and momentum never gets there SGD reaches 95% at epoch 8, Adam at epoch 54 and AdamW at 57; SGD with momentum stalls at 93% and never reaches 95%. The learning rates, not the algorithms, decide this race: momentum with multiplies SGD's step by about 10 and overshoots, while Adam's steps are about its learning rate, 0.001 per weight, fifty times smaller than SGD's. M1 reruns the race with matched step sizes. Solution M1 · Fair learning rates Momentum at 0.005 now matches SGD exactly: 85 percent at epoch 4, 95 percent at epoch 8, 99 percent at the end. Adam at 0.01 also reaches 85 and 95 percent at epochs 4 and 8 and finishes with the lowest loss (0.0095, accuracy 99.5 percent). Once each optimiser gets a sensible learning rate, the differences shrink on a problem this small. Solution B1 · Past the stability limit Each SGD step multiplies by : it flips sign and grows by 10 percent. After 100 steps ≈ 13 , 800 and the loss is around . Momentum is stable up to , so at 0.021 it still converges, though it oscillates. The largest stable learning rate is set by the steepest direction, which is why learning-rate warmup and gradient clipping exist. Use it: the same idea with real libraries PyTorch optimizers handle parameter groups, gradient clipping, and learning rate scheduling: Copy The pattern is always: zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, (clip), step, (schedule). Memorize this order. Getting it wrong (e.g., calling scheduler.step() before optimizer.step()) is a common source of subtle bugs. For CNNs, many practitioners still prefer SGD + momentum (lr=0.1, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=1e-4) with a step or cosine schedule. SGD finds flatter minima, which often generalize better. For transformers and LLMs, AdamW with warmup + cosine decay is the universal default. Don't fight the consensus without a measured reason. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) AdamW with warmup and decay is the standard recipe for transformers; 8-bit AdamW (bitsandbytes) and paged optimizers cut memory when fine-tuning on one GPU. Muon has entered production. Moonshot AI trained Kimi K2 (1T parameters) with MuonClip, and PyTorch ships torch.optim.Muon (since 2.9); it is applied to 2-D weight matrices while AdamW handles embeddings and norms. Optimizer state is the memory bill. AdamW keeps two extra numbers per parameter, which is why sharded optimizers (ZeRO, FSDP) exist. Sources: torch.optim.AdamW , torch.optim.Muon , Kimi K2 report , bitsandbytes optimizers . Explain the mechanism Adam keeps a running average of the gradient and a running average of its square, and divides each by one minus beta to the power t before the update. A teammate deletes those two divisions to simplify the code. What changes in the first steps of training, and when does the change stop mattering? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Both averages start at zero, so at step one the first moment is only (1 - beta1) times the gradient, a tenth of it with beta1 at 0.9, and the second moment is a thousandth of the squared gradient with beta2 at 0.999. The divisions rescale both to unbiased estimates. Without them the square root of the second moment is shrunk more than the first moment, so the ratio and the step come out too large while the averages warm up. The first moment's factor is close to 1 after about 50 steps, but the second moment's factor, 1 - 0.999 to the t, stays well below 1 for thousands of steps, so without the division the step stays too large for that long. The two averages. Copy The first moment is momentum: with beta1 at 0.9 it averages about the last ten gradients, from 1 over (1 - 0.9). The second moment sets a per-parameter step size: a weight with large gradients is divided by a large number and moves less, a weight with small gradients moves more. Why the averages start wrong. At step one, m is 0.1 times the gradient. The average has not warmed up, and the lesson calls that ten times too small. The same holds for v with a factor of 0.001. Dividing m by (1 - 0.9) at step one gives back the gradient. At step 100 the factor (1 - 0.9 to the 100) is about 1.0, so the correction is gone. The lesson's rule for the first moment: it matters for the first 10 steps or so and is irrelevant after 50. The second moment is slower. With beta2 at 0.999 its factor approaches 1 only after thousands of steps, so its correction lasts much longer. What the deletion does. The two moments are shrunk by different factors, and the update takes their ratio after a square root. The first moment is shrunk by 0.1. The second moment is shrunk by 0.001, and its square root by less than 0.1, so the denominator is too small and the step is too large. The early updates take oversized steps on statistics built from one or two gradients. The symptom is a loss that jumps in the first steps and a run that sometimes diverges before it settles. What else guards the first steps. Warmup, a small learning rate that ramps up over the first steps, protects the same period for a different reason: the correction fixes the scale of the averages, not their noise. The lesson's advice on tuning: change the learning rate first, then beta2, almost never beta1 or epsilon. Plausible wrong answers. "The division is a numerical safety term like epsilon." Epsilon guards a zero denominator; the division by one minus beta to the t corrects the zero initialization of the averages. "Without it the first steps are too small, so training is only slower." The second moment's square root is shrunk more than the first moment, so the ratio and the step come out too large. "Both corrections stop mattering after about 50 steps." That holds for the first moment only. With beta2 at 0.999 the second moment's factor stays well below 1 for thousands of steps. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the first moment estimate and what does the second? Expected: the running mean of the gradient, which is momentum, and the running mean of the squared gradient, which sets a per-parameter step size. (level 2) With beta1 at 0.9, how many past gradients does the first moment roughly average? Expected: about ten, from 1 over (1 - 0.9). (level 3) Why does Adam still want a warmup if bias correction exists? Expected: the correction fixes the scale of the averages, not their noise; a few steps of statistics are a poor estimate, so a small early learning rate limits the damage. (level 3) Which Adam hyperparameter do you change first when training is unstable? Expected: the learning rate, then beta2; almost never beta1 or epsilon. Where it is taught. One engineer adds an L2 penalty on the weights to the loss. Another uses an AdamW optimizer with a weight decay argument. They say the two are the same thing. Are they, and which do you choose? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. They are the same only under plain SGD. In Adam, a penalty inside the loss becomes part of the gradient and is divided by the running gradient size like every other term, so weights with large gradient variance get less decay and weights with small variance get more. AdamW subtracts lr times lambda times w after the adaptive update, so every weight shrinks by the same fraction. Choose AdamW; the lesson makes it the default for transformers for this reason. Where they agree. The L2 term lambda over 2 times the sum of w squared has gradient lambda w. Under SGD the update subtracts lr times lambda w from each weight, which is weight decay by definition. Both names describe one operation. Where Adam breaks the equivalence. Adam does not apply the gradient. It averages it into the first moment, squares it into the second, and divides by the root of the second moment. A penalty that rides along in the gradient is rescaled per parameter by that division. A weight with noisy, large gradients has a large second moment and receives a small share of the decay. A weight with quiet gradients receives a large share. The regularization is uneven, and the lesson reports that it converges to worse solutions than the decoupled form on almost every task. What AdamW does instead. Copy The decay term sits outside the adaptive factor. Every weight loses the same fraction lr times lambda at each step. In the lesson's from-scratch class this is one extra line after the Adam update: subtract lr times weight decay times the parameter. Values the lessons give. 0.01 for AdamW on transformers; the fine-tuning default is also 0.01. 1e-4 for SGD on CNNs, where the two forms coincide. Up to 0.1 for a model that overfits heavily. A test that shows the difference. The lesson's exercise: initialize weights with large magnitudes, train Adam with L2 and AdamW with the same decay, and plot the weight norm over training. AdamW shrinks it faster and more evenly. Plausible wrong answers. "Weight decay and L2 are the same by definition." They coincide under SGD; under an adaptive optimizer the penalty is rescaled per parameter. "Use Adam with L2 and a bigger lambda to compensate." A bigger lambda does not fix the unevenness; some weights still receive almost no decay. "Adam adapts, so it does not need weight decay." Adaptation sets step sizes; it does not shrink weights. Overfit transformers still need decay. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is the decay uniform in AdamW? Expected: it is applied to the weights directly, outside the adaptive division, so the fraction removed per step is lr times lambda for every weight. (level 3) Where exactly does the penalty go wrong inside Adam? Expected: it enters the gradient, so it is averaged into the first moment and squared into the second, and the division by the root of the second moment rescales it per parameter. (level 3) What decay values does the lesson give? Expected: 0.01 for AdamW on transformers, 1e-4 for SGD on CNNs, up to 0.1 for a heavily overfit model. (level 4) What experiment shows the difference in a few lines? Expected: start from weights of large magnitude, train both with the same decay, and plot the weight norm; AdamW shrinks it faster and more evenly. Where it is taught. The optimizers lesson builds Adam and AdamW and explains the decoupling, and the regularization lesson gives the decay values. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Your model gets 99% on training data and 60% on test data. It memorized instead of learning. Regularization is the tax you impose on complexity to force generalization. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Overfitting "Model memorized the data" When a model's training performance significantly exceeds its test performance, indicating it learned noise rather than signal Regularization "Preventing overfitting" Any technique that constrains model complexity to improve generalization: dropout, weight decay, normalization, augmentation Dropout "Random neuron deletion" Zeroing random neurons during training with probability $p$, forcing redundant representations; equivalent to training an ensemble Weight decay "L2 penalty" Shrinking all weights toward zero by subtracting $\lambda w$ at each step; penalizes complexity through weight magnitude Batch normalization "Normalize per batch" Normalizing layer outputs across the batch dimension using batch statistics during training and running averages during inference Layer normalization "Normalize per sample" Normalizing across features within each sample; batch-independent, used in transformers where batch size varies RMSNorm "LayerNorm without the mean" Root mean square normalization; drops the mean subtraction from LayerNorm for 10% speedup with equal accuracy Early stopping "Stop before overfit" Halting training when validation loss stops improving; the simplest regularizer, often used alongside others Data augmentation "More data from less" Transforming training inputs (flip, crop, noise) to increase effective dataset size and force invariance learning Generalization gap "Train-test split" The difference between training and test performance; regularization aims to minimize this gap The problem In plain words first A big network can memorise its training set, noise included, and then do worse on new data. Regularisation makes memorising harder: dropout randomly switches neurons off during training so no single one can be relied on, weight decay keeps weights small, early stopping quits before the memorising starts, and data augmentation shows the model more varied examples. Normalisation layers (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) mainly keep each layer's numbers in a steady range so training is stable, which also tends to help. A neural network with enough parameters can memorize any dataset. This is not a hypothetical -- Zhang et al. (2017) showed it by training standard networks on ImageNet with random labels. The networks reached near-zero training loss on completely random label assignments. They memorized a million random input-output pairs with no pattern to learn. Training loss was perfect. Test accuracy was no better than chance. This is the overfitting problem, and it gets worse as models get larger. GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters. The training set has about 500 billion tokens. With that many parameters, the model has enough capacity to memorize significant chunks of the training data verbatim. Without regularization, it would just regurgitate training examples instead of learning generalizable patterns. The gap between training performance and test performance is the overfitting gap. Every technique in this lesson attacks that gap from a different angle. Dropout forces the network to not rely on any single neuron. Weight decay prevents any single weight from growing too large. Batch normalization smooths the loss landscape so the optimizer finds flatter, more generalizable minima. Layer normalization does the same thing but works where batch normalization fails (small batches, variable-length sequences). RMSNorm does it 10% faster by dropping the mean calculation. Each technique is simple. Together, they're the difference between a model that memorizes and one that generalizes. Idea 1 · The Overfitting Spectrum Every model sits somewhere on a spectrum from underfitting (too simple to capture the pattern) to overfitting (so complex it captures noise). The sweet spot is in between, and regularization pushes models toward it from the overfit side. Idea 2 · Dropout The simplest regularization technique with the most elegant interpretation. During training, randomly set each neuron's output to zero with probability . With , half the neurons are zeroed on every forward pass. The network must learn redundant representations because it can't predict which neurons will be available. This prevents co-adaptation -- neurons learning to rely on specific other neurons being present. The ensemble interpretation: a network with neurons and dropout creates possible subnetworks (every combination of which neurons are on or off). Training with dropout approximately trains all subnetworks simultaneously, each on different mini-batches. At test time, you use all neurons (no dropout) and scale outputs by to match the expected value during training. This is equivalent to averaging the predictions of subnetworks -- a massive ensemble from a single model. In practice, the scaling is applied during training instead of testing (inverted dropout): During testing: ​ output = activation ( z ) ⋅ mask / ( 1 − p ) output = activation ( z ) (no change needed) ​ This is cleaner because test code doesn't need to know about dropout at all. Default rates: p = 0.1 for transformers, p = 0.5 for MLPs, p = 0.2-0.3 for CNNs. Higher dropout = stronger regularization = more underfitting risk. Worked example Inverted dropout on eight numbers Input , mean 4.5, with . One training pass might keep positions 1, 2, 5 and 7 and scale them by : output , mean 3.75. Another pass keeps a different half. On average over many passes each value is kept half the time and doubled when kept, so the expected output equals the input, and at test time the layer can simply pass values through unchanged. Check your mental model ✗ "At test time dropout exactly averages all sub-networks." ✓ Using all neurons with matched scaling is a cheap approximation of that average. It is exact only for a linear layer; with non-linear layers it is close, not equal. ✗ "Training accuracy above test accuracy is always overfitting, and the reverse means a bug." ✓ With dropout, training accuracy is measured with neurons switched off, so it understates the model. Step 6's dropout run shows test accuracy above training accuracy for exactly this reason. ✗ "BatchNorm works because it removes internal covariate shift." ✓ That was the original explanation; Santurkar et al. (2018) found the benefit comes mostly from a smoother loss landscape that tolerates larger learning rates. Idea 3 · Weight Decay (L2 Regularization) Add the squared magnitude of all weights to the loss: λ ​ i ∑ ​ w i 2 ​ The gradient of the regularization term is . This means at every step, each weight is shrunk toward zero by a fraction proportional to its magnitude. Large weights get penalized more. The model is pushed toward solutions where no single weight dominates. Why this helps generalization: overfit models tend to have large weights that amplify noise in the training data. Weight decay keeps weights small, which limits the model's effective capacity and forces it to rely on robust, generalizable features rather than memorized quirks. The hyperparameter controls the strength. Typical values: 0.01 for AdamW on transformers 1e-4 for SGD on CNNs 0.1 for heavily overfit models As discussed in lesson 06: weight decay and L2 regularization are equivalent in SGD but not in Adam. Always use AdamW (decoupled weight decay) when training with Adam. Idea 4 · Batch Normalization Normalize the output of each layer across the mini-batch before passing it to the next layer. For a mini-batch of activations at some layer: σ 2 x ^ y ​ = B 1 ​ i ∑ ​ x i ​ = B 1 ​ i ∑ ​ ( x i ​ − μ ) 2 = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x i ​ − μ ​ = γ x ^ + β ​ ​ (batch mean) (batch variance) (normalize) (scale and shift) ​ Gamma and beta are learnable parameters that let the network undo the normalization if that's optimal. Without them, you'd be forcing every layer's output to be zero-mean unit-variance, which might not be what the network wants. Training vs inference split: During training, and come from the current mini-batch. During inference, you use running averages accumulated during training (exponential moving average with momentum = 0.1, meaning 90% old + 10% new). Why BatchNorm works is still debated. The original paper claimed it reduces "internal covariate shift" (the distribution of layer inputs changing as earlier layers update). Santurkar et al. (2018) showed this explanation is wrong. The actual reason: BatchNorm makes the loss landscape smoother. The gradients are more predictive, the Lipschitz constants are smaller, and the optimizer can take larger steps safely. This is why BatchNorm lets you use higher learning rates and converge faster. BatchNorm has a fundamental limitation: it depends on batch statistics. With batch size 1, the mean and variance are meaningless. With small batches (< 32), the statistics are noisy and hurt performance. This matters for tasks like object detection (where memory limits batch size) and language modeling (where sequence lengths vary). Predict before you run A fresh BatchNorm(4) (running mean starts at 0, momentum 0.1) sees ten training batches whose values average about 3.45. What is its running mean afterwards, and what does it output in eval mode for the input ? (Solution P1; the run is under Step 3.) Idea 5 · Layer Normalization Normalize across features instead of across the batch. For a single sample: σ 2 x ^ y ​ = D 1 ​ j ∑ ​ x j ​ = D 1 ​ j ∑ ​ ( x j ​ − μ ) 2 = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x j ​ − μ ​ = γ x ^ + β ​ ​ (feature mean) (feature variance) ​ is the feature dimension. Each sample is normalized independently -- no dependence on batch size. This is why transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm. Sequences have variable lengths, batch sizes are often small (or 1 during generation), and the computation is identical between training and inference. LayerNorm in transformers is applied after each self-attention block and each feed-forward block (Post-LN), or before them (Pre-LN, which is more stable for training). Idea 6 · RMSNorm LayerNorm without the mean subtraction. Proposed by Zhang & Sennrich (2019). y ​ = D 1 ​ j ∑ ​ x j 2 ​ ​ = γ ⋅ rms x ​ ​ That's it. No mean computation, no beta parameter. The observation: the re-centering (mean subtraction) in LayerNorm contributes very little to the model's performance, but costs computation. Removing it gives the same accuracy with about 10% less overhead. LLaMA, LLaMA 2, LLaMA 3, Mistral, and most modern LLMs use RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. At the scale of billions of parameters and trillions of tokens, that 10% savings is significant. Tip How much faster? The RMSNorm paper measured running-time reductions from 7 to 64 percent of the normalisation cost, depending on the model and hardware. Normalisation is a small part of a transformer's total compute, so the end-to-end saving is much smaller; treat "about 10 percent" as a rough figure, not a constant. Idea 7 · Normalization Comparison Idea 8 · Data Augmentation as Regularization Not a model modification but a data modification. Transform training inputs while preserving labels: Images: random crop, flip, rotation, color jitter, cutout Text: synonym replacement, back-translation, random deletion Audio: time stretch, pitch shift, noise addition The effect is identical to regularization: it increases the effective size of the training set, making it harder for the model to memorize specific examples. A model that only sees each image once in its original form can memorize it. A model that sees 50 augmented versions of each image is forced to learn the invariant structure. Idea 9 · Early Stopping The simplest regularizer: stop training when validation loss starts increasing. The model hasn't overfit yet at that point. In practice, you track validation loss every epoch, save the best model, and continue training for a "patience" window (typically 5-20 epochs). If validation loss doesn't improve within the patience window, you stop and load the best saved model. Idea 10 · When to Apply What The same idea as a formula Dropout. During training, each unit is kept with probability and scaled: = q m ⊙ h ​ with ​ ∼ Bernoulli ( q ) . Then ] = h , so at evaluation the layer simply passes through unchanged ("inverted dropout"). Forgetting to switch to evaluation mode keeps the noise on at inference. Weight decay. Adding λ ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 to the loss adds to the gradient, so each SGD step multiplies the weights by before the gradient step. Normalisation layers. For a vector of activations (over a batch for BatchNorm, over the features of one example for LayerNorm): + ϵ ​ x − μ ​ + β , RMSNorm ( x ) = γ ⊙ d 1 ​ ∑ i ​ x i 2 ​ + ϵ ​ x ​ BatchNorm uses batch statistics in training and running averages at evaluation, so it depends on batch size; LayerNorm and RMSNorm use only the example itself, which is why transformers use them. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and : fewer operations, and in practice the same quality (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma). Early stopping keeps the checkpoint with the best validation loss; with gradient descent on a linear model it behaves much like an L2 penalty whose strength falls as training goes on. Recap What to keep from this lesson Overfitting shows as a gap between training and validation performance; measure it before regularising. Dropout zeroes random neurons during training and rescales the rest; at test time it does nothing. Weight decay shrinks weights each step; use AdamW's decoupled version with Adam. BatchNorm normalises across the batch and keeps running statistics for eval; LayerNorm and RMSNorm normalise each sample and suit transformers. Early stopping is often the strongest and cheapest regulariser on small data. Solutions Solution P1 · Running statistics lag behind The running mean ends near 2.2 to 2.4 in each feature, not 3.45: starting from 0, ten updates with momentum 0.1 cover only = 65 percent of the way. In eval mode is normalised with that low mean and comes out between about 2.6 and 3.0 per feature; with fully settled statistics it would be about 1.6. Solution B1 · BatchNorm needs more than one sample ValueError: Expected more than 1 value per channel when training . In training mode BatchNorm normalises each feature across the batch, and one sample has no spread to divide by. In eval mode it uses the running mean and variance instead, so a single sample is fine. The same mismatch causes subtler bugs: forget model.eval() and predictions depend on whichever other samples share the batch. Use it: the same idea with real libraries PyTorch provides all normalization and regularization as modules: Copy The model.train() / model.eval() toggle is critical. It switches dropout on/off and tells BatchNorm to use batch statistics vs running statistics. Forgetting model.eval() before inference is one of the most common bugs in deep learning. Your test accuracy will fluctuate randomly because dropout is still active and BatchNorm is using mini-batch statistics. For transformers, the pattern is different: Copy LayerNorm, not BatchNorm. Dropout p=0.1, not p=0.5. These are the transformer defaults. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLM pretraining uses little dropout. Llama 3 and most modern LLM recipes set dropout to zero for pretraining and rely on weight decay (around 0.1 with AdamW) and huge, deduplicated data; dropout reappears in small-data fine-tuning. Data augmentation in vision. RandAugment, MixUp and CutMix are standard in image classification training (timm, torchvision), as is label smoothing. LoRA as regularisation. Low-rank fine-tuning (PEFT) changes far fewer parameters, which itself limits overfitting on small datasets. Sources: Llama 3 paper , timm training scripts , torchvision v2 MixUp/CutMix , PEFT .
