Read the code This dropout module comes from a mini framework. python class Dropout(Module): def __init__(self, p=0.5): super().__init__() self.p = p self.mask = None def forward(self, x): if not self.training: return x self.mask = [0.0 if random.random() < self.p else 1.0 / (1 - self.p) for _ in x] return [v * m for v, m in zip(x, self.mask)] def backward(self, grad): if self.mask is None: return grad return [g * m for g, m in zip(grad, self.mask)] Why do the kept entries of the mask hold 1 over (1 minus p) rather than 1, and why does backward reuse the same mask? What would change if the forward kept 1 and the scaling moved to evaluation time? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each unit is zeroed with probability p, so the expected value of a unit falls to (1 - p) times its original. Dividing the kept units by (1 - p) restores that expectation during training, so evaluation runs the plain network with no change. Backward multiplies by the same mask because the forward pass was a per-unit scale, and the derivative of a scale is the scale. Moving the factor to evaluation time also works, but then every inference path must know the dropout rate. The expectation argument. A mask entry is 0 with probability p and 1 over (1 - p) otherwise. Its expected value is (1 - p) times 1 over (1 - p), which is 1. So the expected output of each unit in training equals its output with dropout off. The network sees the same scale in both modes, and the evaluation path has no dropout code at all. The lesson calls this inverted dropout. The original form kept the mask at 1 and multiplied by (1 - p) at test time, which forces inference code to know p. The backward pass. Dropout is an element-wise scale by the mask. The gradient of the input is the gradient of the output times the same mask: dropped units get 0, kept units get the gradient scaled by 1 over (1 - p). The mask must be the one from the matching forward pass, because the backward pass differentiates the function that ran forward. A fresh mask would pass gradient to units that were off and scale units that were on. The guard on a missing mask covers only a backward call before any training forward. The evaluation branch returns before it changes the mask, so a backward call after an evaluation forward reuses the mask of the last training forward. What dropout buys. Zeroing random units stops neurons from relying on specific other neurons being present, which the lesson calls co-adaptation. Each mask selects a subnetwork, so training samples from about 2 to the N subnetworks of N units, and evaluation averages them in one pass by running the full network at the scaled expectation. Default rates: 0.1 for transformers, 0.5 for MLPs, 0.2 to 0.3 for CNNs. Higher p is stronger regularization and more risk of underfitting. Plausible wrong answers. "The scale makes the outputs sum to one." It restores the expected value of each unit, not a sum. "Backward should draw a fresh mask for exploration." The backward pass differentiates the function that ran forward; a different mask gives the gradient of a different function. "In evaluation mode multiply by (1 - p) as well." With inverted dropout the scaling already happened in training; scaling again at evaluation shrinks every activation. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What gradient does a dropped unit receive? Expected: zero, because its mask entry is 0. (level 2) Why must backward use the mask from the same forward pass? Expected: the backward pass differentiates the function that ran forward; a new mask would scale active units wrongly and pass gradient to inactive ones. (level 3) What is the ensemble reading of dropout? Expected: each mask defines a subnetwork, so training samples from about 2 to the N subnetworks, and evaluation averages them by running the full network at the scaled expectation. (level 3) Which rate does the lesson give for a transformer, and why is it lower than for an MLP? Expected: 0.1 against 0.5; a higher rate is stronger regularization with more underfitting risk, and the transformer default is the lighter one. Where it is taught. The regularization lesson derives inverted dropout, and the mini framework lesson turns it into this module. Weigh a trade-off A team ports a vision training recipe to a transformer and keeps batch normalization. Training is unstable, and text generation with one sequence at a time produces garbage. Explain why transformers use layer normalization instead, and when you would go a step further to RMSNorm. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Batch normalization normalizes each feature across the batch, so its statistics depend on the batch size and on which sequences share the batch; with small batches they are noisy, with a batch of one they are meaningless, and training and inference run different code paths. Layer normalization normalizes across the features of one sample, so it does not depend on the batch and is identical in both modes, which is what variable length sequences and single sequence generation need. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the shift parameter, keeps the accuracy, and saves about 10 percent of the normalization cost, which is why most recent large language models use it. Batch normalization and its two dependencies. For each feature, batch normalization subtracts the batch mean, divides by the batch standard deviation with an epsilon, and applies a learned scale gamma and shift beta. Two things follow. First, the result for one sample depends on the other samples in its batch. The lesson puts the floor at a batch of about 32; below it the statistics are noisy, and at a batch of one the variance is zero. Second, inference cannot see a batch, so it uses running averages collected in training with a momentum of 0.1, which is a second code path and a second source of bugs. Sequence models hit both problems: lengths vary, memory limits the batch, and generation runs one sequence at a time. Layer normalization. Layer normalization computes the mean and variance over the D features of one sample and normalizes that sample alone. No batch dependence, no running averages, the same computation in training and at inference. Transformers apply it around each attention block and each feed-forward block, after them in the Post-LN layout or before them in the Pre-LN layout, which the lesson notes trains more stably. RMSNorm. RMSNorm divides by the root mean square of the features and multiplies by gamma. There is no mean subtraction and no beta. The observation behind it is that re-centering adds little to accuracy and costs compute, so removing it gives the same accuracy with about 10 percent less normalization overhead. At the scale of billions of parameters that saving is real, and most modern large language models use it. Why batch normalization helps at all. The first published explanation, internal covariate shift, has been shown to be wrong. The gain comes from a smoother loss landscape with more predictive gradients, which lets the optimizer take larger steps. Layer normalization and RMSNorm deliver that effect without the batch dependence. Plausible wrong answers. "Batch normalization only needs a bigger batch." Generation runs one sequence at a time and sequence lengths vary; the fix is a norm that does not look across the batch. "Layer normalization is a weaker regularizer, so it is a compromise." It normalizes across features, which is the right axis for sequences, and it removes the mismatch between training and inference. "RMSNorm is an approximation that loses accuracy." The lesson reports the same accuracy; the re-centering adds little and costs compute. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does batch normalization need at inference that layer normalization does not? Expected: running averages of the mean and variance collected in training; layer normalization computes its statistics from the sample itself. (level 3) Where does a transformer block place the normalization? Expected: after each attention and feed-forward block in Post-LN, or before them in Pre-LN, which trains more stably. (level 4) What does RMSNorm remove and what does it cost? Expected: the mean subtraction and the shift parameter; the lesson reports the same accuracy with about 10 percent less normalization overhead. (level 4) Why did the original explanation for batch normalization fall out of favor? Expected: later work showed the gain comes from a smoother loss landscape with smaller Lipschitz constants, which lets the optimizer take larger steps. Where it is taught. The regularization lesson builds all three normalizations and explains the choice for transformers. Explain the mechanism A saved model gives a different test accuracy each time you evaluate it on the same test set with the same weights. The data loader does not shuffle. What is the most likely cause, and which two layer types are involved? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The model is still in training mode at test time. Dropout keeps zeroing random units, so each forward pass runs a different subnetwork, and batch normalization keeps using the mean and variance of the current batch instead of its running averages. Switch to evaluation mode before inference and turn gradient tracking off. Two layers that behave differently by mode. Layer Training mode Evaluation mode Dropout zero each unit with probability p, scale the rest by 1 over (1 - p) pass everything through unchanged Batch normalization normalize with the batch mean and variance, update the running averages normalize with the running averages Both layers read one flag, the training flag of the module. In the mini framework, a Sequential container's train and eval methods set the flag on the container and on every module inside it. A framework does the same with model.train() and model.eval(). Why the accuracy moves. With dropout active, each forward pass draws a new mask, so the same input gives a different output and some predictions flip across the threshold. With batch statistics active, each prediction depends on which other rows sit in its batch, and a batch of one has a variance of zero, which makes the normalization meaningless. The lesson calls a forgotten eval call one of the most common bugs in deep learning, and this symptom is its signature. The fix and its mirror image. Call eval before inference and wrap the pass in no_grad, which also saves memory. Then call train again before the next epoch. The mirror bug is as common: a model left in evaluation mode after validation trains with dropout off and with batch norm's running averages frozen, so it loses its regularization and its inference statistics go stale. Plausible wrong answers. "Set a random seed before each evaluation." That hides the symptom; the model still evaluates with dropout and batch statistics active, so the accuracy is wrong, just repeatably wrong. "GPU arithmetic is nondeterministic, this is normal." That gives differences far below one changed prediction, not a moving accuracy. "Remove dropout from the architecture." Dropout is a training time regularizer; the fix is to switch modes, not to delete the layer. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does dropout do in evaluation mode? Expected: nothing; it passes every value through unchanged, because the scaling was applied during training. (level 2) Why can batch normalization not use batch statistics for a batch of one at test time? Expected: the variance of one sample is zero, so the statistics are meaningless; the running averages must be used. (level 2) How does a container pass the mode to its children? Expected: its train and eval methods set the flag on the container and on every module inside it. (level 3) You forget to switch back to training mode after validation. What happens in the next epoch? Expected: dropout stays off and batch norm stops updating its running statistics, so the model trains without regularization and its inference statistics go stale. Where it is taught. The regularization lesson builds both layers in both modes, and the mini framework lesson adds the training flag to every module. Sources and further reading Srivastava et al., "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (2014) -- the original dropout paper with the ensemble interpretation and extensive experiments Ioffe & Szegedy, "Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift" (2015) -- introduced BatchNorm and its training procedure, one of the most cited deep learning papers Zhang & Sennrich, "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization" (2019) -- showed RMSNorm matches LayerNorm accuracy with reduced computation; adopted by LLaMA and Mistral Zhang et al., "Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization" (2017) -- the landmark paper showing neural networks can memorize random labels, challenging traditional views of generalization Check your understanding Q1 What is overfitting in neural networks? A The model is too small to learn the data B The model trains too slowly C The model memorizes training data instead of learning generalizable patterns, showing a large gap between train and test accuracy D The loss function is wrong Overfitting occurs when a model achieves high training accuracy but poor test accuracy. It has memorized the training data's noise rather than learning the underlying patterns. Q2 How does dropout regularize a neural network? A It removes the worst-performing neurons permanently B It reduces the learning rate C It randomly zeroes neurons during training, forcing the network to learn redundant representations D It removes outliers from the training data During each forward pass, dropout randomly sets neuron outputs to zero with probability p. This prevents co-adaptation (neurons relying on specific others) and is equivalent to training an ensemble of 2^N subnetworks. Q3 Why do transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm? A BatchNorm causes gradient explosion B LayerNorm was invented more recently C LayerNorm is faster to compute D LayerNorm normalizes across features per sample (batch-independent), which works with variable sequence lengths and small batch sizes BatchNorm depends on batch statistics, which are noisy with small batches and meaningless with batch size 1 (common during generation). LayerNorm normalizes across features within each sample, independent of batch size. Q4 What is the key difference between RMSNorm and LayerNorm? A RMSNorm uses batch statistics B RMSNorm only works on CNNs C RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction, only dividing by the root mean square, giving ~10% speedup with equal accuracy D RMSNorm adds learnable parameters RMSNorm removes the mean subtraction step from LayerNorm, which contributes little to accuracy but adds computation. LLaMA, Mistral, and most modern LLMs use RMSNorm for this efficiency gain. Q5 Why is it critical to call model.eval() before running inference in PyTorch? A It speeds up computation B It enables gradient computation C It disables dropout and switches BatchNorm to use running statistics instead of batch statistics, giving deterministic outputs D It frees GPU memory Without model.eval(), dropout randomly zeroes neurons during inference (causing random output variation) and BatchNorm uses current-batch statistics instead of the stable running averages accumulated during training. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Initialize wrong and training never starts. Initialize right and 50 layers train as smoothly as 3. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Weight initialization "Set starting weights randomly" The strategy for choosing initial weight values that determines whether a network can train at all Symmetry breaking "Make neurons different" Using random initialization to ensure neurons learn distinct features instead of computing identical functions Fan-in "Number of inputs to a neuron" The number of incoming connections, which determines how input variance accumulates in the weighted sum Fan-out "Number of outputs from a neuron" The number of outgoing connections, relevant for maintaining gradient variance during backpropagation Xavier/Glorot init "The sigmoid initialization" $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/(\text{fan} {\text{in}} + \text{fan} )$, designed to preserve variance through sigmoid and tanh activations} Kaiming/He init "The ReLU initialization" $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/\text{fan}_{\text{in}}$, accounts for ReLU zeroing half the activations Variance propagation "How signals grow or shrink through layers" The mathematical analysis of how activation variance changes layer by layer based on weight scale Residual scaling "GPT-2's init trick" Scaling residual connection weights by $1/\sqrt{2N}$ to prevent variance growth through $N$ transformer layers Dead network "Nothing trains" A network where poor initialization causes all gradients to be zero or all activations to saturate Exploding activations "Values go to infinity" When weight variance is too high, causing activation magnitudes to grow exponentially through layers The problem In plain words first Before training, every weight needs a starting value. If they are all equal, every neuron in a layer stays identical forever. If they are random but too large, numbers grow by the same factor at every layer and explode; too small, and they shrink to nothing. Good initialisation picks the spread of the random weights from the number of inputs each neuron has, so that the signal keeps roughly the same size from the first layer to the last. Xavier does this for tanh-like activations, Kaiming (He) for ReLU. Initialize all weights to zero. Nothing learns. Every neuron computes the same function, receives the same gradient, and updates identically. After 10,000 epochs, your 512-neuron hidden layer is still 512 copies of the same neuron. You paid for 512 parameters and got 1. Initialize them too large. Activations explode through the network. By layer 10, values hit 1e15. By layer 20, they overflow to infinity. Gradients follow the same trajectory in reverse. Initialize them randomly from a standard normal distribution. Works for 3 layers. At 50 layers, the signal collapses to zero or detonates to infinity depending on whether the random scale was slightly too small or slightly too large. The boundary between "works" and "broken" is razor-thin. Weight initialization is the most underrated decision in deep learning. Architecture gets papers. Optimizers get blog posts. Initialization gets a footnote. But get it wrong and nothing else matters -- your network is dead before training begins. Idea 1 · The Symmetry Problem Every neuron in a layer has the same structure: multiply inputs by weights, add bias, apply activation. If all weights start at the same value (zero is the extreme case), every neuron computes the same output. During backpropagation, every neuron receives the same gradient. During the update step, every neuron changes by the same amount. You're stuck. The network has hundreds of parameters, but they all move in lockstep. This is called symmetry, and random initialization is the brute-force way to break it. Each neuron starts at a different point in weight space, so each learns a different feature. But "random" is not enough. The scale of the randomness determines whether the network trains. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Xavier initialization sets the weight variance to 2 over the sum of fan in and fan out. Kaiming initialization sets it to 2 over fan in. Both are called variance preserving. Explain what each one preserves, where the 2 in Kaiming comes from, and what happens to a 50 layer ReLU network that starts from a plain standard normal. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A layer's pre-activation variance is fan in times the weight variance times the input variance, so a weight variance of 1 over fan in keeps the signal size constant through a linear layer. Xavier balances that condition between the forward and the backward pass, which gives 2 divided by the total of the two fan counts, and it suits sigmoid and tanh, which are near linear around zero. ReLU zeroes half of its inputs and halves the variance at each layer, so Kaiming doubles the variance of each weight to 2 over fan in to compensate. A standard normal with a fan in of 512 multiplies the variance by 512 at every layer, and the signal explodes within a few layers. Variance through one layer. For z equal to the sum of w_i x_i over fan in terms with independent weights and inputs: Copy The lesson's two failures follow at once. With Var(w) equal to 1 and a fan in of 512, each layer multiplies the variance by 512, and after 10 layers the factor is 512 to the tenth, about 1.2 times 10 to the 27. With Var(w) equal to 0.001 the factor per layer is 0.512, and after 10 layers the signal is at 0.00013 of its size. The goal is Var(z) equal to Var(x). Xavier. Glorot and Bengio asked for constant variance in both directions: forward through fan in, backward through fan out. The compromise is Var(w) equal to 2 over (fan in plus fan out), drawn as a normal with that variance or as a uniform with limit the square root of 6 over the same sum. It holds for sigmoid and tanh because, at a well scaled initialization, their inputs sit in the near linear region around zero. Kaiming. ReLU sets every negative pre-activation to zero. On average half the units are off, so the variance that reaches the next layer is half of what the linear analysis predicts. He and colleagues doubled the weight variance to cancel that: Var(w) equal to 2 over fan in. Without the 2 the signal shrinks by about 0.5 per layer, and over 50 layers that is 0.5 to the 50, about 8.8 times 10 to the minus 16. GELU and Swish use the same rule. A framework's linear layer defaults to a Kaiming uniform draw, which is why shallow networks train with no thought given to it. The check. Push random inputs through the untrained network and log the mean activation magnitude at each layer. The lesson's experiment prints it at layers 1, 5, 10, 25 and 50: a standard normal explodes, a normal with standard deviation 0.01 vanishes, and both Xavier with sigmoid and Kaiming with ReLU hold near 1.0 through layer 50. Plausible wrong answers. "Random is random, the scale does not matter if it is small." Too small vanishes and too large explodes; the lesson shows both, and the margin is thin at 50 layers. "Xavier works for ReLU too, the difference is minor." Xavier under-estimates the variance ReLU needs by a factor of 2, and over 50 layers the signal falls to about 8.8 times 10 to the minus 16. "Kaiming's 2 stands for the forward and backward passes." That 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the activations; Xavier's 2 is the one that balances the two passes. Expected: push random data through the network and log the mean activation magnitude per layer; it should stay in a band such as 0.5 to 2.0 at every depth. (level 4) Why do residual networks need a further scale beyond Kaiming? Expected: each residual addition adds variance, so the stream grows with the layer count; the GPT-2 scheme scales residual weights by 1 over the square root of 2N. Where it is taught. Explain the mechanism A transformer with Kaiming-initialized weights trains without trouble at 20 layers and diverges at 126 layers with the same recipe. Nothing else changed. Explain why depth breaks it even with a variance preserving initialization, and what the GPT-2 style fix does. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Kaiming keeps the variance constant through each sub-layer, but a residual block adds the sub-layer's output back onto its input, and the variance of a sum of independent terms adds. With N residual additions the stream's variance grows in proportion to N, so a deeper stack carries a larger residual signal, and the attention logits and feed-forward activations built from it grow with it. The GPT-2 fix scales the weights of the layers that write into the residual stream by 1 over the square root of 2N, so the accumulated variance stays the same at any depth. Two kinds of variance preservation. Kaiming answers one question: how to draw weights so that a matrix multiply followed by a ReLU returns a signal with the same variance it received. It knows nothing about what happens next. In a residual block the next thing is an addition: Copy If the sub-layer output has about the same variance as x and is roughly independent of it, the sum has about twice the variance. Each block adds again. After N additions the stream has grown in proportion to N. The lesson states this directly: each addition increases variance, and with N residual layers the variance grows proportionally to N. Why it shows up as depth. At 20 layers the growth is a modest factor and the optimizer copes. At 126 layers, the depth the lesson cites for a 405B parameter model, the stream is large enough at initialization that the softmax inside attention and the activations in the feed-forward blocks run far from their intended range, and the first updates are oversized. Without a correction, the lesson says, the residual stream would grow without bound through the stack. The fix. GPT-2 scales the weights of the residual projections, the layers that write into the stream, by 1 over the square root of 2N, where N is the number of layers. The 2 counts the two writes per layer, one from attention and one from the feed-forward block. The sum of 2N contributions each scaled by that factor has the same variance as one, so the stream stays in range at any depth. The lesson notes that the 405B model uses a similar scheme and that a transformer built from scratch must add this scaling itself. How to confirm before you change anything. Push random tokens through the untrained model and log the residual stream magnitude at each layer. Growth with depth confirms the diagnosis. Run it again with the scaling and the curve should be flat. The lesson's exercise does exactly this over 50 layers. Plausible wrong answers. "Deeper models just need a smaller learning rate." A smaller rate slows the growth of the weights; it does nothing about the variance that accumulates in the forward pass at initialization. "Kaiming is variance preserving, so depth cannot be the issue." It preserves variance through each sub-layer, not through the sum of a sub-layer and its input. "Divide the residual stream by N at the output." The fix has to act where the variance accumulates; scaling the writers keeps every intermediate layer in range, not only the last one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does Kaiming not account for this? Expected: it preserves variance through a matrix multiply followed by ReLU; it knows nothing about the addition that follows. (level 3) Why 2N and not N? Expected: each transformer layer writes into the stream twice, once from attention and once from the feed-forward block, so N layers make 2N additions. (level 4) How would you confirm the diagnosis before changing the initialization? Expected: push random input through the untrained model and log the residual stream magnitude per layer; growth with depth confirms it, and the scaled version should be flat. (level 4) Does a Pre-LN layout remove the need for the scaling? Expected: it normalizes what enters each sub-layer and helps stability, but the additions into the stream sit outside the norm, so the lesson still applies the scaling to the writers. Where it is taught. The weight initialization lesson explains residual variance growth and the GPT-2 scaling scheme. Explain the mechanism A network with a hidden layer of 512 units is initialized with every weight and every bias at zero. Training runs for thousands of epochs and the loss barely moves. Learning rate and data both check out. What is wrong, and why does a small random perturbation of each weight fix it? Level 2 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Every neuron in the layer starts identical, so each computes the same output, receives the same gradient and takes the same update. They stay identical for the whole run: the layer holds the parameters of 512 neurons and the function of one. Random initialization gives each neuron its own starting point, so the gradients differ and the neurons learn different features. The scale of that randomness then decides whether the signal survives the depth. The symmetry. All neurons in a layer have the same structure: a weighted sum of the same inputs, a bias, an activation. Whatever makes them different must come from the weights. If the weights are equal, the outputs are equal. Backpropagation then hands each neuron the same gradient, because each contributed the same amount to the loss. The update is the same, and the weights are equal again. Nothing in gradient descent can split them. The lesson's demo builds four zero-initialized neurons, feeds one input, prints four identical outputs, and counts one effective parameter instead of the eight that were allocated. Why zero is only the extreme case. Any constant initialization has the same flaw. Setting every weight to 0.5 produces 512 copies of one neuron just as zero does. Random values are the brute force way to break the tie, and they are also why two runs with different seeds learn different features. Biases can stay at zero. The lesson's layers draw random weights and set the biases to 0.0. That is fine: the weights already differ across neurons, so the biases do not need to. After the symmetry is gone. Random is not enough on its own. The variance of the draw must match the activation: Xavier for sigmoid and tanh, Kaiming for ReLU and GELU. Too small a scale and the signal vanishes through the layers; too large and it explodes. A quick check is to push random inputs through the untrained network and log the activation magnitude at each layer. Plausible wrong answers. "The learning rate is too low." Each neuron moves, but all move together; no learning rate separates identical gradients. "Add more neurons." They are all the same neuron; width adds nothing without symmetry breaking. "Zero init is fine for the first layer because the inputs differ." The neurons in one layer share the same inputs; what differs across neurons has to be the weights. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Is it fine to set the biases to zero? Expected: yes, when the weights are random; the lesson's layers do so. (level 2) Would a nonzero constant for every weight fix it? Expected: no; the neurons are still identical and move in lockstep. (level 3) After the fix, the loss moves but a deeper version trains badly. What do you check next? Expected: the scale of the random draw against the activation; Xavier for sigmoid and tanh, Kaiming for ReLU, verified by activation magnitudes per layer. (level 3) How does the lesson show the symmetry in a few lines? Expected: four zero-initialized neurons on one input give four identical outputs, and it counts one effective parameter instead of eight. Where it is taught. The weight initialization lesson opens with the symmetry problem and demonstrates it with a tiny layer. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in RMSNorm A simpler normalisation layer that divides by the root mean square Lesson 7.8 Pre-norm Normalizing before each sublayer rather than after Lesson 7.8 Feed-forward network The small MLP inside each block that processes every position on its own Lesson 7.8 Fine-tuning Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so that its behaviour changes. A series of practical fixes in the 2010s changed that. Xavier and He initialisation (2010, 2015) chose starting weights that keep signals a steady size; ReLU (popularised in 2011) avoided flat regions; batch normalisation (2015) and layer normalisation (2016) rescaled values inside the network; residual connections (ResNet, 2015) let a 152-layer network win the ImageNet competition; and the Adam optimiser (2014) gave every weight its own step size. A transformer block (the Transformers, step by step section) is these ideas assembled: LayerNorm, a residual connection , and training with AdamW and a warm-up schedule. In plain words first A message passed down a long line of people Whisper a message down a line of twenty people. If each person speaks a little more quietly than they heard, the message fades to nothing; if each speaks a little louder, it ends as a shout. Training a deep network sends signals forwards (the predictions) and backwards (the gradients) through every layer, with the same problem. The fixes are: start everyone at the right volume (initialisation), have each person re-adjust the volume before passing it on (normalisation), and add a direct line that skips past everyone so the original message always gets through (residual connections). He initialisation (Kaiming He and colleagues, 2015) draws weights with spread √(2 / inputs). More layers made it worse , because the signal cannot get through. nn.ModuleList is a list that PyTorch knows contains layers, so their parameters are found and trained. Step 3 · The fixes: normalisation and residual connections Normalisation rescales values inside the network. Layer normalisation (LayerNorm) takes each example's vector of values, subtracts its mean and divides by its spread, then applies a learned scale and shift: Copy What you should see Copy Whatever size the values arrive at, they leave with mean 0 and spread 1, so no layer can drift to huge or tiny values. Batch normalisation does the same across the examples of a batch instead of within each example; it is common in image networks, while transformers use LayerNorm or its simpler cousin RMSNorm later · 7.8 . A residual connection adds a layer's input back to its output: h = h + layer(h) . Two ways to normalise the same grid of activations (rows are examples in the batch, columns are features). Batch normalisation computes its statistics down each column, across the batch. Layer normalisation computes them along each row, for one example on its own, which is why it works for any batch size and is the choice in transformers. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . A residual block. The input skips around the layer and is added back to its output, so the block only has to learn a correction. The skip path also carries gradients straight back to earlier layers. Normalisation first rescales each input vector to a standard size. Every transformer block is built this way ( Lesson 7.8 ). If the layer has nothing useful to add, it can output values near 0 and the block passes h through unchanged; so adding blocks can never make things much worse. On the way back, the + passes the gradient straight through to earlier layers, a "highway" around every layer. Put the two together: Copy What you should see Copy Same depth, same width, same data, same optimiser: 98% instead of chance. The gradient at layer 1 is now larger than at layer 20, because the residual paths deliver the signal to every layer. This " pre-norm later · 7.8 residual block" (normalise, transform, add back) is exactly the skeleton of a transformer block in Lesson 7.8 ; there, the transform is attention or a feed-forward network later · 7.8 . Step 4 · Optimisers: better than plain gradient descent Plain gradient descent uses one learning rate for every weight. Real loss landscapes are steep in some directions and shallow in others ( Lesson 2.4 's long thin valley), and a single rate is too big for one and too small for the other. The same starting point (red dot) on the same loss surface. Plain SGD (left) creeps along the valley; Adam (right) adapts its step for each parameter and reaches the low region in far fewer steps. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . Momentum keeps a running average of recent gradients, so steps build up speed in directions that stay consistent and cancel out in directions that zig-zag. Adam (2014) adds a running average of each weight's squared gradient and divides by its square root, giving every weight its own step size: weights with large, steady gradients take careful steps; weights with tiny gradients take relatively larger ones. AdamW is Adam with weight decay (Step 6) applied separately. It is the default for training and fine-tuning later · 10.10 transformers. Copy What you should see Copy For plain gradient descent the steep direction (slope 50) sets the largest safe learning rate, 2 / 50 = 0.04, exactly as in Lesson 1.7 . Just above it, it explodes; well below it, the shallow direction barely moves. Momentum and Adam both solve the problem. Step 5 · Learning-rate schedules The learning rate usually changes during training. Large models use a warm-up (rise from zero over the first steps, while Adam's running averages settle and the random starting weights get organised) and then decay slowly, often following a cosine curve, so the final steps are small and precise ( Lesson 1.7 's V-shaped valley showed why constant steps cannot settle). Copy What you should see Copy In PyTorch, schedules live in torch.optim.lr_scheduler ; you call scheduler.step() after each optimizer.step() . Fine-tuning ( Lesson 14.139 ) uses the same shape over a shorter run, typically with a peak around 1e-4 to 2e-4 for LoRA later · 3.24 . Step 6 · Regularisation and safety rails Three more tools, each a line or two of PyTorch: Dropout . During each training step, a random set of hidden units is switched off (right), so the network cannot lean on any one unit. At prediction time all units are used. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Weight decay : shrink every weight slightly at each step, the neural-network version of ridge regularisation ( Lesson 2.16 ). In AdamW it is the weight_decay argument (often 0.01 to 0.1). Dropout : during training, randomly set a fraction of a layer's outputs to zero, so the network cannot rely on any single neuron. At evaluation time it is switched off, which is why model.eval() matters. Gradient clipping : if the gradient's overall size exceeds a limit, scale it down before the update, so one unusual batch cannot wreck training. Large models almost always clip, typically at a size of 1.0. Copy What you should see Copy Clipping keeps the gradient's direction (30 : 40 stays 0.6 : 0.8) and caps only its size. Step 7 · When training goes wrong: an order to try things What you see First things to try Loss is nan or explodes lower the learning rate; add gradient clipping; add warm-up; check inputs for huge values Loss does not move at all check the loop ( Lesson 3.16 ); raise the learning rate; check initialisation and that gradients are not 0 Deep model trains worse than a shallow one add residual connections and normalisation Training loss falls, validation loss rises more data; weight decay; dropout; early stopping ; a smaller model Both losses high and flat a bigger model; train longer; better features or data The standard advice (from Karpathy's recipe and every practitioner's experience): start from a known-good setup, change one thing at a time , and always watch both training and validation curves. The same idea as a formula He initialisation: W ~ N(0, 2 / n_in) for ReLU layers LayerNorm: y = γ · (x − mean(x)) / √(var(x) + ε) + β, per example pre-norm residual block: h ← h + F(LayerNorm(h)) momentum: v ← β v + g , w ← w − η v Adam: m ← β₁ m + (1 − β₁) g , v ← β₂ v + (1 − β₂) g ², w ← w − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) AdamW adds a separate decay: w ← w − ηλ w Check your mental model ✗ "Deeper networks are always more powerful, so they always train better." ✓ A plain 20-layer network trained worse than a 1-layer one here. Depth helps only with the tools that keep signals flowing. ✗ "Adam removes the need to choose a learning rate." ✓ It adapts step sizes per weight, but the overall learning rate still matters a lot, and schedules still help. ✗ "Dropout is used when the model makes predictions." ✓ It is only active in training; model.eval() switches it off. Exercises Predict before you run In the ResidualDeep class, what happens to accuracy if you remove the norm(...) call but keep the residual connection ( h = h + torch.relu(layer(h)) )? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Change PlainDeep to use ReLU instead of sigmoid (replace both torch.sigmoid calls with torch.relu ) and train it. Does it do better than sigmoid? Then try a depth of 4. (Solution M1.) Debugging exercise A fine-tuning run's loss goes 2.1, 1.9, 1.8, then suddenly 9.7 and nan on one step, around step 400. The learning rate is constant at 5e-4 with no warm-up and no clipping. List two changes to try first. (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Residuals without normalisation It still trains very well here: about 98.3%, the same as with LayerNorm. On this small problem the residual path alone keeps gradients flowing. Without normalisation, though, each block adds a ReLU output (never negative) to h , so the values in the residual stream later · 7.8 tend to grow block after block. That matters more in wider and deeper networks trained for longer at higher learning rates, where it makes training unstable. That is why transformers use both. Solution M1 · ReLU, and fewer layers At depth 20, ReLU does no better: about 8%, still chance, because gradients still shrink through 20 plain layers with PyTorch's default initialisation. At depth 4, ReLU reaches about 93% in 15 epochs, while sigmoid manages only about 19%: sigmoid's flat ends slow learning even in a fairly shallow network. That is one reason ReLU replaced sigmoid inside networks. Plain networks are fine at modest depth; residual connections are what make depth of 20, 100 or more practical. Solution D1 · A sudden spike Add gradient clipping ( clip_grad_norm_ with max_norm=1.0 ), so one unusual batch cannot produce a huge update; and lower the learning rate , ideally with a short warm-up and a decaying schedule. Also check the batch at that step for unusual data (very long or corrupted examples). Restarting from the last good checkpoint with these changes is standard practice. Recap In deep plain networks, signals and gradients shrink or blow up layer by layer; early layers stop learning. Good initialisation (such as He) starts signals at a steady size; LayerNorm keeps them there throughout training. Residual connections add each block's input to its output, giving gradients a highway; with LayerNorm they let very deep networks train. Adam and AdamW give each weight its own step size; warm-up plus cosine decay is the common schedule. Weight decay and dropout reduce overfitting , gradient clipping prevents blow-ups, and changing one thing at a time is how you debug training. In plain words first The idea in one line The learning rate is the single most important hyperparameter. Not the architecture. Not the dataset size. Not the activation function. The learning rate. If you tune nothing else, tune this. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Learning rate "How fast the model learns" The scalar that multiplies the gradient to determine the parameter update size Schedule "Change the LR over time" A function that maps training step to learning rate, designed to optimize convergence Warmup "Start with a small LR" Linearly ramping the LR from near-zero to the target value over the first $N$ steps to stabilize optimizer statistics Cosine annealing "Smooth LR decay" Decreasing the LR following a cosine curve from $\text{lr} {\max}$ to $\text{lr} $ over training Step decay "Drop LR at milestones" Multiplying the LR by a factor (usually 0.1) at fixed epoch intervals 1cycle policy "Up then down" Leslie Smith's method of ramping LR up then down in a single cycle for faster convergence LR range test "Find the best learning rate" Training briefly while increasing LR to find the value where loss starts diverging Cosine with warm restarts "Reset and repeat" Periodically resetting the LR to $\text{lr} _{\max}$ and decaying again (SGDR) Eta min "The floor for the LR" The minimum learning rate that the schedule decays to Peak learning rate "The maximum LR" The highest LR reached during training, typically after warmup The problem In plain words first A learning-rate schedule changes the step size during training. Early on, warmup starts small and ramps up, so the first noisy updates cannot throw the model somewhere bad. Later, decay (cosine, step or 1cycle) shrinks the steps, so the model can settle into a minimum instead of bouncing around it. The peak value still matters most; the schedule decides how you get there and how you finish. Set the learning rate to 0.1. Training diverges -- loss jumps to infinity in 3 steps. Set it to 0.0001. Training crawls -- after 100 epochs, the model has barely moved from random. Set it to 0.01. Training works for 50 epochs, then the loss oscillates around a minimum it can never reach because the steps are too large. The optimal learning rate is not a constant. It changes during training. Early on, you want large steps to cover ground quickly. Late in training, you want tiny steps to settle into a sharp minimum. The difference between a 90% accurate model and a 95% accurate model is often just the schedule. Every major model published in the last three years uses a learning rate schedule. Llama 2 (7B and 13B) used a peak of 3e-4 with 2,000 warmup steps and cosine decay to 10 percent of the peak; Llama 3 405B used a peak of 8e-5 with 8,000 warmup steps, decaying to 8e-7 over 1.2 million steps. GPT-3 175B used a peak of 6e-5 with warmup over 375 million tokens. These are not arbitrary choices. They are the result of extensive hyperparameter sweeps that cost millions of dollars. You need to understand schedules because the defaults will not work for your problem. When you fine-tune a pretrained model, the right schedule is different than training from scratch. When you increase batch size, the warmup period needs to change. When training breaks at step 10,000, you need to know whether it's a schedule problem or something else. Idea 1 · Constant Learning Rate The simplest approach. Pick a number, use it for every step. ​ Rarely optimal. It's either too high for the end of training (oscillation around the minimum) or too low for the beginning (wasted compute on tiny steps). Works fine for small models and debugging. A terrible choice for anything that trains for more than an hour. Idea 2 · Step Decay The old-school approach from the ResNet era. Cut the learning rate by a factor (usually 10x) at fixed epochs. ​ ⋅ γ ⌊ epoch / step_size ⌋ Where and step_size = 30 means: lr drops by 10x every 30 epochs. ResNet-50 used this -- lr=0.1, drop by 10x at epochs 30, 60, and 90. The problem: the optimal decay points depend on the dataset and architecture. Move to a different problem and you need to re-tune when to drop. The transitions are abrupt -- loss can spike when the rate suddenly changes. Idea 3 · Cosine Annealing Smooth decay from the maximum learning rate to a minimum, following a cosine curve: ​ + 0.5 ⋅ ( lr m a x ​ − lr m i n ​ ) ⋅ ( 1 + cos ( T π t ​ ) ) Where is the current step and is the total number of steps. At , the cosine term is 1, so ​ . At , the cosine term is -1, so ​ . The decay is gentle at first, accelerates in the middle, and becomes gentle again near the end. This is the default for most modern training runs. No hyperparameters to tune beyond ​ and ​ . The cosine shape matches the empirical observation that most learning happens in the middle of training -- you want reasonable step sizes during that critical period. Worked example Cosine by hand With ​ = 0.01 , ​ = 1 0 − 5 and steps: Step Learning rate 0 1 0.01 250 0.707 0.00854 500 0 0.00501 750 −0.707 0.00147 1000 −1 0.00001 The first quarter loses only 15 percent of the rate, the middle half most of it, and the last quarter creeps down to the floor. Idea 4 · Warmup: Why You Start Small Adam and other adaptive optimizers maintain running estimates of gradient mean and variance. At step 0, these estimates are initialized to zero. The first few gradient updates are based on garbage statistics. If your learning rate is large during this period, the model takes huge, poorly-directed steps. Warmup fixes this. Start with a tiny learning rate (often lr_max / warmup_steps or even zero) and linearly ramp up to ​ over the first steps. By the time you reach the full learning rate, Adam's statistics have stabilized. ​ ⋅ warmup_steps t ​ for t < warmup_steps Typical warmup: 1-5% of total training steps. Llama 2 trained on about 2 trillion tokens and warmed up for 2,000 steps. GPT-3 warmed up over 375 million tokens. Warmup also helps plain SGD at large batch sizes (Goyal et al., 2017) and protects against the large, badly aimed gradients of a freshly initialised network. ✗ "Copy the published learning rate." ✓ Peaks shrink as models grow: 3e-4 for Llama 2 7B, 8e-5 for Llama 3 405B, 6e-5 for GPT-3 175B. Idea 5 · Linear Warmup + Cosine Decay The modern default. Ramp up linearly, then decay with cosine: Copy This is what Llama, GPT, PaLM, and most modern transformers use. The warmup prevents early instability. The cosine decay settles the model into a good minimum. Idea 6 · 1cycle Policy Leslie Smith's discovery (2018): ramp the learning rate up from a low value to a high value in the first half of training, then ramp it back down in the second half. Counterintuitive -- why would you increase the learning rate midway through? The theory: a high learning rate acts as regularization by adding noise to the optimization trajectory. The model explores more of the loss landscape during the ramp-up phase, finding better basins. The ramp-down phase then refines within the best basin found. Copy 1cycle often trains faster than cosine annealing for a fixed compute budget. The tradeoff: you must know the total number of steps in advance. Idea 7 · Schedule Shapes Idea 8 · Decision Flowchart Idea 9 · Real Numbers from Published Models The same idea as a formula For step out of , peak rate ​ , final rate ​ : Step decay: ​ = η 0 ​ ⋅ γ ⌊ t / s ⌋ (multiply by , e.g. 0.1, every steps). Linear warm-up over ​ steps: ​ = η m a x ​ t / T w ​ . Cosine decay after warm-up: ​ = η m i n ​ + 2 1 ​ ( η m a x ​ − η m i n ​ ) ( 1 + cos ( π T − T w ​ t − T w ​ ​ ) ) . Warm-up, stable, decay (WSD): warm up, hold ​ for most of training, then decay quickly over the last 10–20%. A checkpoint from the stable phase can be decayed at any time, so training can be extended without restarting. 1cycle: rise to ​ over about 30% of training, then fall far below the start. Why warm up. At the start the weights are random and Adam's second-moment estimate rests on a handful of gradients, so its per-weight steps are unreliable; a large rate then can push the model into a region it never recovers from. A short ramp (often 0.1–2% of the steps) avoids it. Why decay. Near the end, the noise in mini-batch gradients keeps the weights bouncing around a minimum at a distance that grows with ; lowering lets them settle, which is why the loss often drops sharply during the final decay. Recap What to keep from this lesson The peak learning rate matters most; the schedule shapes the start and the finish. Warmup ramps up from near zero so early noisy updates cannot do damage. Cosine decay is the common default; step decay and 1cycle are alternatives. Decay matters when gradient noise sets a loss floor; on easy, nearly noiseless problems a constant rate can do fine. Find the sweet spot where training is most stable. Implement cosine annealing with warm restarts (SGDR): reset the learning rate to ​ every steps and decay again. Compare to standard cosine on a longer training run. Build a "schedule surgeon" that monitors training loss and automatically switches from warmup to cosine when the loss stabilizes, and reduces lr if the loss plateaus for too long. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Take-home Take-home. Implement a learning rate schedule as one function of the step: a linear ramp from zero to a peak, a cosine decay from the peak to a floor, and a fixed floor after the last step. Deliver tests that pin the value at every boundary, prove the curve has no jumps, and show that a resumed run lands on the right value. Describe your design and your tests. Level 4 of 4 · about 25 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Write one function with three branches: up to the warmup step, the peak times the step over the warmup length; between the warmup step and the total, the floor plus half the gap times one plus the cosine of pi times the progress since warmup ended; past the total, the floor. Test the fixed points: zero at step zero, the peak at the end of warmup from both branches, the floor at the last step and the floor one step later. Add a continuity test that bounds each one step change, and a resume test that computes the schedule from a saved global step. The function. Copy The cosine evaluates to 1 at the end of warmup, which gives the peak and matches the ramp's endpoint, and to -1 at the total, which gives the floor. The capstone lesson makes the point that this continuity is the reason to write one function over the step rather than three pieces glued together: a glued schedule loses a boundary the first time the peak or a step count changes. Two guards: the ramp branch runs only when the warmup is above zero, so a warmup of zero steps starts at the peak and decays at once, with no division by zero. The constructor rejects a warmup that is not less than the total, as the lesson's code does with an error, because the rate would hold the peak at the last step and drop to the floor one step later. Why the floor is pinned, not an error. A trainer that overshoots the configured total keeps a usable rate and logs a warning. Extending a run means changing the total in the config, not editing the loop. The floor is non-zero on purpose: the lesson keeps it near 10 percent of the peak so the optimizer keeps learning in the long tail, and warns that a floor of zero looks good on a plot and leaves the model under-trained. The tests. Fixed points. With a non-zero warmup, lr(0) is 0, lr(warmup) equals the peak from the ramp branch and from the cosine branch, lr(total) equals the floor, lr(total + 1) equals the floor. Continuity. For every step from 0 to total, the change between consecutive steps is at most the larger of the warmup slope, peak over warmup steps, and the steepest cosine slope, pi times the gap over twice the decay length. The lesson's exercise notes that a short cosine segment can be steeper than the ramp, so the ramp slope alone is not a safe bound. Resume. Save a checkpoint with a global step, reload, and assert that the next value equals lr(global step + 1). The schedule reads a monotonic global step from the checkpoint, not an epoch counter or a loop variable, because sharded datasets and restarted loaders break the epoch to step mapping. Shape. Render the schedule to a text plot and a CSV, with one row per step, and check the plot into the run directory so a reviewer can see the curve without running anything. Production notes from the lesson. The schedule's four numbers live in a versioned config, not in code. The warmup is a fraction of the total, around 1 to 3 percent, so the shape survives a longer run. The log row is step, learning rate, gradient L2 norm and loss, in that order, so dashboards can read it. Plausible wrong answers. "Set the floor to zero so the schedule finishes cleanly." The lesson keeps a non-zero floor near 10 percent of the peak so the optimizer keeps learning in the tail; a zero floor looks clean and leaves the model under-trained. "Test a few steps in the middle, the boundaries follow from the formula." An off by one at a boundary is the bug the lesson warns about; it shows up hours into a run as a rate that is 1 percent off at the moment it matters. "Compute the rate from the epoch and the batch index." Sharded datasets and restarted loaders break that mapping; the global step is the durable axis. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why implement the three regions in one function? Expected: so the ramp endpoint and the cosine start share one formula for the peak, and a change to the peak or the step counts cannot open a gap at a boundary. (level 4) What is the right bound for the continuity test? Expected: the larger of the ramp slope, peak over warmup steps, and the steepest cosine slope, pi times the gap over twice the decay length; a short cosine segment can be steeper than the ramp. (level 4) Why pin at the floor after the last step instead of raising? Expected: a trainer that overshoots keeps a usable rate and logs a warning; extending training means changing the total in the config, not the loop. (level 4) What makes a resumed run land on the right value? Expected: the schedule reads a monotonic global step saved in the checkpoint, not an epoch counter or a local loop variable. Where it is taught. The cosine warmup capstone builds this schedule with its boundary contract and production patterns, and the learning rate schedules lesson compares it with the other schedules. Explain the mechanism A transformer recipe starts the learning rate at zero and ramps it linearly up to the peak during the first steps, then decays it with a cosine. A teammate wants to start at the peak to save those steps. Explain what the ramp protects, how long it should be, and how to write it down so the recipe scales to a longer run. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The first updates are the fragile ones: the weights sit near their initialization, Adam's running estimates of the gradient mean and variance are built from a handful of samples, and the gradient norm is large and noisy. A full size step on that footing diverges or drops the model into a plateau it never leaves. Warmup keeps the effective step small until the statistics settle, over about 1 to 5 percent of the total steps, and the schedule should express that length as a fraction of the run rather than as a fixed step count. What is wrong at step zero. Adam's two moment estimates start at zero. Bias correction fixes their scale, but the first steps still use statistics from one or two gradients, which the schedules lesson calls garbage statistics. At the same time the weights are at their random initialization and the gradient norm is at its largest and noisiest. A peak step on that mix is a large, poorly directed move. The capstone lesson gives the two outcomes: the run diverges outright, or it settles into a loss plateau it never escapes. What warmup does. Copy The rate climbs from zero to the peak over the warmup steps. By the time the full rate arrives, the moment estimates have seen hundreds of gradients and the weights have moved off their starting point. The schedules lesson's examples of published runs use a warmup of 2000 steps to a peak of 3e-4 followed by a cosine decay to 3e-5, and a warmup over 375 million tokens to a peak of 6e-4. How long. The schedules lesson gives 1 to 5 percent of the total steps and, when in doubt, 3 to 5 percent. The capstone lesson gives 1 to 3 percent and makes the stronger point: write the warmup as a fraction. A run of 200 million steps with 2,000 warmup steps is at the peak almost at once, and a run of 20,000 steps with the same count warms up for 10 percent. The same number describes two different schedules. How to see that it worked. Log the gradient norm next to the learning rate at each step. In a well tuned warmup the norm rises roughly in step with the rate and settles after the peak. A norm that stays high after the ramp ends says the peak is too aggressive. A divergent run shows the norm spike before the loss does. Plausible wrong answers. "Warmup wastes steps at a low rate." The lessons spend 1 to 5 percent of training on it, and a run that diverges in its first steps wastes all of them. "Bias correction already handles Adam's cold start, so warmup is redundant." The correction rescales the averages; it cannot turn two samples into a good estimate. "Set the warmup to 2000 steps, the big runs use that." That count was a fraction of one specific run; on a short run it is most of the training, and on a longer one it is nothing. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is Adam sensitive at step zero in particular? Expected: its moment estimates start at zero and the first steps use statistics from one or two gradients; bias correction fixes their scale but not their noise. (level 3) What does the gradient norm look like during a healthy warmup? Expected: it rises roughly in step with the learning rate and settles after the peak; a norm that stays high after the ramp says the peak is too aggressive. (level 4) Why does a fixed warmup step count break when the run gets longer? Expected: 2000 steps is 10 percent of a 20,000 step run and a vanishing share of a 200 million step run, so the same count gives two different schedules; a fraction keeps the shape. (level 4) You change the batch size. What do you revisit? Expected: the warmup length and the peak; the schedules lesson lists the warmup period as the setting that must change when the batch size changes. Where it is taught. The learning rate schedules lesson explains warmup and gives the published configurations, and the cosine warmup capstone argues for a fractional warmup and logs the gradient norm beside the rate. Sources and further reading Loshchilov & Hutter, "SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts" (2017) -- introduced cosine annealing and warm restarts Smith, "Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates" (2018) -- the 1cycle policy paper Touvron et al., "Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models" (2023) -- documents the warmup + cosine schedule used at scale Goyal et al., "Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour" (2017) -- linear scaling rule and warmup for large batch training Check your understanding Q1 Why is a constant learning rate usually suboptimal for training neural networks? A It uses too much memory B It's either too high for late training (causes oscillation) or too low for early training (wastes compute) C Constant learning rates cause overfitting D They only work with SGD The optimal step size changes during training. Early on, large steps cover ground quickly. Late in training, small steps are needed to settle into a minimum. A constant rate can't serve both needs. Q2 What is the purpose of learning rate warmup? A To let adaptive optimizer statistics (momentum, variance) stabilize before taking large steps B To prevent overfitting C To increase the batch size gradually D To initialize weights properly Adam's moment estimates are initialized to zero. Early gradient updates are based on unreliable statistics. Warmup starts with a tiny LR and ramps up, giving Adam time to accumulate meaningful estimates. Q3 What learning rate schedule do Llama 3, GPT-3, and most modern LLMs use? A Constant learning rate B Step decay every 30 epochs C Exponential decay D Linear warmup followed by cosine decay Linear warmup + cosine decay is the standard for transformer training. Llama 3 used 2000 warmup steps with cosine decay from 3e-4 to 3e-5. This schedule requires no milestone tuning. Q4 What makes the 1cycle policy different from other schedules? A It requires no hyperparameter tuning B It only works with SGD C It uses a constant learning rate D It ramps the learning rate UP in the first half of training, then back down -- the high LR phase acts as regularization Leslie Smith's 1cycle ramps LR from low to high (first half) then high to very low (second half). The high-LR phase helps the model explore more of the loss landscape before settling into the best basin. Q5 If training loss suddenly spikes and diverges, what is the most likely learning rate issue? A Learning rate is too low B Learning rate is too high, causing the optimizer to overshoot the minimum C The warmup period is too long D The schedule decays too slowly A learning rate that's too high causes the optimizer to take steps larger than the loss basin, overshooting the minimum and causing the loss to increase. This manifests as sudden divergence. In plain words first The idea in one line You have built neurons, layers, networks, backprop, activations, loss functions, optimizers, regularization, initialization, and LR schedules. All as separate pieces. Now wire them together into a framework. Not PyTorch. Not TensorFlow. Yours. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Module "A layer" The base abstraction in a framework -- anything with forward(), backward(), and parameters() Sequential "Stack layers in order" A container that chains modules, applying them in sequence for forward and reverse for backward Forward pass "Run the network" Computing the output by passing input through each module in order Backward pass "Compute gradients" Propagating the loss gradient through each module in reverse to compute parameter gradients Parameters "The trainable weights" All values in the network that the optimizer can update -- weights and biases Optimizer "The thing that updates weights" An algorithm that uses gradients to update parameters, implementing SGD, Adam, or other rules DataLoader "The thing that feeds data" An iterator that splits a dataset into batches, optionally shuffling between epochs Training mode "model.train()" A flag that enables stochastic behavior like dropout and batch normalization with batch stats Evaluation mode "model.eval()" A flag that disables dropout and uses running statistics for batch normalization Zero grad "Clear the gradients" Resetting all parameter gradients to zero before computing the next batch's gradients The problem In plain words first A framework is a handful of agreements. Every layer is a Module with forward , backward and parameters . A Sequential runs modules in order forwards and in reverse backwards. A loss turns predictions into one number and its gradient. An optimizer only sees a flat list of parameters and their gradients. A DataLoader hands out shuffled batches. Once every piece keeps those agreements, any network is a few lines, and that is all PyTorch's nn.Module is, plus automatic gradients and a GPU. You have ten lessons of building blocks scattered across separate files. A Value class here, a training loop there, weight initialization in another file, learning rate schedules in yet another. To train a network, you copy-paste from five different lessons and wire them together by hand. That is what frameworks solve. PyTorch gives you nn.Module , nn.Sequential , optim.Adam , DataLoader , and a training loop pattern that ties them together. TensorFlow gives you keras.Layer , keras.Sequential , keras.optimizers.Adam . These are not magic. They are organizational patterns that make it possible to define, train, and evaluate networks without reinventing the plumbing every time. You are going to build the same thing in ~500 lines of Python. No numpy. No external dependencies. A framework that can define any feedforward network, train it with SGD or Adam, batch the data, apply dropout and batch normalization, use any activation, and schedule the learning rate. When you finish, you will understand exactly what happens when you write model = nn.Sequential(...) in PyTorch. You will understand why model.train() and model.eval() exist. You will understand why optimizer.zero_grad() is a separate call. You will understand all of it, because you built all of it. Idea 1 · The Module Abstraction Every layer in PyTorch inherits from nn.Module . A Module has three responsibilities: forward() -- compute the output given inputs parameters() -- return all trainable weights backward() -- compute gradients (handled by autograd in PyTorch, explicit in ours) A Linear layer is a Module. A ReLU activation is a Module. A dropout layer is a Module. A batch normalization layer is a Module. They all have the same interface. Predict before you run Step 10's model is Linear(2, 16) , Linear(16, 16) , Linear(16, 8) and Linear(8, 1) , with ReLUs and a final Sigmoid between them. How many parameters does model.parameters() return, and how many moving averages does Adam keep for them? (Solution P1.) Idea 2 · Sequential Container nn.Sequential chains Modules. Forward pass: feed data through Module 1, then Module 2, then Module 3. Backward pass: reverse the chain. The container itself is a Module -- it has forward(), parameters(), and backward(). This is the composite pattern: a sequence of Modules is itself a Module. Idea 3 · Training vs Evaluation Mode Dropout randomly zeroes neurons during training but passes everything through during evaluation. Batch normalization uses batch statistics during training but running averages during evaluation. The train() and eval() methods toggle this behavior. Every Module has a training flag. Idea 4 · Optimizer The optimizer updates parameters using their gradients. SGD: param -= lr * grad . Adam: maintains momentum and variance estimates, then updates. The optimizer does not know about the network architecture -- it only sees a flat list of parameters and their gradients. Check your mental model ✗ "With batch_size=16 , each update averages 16 examples." ✓ Not in Step 10: the loop calls zero_grad , backward and step once per example, so the DataLoader only decides the order. Averaging over a batch is Exercise 5. ✗ " zero_grad is housekeeping; skipping it just wastes memory." ✓ Linear.backward adds into its gradient buffers with += . Skip zero_grad and every step uses the sum of all past gradients (Solution B1). ✗ "Activations have no parameters, so they need no backward." ✓ They own no weights, but they must still pass the gradient through, scaled by their slope; that is the whole of ReLU.backward . Idea 5 · DataLoader Batching matters for two reasons. First, you cannot fit the entire dataset in memory for large problems. Second, mini-batch gradient descent provides noise that helps escape local minima. The DataLoader splits data into batches and optionally shuffles between epochs. Solution B1 · Gradients that pile up The loss climbs instead of falling (about 0.83 at the end) and test accuracy collapses to 35 percent , worse than always answering "outside". Reference solution and notes Copy Why depth helps here Each tanh unit of the first layer makes one soft line in the plane. The second layer combines these lines into curved regions. The spirals need many bends, and two layers of 24 units give enough of them inside the step budget. Why the shuffle matters The rows come sorted by label. Without a shuffle, the batches near the start hold only label 0 and the batches near the end hold only label 1. Each run of such batches pulls the output toward one class. A new random order for each pass over the data gives batches that look like the whole set. The order comes from rng , so the run stays reproducible. Why Adam Adam divides each step by a running estimate of the gradient size. Each weight then moves at a similar speed, also when its gradients are very small or very large. Plain gradient descent with one learning rate can reach the target too, but it needs a careful choice of the rate and more steps. A Load data, preprocess data, augment data B forward() for computation, backward() for gradients, parameters() for trainable weights C Compile, optimize, deploy D Tokenize, embed, decode Every Module implements forward() to compute output, backward() to propagate gradients, and parameters() to expose trainable weights. A Reverse order uses less memory B Gradients flow from the loss backward through the network, so the last layer computes gradients first C It prevents gradient explosion D It's arbitrary -- either direction works The backward pass starts at the loss and propagates gradients toward the input. The last layer receives the loss gradient first, computes its local gradients, and passes them to the previous layer. Q3 Why is optimizer.zero_grad() a separate call instead of being done automatically? A It allows gradient accumulation across multiple batches before taking a single optimizer step B It makes debugging easier C It saves memory D It's a PyTorch design mistake Separating zero_grad from step enables gradient accumulation: you can run backward() multiple times (across mini-batches) and sum the gradients before calling step(). This simulates larger batch sizes. Q4 What is the correct order of operations in a training loop? A backward, forward, zero_grad, step B forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step C forward, zero_grad, backward, loss, step D zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, step The standard pattern: zero_grad (clear old gradients), forward (compute predictions), loss (compute scalar loss), backward (compute gradients), step (update parameters). A It splits data into batches and optionally shuffles between epochs for mini-batch gradient descent B It computes the loss function C It initializes the weights D It trains the model The DataLoader handles two practical concerns: batching (you can't fit all data in memory) and shuffling (random order prevents the model from memorizing data sequence).
