Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Tensor "A multi-dimensional array" A typed, device-aware array with automatic differentiation support baked into every operation Autograd "Automatic backprop" A tape-based system that records operations during forward pass, then replays them in reverse to compute exact gradients nn.Module "A layer" The base class for any differentiable computation block -- registers parameters, supports nesting, handles train/eval modes state_dict "The model weights" An OrderedDict mapping parameter names to tensors -- the portable, serializable representation of a trained model .backward() "Compute gradients" Traverse the computational graph in reverse, computing and accumulating gradients for every leaf tensor with requires_grad=True .to(device) "Move to GPU" Recursively transfer all parameters and buffers to the specified device (CPU, CUDA, MPS) DataLoader "The data pipeline" An iterator that batches, shuffles, and optionally parallelizes data loading from a Dataset Mixed precision "Use float16" Train with float16 forward/backward for speed while keeping float32 master weights for numerical stability Eager execution "Run it now" Operations execute immediately when called, not deferred to a later compilation step -- the core design choice that differentiates PyTorch from TF 1.x zero_grad "Reset gradients" Set all parameter gradients to zero before the next backward pass, since PyTorch accumulates gradients by default The problem In plain words first PyTorch is the framework you built in Lesson 3.14, with three big upgrades. Tensors hold whole batches and run on fast C++ or GPU kernels. Autograd records every operation and writes the backward pass for you. nn.Module finds all the weights inside your layers automatically. The training loop stays the one you know: zero the gradients, run forward, compute the loss, call backward, step the optimiser. You have a working mini framework. Linear layers, ReLU, dropout, batch norm, Adam, a DataLoader, a training loop. It trains a 4-layer network on a circle classification problem in pure Python. It is also 500x slower than PyTorch on the same problem. Your mini framework processes one sample at a time with nested Python loops. PyTorch dispatches the same operations to optimized C++/CUDA kernels that run on GPU. On a single NVIDIA A100, a well-tuned PyTorch pipeline with mixed precision processes a few thousand ImageNet images per second, so the standard 90-epoch ResNet-50 run (25.6M parameters, 1.28M images) takes on the order of half a day. Your framework would take roughly 3,000 hours on the same task -- if it didn't run out of memory first. Speed is not the only gap. Your framework has no GPU support. No automatic differentiation -- you hand-wrote backward() for every module. No serialization. No distributed training. No mixed precision. No way to debug gradient flow without print statements. PyTorch fills every one of these gaps. And it does so while keeping the exact same mental model you already built: Module, forward(), parameters(), backward(), optimizer.step(). The concepts transfer one-to-one. The syntax is nearly identical. The difference is that PyTorch wraps a decade of systems engineering behind the same interface you designed from scratch. Idea 1 · Why PyTorch Won In 2015, TensorFlow required you to define a static computation graph before running anything. You built the graph, compiled it, then fed data through it. Debugging meant staring at graph visualizations. Changing the architecture meant rebuilding the graph from scratch. PyTorch launched in 2017 with a different philosophy: eager execution. You write Python. It runs immediately. y = model(x) actually computes y right now, not "add a node to a graph that will compute y later." This meant standard Python debugging tools worked. print() worked. pdb worked. if/else in your forward pass worked. By 2020, the market had spoken. PyTorch's share in ML research papers went from 7% (2017) to over 75% (2022). Meta, OpenAI and Hugging Face build mainly on PyTorch; Google DeepMind is the best-known exception and builds mainly on JAX (Lesson 3.17). TensorFlow 2.x adopted eager execution in response -- tacit admission that PyTorch's design was correct. The lesson: developer experience compounds. A framework that is 10% slower but 50% faster to debug wins every time. Idea 2 · Tensors A tensor is a multi-dimensional array with three critical properties: shape, dtype, and device. Copy Shape is the dimensionality. A scalar is shape (), a vector is (n,), a matrix is (m, n), a batch of images is (batch, channels, height, width). Dtype controls precision and memory. dtype Bits Range Use case float32 32 ~7 decimal digits Default training float16 16 ~3.3 decimal digits Mixed precision bfloat16 16 Same range as float32, less precision LLM training int8 8 -128 to 127 Quantized inference Device determines where computation happens. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Every operation requires all tensors on the same device. This is the #1 PyTorch error beginners hit: RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device . Fix it by moving everything to the same device before computation. Reshaping is constant-time -- it changes the metadata, not the data. Copy Worked example Shapes, step by step Start with x = torch.randn(2, 3, 4) : 24 numbers. Call Result shape What happened x.view(2, 12) (2, 12) same memory, read as 2 rows of 12 x.reshape(6, 4) (6, 4) same, works even when view cannot x.permute(2, 0, 1) (4, 2, 3) axes reordered; memory untouched, so no longer contiguous x.unsqueeze(0) (1, 2, 3, 4) new axis of size 1 at the front x.unsqueeze(0).squeeze() (2, 3, 4) size-1 axes removed again The total, 24, never changes. A shape error almost always means two of these steps disagree about which axis is which. Idea 3 · Autograd Your mini framework required you to implement backward() for every module. PyTorch does not. It records every operation on tensors into a directed acyclic graph (the computational graph) and then traverses that graph in reverse to compute gradients automatically. The key difference from your framework: PyTorch uses tape-based autodiff. Every operation appends to a "tape" during the forward pass. Calling .backward() replays the tape in reverse. Copy When you assign an nn.Module or nn.Parameter as an attribute in __init__ , PyTorch automatically registers it. model.parameters() recursively collects every registered parameter. A training loop repeats four actions for every batch of data: run the model forward to get predictions, measure the loss, call backward() to compute gradients, and let the optimiser nudge the weights. a0312: Course home / Phase 3 · Deep Learning and Neural Networks JAX Fundamentals Lesson 3.17 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write pure-function neural network code using JAX's functional API (jax.numpy, jax.grad, jax.jit, jax.vmap) Explain the key design difference between PyTorch's eager mutation and JAX's functional compilation model Apply jit compilation and vmap vectorization to accelerate training loops compared to naive Python Train a simple network in JAX and contrast the explicit state management with PyTorch's object-oriented approach Before you start Needs : Lessons 3.2 to 3.14, basic NumPy Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line PyTorch mutates tensors. TensorFlow builds graphs. JAX compiles pure functions. That last one changes how you think about deep learning. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means XLA "The thing that makes JAX fast" Accelerated Linear Algebra -- a compiler that fuses operations and generates optimized GPU/TPU kernels from a computation graph JIT "Just-in-time compilation" JAX traces the function on first call, compiles to XLA, then runs the compiled version on subsequent calls Pure function "No side effects" A function where the output depends only on inputs -- no global state, no mutation, no randomness without explicit keys vmap "Auto-batching" Transforms a function that processes one example into one that processes a batch, without rewriting pmap "Auto-parallelism" Replicates a function across multiple devices and splits the input batch Pytree "Nested dict of arrays" Any nested structure of lists, tuples, dicts, and arrays that JAX can traverse and transform Tracing "Recording the computation" JAX executes the function with abstract values to build a computation graph, without computing real results Functional autodiff "grad of a function" Computing derivatives by transforming functions, not by attaching gradient storage to tensors Optax "JAX's optimizer library" A composable library of gradient transformations -- Adam, SGD, clipping, scheduling -- that chain together Flax "JAX's nn.Module" Google's neural network library for JAX, adding layer abstractions while keeping state explicit The problem In plain words first JAX looks like NumPy, but every function you write can be transformed : grad turns a loss function into its gradient function, jit compiles a function into fast machine code, and vmap turns a one-example function into a batch function. The price is that functions must be pure : parameters go in as arguments and come out as return values, arrays are never changed in place, and randomness needs an explicit key. PyTorch keeps state inside objects; JAX passes it around. You know how to build neural networks in PyTorch. You define an nn.Module , call .backward() , step the optimizer. It works. Millions of people use it. But PyTorch has a constraint baked into its DNA: it traces operations eagerly, one at a time, in Python. Every tensor + tensor is a separate kernel launch. Every training step re-interprets the same Python code. This works fine until you need to train a 540-billion-parameter model across 2,048 TPUs. Then the overhead kills you. Google DeepMind trains Gemini with JAX on TPUs, and other labs with large TPU fleets use it too. These are not small operations -- they are the largest neural network training runs on Earth. They chose JAX because it treats your training loop as a compilable program, not a sequence of Python calls. JAX is NumPy with three superpowers: automatic differentiation, JIT compilation to XLA, and automatic vectorization. You write a function that processes one example. JAX gives you a function that processes a batch, computes gradients, compiles to machine code, and runs across multiple devices. All without changing the original function. Idea 1 · The JAX Philosophy JAX is a functional framework. No classes, no mutable state, no .backward() method. Instead: PyTorch JAX nn.Module class with state Pure function: f(params, x) -> y loss.backward() jax.grad(loss_fn)(params, x, y) Eager execution JIT compilation via XLA for x in batch: manual loop jax.vmap(f) auto-vectorization DataParallel / FSDP jax.pmap(f) auto-parallelism Mutable model.parameters() Immutable pytree of arrays This is not a style preference. It is a compiler constraint. JIT compilation requires pure functions -- same inputs always produce same outputs, no side effects. That restriction is what makes 100x speedups possible. Idea 2 · jax.numpy: The Familiar Surface JAX reimplements the NumPy API on accelerators: Copy Same function names. Same broadcasting rules. Same slicing semantics. But the arrays live on GPU/TPU, and every operation is traceable by the compiler. One critical difference: JAX arrays are immutable. No a[0] = 5 . Instead: a = a.at[0].set(5) . This feels awkward for a week, then it clicks -- immutability is what makes transformations like grad , jit , and vmap composable. Idea 3 · jax.grad: Functional Autodiff PyTorch attaches gradients to tensors ( .grad ). JAX attaches gradients to functions. Copy jax.grad takes a function and returns a new function that computes the gradient. No .backward() call. No computation graph stored on tensors. The gradient is just another function you can call, compose, or JIT-compile. This composes arbitrarily: Copy Second derivatives. Third derivatives. Jacobians. Hessians. All by composing grad . PyTorch can do this too ( torch.autograd.functional.hessian ), but it is bolted on. In JAX, it is the foundation. The constraint: grad only works on pure functions. No print statements inside (they run during tracing, not execution). No mutation of external state. No random number generation without explicit key management. Worked example grad, by hand and by JAX For : jax.grad(f) is , so df(3.0) returns 6.0 ; jax.grad(jax.grad(f)) is the constant 2, so d2f(3.0) returns 2.0 . Nothing was stored on any array: df is an ordinary function you can call on any number, pass to jit , or differentiate again. With several arguments, jax.grad(loss_fn)(params, x, y) differentiates with respect to the first one, params , and returns gradients with the same nested shape as params . Idea 4 · jit: Compile to XLA Copy On the first call, JAX traces the function -- it records which operations happen, without executing them. Then it hands that trace to XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra), Google's compiler for TPUs and GPUs. XLA fuses operations, eliminates redundant memory copies, and generates optimized machine code. Subsequent calls skip Python entirely. The compiled code runs on the accelerator at C++ speed. When JIT helps: - Training steps (same computation repeated thousands of times) - Inference (same model, different inputs) - Any function called more than once with similar-shaped inputs When JIT hurts: - Functions with Python control flow that depends on values ( if x > 0 where x is a traced array) - One-shot computations (compilation overhead exceeds runtime) - Debugging (tracing hides the actual execution) The control flow restriction is real. jax.lax.cond replaces if/else . jax.lax.scan replaces for loops. These are not optional -- they are the price of compilation. Check your mental model ✗ "A print inside a jitted function prints on every call." ✓ It runs only while JAX traces the function, so you see it once, with a placeholder instead of a value. jax.debug.print prints the real value on every call (see the run under Step 4). ✗ " jit makes every function faster." ✓ It compiles once per input shape and dtype. A new batch size triggers a fresh compilation, which is why Step 5 drops the last partial batch. ✗ "Python if works on JAX arrays inside jit ." ✓ During tracing the array has no value yet, so if x > 0 raises an error. Use jnp.where or jax.lax.cond . Idea 5 · vmap: Automatic Vectorization You write a function that processes one example: Copy vmap lifts it to process a batch: Copy in_axes=(None, 0) means: do not batch over params (shared), batch over axis 0 of x . No manual for loop. No reshaping. No batch dimension threading. JAX figures out the batch dimension and vectorizes the entire computation. This is not syntactic sugar. vmap generates fused vectorized code that runs 10-100x faster than a Python loop. And it composes with jit and grad : Copy Per-example gradients. One line. PyTorch has since added the same ability in torch.func , modelled on JAX. Idea 6 · pmap: Data Parallelism Across Devices Copy pmap replicates the function across all available devices (GPUs/TPUs) and splits the batch. Inside the function, jax.lax.pmean and jax.lax.psum synchronize gradients across devices. Google trains Gemini on fleets of thousands of TPU chips with JAX; at that scale pmap has largely given way to its successors, jit with sharded arrays and shard_map . The programming model: write the single-device version, wrap with pmap , done. Idea 7 · Pytrees: The Universal Data Structure JAX operates on "pytrees" -- nested combinations of lists, tuples, dicts, and arrays. Your model parameters are a pytree: Copy Every JAX transformation -- grad , jit , vmap -- knows how to traverse pytrees. jax.tree.map(f, tree) applies f to every leaf. This is how optimizers update all parameters at once: Copy What you should see Copy Copy No .parameters() method. No parameter registration. The tree structure is the model. Idea 8 · Functional vs Object-Oriented PyTorch stores state inside objects: Copy What you should see Copy Copy JAX uses pure functions with explicit state: Copy The params are passed in. Nothing is stored. Nothing is mutated. This makes every function testable, composable, and compilable. It also means you manage the params yourself -- or use a library like Flax or Equinox. Idea 9 · The JAX Ecosystem JAX gives you primitives. Libraries give you ergonomics: Library Role Style Flax (Google) Neural network layers nn.Module with explicit state Equinox (Patrick Kidger) Neural network layers Pytree-based, Pythonic Optax (DeepMind) Optimizers + LR schedules Composable gradient transforms Orbax (Google) Checkpointing Save/restore pytrees CLU (Google) Metrics + logging Training loop utilities Optax is the standard optimizer library. It separates the gradient transformation (Adam, SGD, clipping) from the parameter update, making it trivial to compose: Copy Idea 10 · When to Use JAX vs PyTorch Factor JAX PyTorch TPU support First-class (Google built both) Community-maintained (torch_xla) GPU support Good (CUDA via XLA) Best-in-class (native CUDA) Debugging Hard (tracing + compilation) Easy (eager, line-by-line) Ecosystem Research-focused (Flax, Equinox) Massive (HuggingFace, torchvision, etc.) Hiring Niche (Google, DeepMind and other TPU users) Mainstream (everywhere) Large-scale training Superior (XLA, pmap, mesh) Good (FSDP, DeepSpeed) Prototyping speed Slower (functional overhead) Faster (mutate and go) Production inference TensorFlow Serving, Vertex AI TorchServe, Triton, ONNX Who uses it Google DeepMind (Gemini) Meta (Llama), OpenAI (GPT), Stability AI The honest answer: use PyTorch unless you have a specific reason to use JAX. Those reasons are -- TPU access, need for per-example gradients, multi-device training at massive scale, or joining a team whose stack is already built on JAX. Idea 11 · Random Numbers in JAX JAX does not have a global random state. Every random operation requires an explicit PRNG key: Copy This is annoying at first. But it guarantees reproducibility across devices and compilations -- a property that PyTorch's torch.manual_seed cannot guarantee in multi-GPU settings. The same idea as a formula Functions in, functions out. JAX transformations take a pure function and return a new function: ​ = f ( X i ​ ) , jit ( f ) = f compiled with XLA and they compose: jit(vmap(grad(loss))) computes per-example gradients for a whole batch in one compiled program. grad differentiates with respect to the first argument by default ( argnums chooses others), and the argument may be any pytree, a nested structure of arrays such as a dict of layer parameters. Purity is required. A jitted function is traced once per input shape and dtype; Python side effects run only during tracing, and values must not depend on hidden state. Changing a shape triggers a new compilation, so variable-length inputs are padded to a few fixed sizes. Explicit randomness. A key is split into independent keys, ​ , k 2 ​ ) , and each random call consumes one. The same key always gives the same numbers, so experiments are reproducible by construction and parallel devices never share a random stream by accident. Parallelism. pmap (and the newer shard_map and sharding API) runs the same function on several devices, each with a slice of the batch, and averages gradients across them: data parallelism. Recap What to keep from this lesson JAX is NumPy plus transformations: grad , jit , vmap (and sharding for many devices). Solutions Solution P1 · Compilation comes first The first epoch, at roughly twice the time of the others: it pays for tracing and compiling train_step and accuracy . Solution B1 · Python if on a traced value TracerBoolConversionError: Attempted boolean conversion of traced array with shape bool[] . While jit traces the function, x is a placeholder with a shape but no value, so Python cannot decide which branch to take. Write it with array operations instead: return jnp.where(x > 0, x, 0.0) , or use jax.lax.cond(x > 0, lambda v: v, lambda v: 0.0 * v, x) when the two branches do different work. It ran. It produced a number. The number is wrong and nothing crashed. Welcome to the hardest kind of debugging -- the kind where there is no error message. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Silent bug "It runs but gives bad results" A bug that produces no error but degrades model quality -- the dominant failure mode in ML Dead ReLU "The neurons died" A ReLU neuron whose input is always negative, so it outputs 0 and receives 0 gradient permanently Vanishing gradients "Early layers stop learning" Gradients shrink exponentially through layers, making weights in early layers effectively frozen Exploding gradients "Loss went to NaN" Gradients grow exponentially through layers, causing weight updates so large they overflow Gradient checking "Verify backprop is correct" Comparing analytical gradients from backprop to numerical gradients from finite differences Overfit-one-batch "The most important debug test" Training on a single small batch to verify the model CAN learn -- if it cannot, something is fundamentally broken LR finder "Sweep to find the right learning rate" Exponentially increasing the learning rate over one epoch and picking the rate just before loss diverges Data leakage "Test data leaked into training" When information from the test set contaminates training, producing artificially high accuracy Activation statistics "Monitor layer health" Tracking mean, std, and zero-fraction of each layer's output to detect dead, saturated, or exploding neurons Gradient clipping "Cap the gradient magnitude" Scaling gradients down when their norm exceeds a threshold, preventing exploding gradient updates The problem In plain words first When a neural network is wrong it usually does not crash: it trains, prints falling losses and makes confident predictions. So debugging means measuring. Check that the model can memorise one small batch, that backprop agrees with numerical gradients, that each layer's activations and gradients stay in a sensible range, and that the learning rate suits the problem. Each check rules out one family of bugs; none of them alone proves the model is right. Traditional software crashes when it is broken. A null pointer throws an exception. A type mismatch fails at compile time. An off-by-one error produces a clearly wrong output. Neural networks do not give you that luxury. A broken neural network runs to completion, prints a loss value, and outputs predictions. The loss might decrease. The predictions might look plausible. But the model is silently wrong -- learning shortcuts, memorizing noise, or converging to a useless local minimum. Practitioners consistently report that most of their debugging time goes to "silent" bugs that produce no errors but degrade model quality. The difference between a working model and a broken one is often a single misplaced line: a missing zero_grad() , a transposed dimension, a learning rate off by 10x. Andrej Karpathy's widely read "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" (2019) makes the same point: neural network training fails silently. This lesson teaches you to find those bugs. Idea 1 · The Debugging Mindset Forget print-and-pray debugging. Neural network debugging requires a systematic approach because the feedback loop is slow (minutes to hours per training run) and the symptoms are ambiguous (bad loss could mean 20 different things). The golden rule: start simple, add complexity one piece at a time, and verify each piece independently. Idea 2 · Symptom 1: Loss Not Decreasing This is the most common complaint. The training loop runs, epochs tick by, and the loss stays flat or oscillates wildly. Wrong learning rate. Too high: loss oscillates or jumps to NaN. Too low: loss decreases so slowly it looks flat. For Adam, start at 1e-3. For SGD, start at 1e-1 or 1e-2. Always try 3 learning rates spanning 10x each (e.g., 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4) before concluding something else is wrong. Dead ReLUs. If a ReLU neuron receives a large negative input, it outputs 0 and its gradient is 0. It never activates again. If enough neurons die, the network cannot learn. Check: print the fraction of activations that are exactly 0 after each ReLU layer. If >50% are dead, switch to LeakyReLU or reduce the learning rate. Vanishing gradients. In deep networks with sigmoid or tanh activations, gradients shrink exponentially as they propagate backward. By the time they reach the first layer, they are ~0. The first layers stop learning. Fix: use ReLU/GELU, add residual connections, or use batch normalization. Exploding gradients. The opposite problem -- gradients grow exponentially. Common in RNNs and very deep networks. Loss jumps to NaN. Fix: gradient clipping ( torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ ), lower learning rate, or add normalization. Idea 3 · Symptom 2: Loss Decreasing But Model is Bad The loss goes down. Training accuracy hits 99%. But test accuracy is 55%. Or the model produces nonsensical outputs on real data. Overfitting. The model memorizes training data instead of learning patterns. Gap between training and validation loss grows over time. Fix: more data, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, data augmentation. Data leakage. Test data leaked into training. Accuracy is suspiciously high. Common causes: shuffling before splitting, preprocessing with statistics from the full dataset, duplicate samples across splits. Fix: split first, preprocess second, check for duplicates. Label errors. Popular benchmark test sets contain wrong labels too, about 3 percent on average and roughly 6 percent in ImageNet's validation set (Northcutt et al., 2021 -- "Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets"). The model learns the noise. Fix: use confident learning to find and fix mislabeled examples, or use loss truncation to ignore high-loss samples. Idea 4 · Symptom 3: NaN or Inf in Loss The loss value becomes nan or inf . Training is dead. Learning rate too high. Gradient updates overshoot so far that weights explode. Fix: reduce by 10x. log(0) or log(negative). Cross-entropy loss computes log(p) . If your model outputs exactly 0 or a negative probability, the log explodes. Fix: clamp predictions to [eps, 1-eps] where eps=1e-7 . Division by zero. Batch normalization divides by standard deviation. A batch with constant values has std=0. Fix: add epsilon to the denominator (PyTorch does this by default, but custom implementations might not). Numerical overflow. Large activations fed into exp() produce Inf. Softmax is especially prone. Fix: subtract the max before exponentiating (the log-sum-exp trick). Worked example Reading a stuck loss A model that knows nothing and spreads probability evenly over classes has cross-entropy : 0.693 for 2 classes, 2.303 for 10, 6.908 for 1,000. So a loss that sits at 0.69 on a yes/no task means "the model is guessing". Bug 2 in Step 5 ends at 0.6884: its ReLUs are dead, the output layer only sees zeros, and the prediction is barely more than a coin toss. Check your mental model ✗ "A falling loss means no bug." ✓ In Step 5, Bug 3 (no zero_grad ) has a lower loss after 20 steps than the healthy network, and the debugger calls it HEALTHY. Accumulated gradients act like an ever-growing learning rate: fast at first, unstable later. ✗ "More than half the activations at zero means dead neurons." ✓ A ReLU zeroes every negative input, so about half its outputs are zero in a perfectly healthy layer. A dead neuron is one that is zero for every input; count those per neuron. ✗ "If the gradient check passes, the model will train." ✓ It only proves the backward pass matches the forward pass. Wrong labels, a bad learning rate or leaked data all pass it. Idea 5 · Technique 1: Gradient Checking Compare your analytical gradients (from backprop) to numerical gradients (from finite differences). If they disagree, your backward pass has a bug. Numerical gradient for parameter w : loss ( w + eps ) − loss ( w − eps ) ​ Agreement metric (relative difference): ) ∣ grad_analytical − grad_numerical ∣ ​ If rel_diff < 1e-5 : correct. If rel_diff > 1e-3 : almost certainly a bug. Idea 6 · Technique 2: Activation Statistics Monitor the mean and standard deviation of activations after each layer during training. Healthy networks maintain activations with mean near 0 and std near 1 (after normalization) or at least bounded. Health indicator Mean Std Diagnosis Healthy ~0 ~1 Network is learning normally Saturated >>0 or <<0 ~0 Activations stuck at extreme values Dead 0 0 Neurons are dead (all zeros) Exploding >>10 >>10 Activations growing without bound Idea 7 · Technique 3: Gradient Flow Visualization Plot the average gradient magnitude for each layer. In a healthy network, gradient magnitudes should be roughly similar across layers. If early layers have gradients 1000x smaller than later layers, you have vanishing gradients. Idea 8 · Technique 4: The Overfit-One-Batch Test The single most important debugging technique in deep learning. Take one small batch (8-32 samples). Train on it for 100+ iterations. The loss should go to nearly zero and training accuracy should hit 100%. If it does not, your model or training loop has a fundamental bug -- do not proceed to full training. This test catches: - Broken loss functions - Broken backward passes - Architecture too small to represent the data - Optimizer not connected to model parameters - Data and labels misaligned This takes 30 seconds to run and saves hours of debugging full training runs. Predict before you run Step 5 runs three deliberately broken networks through the debugger: a learning rate of 10, ReLUs killed by a large negative bias, and a loop with no zero_grad . Which of the three will the debugger's report call HEALTHY? (Solution P1.) Idea 9 · Technique 5: Learning Rate Finder Leslie Smith (2017) proposed sweeping the learning rate from very small (1e-7) to very large (10) over one epoch while recording the loss. Plot loss vs learning rate. The optimal learning rate is roughly 10x smaller than the rate where loss starts decreasing fastest. Best LR in this example: ~1e-3 (one order of magnitude before the steepest point). Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A run trains for hours with a smooth loss. Then, within three logging intervals, the loss jumps, becomes inf, and every value after that is NaN. The same recipe worked on a smaller model. Give your ranked list of causes, the evidence that separates them, and the changes that keep it from happening again. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A clean run that dies late is almost always an oversized update: the peak learning rate is too high for the larger model, a rare batch produced a huge gradient, or the schedule reached its peak at a point where the model was already sensitive. The logs separate the cases: for an explosion the gradient norm spikes before the loss does, while a forward pass overflow, such as a softmax without the max shift or a normalization over a zero variance, shows a normal norm and a loss that goes to inf in one step. Fix with gradient clipping by norm at 1.0, a lower peak with warmup, and a loss computed from logits, then resume from the last good checkpoint. Rank the causes. Update too large for this model. The debugging lesson's table: a loss that goes NaN after some steps means the learning rate is too high, and the first move is to reduce it by 10 times. The peak that was safe on the smaller model is close to the edge on the larger one. The capstone lesson advises sweeping the peak on a small model as a prior, and says the optimum shifts with size, so confirm rather than copy. One bad batch. A single outlier batch produces a gradient large enough to corrupt every weight in one step. Without clipping, nothing stops it. Schedule position. Check where the schedule was when the loss jumped. A short warmup or a peak reached at the wrong time puts the largest steps on a model that cannot take them. Forward pass overflow. An exp in a hand written softmax without the max shift, a log of zero, or a division by a zero variance in a normalization. These produce inf at once, usually at the first step, so they rank low for a run that was clean for hours, but a rare batch can trigger them late. What the logs show. The gradient L2 norm logged beside the learning rate every step. The capstone lesson's rule: a divergent run shows the norm spike before the loss does. An overflow shows a normal norm and a loss that is inf in a single step. Per-layer gradient statistics. The debugging lesson flags a layer whose mean absolute gradient exceeds 100 as exploding and shows which layer went first. Replay. Load the last good checkpoint, feed the batch from the failing step, and watch the norm. If that batch alone reproduces the spike, it is the trigger; if it does not, the schedule or the rate is. Anomaly detection in the autograd engine, to name the operation that produced the first NaN. Changes that prevent a repeat. Clip the gradient by its global norm at 1.0 before the step. Clipping by norm keeps the direction; clipping each element does not. Lower the peak and keep a warmup of 1 to 5 percent of the steps, so the largest steps arrive after the optimizer statistics settle. Compute the loss from logits with a fused, stable function, and keep epsilons in logs and divisions. Checkpoint often enough that a resume costs minutes, and alert on a NaN loss so the run stops at the first bad step rather than hours later. Plausible wrong answers. "Add an epsilon to the loss and restart." An epsilon fixes a log of zero at step one; a late explosion comes from the update size, and the run will die again. "Halve the learning rate and hope." Halving is a guess; the lesson's move is a 10 times reduction, together with clipping and a check of the schedule position. "NaN means the data has a bad row." A bad row shows in the first epoch, not after hours of clean training; replay the failing batch on the checkpoint before you blame it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What in the logs separates an oversized update from a forward pass overflow? Expected: the gradient norm rises over several steps before the loss for an explosion; an overflow shows a normal norm and a loss that goes to inf in a single step. (level 4) Why clip by norm rather than by value? Expected: clipping by norm scales the whole gradient and keeps its direction; clipping each element changes the direction. (level 4) Why did the recipe work on the smaller model? Expected: the peak that was safe there sits near the edge for the larger one; a sweep on the small model is a prior, and the optimum shifts with size, so verify rather than copy. (level 4) What do you add so the run never dies silently again? Expected: log the gradient norm beside the learning rate each step, alert on a NaN loss, checkpoint often enough to resume, and restart with clipping and a warmup. Where it is taught. Debug a failure A ten class classifier trains for many epochs, and the cross-entropy loss sits at about 2.3 the whole time, on training data and on validation data. Nothing crashes. What does that number tell you, and in which order do you debug? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Minus the natural log of one tenth is about 2.3, the loss of a model that gives every class the same probability, and the lesson's table reads a loss stuck there as a uniform prediction with no usable signal. The mean alone does not say why. Run the one batch overfit test first: a failure points at the loss, the backward pass, the optimizer hookup or misaligned labels, and a pass sends you to the data path to check that labels line up with inputs. Only then look at the learning rate, the gradients and the architecture. Reading the number. Categorical cross-entropy on a one-hot target is minus the log of the probability of the true class. A random guess among 10 classes gives each class probability 0.1 and a loss of minus log 0.1, about 2.3. The debugging lesson's master table has this row: a loss stuck at minus log of 1 over the class count means the model predicts a uniform distribution, and the first thing to check is the data pipeline and whether labels match inputs. A model with no usable signal settles on equal logits, because that is what minimizes the expected loss over a balanced label set. The order. Overfit one batch. Take 8 to 32 samples and train on them for a few hundred steps. The loss must go to near zero and the training accuracy to 100 percent. If it does not, the model or the loop is broken: a wrong loss, a broken backward pass, an optimizer not connected to the parameters, or inputs and labels out of step. The lesson's threshold for a pass is a final loss below 0.1. Look at the data. Print 5 random samples with their labels. Check that the shuffle keeps each input paired with its label, that inputs are normalized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and that labels have the integer type the loss expects. Learning rate. Try three values 10 times apart, such as 1e-2, 1e-3 and 1e-4. A rate that is far too low looks flat, but it would not sit exactly on the uniform value for many epochs. Gradients. All zeros points at dead ReLUs or a detached graph. Architecture. Only after the above: a model too small underfits, but it still beats a uniform guess on its own training data. How this differs from a slow start. A loss that starts near 2.3 and falls slowly is a learning rate or capacity question. A loss that holds at 2.3 for many epochs on the training set means no signal reaches the model at all. Plausible wrong answers. "Train longer, it is a slow start." A flat value at the uniform loss for many epochs means no signal, not a slow one. "Make the model bigger." Capacity is not the issue when the model cannot beat a uniform guess on its own training data. "Lower the learning rate." The rate changes how fast the loss moves, and here it does not move at all; check the data first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why uniform rather than some other wrong answer? Expected: with no usable signal, equal logits minimize the expected cross-entropy over a balanced label set, and that costs the log of the class count. (level 3) What does the overfit one batch test tell you here? Expected: whether the model and loop can learn at all; a healthy setup drives a small batch to near zero loss in a few hundred steps, and a failure means a broken loss, backward pass, optimizer hookup or misaligned labels. (level 4) The one batch test passes and full training still sits at 2.3. Where next? Expected: the full data path, such as a shuffle that breaks the pairing of inputs and labels, or unnormalized inputs, since the model can learn when given a consistent batch. (level 4) What distinguishes this symptom from a loss that starts at 2.3 and falls slowly? Expected: a slow fall is a learning rate or capacity question; a flat 2.3 for many epochs means no signal reaches the model. Where it is taught. Read the code This loop trains a small network with plain SGD at a small learning rate on a fixed batch. python for step in range(50): out = model(x) loss = criterion(out, y) loss.backward() optimizer.step() The loss falls for a few steps and then swings up and down. Read the loop, name the bug, explain the mechanism, and say where the fix goes. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The loop never zeroes the gradients, so each backward call adds the new gradient on top of all the earlier ones. The step applies a growing sum, which acts like a learning rate that rises at every step, and the loss oscillates. Add the optimizer's zero_grad call before backward, which is where the lesson's correct loop puts it. Why the gradient grows. Gradient storage is an accumulator by design. A parameter used in several places sums its contributions, and a backward call adds into the stored gradient rather than replacing it. In the mini framework the Linear layer's backward does exactly that, with a plus-equals into the weight gradients, and the optimizer's zero_grad sets every gradient container back to 0.0. A framework does the same. Without the reset, step one applies g1, step two applies g1 plus g2, step three applies the sum of three, and so on. The direction stays roughly right for a while and the magnitude climbs until the updates overshoot. The lesson's order. Copy The debugging lesson lists a forgotten zero_grad first among the bugs that waste the most hours, with this symptom: gradients accumulate across batches and the loss oscillates. Its demo reproduces the exact loop above and reports it. The optimizers lesson adds the ordering rule for the two trailing calls: the scheduler steps after the optimizer, and swapping them is a subtle bug. How to see it in logs. On a fixed batch the gradient norm should fall or hold as the loss falls. With this bug it grows step after step while the loss first improves and then swings with increasing amplitude. The overfit one batch test, which this loop resembles, would fail to reach a near zero loss. When accumulation is on purpose. Gradient accumulation across several small batches emulates one large batch: run backward on each micro batch without zeroing, then take one step and one zero_grad for the group, with the loss scaled by the group size. That is an exercise in the framework lesson. The difference from the bug is the single step per group and the division. Plausible wrong answers. "The learning rate is too high." The rate is small; the accumulated gradient is what grows. "Reset the gradients only every few steps to smooth them." That is accumulation without the division; the step size scales with the group size and the loss swings. "Detach the loss each step to stop the buildup." Detaching stops the graph, not the stored gradients; the gradient buffers still hold the sum. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why do frameworks accumulate gradients instead of overwriting them? Expected: a parameter used in several places sums its contributions, and accumulation across micro batches emulates a larger batch; the reset is left to the caller. (level 3) Where do clipping and the schedule go in the order? Expected: zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, clip, step, schedule; the scheduler steps after the optimizer. (level 4) How would you detect this bug from logs without reading the code? Expected: the gradient norm grows step after step on a fixed batch where it should shrink or hold, and the loss oscillates with growing amplitude. (level 4) When is skipping zero_grad on some steps correct? Expected: deliberate accumulation over several micro batches, with one step and one zero_grad after the group and the loss scaled by the group size. Where it is taught. List the classes of bugs it catches and the ones it does not. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Take one small batch of 8 to 32 samples and train on it alone for a few hundred steps. The loss must fall to near zero and the training accuracy must reach 100 percent. A pass shows that the loss function, the backward pass and the optimizer hookup work, and that the model can fit this batch, but not that each input has its correct label, because a model can memorize a wrong but consistent pairing as well. It says nothing about generalization, leakage or the full data loader, so it is the first gate and not the last. The test. The debugging lesson calls this the single most important technique in deep learning. Fix a batch, build a fresh model and optimizer, and loop: zero the gradients, forward, loss, backward, step. Print the loss and accuracy every 50 steps. The lesson's implementation runs 200 steps and treats a final loss above 0.1 as a failure. What a failure means. Any of these, and the lesson lists them: a loss function that does not match the output layer; a broken backward pass or a detached graph; an optimizer built before the model's parameters existed, so it updates nothing; inputs and labels out of step; an architecture too small to represent even this batch. Each of these would also break the full run, and there it would show up hours later as a slow or flat loss with twenty possible causes. Here it shows up in seconds with five. What a pass does not prove. The test overfits by design, so it says nothing about generalization. A model can memorize any consistent labels, so a wrong pairing of inputs and labels inside the fixed batch also passes. It uses one batch, so a shuffle that unpairs inputs and labels across the full set, a normalization computed on the full dataset, duplicate rows across splits, or label noise can all survive it. The lesson's checklist continues after it: print the model summary and check the parameter count, run one forward pass on random data and check the output shape, train for 5 epochs and confirm the loss falls, check activation statistics for dead or exploding layers, check the gradient flow across layers, and print 5 random samples with their labels. Make it a gate. Run it at startup on a fixed batch, assert the final loss is below the threshold, and refuse to start the long run when it fails. Run it again whenever the architecture or the pipeline changes. Plausible wrong answers. "A passing test means the model will generalize." It proves the model can memorize one batch; generalization needs the validation curve. "Skip it, the full run shows problems soon enough." The run shows a symptom hours later and the symptom fits many causes; the test isolates the loop in seconds. "Use the whole training set for a few epochs instead." That is the full run; a small batch is what makes a failure unambiguous and fast. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The loss on the one batch stalls well above the threshold. Name three suspects. Expected: a loss that does not match the output layer, an optimizer built before the model's parameters were created, or a model too small to fit the batch. (level 3) Why 8 to 32 samples? Expected: small enough that a correct model memorizes it in a few hundred steps, so a failure is unambiguous and the test stays fast. (level 4) The test passes and the full run later shows training accuracy at chance. What does the pass rule out, and what remains? Expected: the model and loop can learn, so what remains is the full data path: a shuffle that unpairs inputs and labels, or normalization computed differently for the full set. (level 4) How do you turn this into a gate in a training script? Expected: run it on a fixed batch at startup, assert the final loss is below the threshold, refuse to start the long run on a failure, and rerun it whenever the architecture or pipeline changes. Where it is taught. The debugging lesson implements the test, lists what it catches, and places it first in the pre-training checklist. Defend a design You inherit a model with no known good learning rate and a compute budget of a few hours. Design the procedure that picks the peak learning rate and the schedule for the run, and say what you log to defend the choice. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run a learning rate range test first: train for about a hundred steps while the rate grows exponentially from 1e-7 toward 10 and record the loss at each rate. Take the rate where the loss falls fastest and set the peak about 10 times lower. Then run a linear warmup over 1 to 5 percent of the steps into a cosine decay with a floor near a tenth of the peak, or the 1cycle policy when the budget is short and the total step count is fixed. Log the range test curve, the schedule curve and the gradient norm beside the learning rate at every step. Step one: measure, do not guess. The debugging lesson's range test: save the weights, start at 1e-7, multiply the rate by a constant factor each step so it reaches about 10 after a hundred steps, record the loss, and stop when the loss turns NaN or exceeds ten times the best value seen. Restore the weights. The loss is flat at the low end, falls fastest around some rate, reaches its minimum, and diverges. The suggested peak is about 10 times below the steepest fall, which in the lesson's example puts the best rate near 1e-3 when the steepest point sits near 1e-2. The lesson's second rule covers the case where the curve is unclear: try three rates 10 times apart, such as 1e-2, 1e-3 and 1e-4, and read the loss after a few epochs. Step two: pick the shape from the budget. Situation Schedule Why Total steps unknown constant, with manual drops nothing else can be computed Hours, step count fixed 1cycle fastest convergence for a fixed budget Moderate budget cosine, floor at a tenth of the peak safe default with no extra knobs Days or weeks warmup plus cosine the default for large transformer runs For a few hours with a known step count the schedules lesson points at 1cycle, which ramps from the peak over 25 up to the peak over the first half and down to the peak over 10000 in the second half. For anything longer, warmup plus cosine with a warmup of 1 to 5 percent. With an adaptive optimizer the warmup is not optional: its moment estimates are poor for the first steps. Step three: sanity check the peak. The schedules lesson's sensitivity run trains a few epochs at a constant rate and labels each run diverged, barely moved, learning or converged. Run it at the chosen peak and at the rates one step above and below. The peak should land in learning or converged, and the rate above it should show the first signs of trouble. What to log. The range test curve, loss against rate on a log axis, with the chosen peak marked. The schedule rendered over the step axis, saved in the run directory so a reviewer can read it without running anything. Per step: step, learning rate, gradient L2 norm and loss, in that order. The capstone lesson's rule is that a healthy warmup shows the norm rising with the rate and settling after the peak, and that a peak set too high shows a norm that stays high. The four schedule numbers in a versioned config, with the warmup as a fraction of the total so the choice survives a longer run. Defaults for when there is no time. The optimizers lesson's fallback: AdamW at 3e-4 with weight decay 0.01 for an unknown model, 2e-5 for fine-tuning a pretrained one. Treat these as the starting point of the range test, not as its result. Plausible wrong answers. "Use 3e-4 for Adam, it always works." It is the lesson's starting default when nothing is known, not a result; the range test takes minutes and replaces a guess with a measurement. "Pick the rate with the lowest loss in the range test." The lowest point sits next to divergence; the lesson picks about 10 times lower than the steepest fall. "A constant rate is fine if it is the right one." The right rate changes during training; a constant that fits the start is too large at the end, and the lesson keeps constant rates for small models and debugging. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why set the peak below the steepest point rather than at it? Expected: the steepest point is close to where the loss starts to diverge, and a long run needs a margin; one order of magnitude lower keeps it. (level 4) When do you choose 1cycle over warmup plus cosine? Expected: a short, fixed budget where the total step count is known; it converges faster for a fixed compute and needs the step count in advance. (level 4) The peak is right and the loss still oscillates near the end. What do you adjust? Expected: the decay, not the peak; a schedule that ends too high leaves steps too large for the final minimum, so lower the floor or lengthen the decay. (level 4) How does the model's size change the plan? Expected: sweep the peak on a smaller version first as a prior, then confirm with the range test on the full model, because the optimum shifts with size. Where it is taught. The debugging lesson builds the range test, the learning rate schedules lesson compares the schedules and gives the decision flow, the optimizers lesson gives the fallback defaults, and the cosine warmup capstone sets the logging schema. A There are no debugging tools for neural networks B Networks can produce wrong outputs without any error messages or crashes -- the code runs but the results are silently incorrect C Neural networks use different programming languages D Neural networks can't be tested Traditional bugs crash or throw exceptions. Neural network bugs produce a number that's just wrong -- a loss that doesn't decrease, accuracy that plateaus, or outputs that are subtly incorrect. No error message tells you what went wrong. Q2 What is the 'overfit one batch' debugging technique? A Training on the full dataset until it overfits B Overfitting the validation set C Using a very large batch size D Training on a single small batch until the loss reaches near-zero, verifying the model can memorize at least a few examples If your model can't memorize a tiny batch (e.g., 4-8 samples) to near-zero loss, something is fundamentally broken: wrong architecture, broken loss function, or incorrect training loop. This is the first diagnostic to run. Q3 Your loss is NaN after a few training steps. What is the most likely cause? A The model has too few parameters B The activation function is wrong C Exploding gradients or numerical overflow, often from a learning rate that's too high or missing gradient clipping D The dataset is too small NaN loss typically comes from numerical overflow: gradients explode, weights grow unbounded, and operations like log(0) or exp(1000) produce infinity/NaN. Lower the learning rate or add gradient clipping. Q4 Your training loss decreases but validation loss stays flat from the start. What does this indicate? A The model is learning training data patterns but they don't generalize -- likely a data pipeline issue (train/val data mismatch) or severe overfitting B The learning rate is too low C The model needs more layers D The model is overfitting If validation loss never improves, the model is either memorizing training noise (overfitting), or there's a data pipeline bug where train and validation distributions are fundamentally different. Q5 What should you check first when your loss curve is completely flat (loss doesn't decrease at all)? A Try a different architecture B Switch to a different optimizer C Verify gradients are nonzero, the learning rate is high enough, and the loss function actually depends on the model's predictions D Add more training data A flat loss means the model isn't updating. Common causes: zero gradients (dead neurons, detached tensors), learning rate too small, or a loss function that doesn't flow gradients to the model (e.g., using .item() before .backward()). Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Word2vec The 2013 method that learns word vectors by predicting nearby words Lesson 5.7 Embedding model A model that turns a piece of text into one vector that captures its meaning Lesson 7.13 Vector search Finding text by meaning: embed the query and return the stored passages whose vectors are closest Lesson 14.26 GloVe Word vectors learned from counts of how often words appear together Lesson 5.7 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.37 Why this came about Networks need numbers, but much of the world comes in categories: words, products, users, cities. Early systems used hand-made codes or giant one-hot vectors. In 2003 Yoshua Bengio and colleagues trained a language model that learned a small vector for every word as part of predicting the next word, and noticed that similar words ended up with similar vectors. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov's word2vec later · 5.7 at Google made learning such vectors fast enough to run on billions of words, and showed they captured meaning ("Paris" relates to "France" as "Tokyo" relates to "Japan"). The same trick spread to products, songs and users in recommendation systems. Every language model begins with an embedding table, and the embedding models later · 7.13 used for search in the Retrieval (RAG) section are its descendants. In plain words first Giving everything an address on a map of meaning Imagine placing every product in a supermarket on a map, so that things bought together sit close to each other: bread near butter, tea near biscuits, diapers near baby wipes. Each product's position (a few coordinates) is its embedding . You do not draw the map by hand: you start with everything scattered randomly, then repeatedly nudge products that appear in the same baskets closer together and unrelated ones apart. After enough nudges, the map's layout reflects how products are actually used. Word embeddings are the same map, for words, learned from which words appear near each other in text. Step 1 · Categories are not numbers Suppose a network should use "which product" as an input. Two obvious encodings both have problems: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output ID numbers suggest a false order and size: to a network, diapers (8) would be "more" than tea (5), and halfway between them would mean something. It means nothing. One-hot vectors avoid that, but every product is exactly as different from every other (cosine 0, Lesson 1.2 ): bread is no closer to butter than to a sponge. They are also as long as the number of categories: a language model's vocabulary of 50,000 to 200,000 tokens would need vectors that long, almost all zeros. What you want is a short vector per item, where similar items have similar vectors . That is an embedding. Three ways to turn a category into numbers. An ID number implies a false order. A one-hot vector makes every product equally different from every other. An embedding table gives each product a short learned vector; looking up its row is the same as multiplying the one-hot vector by the table, and training moves similar products to similar rows. Step 2 · An embedding is a lookup table An embedding table has one row per item and a chosen number of columns (the embedding dimension , from a handful to several thousand). The vector for item i is simply row i . Multiplying a one-hot vector by the table gives exactly that row, so an embedding layer is a linear layer whose input is one-hot, done efficiently by looking the row up. Copy What you should see Copy The rows start random, and they are parameters like any weight: backpropagation updates the rows that were used, so training moves them wherever they help reduce the loss. What the vectors end up meaning depends entirely on the task they were trained for. Step 3 · Learning embeddings from baskets Here are 400 shopping baskets. Behind the scenes there are four kinds of shopping trip (breakfast, tea time, baby, cleaning), and milk belongs to three of them, plus some random noise. The model is never told about the groups. Copy What you should see Copy The training task: for a pair bought together, make the dot product of their two vectors large (so the sigmoid of it is near 1, "yes, these go together"). For randomly chosen pairs, called negative samples , make it small. That is logistic regression ( Lesson 2.6 ) where the "features" are the embeddings themselves, and it is how word2vec works. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code emb(a) looks up a vector for every pair's first product: shape (number of pairs, 8). * emb(b) then .sum(dim=-1) is a row-by-row dot product. unsqueeze(1) adds a dimension so each pair's vector lines up with its 3 negatives: (pairs, 1, 8) times (pairs, 3, 8) broadcasts to (pairs, 3, 8). F.logsigmoid(s) is log(sigmoid(s)) , computed safely. The loss is binary cross-entropy ( Lesson 2.6 ): label 1 for real pairs, label 0 for negatives (since 1 − sigmoid(s) = sigmoid(−s)). The loss levels off rather than reaching 0: random negatives sometimes happen to be products that do go together, and the noisy baskets add contradictions. That is normal. word2vec keeps two separate tables (one for the item, one for its neighbours); a single shared table is simpler and works well here. Now ask which products ended up closest to each other, by cosine similarity : Copy What you should see Copy The 15 product embeddings learned in Step 3 of Lesson 3.19, squashed from 8 numbers to 2 with PCA ( Lesson 2.11 ). Nobody told the model about breakfast, tea, babies or cleaning; it learned the groups from which products appear in the same baskets. Milk, bought with three of the four groups, belongs to none of the clusters: it sits on its own, partly similar to each. Reading this output Diapers sit next to baby wipes and baby food, tea next to biscuits and sugar, the sponge next to the other cleaning products, with similarities near 1. The groups were discovered purely from what was bought together. Milk is moderately similar (about 0.5) to products from three different groups, because it belongs to all three. One vector has to compromise between its uses. unit @ unit.T computes every pairwise cosine similarity in one matrix multiplication : once vectors have length 1, a dot product is the cosine ( Lesson 1.2 ). Vector search later · 14.26 in Lesson 14.26 does exactly this, at scale. Step 4 · Embeddings inside a language model The first layer of every language model is an embedding table with one row per token in its vocabulary. GPT-2's has 50,257 rows of 768 numbers: Copy What you should see Copy About 38.6 million of GPT-2 small's 124 million parameters are this one table. Its rows are trained, like your product vectors, by backpropagation from the next-token prediction loss: tokens used in similar ways end up with similar rows. Many models also reuse the same table, transposed, as the final layer that produces one score per token ( Lesson 2.6 ), called weight tying ; GPT-2 does this. There is one important difference from your products. A token's row in the table is the same wherever the token appears, so "bank" in "river bank" and in "bank account" starts from the same vector. These are static embeddings . Inside a transformer , every layer mixes in information from the surrounding tokens (attention, the Transformers, step by step section), so by the upper layers each token has a contextual embedding that depends on its sentence. Modern text embedding models used for search ( Lesson 14.26 ) take these contextual vectors and combine them into one vector per sentence or paragraph ( Lesson 7.13 ). First explained in Lesson 10.10; the hands-on workshop is Lessons 7.25 to 11.17 Lesson 10.10 LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 Why this came about Neural networks are old; what changed around 2012 was compute. Graphics cards (GPUs), built to colour millions of pixels at once for video games, turned out to be ideal for the matrix multiplications at the core of networks. In 2012 AlexNet , trained on two gaming GPUs, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a wide margin, and deep learning took off. Since then the compute used to train the largest models has grown roughly four- to fivefold per year, and a big part of the engineering of modern AI is squeezing more useful arithmetic out of each chip: lower-precision numbers, careful memory use, and splitting work across thousands of GPUs. In plain words first A kitchen with many cooks A CPU is like a kitchen with a few master chefs: each can cook anything, quickly, one dish after another. A GPU is like a kitchen with ten thousand assistants who can each only chop, but all chop at the same time. Making one complicated dish? Use the chefs. Chopping a mountain of onions? The assistants win by a mile. Training and running neural networks is a mountain of onions: billions of identical multiply-and-add steps. Step 1 · Counting the arithmetic Multiplying an (m × k) matrix by a (k × n) matrix does m × n × k multiplications and about as many additions: 2 × m × n × k floating-point operations (FLOPs) . A layer with d_in inputs and d_out outputs, applied to one input vector, is 2 × d_in × d_out FLOPs: two per weight. So a whole model costs about 2 × (number of parameters) FLOPs per token to run. Copy What you should see Copy A modern data-centre GPU (an NVIDIA H100, say) can do roughly 10¹⁵ FLOPs per second in 16-bit arithmetic. On paper that is over 60,000 tokens per second for an 8B model. Real generation is much slower, for a reason Step 5 explains: memory, not arithmetic, is usually the bottleneck. Step 2 · Why GPUs A CPU has a few powerful cores that run varied tasks one after another very quickly. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that all do the same kind of arithmetic at once. A neural network is mostly matrix multiplication, millions of independent multiply-adds, which is exactly the GPU's kind of work. Even on a CPU, the gap between doing arithmetic one number at a time in Python and handing a whole array to optimised code is huge: Copy What you should see Copy On a typical laptop the loops take around a second and NumPy well under a millisecond: thousands of times faster (the exact ratio depends on your machine, which is why the code prints a yes/no instead). NumPy uses the CPU's vector instructions and several cores. A GPU takes the same idea much further, with thousands of cores and special tensor cores that multiply small blocks of matrices in one step, and very fast memory next to them. That is why PyTorch code that moves tensors .to("cuda") ( Lesson 3.16 ) can run tens to hundreds of times faster than on a CPU. Step 3 · Number formats: range versus precision How computers store decimal numbers. A floating-point number has a sign bit, exponent bits (how big: the range) and mantissa bits (how precise). float16 and bfloat16 both use 16 bits but split them differently: bfloat16 keeps float32 's range and gives up precision, which suits training. int8 and int4 store whole numbers plus a shared scale. Every number in a model takes space and time to move. Using fewer bits per number means less memory and faster arithmetic, but each format makes a different trade-off between range (how big or small a number can be) and precision (how finely it can distinguish nearby values): Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output float32 handles all three cases well. It was the standard for training until about 2017. float16 overflows: its largest number is 65,504, so 70,000 becomes inf . Large activations or gradients in float16 training can overflow, which is why float16 training needs a trick called loss scaling. bfloat16 ("brain float", from Google) keeps float32's range (70,000 is fine, stored as 70,144) but has very little precision: 256 + 1 = 256, because the gap between neighbouring bfloat16 numbers near 256 is 2. Training mostly tolerates that, and bfloat16 is today's standard format for training and running LLMs . In practice, training uses mixed precision : the big matrix multiplications run in bfloat16, while a float32 master copy of the weights collects the small updates, which would otherwise be rounded away (as the +1 was). Newer GPUs add fp8 (one byte, used for parts of training and serving the largest models) and even 4-bit floating-point formats. The direction of travel is clear: fewer bits per number, used carefully. Step 4 · Quantisation: storing weights as small integers To run a trained model, you can go further and store weights as 8-bit or 4-bit integers plus a scale factor, called quantisation . Each weight becomes a whole number from −127 to 127 (8 bits) or −7 to 7 (4 bits), and is multiplied back by the scale when used. Copy What you should see Copy 8-bit is nearly lossless here. 4-bit with a single scale for all 4,096 weights is crude, because the one largest weight sets the step size for everyone. Giving each group of 32 weights its own scale nearly halves the error, at the cost of storing the extra scales. Real 4-bit methods ( GPTQ later · 3.25 , AWQ later · 3.25 , the GGUF later · 10.33 formats used by llama.cpp later · 10.33 and Ollama later · 10.33 ) use groups like this plus cleverer rounding, and a good 4-bit version of a model usually performs close to the original. That is how an 8B model runs on a laptop ( Lesson 10.33 ). Step 5 · Memory: the real bottleneck To run a model, its weights must fit in the GPU's memory: parameters × bytes per parameter. To generate each token, every weight must be read from memory once, so generation speed is usually limited by memory bandwidth (how many bytes per second can be read), not by arithmetic. To train , you need far more ( Lesson 3.6 ): gradients, the optimiser's two running averages per weight ( Lesson 3.12 ), and a float32 master copy, about 16 bytes per parameter with AdamW in mixed precision, before counting activations. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output An 8B model needs 16 GB in bfloat16: one 24 GB gaming GPU can run it. In 4-bit it needs 4 GB, which fits on a laptop. A 70B model needs 140 GB in bfloat16 (two 80 GB data-centre GPUs) but 35 GB in 4-bit, which fits on one 48 GB card. Add memory for the KV cache later · 7.19 , the stored attention values for every token of the conversation so far, which grows with context length and the number of users (Lessons 11.21 and 7.19 ). Training even the 8B model needs about 128 GB just for weights, gradients and optimiser state: more than one GPU. That is why fine-tuning later · 10.10 usually uses LoRA later · 3.24 , which trains a small set of extra weights instead of all of them ( Lesson 14.139 ). Step 6 · The cost of training The rule of thumb from Lesson 3.6 : training costs about 6 FLOPs per parameter per training token (2 for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass). With the GPU's speed and a realistic utilisation (about 40% of the peak is good in practice), you get GPU-hours: Copy What you should see Copy These are lower bounds. Meta reported about 1.3 million H100 hours for Llama 3 8B and 6.4 million for Llama 3 70B (2024); real runs lose time to restarts, slower phases and experiments. At a few dollars per GPU-hour, pretraining a frontier-scale model costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, which is why most teams start from a pretrained model and adapt it (the From language model to assistant and Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning sections). Step 7 · Many GPUs at once A big model does not fit on one GPU, and a big training run would take years on one. Work is split in a few standard ways, often combined: Technique What is split When it is used Data parallelism each GPU has the whole model and trains on different batches; gradients are averaged whenever the model fits on one GPU FSDP / ZeRO weights, gradients and optimiser state are sharded across GPUs and gathered when needed the usual way to train models too big for one GPU Tensor parallelism each layer's matrices are split across the GPUs in one server very large layers; also used to serve big models Pipeline parallelism different layers live on different GPUs very deep models spread over many servers You do not need to implement these; libraries such as PyTorch FSDP, DeepSpeed and the serving engines in Lesson 14.111 do. But they explain the hardware words you will hear: GPUs inside one server are linked by very fast connections (such as NVLink), and servers by fast networks, because these methods constantly exchange data. The same idea as a formula matrix multiplication (m × k) @ (k × n): 2mkn FLOPs inference: ≈ 2N FLOPs per token for a model with N parameters training: ≈ 6ND FLOPs for N parameters and D training tokens memory for weights: N × bytes per parameter (4 fp32, 2 bf16, 1 int8 or fp8, 0.5 for 4-bit) training with AdamW in mixed precision: ≈ 16N bytes, plus activations symmetric quantisation: q = round(w / s), s = max|w| / (2^(b−1) − 1), ŵ = q · s Check your mental model ✗ "A bigger GPU always makes my chatbot answer faster." ✓ Generation speed is mostly limited by how fast weights can be read from memory. More memory bandwidth, smaller (quantised) weights or batching many users together help most. ✗ "Lower precision always ruins accuracy." ✓ bfloat16 is the standard for training, and good 4-bit quantisation loses little for running models. Range problems (float16 overflow) and very crude quantisation are the real risks. ✗ "If a GPU can run a model, it can fine-tune it." ✓ Full training needs roughly eight times the memory of bf16 inference. That gap is why LoRA and QLoRA exist. Exercises Predict before you run In bfloat16, what is torch.tensor(1000.0, dtype=torch.bfloat16) + 3 ? (Hint: bfloat16 has 8 bits of precision, so between 512 and 1024 the gap between neighbouring numbers is 4.) (Solution P1.) Make it your own Use weights_gb to find the largest model that fits in 4-bit on a laptop GPU with 12 GB of memory, keeping 3 GB free for the KV cache and everything else. (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A team wants to fine-tune a 3B model fully (not LoRA) with AdamW in mixed precision. Roughly how much memory do the weights, gradients and optimiser state need, and does that fit on one 80 GB GPU? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Rounding in bfloat16 1000 + 3 = 1003 , which bfloat16 cannot store; neighbouring representable numbers near 1000 are 4 apart (..., 996, 1000, 1004, ...), so it rounds to 1004 (the nearest). Small additions to large numbers get rounded, sometimes to nothing: the reason training keeps a float32 master copy of the weights. Solution M1 · Fitting a laptop 12 − 3 = 9 GB for weights. At 0.5 bytes per parameter, that is 9 / 0.5 = 18 billion parameters. In practice 4-bit files also store scales and keep some layers at higher precision, so models up to about 14B are a comfortable fit, and 8B models leave plenty of room for long contexts. Solution X1 · Full fine-tuning memory 16 bytes × 3 billion = 48 GB before activations. It fits on one 80 GB GPU if activations are kept modest (small batches, shorter sequences, or activation checkpointing, which recomputes activations instead of storing them). A 7B or 8B model (112 to 128 GB) would not fit on one GPU, so it needs sharding across several GPUs or LoRA. Recap A matrix multiply costs 2mkn FLOPs; running a model costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, training about 6 per parameter per token. GPUs run thousands of identical multiply-adds in parallel, which is exactly what neural networks need. float16 risks overflow; bfloat16 keeps the range with less precision and is the training standard; mixed precision keeps a float32 master copy. Quantisation stores weights as small integers plus scales; 8-bit is nearly lossless and grouped 4-bit is good enough to run large models on small hardware. Memory decides what you can run (weights plus KV cache) and train (about 16 bytes per parameter); large training runs split work across many GPUs.
