l2407: Course home / Phase 3 · Deep Learning and Neural Networks Networks that see: convolution, CNNs and the road to vision transformers Lesson 3.21 60 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Describe an image as a grid of numbers, and apply a convolution filter to it by hand Explain why sharing one small filter across the whole image needs far fewer weights and recognises a pattern wherever it appears Build and train a small convolutional network in PyTorch, and read the shape of the data at every layer Place CNNs in the history of AI, and say how vision transformers and today's multimodal models relate to them Before you start Needs : Lesson 3.16 (PyTorch and the training loop) and Lesson 3.4 (layers). Lesson 0.14 (NumPy arrays and shapes) is used throughout. Depth : Core, and short. You will not build vision systems in this course, but convolution is one of the central ideas of deep learning, and image encoders sit inside every multimodal model. Time : about 60 minutes. Next : the Language as data: NLP foundations section turns to language. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Convolutional neural network (CNN) A network that slides small filters across an image, so the same pattern detector is used everywhere Vision Filter A small grid of weights that responds to one local pattern, such as an edge CNNs Feature map The output of sliding one filter across an image CNNs Weight sharing Using the same weights at every position CNNs Max pooling Shrinking a feature map by keeping the largest value in each small window CNNs Data augmentation Making extra training examples by altering existing ones, such as shifting or flipping Training Transfer learning Starting from a model trained on one task and adapting it to another Fine-tuning Vision transformer (ViT) A transformer that treats patches of an image as tokens Multimodal models Mentioned here, taught later 5 Transformer, Encoder-decoder, Diffusion model, CLIP, Fine-tuning This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.8 Encoder-decoder A transformer with both parts, such as T5 Lesson 7.13 Diffusion model A model that learns to remove noise step by step, and generates by starting from pure noise Lesson 10.34 CLIP A model trained to place images and their captions near each other in one vector space Lesson 10.34 Fine-tuning Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so that its behaviour changes. First explained in Lesson 10.10; the hands-on workshop is Lessons 7.25 to 11.17 Lesson 10.10 Why this came about Early neural networks treated an image as one long list of pixels, with a separate weight from every pixel to every neuron. That wastes weights and has to relearn a pattern at every position where it might appear. In 1989 Yann LeCun trained a network for reading handwritten postcodes that instead slid small shared filters across the image: a convolutional neural network (CNN). It worked, banks used it to read cheques, and then the idea waited for data and computing power. In 2012 a larger CNN, AlexNet , trained on GPUs , won the ImageNet competition by a margin that surprised the whole field. That result started the deep learning era ( Lesson 3.1 ). CNNs dominated computer vision for the next eight years, until transformers later · 7.8 arrived there too. In plain words first A small stencil slid across the picture Imagine checking a page for the letter "T" with a small cardboard stencil. You place the stencil on the top-left corner, see how well what is underneath matches, move it one step, and repeat until you have covered the page. You end up with a map of where the pattern appears. A convolutional layer does this with many stencils at once, and it learns what the stencils should look for. The first layer learns simple stencils such as edges; the next layer slides stencils over the first layer's maps and finds combinations such as corners and loops; and so on up to whole objects. Step 1 · An image is a grid of numbers A greyscale image is a table of brightness values. scikit-learn ships with 1,797 small handwritten digits, each 8 pixels by 8, with brightness from 0 (black) to 16 (white). A colour image is three such grids stacked (red, green, blue), called channels . Copy What you should see Copy On the left are the numbers the computer sees; on the right the same numbers drawn as characters, so you can see the 7. Step 2 · Convolution by hand A filter (or kernel ) is a small grid of weights. To apply it, lay it over a 3 × 3 patch of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel under it, and add the nine products into one number. Then slide one pixel along and repeat. This filter has −1 on the left and +1 on the right, so it gives a large positive number wherever the image gets brighter from left to right: a vertical-edge detector . Convolution. A small grid of weights (the filter, here 3 × 3) is placed on a patch of the image; the nine pairs of numbers are multiplied and added to give one output number. The filter then slides one step and repeats. The same nine weights are used at every position, so a pattern is recognised wherever it appears. Copy What you should see Copy The output is 6 × 6 because a 3 × 3 window fits in 6 positions across an 8-pixel row. Large positive numbers mark places where the stroke of the 7 begins as you move right; large negative numbers mark where it ends. The output is called a feature map : a map of where the feature was found. Reading this output Four things to notice The filter has 9 weights and they are reused at all 36 positions. A fully connected layer from 64 pixels to 36 outputs would need 2,304 weights. This is weight sharing . Each output looks only at a small local patch. Nearby pixels matter to each other far more than distant ones, and convolution builds that assumption in. If the digit moves two pixels right, the feature map moves two pixels right too, with the same values. This is translation equivariance : the network does not have to relearn the pattern at each position. In a CNN nobody designs the filters. They start random and are learned by gradient descent , like every other weight ( Lesson 3.6 ). Step 3 · A fair test: digits that move To see what convolution buys, set up an experiment. Put each digit on a larger 12 × 12 black canvas. Train on digits placed in the centre. Then test on digits moved a few pixels, which a person would find no harder. Copy What you should see Copy PyTorch expects images as (number of images, channels, height, width). There is one channel because the images are greyscale. Step 4 · Two networks The first model is the kind you built in Lesson 3.16 : flatten the 144 pixels and pass them through fully connected layers (a multi-layer perceptron , MLP). The second is a small CNN. The small CNN of this lesson. Convolution layers detect local patterns; pooling shrinks the grid and keeps the strongest responses; the last pooling asks only whether each pattern appeared anywhere, which is what makes the result insensitive to where the digit sits. A final linear layer turns the 32 answers into 10 scores. Max pooling on a 6 by 6 feature map with 2 by 2 windows: each window is replaced by its largest value, giving a 3 by 3 map. The strongest response survives; its exact position inside the window is forgotten, which is what makes the network tolerant of small shifts. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Follow the shape down the table. The first convolution turns 1 channel into 16 feature maps of the same size ( padding=1 adds a border of zeros so the size is kept). Max pooling keeps the largest value in each 2 × 2 block, halving the grid: small shifts and details are thrown away, strong responses are kept. The second convolution builds 32 maps from the 16. The last pooling keeps one number per map: the strongest response anywhere. The CNN has about half as many parameters as the MLP. Reading this output Reading the layer names Layer What it does Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1) 16 filters of 3 × 3, each applied to 1 input channel: 16 × 9 weights + 16 biases = 160 ReLU() Sets negative responses to zero ( Lesson 3.4 ) MaxPool2d(2) Keeps the maximum of each 2 × 2 block Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1) 32 filters, each 3 × 3 across all 16 input channels: 32 × 16 × 9 + 32 = 4,640 AdaptiveMaxPool2d(1) Reduces each map to its single largest value ( global pooling ) Linear(32, 10) One score per digit class Step 5 · Train both, then move the digits The experiment that shows what convolution buys. Train the fully connected network (the MLP) and the convolutional network on the same centred digits, measure both, and then measure again after shifting every test digit a few pixels sideways. The digits have not changed; only their position has. Copy What you should see Copy On centred digits the two models are equally good. Move the digit and the MLP collapses: it learned "this pixel is usually bright for a 7", and now the 7 is somewhere else. The CNN, with half the parameters and no shifted examples in training, still reads most of them, because its filters respond to strokes wherever they are and the global pooling asks only whether each pattern appeared. (It does better on a 2-pixel shift than a 1-pixel shift because 2 pixels lines up exactly with the 2 × 2 pooling grid; real networks reduce this effect with more layers and with training on shifted, rotated and cropped copies, called data augmentation .) What did the first layer learn? Copy What you should see Copy These are less tidy than the hand-made filter of Step 2, but the pattern is the same: positive weights next to negative ones, so each filter responds to a change in brightness in some direction. Nobody told the network to look for edges and strokes; it found that they are useful. In networks trained on photographs the first-layer filters reliably become edge, colour and texture detectors, which is one of the most reproduced findings in deep learning. From CNNs to today Year Model What it added 1989–1998 LeNet Convolution and pooling, trained by backpropagation ; read cheques and postcodes 2012 AlexNet A deep CNN on GPUs with ReLU and dropout ; won ImageNet and started the deep learning boom 2014 VGG , GoogLeNet Much deeper stacks of small filters 2015 ResNet Residual connections ( Lesson 3.12 ) made 100-layer networks trainable; still a standard backbone 2015 U-Net An encoder-decoder later · 7.13 CNN for labelling every pixel; later the core of image diffusion models later · 10.34 ( Lesson 10.34 ) 2015 on YOLO and relatives Fast object detection: boxes and labels in one pass 2020 Vision Transformer (ViT) Cuts the image into patches, treats each patch as a token, and applies a transformer (the Transformers, step by step section). No convolutions 2021 CLIP later · 10.34 An image encoder and a text encoder trained so that a picture and its caption get similar vectors ( Lesson 10.34 ) 2023 on Vision-language models An image encoder (usually a ViT) feeding a large language model Two landmark CNNs drawn layer by layer, input at the bottom. LeNet (left, 1998) read 28 by 28 digit images with two convolution layers. AlexNet (right, 2012) used the same recipe, only deeper and wider, on 224 by 224 photographs, and started the deep learning era. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . A vision transformer. The image is cut into patches (bottom left), each patch becomes a vector like a token embedding, a position encoding is added, and the sequence goes through an ordinary transformer encoder. No convolution is involved. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . Transfer learning , the practice that made pretrained vision models useful to everyone: copy every layer of a model trained on a large dataset (left), replace only the output layer for your own classes (right), and train briefly on your smaller dataset. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Two ideas from this history are used every day in the rest of this course. Transfer learning began here: take a network pretrained on ImageNet, keep its layers as a general feature extractor, and train only a new final layer on a few hundred of your own images. That is the same move as fine-tuning later · 10.10 a language model (the Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning section). And the patch-as-token idea of the ViT is how language models "see": Lesson 10.34 shows an image entering a language model as a row of patch vectors. Reading this output Do CNNs still matter? Yes. Transformers win on very large datasets, but convolutions remain efficient and data-frugal. CNNs and hybrids run most on-device and real-time vision: phone cameras, factory inspection, medical imaging, number-plate and document readers. Convolution layers also sit inside speech models such as Whisper (to shorten the audio sequence) and inside image generators. When this course uses a vision model, it will be through an API or a pretrained model , and you now know the two kinds of machinery that can be inside. Check your mental model ✗ "A CNN is a different kind of learning." ✓ It is an ordinary neural network trained by backpropagation, with layers whose weights are shared across positions. ✗ "Someone programs the filters to find edges." ✓ Filters start random and are learned. Edge detectors emerge because they are useful. ✗ "Pooling loses information, so it must hurt." ✓ It deliberately discards exact positions, which makes the network tolerant of small shifts and cheaper to run. ✗ "Vision transformers made convolution obsolete." ✓ Both are in wide use. Many strong models combine them. See it drawn These are well-known explanations whose pictures belong to their authors, so they are linked here and not copied. If the input were a colour image with 3 channels, how many parameters would that layer have? What if the filters were 5 × 5 on 1 channel? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Write a horizontal-edge filter (−1 in the top row, +1 in the bottom row) and apply it with convolve to the same digit. Where are the largest responses, and which part of the 7 do they mark? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Replace nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d(1) with nn.MaxPool2d(2) followed by nn.Flatten() and a nn.Linear(32 * 3 * 3, 10) layer, retrain, and run the shift test again. Explain the result using the idea of "where" against "whether". (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Counting convolution weights Each filter spans all input channels. With 3 channels: 16 × (3 × 3 × 3) + 16 = 448. With 5 × 5 on 1 channel: 16 × 25 + 16 = 416. The number of parameters does not depend on the size of the image at all, which is why CNNs scale to large pictures. Solution M1 · A horizontal-edge detector np.array([[-1, -1, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]) . Positive responses appear where the image gets brighter going down, such as the top edge of the bar across the 7 and the top of its long stroke; negative responses appear under the bar. Vertical and horizontal detectors together already describe much of a digit's shape, and the network learns 16 such detectors at many angles. Solution X1 · Where against whether With a flatten-and-linear ending, the last layer has a separate weight for each of the 3 × 3 positions of each map, so it learns where each pattern usually is for centred digits. Accuracy on shifted digits drops sharply, closer to the MLP. Global pooling throws the position away and keeps only whether the pattern appeared, which is what makes the classifier tolerant of shifts. Many modern networks end with global pooling for this reason. Recap An image is a grid of numbers per colour channel. A convolution slides a small filter over it and produces a feature map of where the filter's pattern occurs. Sharing the filter's weights across positions means few parameters and the same response wherever the pattern appears. A CNN stacks convolution, ReLU and pooling; early layers learn edges, later layers combinations. Filters are learned. On digits moved a few pixels, a small CNN kept working where a fully connected network failed. AlexNet (2012) began the deep learning era. Vision transformers treat image patches as tokens, and image encoders now feed language models. Check your understanding Q1 What does "weight sharing" mean in a convolutional layer? A Two layers use the same weights B The same small filter is applied at every position of the image C All filters have identical values D The weights are copied from a pretrained model One set of filter weights is reused across the whole image, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears. Q2 Why did the fully connected network fail on digits moved two pixels to the right? A It had too few parameters B It was trained for too few epochs C It learned which exact pixels are bright for each digit, and those pixels changed D The images became darker With a separate weight per pixel, a shifted image is a different input as far as the network is concerned. Q3 How does a vision transformer turn an image into something a transformer can process? A It converts the image to text with OCR B It applies a convolution to every pixel C It cuts the image into patches and treats each patch as a token D It lists the pixels one by one as tokens Each patch becomes one vector, and attention then relates the patches to each other. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Catastrophic forgetting Losing general skills after fine-tuning hard on a narrow task Lesson 3.23 Why this came about General embedding models do not know a company's vocabulary, acronyms or product names. Fine-tuning embedding models on pairs of queries and relevant passages became practical with open models and libraries, as a way to lift retrieval after the cheaper fixes were exhausted. In plain words first Teaching the search your company's vocabulary General embedding models do not know that "SKU" and "item code" mean the same in your company, or that two product names are related. Fine-tuning an embedding model on pairs of queries and the passages that answer them pulls those together in its space. It can lift retrieval noticeably, but needs good training pairs, re-embedding the whole collection, and careful evaluation against the original model. Fine-tuning an embedding model How this connects Lesson 14.26 used an embedding model as it came. Lesson 7.13 showed where such models come from: a transformer encoder trained so that matching texts get nearby vectors. This lesson trains one further on your own vocabulary. It is the same kind of training as the fine-tuning workshop of the Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning section (Lessons 7.25 to 3.25 ), applied to an embedding model instead of a chat model; you do not need that workshop first, only the PyTorch training loop of Lesson 3.16 . Off-the-shelf embedding models are trained on general web text. When your queries use internal jargon, product codes or a specialist domain (legal clauses, part numbers, medical coding), fine-tuning the embedding model on your own query-and-passage pairs often lifts recall more than any index setting. The shape of the model being trained. Both texts go through the same encoder (the diagram says BERT; any encoder works), each is pooled to one vector, and the loss rewards a high cosine similarity for matching pairs and a low one for the rest. Figure: Sentence Transformers documentation , Apache 2.0 . Embedding models are bi-encoders : the query and the document are embedded separately, so documents can be embedded once and searched fast. (A reranker is a cross-encoder , which reads query and document together: more accurate, too slow to run over a whole corpus; Lesson 5.22 .) Bi-encoders are trained with a contrastive loss, usually InfoNCE : in each batch, the matching passage must score higher than every other passage, which act as negatives. The negatives decide how much the model learns. Random passages are too easy; hard negatives , passages on the same topic that do not answer the query, are where the signal is. Copy What you should see Copy With random negatives the loss is already near zero, so there is nothing to learn. With hard negatives the loss is large, and reducing it teaches exactly the fine distinctions your search needs. The practical recipe: Collect pairs : real queries with the passage a person clicked, accepted or cited; or generate synthetic questions for each chunk with an LLM and filter them. Mine hard negatives : retrieve the top results for each query with the current model and keep the ones labeled wrong (check they are truly wrong, or you teach the model to push away correct answers). Train : Sentence Transformers' MultipleNegativesRankingLoss implements in-batch InfoNCE; larger batches give more negatives. A few thousand good pairs and one to three epochs is a typical start. Evaluate on held-out queries with recall@k and nDCG ( Lesson 14.27 ) against the base model , then re-embed the whole corpus, because vectors from the old and new models are not comparable. Related ideas: Matryoshka training makes the first dimensions of a vector carry the most meaning, so vectors can be truncated to save memory; late interaction models such as ColBERT keep one vector per token and match token by token, between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder in cost and accuracy. Do it for real: teach an embedding model your company's shorthand The loss at the start of this lesson was computed on made-up vectors. Here is the whole recipe on a real model, in under a minute on a laptop. The setting is one every company has: internal shorthand. ShopKart's operations team talks in codes (RTO, NDR, OFD), while the wiki pages that explain each process are written in plain words and never use the codes. A general embedding model has never seen this vocabulary, so a question that uses a code cannot find its page. First, measure the problem. Copy What you should see Copy One in sixteen is what random guessing gives: 6%. The model is not weak; on ordinary customer questions it matches four of five. It simply has no idea that "RTO" has anything to do with a parcel travelling back to the seller. Now train it. The loop is the PyTorch loop of Lesson 3.16 with the InfoNCE loss from above. Each batch holds sixteen questions and their sixteen pages; every question is scored against every page, and the loss pushes the matching page to the top of its row. The other fifteen pages in the batch serve as the negatives, at no extra cost ( in-batch negatives ). Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The loss falls from 2.8 to 0.2. A loss of 2.77 is what a model gets when it is guessing among 16 pages (the natural logarithm of 16), so it started from nothing and learned the mapping in four passes. Trained wordings: 6% to 100%. Expected; the model saw those. New wordings: 6% to 100%. This is the result that matters. "ticket mentions RTO, please advise" was never in the training data, and it now finds the right page. The model did not memorise sentences; it learned what each code means and moved its vector next to the page that explains it. General questions: 4 of 5 before, 4 of 5 after. Fine-tuning on a narrow task can damage what a model already knew ( catastrophic forgetting later · 3.23 , Lesson 3.23 ). Here 96 examples and four passes did no harm to this small check. Always measure it; with more data, more passes or a higher learning rate it can go the other way. What made this work with so little data is that the task is narrow and the signal is clean: sixteen facts, each repeated in six wordings. Real projects have thousands of pages and messier pairs, which is why the recipe above spends most of its effort on collecting pairs and choosing negatives. And remember the last step: after fine-tuning, every stored vector is out of date. Vectors from the old and the new model live in different spaces, so the whole corpus must be embedded again before the new model is used for search. Check your mental model ✗ "Fine-tuning is the first fix for poor retrieval." ✓ Try hybrid search , reranking and better chunking first; they are cheaper. ✗ "After fine-tuning, only new documents need re-embedding." ✓ All stored vectors must be recomputed with the new model. ✗ "More training pairs are always better." ✓ Quality and hard negatives matter more than volume. Exercises Predict before you run In info_nce , the temperature is lowered from 0.05 to 0.01. How does that change what the loss focuses on? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Train with random negatives only. Why does the model improve little on ShopKart's confusing pairs (COD fee against COD refund)? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise After fine-tuning, recall improved on training questions but fell on new ones. Explain and fix. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Write the evaluation plan for a fine-tuned embedding model: the held-out set, the metrics, the baseline, and the re-indexing step. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Temperature sharpens A lower temperature makes the softmax sharper, so the loss concentrates on the hardest negatives, the ones scored closest to the positive. Too low makes training unstable; tune it. Solution B1 · Easy negatives teach little Random negatives are already far from the positive, so the loss is small and the model learns nothing about fine distinctions. Mine hard negatives: passages on the same topic that do not answer the query. Solution D1 · Overfitting and leakage The model memorized training pairs, or test questions leaked into training. Hold out questions (by document, not just by question), evaluate on them, use more varied data, and stop earlier. Solution M1 · Measure before you switch Held-out questions from documents not used in training; recall@k and nDCG against the base model and the current production model; then a full re-embed into a new index, compared side by side before switching an alias. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How are embedding models fine-tuned, and when is it worth it? Worked answer. With contrastive learning : pairs of a query and a relevant passage, trained so the pair scores higher than negatives in the batch (InfoNCE), with hard negatives mined from the corpus. Worth it when a domain's vocabulary or notion of relevance differs from general data and the eval shows a retrieval gap that hybrid search and reranking do not close. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tune whenever retrieval is bad." Cheaper fixes come first. Follow-ups. Where do you get training pairs? Debug a failure A fine-tuned embedding model performs worse in production than in the eval. Why? Worked answer. Production queries differ from the training and eval distribution (shorter, more Hinglish, more typos), the index was built with a different model version, or documents were embedded without the same preprocessing. Compare query and document preprocessing, and sample production queries into the eval. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tuning does not work." Distribution mismatch is the usual cause. Follow-ups. How would you collect production pairs safely? Defend a design Fine-tune an embedding model, or add a reranker? Worked answer. A reranker first: no re-indexing, and it often gives a larger precision gain. Fine-tune when recall at the candidate stage is the problem (the right passage is not in the top 50 at all), which a reranker cannot fix. Measure both. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tuning is always better because it is custom." It is more work and requires re-embedding everything. Follow-ups. How would you combine both? Check your understanding Q1 What does contrastive training teach an embedding model? A To score a query and its relevant passage higher than the negatives B To write longer answers C To compress documents D To translate queries Each query is pulled towards its relevant passage and pushed away from the others. Hard negatives carry most of the signal. Q2 The right passage is not even among the top 50 candidates. Which fix addresses that? A Adding a reranker B Improving first-stage retrieval, for example by fine-tuning the embedding model C A longer system prompt D A lower temperature A reranker can only reorder what the first stage found. When recall at the candidate stage is the problem, the retriever has to improve. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 Why this came about The recipe "pretrain on everything, then fine-tune on your task" was established for language in 2018 by ULMFiT, GPT-1 and BERT . Before it, every task needed its own model trained from nothing on its own labelled data. After it, a few hundred or thousand examples were enough, because the model arrived already knowing the language. The same recipe turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT ( Lesson 10.10 ): supervised fine-tuning on conversations. What you do in this lesson is the same procedure with the same loss function, on a model about ten thousand times smaller. In plain words first More of the same training, on your examples A fine-tune is not a new kind of training. It is the model's original training (predict the next token, measure the error, nudge the weights) continued for a short while on your examples instead of the internet. Three practical details make it work: the examples are written in the model's own chat template , so they look like conversations it already understands; the model is graded only on the answer part, so it learns to respond and is not trained to imitate customers; and the nudges are small , so it adjusts what it knows without wrecking it. Step 1 · What the model actually reads A chat is a list of messages, but a model reads one string of tokens. The tokenizer 's chat template ( Lesson 10.10 ) joins the messages with special markers. Here is one training example as the model will see it: Copy What you should see Copy <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> mark where each message begins and ends, followed by the role. This model was instruction-tuned on text in exactly this layout, which is why fine-tuning data must use it too. Never build this string by hand: always call apply_chat_template , so the format stays right if you switch models. Step 2 · Labels: grade the answer, not the question What the model is graded on. The whole conversation goes in as tokens, but the labels are set to -100 (ignored) for the system and user parts. The loss is computed only where the assistant's answer is, so the model learns to write answers and is not trained to imitate customers. Training needs two lists of the same length: the input ids (the tokens above) and the labels (what the model should predict at each position). For a causal language model the label at each position is simply the next token, and the loss function shifts them by one for you. The one decision you make is which positions count . A label of -100 tells PyTorch 's loss function to ignore that position. encode in ft_model.py sets -100 for the whole prompt and real token ids for the answer: Copy What you should see Copy The boundary is at the first token of the JSON . Everything before it, including the assistant marker, has label -100 : the model reads it as context but is not graded on predicting it. From {" onward the labels equal the token ids, ending with <|im_end|> . That last token matters: it teaches the model to stop after the JSON. A fine-tune that forgets the end marker produces models that answer correctly and then keep talking. Reading this output Why not train on the whole conversation? You can, and for general chat data it makes little difference. For a task like this one it wastes effort and can hurt: the model would spend most of its updates learning to predict what customers write, which is not its job, and the prompt is about two thirds of every example. Libraries call this option assistant-only loss or train on responses only . Step 3 · A batch Examples have different lengths, and a batch must be a rectangle. make_batch pads the shorter ones with a padding token, and builds an attention mask so the model ignores the padding ( Lesson 7.5 ): Copy What you should see Copy About a third of the real tokens are answer tokens; only those contribute to the loss. The loss before training is the model's average surprise at the correct answers ( Lesson 1.10 ): it currently gives the right next token a probability of roughly one in nine. Training will push that close to 1. One more measurement before training, to compare with afterwards: a question that has nothing to do with tickets. Copy What you should see Copy Step 4 · Train The loop in ft_model.py is the loop from Lesson 3.16 with three additions that almost every fine-tune uses: Line in train What it does Why AdamW(params, lr=5e-5) A small learning rate The weights are already good. Typical values for full fine-tuning are 1e-5 to 1e-4, ten to a hundred times smaller than training from scratch lr * min(1.0, step / 10) Warm-up : the rate climbs from zero over the first steps The first gradients on new data are large and noisy; easing in avoids damaging the model clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0) Gradient clipping Caps the size of any single update ( Lesson 3.12 ) the val_rows branch Loss on the validation set every 20 steps To see whether the model is still improving on tickets it is not training on It runs 80 steps of 8 tickets each, which is two passes ( epochs ) over the 320 training tickets: Copy What you should see Copy Both losses fall quickly and together. By step 40 the model predicts the answer tokens almost perfectly, and the second half of the run changes little. Validation loss tracks training loss closely, which here says only that validation tickets resemble training tickets. Your time will differ with your processor; with a GPU this run takes a few seconds. Reading this output Reading a loss curve during fine-tuning Both fall, then flatten : normal. Stop when validation loss stops improving. Training falls, validation rises : overfitting . The model is memorising. Stop earlier, lower the learning rate, or add data ( Lesson 2.16 ). Neither falls : the learning rate is too low, the labels are all -100 by mistake, or the weights are frozen. Loss jumps or becomes nan : the learning rate is too high. Divide it by 3 to 10. Loss is near zero from the first step : the answer has leaked into the prompt, or the model is being graded on the wrong tokens. Step 5 · Did it work? Loss is not the goal; correct routing is. Evaluate with the same function and the same test tickets as the baseline: Copy What you should see Copy Compare with Lesson 7.25 : the baseline scored 0% fully correct with instructions alone and 15% with five examples in the prompt. After a few minutes of training the format is perfect (every reply is valid JSON), and order numbers and urgency are right on every ticket, including tickets phrased in ways the model never saw. Now look at the two rows separately. On validation tickets, which use phrasings from training, everything is correct. On test tickets, with unseen phrasings, the intent is wrong more often than it is right. The model learned the output format and the copying task completely, but for the intent it leaned on the sentence patterns it was shown. In the third example it even invents an intent, pay , that is not one of the five. Four phrasings per intent were not enough for it to learn what a refund request means . Watch out The most important lesson of the workshop If you had evaluated only on the validation set, you would have shipped this model believing it was perfect. The honest number is the test score. The gap between them is not a training problem and no setting will fix it: it is a data problem, and Lesson 14.137 fixes it by adding variety, not by training harder. Step 6 · Save, reload, use A fully fine-tuned model is a complete new copy of the weights. Save it with its tokenizer (which carries the chat template), then load it back as you would any model: Copy What you should see Copy The folder holds every weight of the model as 32-bit numbers, plus the tokenizer files, the chat template and the configuration. The reloaded model routes a ticket it has never seen, written in a different style. Each fully fine-tuned variant costs this much storage; Lesson 3.24 reduces that to a few megabytes. Step 7 · What did the model forget? Fine-tuning moves the weights towards your task, and can move them away from everything else. Ask the earlier general question again, with and without the router's system prompt : Copy What you should see Copy Before training, this question got a one-sentence answer. Now, even with no system message at all, the model replies with a router-shaped JSON object and invents a key to do it. Two passes over 320 examples of one narrow job were enough to overwrite its general chat behaviour: it has become a ticket router and little else. With the router's system message it does the sensible thing for a router and files the question under other . Reading this output Catastrophic forgetting, and how to limit it Training on one narrow task pulls every weight towards that task, and abilities that the new data never exercises fade. This is catastrophic forgetting . For a model whose only job is routing it may not matter. For a model that must also chat, summarise or call tools, it is a serious regression, and you will only notice it if you test for it. The usual protections: stop as soon as validation loss flattens (here the loss was near zero by step 40, and the remaining steps only deepened the specialisation); use a smaller learning rate; mix some general examples into the training data; use a parameter-efficient method such as LoRA later · 3.24 ( Lesson 3.24 ), which leaves the original weights untouched and can be removed; and keep a short regression test of general prompts, run before and after, like the one above. The settings, and sensible starting values Setting What it controls Starting point for full fine-tuning Learning rate Size of each update 1e-5 to 5e-5 for larger models; up to 1e-4 for very small ones Epochs Passes over the training set 1 to 3. More invites memorising Batch size Examples per update As many as memory allows (8 to 32); use gradient accumulation to imitate a larger batch Warm-up Steps before the full learning rate 3% to 10% of all steps Schedule How the rate changes afterwards Constant, linear decay or cosine decay to zero Weight decay A pull towards smaller weights 0 to 0.01 Max length Longest example in tokens Long enough for your longest example; memory grows with it The same loop is what Trainer in Hugging Face Transformers and SFTTrainer in TRL run for you, with logging, checkpoints and multi-GPU support added. Lesson 14.139 shows that script; having written the loop once, every argument in it will make sense. Only held-out data that resembles real use says whether it is good. ✗ "The chat template is a formatting detail." ✓ It is the format the model was trained to understand. A different template at training or serving time quietly ruins results. ✗ "Fine-tuning adds a skill on top of what the model knew." ✓ It moves the same weights, so it can also remove abilities. Check for that. Exercises Predict before you run Change the learning rate from 5e-5 to 5e-3 (a hundred times larger) and train for 20 steps. What do you expect the loss to do, and what will the model's replies look like? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Change encode so that the labels cover the whole conversation (no -100 ). Train again for 80 steps and compare the test scores and the starting loss. Then explain the difference in starting loss. (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A colleague fine-tunes a model and reports: "training loss 0.01, validation loss 0.9 and rising after the first epoch." List three things you would check or change, in order. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A learning rate a hundred times too large The loss jumps around or grows instead of falling, and may become nan . Each update overshoots, and because every weight is being trained, a few such steps overwrite what pretraining learned. The replies turn into repeated tokens or nonsense, including for the general question. This is why fine-tuning rates are so small, and why warm-up and clipping are standard. Solution M1 · Training on the prompt as well Return p + a, p + a from encode . The starting loss is higher, because customer tickets are much harder to predict than the JSON answer and now make up most of the graded tokens. The final loss stays higher for the same reason: no model can predict a random order number or product. Test scores are usually similar or slightly worse for the same number of steps, because the updates were shared between two jobs, one of which you do not need. Solution X1 · Training loss falling, validation loss rising This is overfitting. In order: (1) check the data for duplicates and for a training set that is too small or too uniform, because that is the usual cause; (2) stop at the step where validation loss was lowest ( early stopping ) and reduce epochs; (3) lower the learning rate, or switch to LoRA with a modest rank, which has less capacity to memorise. Also confirm that validation data is formatted exactly like training data. Recap Fine-tuning is next-token training continued on your examples, written in the model's chat template. Labels of -100 hide the prompt from the loss, so the model is graded only on the answer, including the end-of-turn token. Small learning rate, warm-up and clipping protect what the model already knows. A few minutes of training took the router from 0% to 100% on phrasings it had seen, with perfect format, order numbers and urgency everywhere. On unseen phrasings the intent is often wrong: a data problem that the validation score hid. Full fine-tuning saves a complete copy of the model, and can cause forgetting. Test for it. A The token is deleted from the input B The model's prediction at that position is not counted in the loss C The token is padding and the model cannot see it D The learning rate is negative there The model still reads the token as context; the loss function just skips it. Q2 Validation accuracy is 100% and test accuracy on new phrasings is much lower. What is the most likely cause? A The learning rate was too low B The model is too small to output JSON C The training data lacks variety, so the model learned its phrasings D The test set is too large Validation data resembles training data; the gap shows what the training data failed to cover. Q3 Why must the end-of-turn token be included in the answer labels? A So the model learns to stop after the answer B So the tokenizer can decode the output C Because padding requires it D To make the loss larger Without it the model is never trained to end its turn and keeps generating. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in vLLM An open-source server for running language models with high throughput Lesson 3.25 Why this came about Full fine-tuning updates every weight and saves a complete copy of the model. For a 135-million-parameter model that is tolerable. For a 7-billion-parameter model it needs tens of gigabytes of GPU memory for training and 14 GB or more of disk for every tuned variant, and a company with fifty tasks would store and serve fifty full models. Researchers looked for ways to train only a small number of new parameters: adapters (2019) inserted small layers, prefix tuning and prompt tuning (2021) learned extra input vectors. In 2021 Edward Hu and colleagues at Microsoft published LoRA : leave every original weight frozen and learn a small low- rank correction beside it. It matched full fine-tuning on many tasks with a thousand times fewer trainable parameters, added no delay at inference, and produced a file of a few megabytes. In 2023 QLoRA combined it with 4-bit quantisation so that large models could be tuned on one consumer GPU. Together they are why fine-tuning open models became something a single engineer can do in an afternoon. In plain words first A sticky note on a textbook Full fine-tuning is rewriting a textbook to add your company's conventions: you get a whole new book. LoRA leaves the printed book untouched and adds a thin sticky note to some pages, saying "on this page, adjust the result like so". The notes are tiny compared with the book, you can peel them off to get the original back, and you can keep several sets of notes for different jobs and swap them over the same book. The surprising finding is that for most tasks a few thin notes are enough. Step 1 · The idea: a small correction beside a frozen matrix A linear layer multiplies its input by a weight matrix W ( Lesson 1.5 ). Fine-tuning changes W into W + ΔW . Full fine-tuning learns every entry of ΔW . LoRA makes a bet: the change a task needs is simple enough to be written as the product of two thin matrices, ΔW = B × A , where A squeezes the input down to a handful of numbers (the rank , r ) and B expands it back. LoRA on one layer of the 135M model. The original 576 × 576 weight matrix W is frozen. Two small matrices are trained beside it: A squeezes the input down to r = 8 numbers and B expands it back. Their product is added to the layer's output. B starts at zero, so training begins from exactly the original model. The same idea as a formula output of the layer: h = W x + (alpha / r) · B A x W has shape (d_out, d_in) and is frozen; A has shape (r, d_in); B has shape (d_out, r) at the start A holds small random numbers and B holds zeros, so B A = 0 and training begins from exactly the pretrained model trainable parameters: r × (d_in + d_out), instead of d_in × d_out alpha / r (alpha over rank) scales the correction Here is the whole method as one small PyTorch module, tried on a single layer the size of this model's attention matrices: Copy What you should see Copy The wrapped layer gives the same output as the original, because B is all zeros. And the two thin matrices hold under 3% as many numbers as the matrix they correct. Reading this output Reading this code self.base is the original layer. Setting requires_grad = False freezes it: no gradients are stored for it and the optimiser never touches it. x @ self.A.T takes the 576 input numbers down to 8; @ self.B.T takes those 8 back up to 576. Everything the layer learns about your task must pass through those 8 numbers. That bottleneck is the "low rank". self.scale = alpha / r . A common convention is alpha = 2 × r (a scale of 2). Because of this factor, changing r does not also force you to re-tune the learning rate very much. Step 2 · Add LoRA to the real model Which layers get a LoRA? The original paper adapted the query and value matrices of every attention layer ( Lesson 7.3 ), and that is still a sensible minimum. Freeze the whole model, then wrap those two layers in each of the 30 blocks: Copy What you should see Copy About one weight in three hundred will be trained. The other 134.5 million stay exactly as they were pretrained. Step 3 · Train it The training function is unchanged from Lesson 3.23 : it trains whatever parameters have requires_grad = True . The one setting that changes is the learning rate. LoRA matrices start at or near zero and there are few of them, so they need much larger steps: 1e-4 to 1e-3 is typical, where full fine-tuning used 5e-5 . Copy What you should see Copy With one weight in three hundred trainable, the model has learned the output format perfectly (every reply is valid JSON ) and copies order numbers without error, exactly as the full fine-tune did. It is weaker on urgency, and on unseen phrasings its intent accuracy is about the same as the full fine-tune's. Two attention matrices per block at rank 8 is a very small adapter; Step 5 gives it more room. Step 4 · A tiny file, and merging Only the LoRA matrices changed, so only they need saving. And because W + scale × B A is just another matrix of the same shape as W , the correction can be merged into the frozen weight afterwards, giving a plain model with no extra layers: LoRA during training (left) and after merging (right). During training the pretrained weights W are frozen (blue) and only the two small matrices A and B (orange) learn. Afterwards their product can be added into W once, giving a single merged matrix with no extra work at prediction time. Figure: Hugging Face documentation , Apache 2.0 . Copy What you should see Copy One hundred and twenty small tensors (an A and a B for each of two layers in 30 blocks) in a file almost three hundred times smaller than the model. After merging, the model produces the same outputs to within rounding error and has exactly the original number of parameters, so it runs at exactly the original speed. Reading this output Keep adapters separate, or merge them? Merged : one ordinary model. Simplest to serve, and required for some export formats ( Lesson 3.25 ). You lose the ability to remove the adapter. Separate : one base model in memory and many small adapters, chosen per request. Serving systems such as vLLM later · 3.25 load a base model once and apply the adapter each request names ( multi-LoRA serving ). This is how one deployment serves many customers' or many tasks' tuned variants. Step 5 · The same thing with the peft library Nobody wraps layers by hand in practice. Hugging Face's PEFT library (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) does it from a short configuration, handles saving and loading, and supports many methods besides LoRA. This time, adapt every linear layer in the transformer blocks (attention and feed-forward), which is the current common default, with a higher rank: Copy What you should see Copy print_trainable_parameters reports about 4.9 million trainable weights, 3.5% of the total: adapting all seven weight matrices in every block at rank 16 is a much larger adapter than Step 2's, though still a small fraction of the model. (On a 7-billion-parameter model the same settings come to well under 1%.) It reaches almost the full fine-tune's score on validation, and on the unseen phrasings of the test set it does clearly better than the full fine-tune did. Higher holds more, costs more, and overfits small data more easily lora_alpha The scale numerator; the correction is multiplied by lora_alpha / r Equal to r or 2 × r lora_dropout Dropout applied to the LoRA path during training ( Lesson 3.12 ) 0 to 0.1 target_modules Which layers get a LoRA ["q_proj", "v_proj"] (minimal), or "all-linear" (stronger, more parameters) task_type Tells PEFT how the model is used "CAUSAL_LM" for text generation Save and reload. To use it you need the base model (downloaded once, shared by every adapter) plus this file. merge_and_unload() folds the adapter in and returns an ordinary model, as Step 4 did by hand. Step 6 · What you have measured so far Model Weights trained Size of what you save Validation, all correct Test, all correct Base model, instructions only ( Lesson 7.25 ) none nothing not measured 0% Base model, five examples in the prompt ( Lesson 7.25 ) none nothing not measured 15% Full fine-tune ( Lesson 3.23 ) 134.5 million (100%) 542 MB 100% 42.5% LoRA, rank 8, query and value only 0.46 million (0.34%) 1.9 MB 75% 35% LoRA, rank 16, all linear layers 4.9 million (3.5%) 19.6 MB 97.5% 60% Two things stand out. The larger LoRA matches full fine-tuning on the data it was shown, while saving a file 27 times smaller. And it generalises better to phrasings it never saw. That is not a law, but it is a common observation: with fewer weights free to move and the original model held fixed underneath, a LoRA has less room to memorise the training sentences and keeps more of what the base model already understood about language. The full fine-tune drove its training loss to almost exactly zero, which on 320 templated tickets means it memorised them. None of these models is good enough yet. The intent is still wrong on four test tickets in ten, and Lesson 3.23 already diagnosed why: the training data has too few ways of saying each thing. Lesson 14.137 fixes that. The rest of the family Where each parameter-efficient method adds its trainable numbers. All of them freeze the pretrained weights; they differ in where the small trainable part sits. LoRA is the most used because it adds nothing to the model's speed once merged. Method What is trained Where it is used today LoRA Low-rank matrices beside chosen weight matrices The default for tuning language and image models QLoRA LoRA on a base model stored in 4 bits ( Lesson 3.25 ), with the adapters in 16-bit Tuning 7B to 70B models on a single GPU. Slightly slower training, much less memory DoRA Splits each weight into a direction and a magnitude; LoRA adjusts the direction, a small vector the magnitude Often a little better than LoRA at low ranks. LoraConfig(use_dora=True) rsLoRA LoRA with the scale alpha / √r , which behaves better at high ranks LoraConfig(use_rslora=True) when r is 64 or more Adapters Small bottleneck layers inserted after sublayers The original 2019 method. Adds a little inference delay; mostly replaced by LoRA Prefix tuning Trainable vectors fed to the attention of every layer Rare now Prompt tuning (soft prompts) A few trainable vectors placed before the input tokens Very few parameters; used by some hosted services; weaker on small models (IA)³ Vectors that rescale activations Extremely small; niche Full fine-tuning Everything When you have a lot of data and want the last point of quality, or the model is small Three facts are enough to navigate this in practice. First, LoRA with all-linear targets and a rank of 16 to 32 is the standard starting point . Second, QLoRA is what you use when the model does not fit in memory ; it is the method behind most tutorials for tuning 7B and larger models on a free or single GPU, and tools such as Unsloth and Axolotl wrap it. Third, the quality gap to full fine-tuning is usually small and sometimes zero, so start with LoRA and switch only if your evaluation shows a gap that matters. Tip Memory, roughly Training needs memory for the weights, the gradients of the trainable weights, the optimiser's two running averages per trainable weight ( Lesson 3.12 ), and the activations. Full fine-tuning of a 7B model in 16-bit needs on the order of 60 GB or more. LoRA removes the gradients and optimiser state for 99% of the weights, bringing it to roughly 16 to 24 GB. QLoRA also shrinks the stored weights to about 4 to 5 GB, which is how it fits a 7B model on a 12 to 16 GB consumer GPU. Activations still grow with batch size and sequence length, which is why gradient checkpointing and small batches with gradient accumulation are common. Check your mental model ✗ "LoRA trains a small separate model." ✓ It trains a small correction to the big model's own weight matrices; the base model still does the work. ✗ "A LoRA model is slower because of the extra matrices." ✓ Once merged there are no extra matrices. Unmerged, the overhead is small. ✗ "Higher rank is always better." ✓ Higher rank has more capacity, including capacity to memorise. On small datasets a modest rank often tests better. ✗ "LoRA cannot forget, because the base weights are frozen." ✓ The combined model can still behave worse on other tasks. But you can remove the adapter and have the original back, which full fine-tuning cannot offer. ✗ "An adapter works with any model." ✓ It works only with the exact base model it was trained on. Exercises Predict before you run The q/v-only LoRA in Step 2 has rank 8 and 460,800 trainable parameters. Without running code, how many would it have at rank 16? At rank 1? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Train the hand-made LoRA with r=1 (and alpha=2 ). Compare validation and test scores with rank 8. What does the result suggest about how complicated the change needed for this task is? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Your team serves a 7B base model and needs separately tuned behaviour for 40 enterprise customers. Compare three designs: 40 fully fine-tuned models, 40 merged LoRA models, and one base model with 40 adapters. Consider storage, GPU memory, switching between customers and what happens when the base model is upgraded. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Parameters scale with rank Each wrapped layer has r × (576 + 576) parameters, and there are 60 of them. Rank 16 doubles the count to 921,600; rank 1 gives 69,120, about one twentieth of one percent of the model. Solution M1 · Rank 1 Create the layers with LoRALinear(..., r=1, alpha=2) . On this task even rank 1 learns the output format well, because "answer in this JSON shape and copy the order number" is a simple change in behaviour. It usually does somewhat worse on intent. The lesson is that the rank needed depends on how far the task is from what the model already does, not on the size of the model. Solution X1 · Forty customers Forty full fine-tunes: 40 × 14 GB of storage and, to serve them all, 40 models in GPU memory or slow swapping; clearly impractical. Forty merged LoRA models: the same serving problem, since each merged model is full size. One base model with 40 adapters: about 14 GB plus 40 files of tens of megabytes; one model in GPU memory; the adapter is chosen per request by a multi-LoRA server. When the base model is upgraded, every option needs retraining, because adapters are tied to their exact base; keep the training data and scripts so that retraining is a routine job. Recap LoRA freezes the model and learns a low-rank correction B × A beside chosen weight matrices; B starts at zero so training starts from the pretrained model. Trainable parameters drop to well under 1% of the model, the saved adapter is a few megabytes, and merging removes any inference overhead. LoRA needs a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning (around 1e-4 to 1e-3). peft does this from a LoraConfig : rank, alpha, dropout and target modules. QLoRA adds 4-bit storage of the base model so large models fit on one GPU; DoRA and rsLoRA are refinements; adapters, prefix and prompt tuning are older or niche relatives. Q2 What does merging a LoRA adapter do? A Deletes the adapter and keeps the base model B Converts the model to 4 bits C Adds scale × B × A into the frozen weight, giving an ordinary model of the original size D Doubles the number of parameters The correction has the same shape as W, so it can be added in and the extra matrices dropped. Time : about 65 minutes; the runnable parts take about four minutes. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up NF4 The 4-bit number format used by QLoRA, with levels spaced for bell-shaped weights Quantisation GPTQ A quantisation method that adjusts the remaining weights to compensate for rounding error Quantisation AWQ A quantisation method that protects the weights that matter most for activations Quantisation vLLM An open-source server for running language models with high throughput Serving Model merging Combining the weights of several fine-tunes into one model Open models Mentioned here, taught later 2 Microsoft Foundry, Data flywheel This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Microsoft Foundry Microsoft's platform for models, agents, knowledge and governance (formerly Azure AI Foundry) Lesson 14.130 Data flywheel The loop where production traffic yields examples that improve the model or prompts, which improves the product, which brings more traffic Lesson 14.138 Why this came about A trained model is a large file of 32-bit or 16-bit numbers that needs an expensive GPU to run. From 2022, as open-weight language models reached quality worth using, the community worked on making them smaller and cheaper to run. Quantisation , storing each weight in 8, 5 or 4 bits, turned out to cost surprisingly little accuracy when done carefully. Georgi Gerganov's llama.cpp (2023) ran quantised models on ordinary laptops and phones, and its GGUF file format became the common way to share them. For servers, vLLM and similar engines made one GPU serve many requests at once. Together with LoRA ( Lesson 3.24 ), these tools are what made " fine-tune a small model and run it yourself" a practical alternative to calling a large hosted model. In plain words first Rounding to save space A weight such as 0.16234871 is stored in 32 bits. Quantising it is rounding it to one of a small set of allowed values, and storing only which value: with 8 bits there are 256 to choose from, with 4 bits only 16. It is like recording heights to the nearest centimetre, and then to the nearest ten centimetres: each step saves space and loses a little truth. Neural networks tolerate a good deal of this, because their answers depend on millions of weights acting together, and a small rounding error in each one mostly cancels out. Past a certain point the errors stop cancelling and the model breaks, suddenly. Step 1 · Rounding one matrix by hand Quantisation stores each weight as a small whole number instead of a 32-bit decimal. With 4 bits there are only 16 allowed values, so every weight snaps to the nearest one and a little accuracy is lost. With 8 bits there are 256 values and the error is usually too small to matter. The simplest scheme: find the largest weight in the matrix, divide the range from its negative to its positive into equal steps, and store each weight as the number of its nearest step. To use the weights again, multiply back by the step size (the scale ). Copy What you should see Copy At 8 bits the five weights come back close to their originals, with an average error of a few percent. At 4 bits the three small weights have all become zero, and at 2 bits everything has. The reason is one outlier : somewhere in this matrix is a weight far larger than the rest, the scale is set by it, and so nearly all the allowed values lie where there are almost no weights. Most of the range is wasted. Reading this output What real quantisers do about it Finer scales : one scale per row or per small block of weights instead of one for the whole matrix, so an outlier only affects its neighbours. Unequal steps : put more of the allowed values near zero, where most weights are. The 4-bit format used by QLoRA ( NF4 ) does this. Calibration : run a few hundred real examples through the model and choose the rounding that changes the layer's outputs least, not the weights. GPTQ and AWQ work this way. Mixed precision : keep the most sensitive layers at higher precision. GGUF's "K-quants" such as Q4_K_M do this. Step 2 · The whole model, at fewer and fewer bits What matters is the task score, not the rounding error. Round every weight matrix in the transformer blocks of the fine-tuned router, with one scale per row, and evaluate on the test set : Copy What you should see Copy At 8 bits the model is a quarter of the size and scores exactly the same. At 6 bits it starts to slip. At 4 bits, with this simple rounding, it is badly damaged, and at 3 bits it produces nothing usable. The fall is a cliff, not a slope. Two points to take from this. First, 8-bit quantisation is close to free and is safe to use almost everywhere. Second, the popular 4-bit formats work because they use the smarter methods in the box above; plain rounding does not get there. Small models are also more fragile than large ones: a 7-billion-parameter model usually loses very little at a good 4-bit setting, where this 135-million-parameter model has no redundancy to spare. Always re-run your evaluation on the quantised model you will actually serve. Step 3 · Formats and methods you will meet Name What it is Where you use it safetensors The standard file for full-precision weights (what save_pretrained wrote) Training, GPU serving GGUF One file holding quantised weights, tokenizer and chat template , for llama.cpp Laptops, CPUs, Apple Silicon, phones; Ollama and LM Studio use it. Variants are named by bits and method: Q8_0 , Q5_K_M , Q4_K_M (the usual default) bitsandbytes (4-bit NF4, 8-bit) Quantises a model as it is loaded in PyTorch QLoRA training; quick experiments on a GPU AWQ , GPTQ Calibrated 4-bit quantisation for GPUs High-throughput GPU serving with vLLM or TGI EXL2 / EXL3 Variable bits per weight, for the ExLlama engine Enthusiast GPU setups MLX Apple's array framework and its model format Fast inference and fine-tuning on Macs ONNX , TensorRT , OpenVINO Hardware-specific export formats Embedded and edge devices, browsers (with WebGPU) A working rule: for a laptop or CPU, convert to GGUF at Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M and check the score. For a GPU server, serve 16-bit weights if they fit, otherwise AWQ or GPTQ. Step 4 · From files to a running model The commands below are the standard route for each target. They are shown for reference and are not run by this course's checker, because they need tools outside Python or a GPU. On a laptop, with llama.cpp and Ollama. Convert the saved model to GGUF, quantise it, and register it with Ollama, which then serves it through a local API: Copy A LoRA adapter must be merged into the base model first ( Lesson 3.24 ), or converted to a GGUF adapter with the script convert_lora_to_gguf.py and attached with an ADAPTER line. After converting, check that the chat template in the GGUF matches the one you trained with ( Lesson 14.137 ). On a GPU server, with vLLM. vLLM serves a base model with an OpenAI-compatible API, and can attach several LoRA adapters to the same base, chosen per request by name: Copy Copy Because the endpoint speaks the same protocol as the hosted APIs of the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context section, the rest of your application does not change. Lesson 14.111 covers batching, throughput and autoscaling for self-hosted models. Step 5 · The other route: a hosted fine-tuning service You do not have to run any of this yourself. Model providers and clouds offer fine-tuning as a service: you upload the JSONL files from Lesson 7.25 , start a job, and receive the name of a private model that you call like any other. The outline is the same everywhere; with the OpenAI SDK it looks like this (not run here; it needs an account, and the list of tunable models changes): Copy Route You manage Good when Hosted fine-tuning (OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry later · 14.130 , Together, Fireworks and others) Data and evaluation only You want a stronger base model than you could host, no infrastructure, and your data may leave your environment under the provider's terms Open tools on rented GPUs (Hugging Face TRL and PEFT , Unsloth, Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory) Training scripts, GPUs, serving You need a specific open model, full control of the weights, or data that must stay in-house A platform's managed training (SageMaker, Azure ML, Vertex AI custom jobs, Databricks) Scripts, within a governed environment You already run on that platform and need its security and lineage controls Whichever route you choose, the steps of this workshop are the same: the task and metric, the baseline, the dataset, the evaluation and the error analysis are yours. Only the training loop is outsourced. Step 6 · What does it cost? The case for a small tuned model is usually economic. A rough comparison for the router, with illustrative prices: Copy What you should see Copy The large model with a long few-shot prompt costs about a hundred times more than a small tuned model on a hosted service, almost entirely because of the input tokens: 460 per ticket against 50. Renting your own GPU costs a fixed amount whatever the volume, so it loses to the hosted small model at this volume and wins only at much higher volumes, or when the data may not leave your network. Add the costs the table leaves out: engineering time to build and evaluate the dataset, retraining when the base model changes, and running the fallback path. Watch out Prices in this lesson are placeholders Token and GPU prices change every few months and differ between providers. The structure of the calculation is what to keep: tokens in and out per request, requests per day, price per million tokens, and for self-hosting the hourly cost and how many requests one machine serves. Put in current numbers before using it for a decision ( Lesson 14.116 ). Step 7 · After release A fine-tuned model is a piece of software with a dataset as its source code. Treat it that way: Version everything together : the training data, the base model's exact name and revision, the training settings, the adapter or weights, and the evaluation results. You must be able to rebuild any model you have served. Gate releases on the evaluation set : a new model replaces the old one only if it scores at least as well overall and on every important class ( Lesson 14.122 ). Watch production : sample real inputs and outputs, track the rate of invalid outputs and of fallbacks to the larger model, and review a sample by hand each week. Inputs drift: new products, new phrasings, new languages. Feed failures back : every production error becomes a test example, and later a training example. This is the data flywheel later · 14.138 of Lesson 14.138 . Plan for the base model to change : adapters work only with the exact base they were trained on. When a better base model appears, retrain and re-evaluate. Keep that a routine job, not a rescue mission. Keep a fallback : route low-confidence or invalid outputs to a larger model or a person. Go deeper (optional) Model merging Because fine-tuned models and adapters built on the same base are just sets of numbers of the same shape, they can be merged without any training: averaged, or combined with methods such as SLERP , TIES and DARE (implemented in the mergekit tool). A merge of a coding fine-tune and a chat fine-tune can keep much of both abilities. Merging is popular in the open-model community and occasionally useful in production for combining several task adapters into one, but the result must be evaluated like any other model: it sometimes inherits the weaknesses of both parents. At 4 bits it depends on the method and the model's size; measure it. ✗ "A 4-bit model is 4-bit everywhere." ✓ Good formats mix precisions and scales, and keep sensitive parts at higher precision. ✗ "Self-hosting a small model is always cheaper." ✓ A GPU costs the same whether busy or idle. It wins at high, steady volume or when data must stay in-house. ✗ "Once a fine-tuned model passes evaluation, the work is done." ✓ Inputs drift and base models are replaced. Plan monitoring, a fallback and retraining from the start. Exercises Predict before you run quantise in Step 1 uses one scale for the whole matrix. If you instead used one scale per row, as quantise_model does, would the 4-bit average error go up or down, and why? Change the function to check. (Solution P1.) Make it your own In the cost calculation, find the number of tickets per day at which one rented GPU becomes cheaper than the hosted small model. Then change few_shot_in to 2,000 (a realistic long prompt with policies included) and see what happens to the first line. (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it You have a LoRA adapter for a 7B model, and three places to run it: a product manager's MacBook for demos, a cloud GPU serving 50 requests a second, and an offline tablet used in warehouses. Choose a format and tool for each, and name one check you would make before trusting the result. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A scale per row The error goes down sharply. An outlier now stretches the scale only for its own row, and the other 575 rows use scales that fit their weights. Compute scale = w.abs().amax(dim=1, keepdim=True) / levels . This is the first of the improvements listed under Step 1, and it is why the whole-model experiment in Step 2 held up at 8 and 6 bits. Solution M1 · Break-even volume The hosted small model costs about $97 a month at 200,000 tickets a day, so its cost per ticket is tiny, and one GPU at $864 a month breaks even at roughly nine times that volume, about 1.8 million tickets a day. Below that, the hosted route is cheaper. With a 2,000-token prompt the large-model line rises to about $38,500 a month: long prompts repeated on every request are what make large models expensive at volume, which is also why prompt caching matters ( Lesson 11.4 ). Solution X1 · Three targets MacBook: merge the adapter, convert to GGUF at Q4_K_M , run with Ollama or LM Studio (or use MLX); check that the chat template survived conversion. Cloud GPU: vLLM with the base model in 16-bit and the adapter attached, or an AWQ build if memory is short; check throughput and the test-set score of the served endpoint. Offline tablet: a smaller base model is probably needed; GGUF with llama.cpp, or an ONNX export; check speed, battery use and the score at the chosen bit width. In every case, the check that matters is re-running your evaluation against the thing you actually deployed. Recap Quantisation stores weights in fewer bits. 8-bit is nearly free; good 4-bit methods use per-block scales, uneven steps, calibration and mixed precision. Small models are more fragile. GGUF with llama.cpp or Ollama is the route for laptops and CPUs; vLLM with 16-bit, AWQ or GPTQ weights for GPU servers; adapters can be merged or served on top of a shared base. Hosted fine-tuning services take your JSONL files and return a private model; the task definition, data and evaluation remain your work. A small tuned model with a short prompt can cost around a hundredth of a large model with a long one. A dedicated GPU pays off only at high, steady volume. After release: version data and models together, gate on evaluation, monitor, keep a fallback, and expect to retrain. Its moment estimates start at zero. Early steps use bad statistics. Why AdamW over Adam plus L2? Every parameter gets the same proportional shrinkage. Why SGD for CNNs? SGD finds flatter minima. They often generalize better. What does 1cycle need? The total number of steps in advance. Does accumulation save time? No. Doubling accum_steps doubles the wall time per optimizer step. Does CPU autocast need loss scaling? No. CPU autocast uses BF16 by default.
